all_proposals.one_line: Wrap the implementer call in a tight cslc-grounded micro-loop: draft -> compile -> if errors, feed top-3 error lines back to the SAME model -> redraft, up to k=4 micro-iterations before the result ever leaves the implementer step.
all_proposals.mechanism: Today cuda2csl.py::translate() calls _llm_call once at line 1407, then hands the output to _benchmark_current_code which runs the full launch contract. That's a heavy outer loop (compile + simulate + reviewer + bucket-routed repair). Insert a much tighter inner loop: after extract_code_block(reply, 'csl'), shell out to cslc on the kernel's actual layout.csl + commands_wse3.sh (NOT the synthetic harnesses in ground_gotcha.py::HARNESSES which were too minimal for halo gotcha r4). If cslc returns non-zero, parse the first 3 error lines (file:line: error: ... pattern) and re-prompt the same Opus session with 'cslc reports the following errors on the file you just wrote: <errors>. Patch only the lines named in those errors and return the full file.' Up to 4 inner iterations, then exit to the outer reviewer. Reuse ground_gotcha.py::_run_cslc — already handles SDK PATH + singularity gate + ANSI stripping. The new piece is a per-kernel cslc-invocation wrapper that points at the real bundle directory, not a synthetic harness.
all_proposals.why_now: Current failure clusters are syntax-shaped: halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail) is about wrong @bind_local_task / @activate / fabric DSD field names; dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fail) is about wrong .queues / .dsr_ids tuple shapes; collectives_2d (2/4 fail) is about c2d_params.x vs .y. These are exactly the errors cslc names precisely on a specific file:line. Today the outer benchmark loop sees them but only on attempt N+1, and by then bucket-routed repair (A/B/C) has been triggered which re-builds prose. A tight inner compile loop fixes 'undeclared identifier in @import_module call' before the architect ever gets called back.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: Eng: 1-2 days (wrapper around _run_cslc, integration into translate() before benchmark, integration test on halo + dsr kernels). Per-attempt cost: +1-4 extra Opus calls (the inner iterations), but each call is ~5x shorter than today's full implementer prompt because it sends only the file + 3 error lines, not the full knowledge_base + layout + cuda. Net: roughly +$0.10/kernel/attempt. Wall: cslc takes 30-90s per invocation on these bundles; 4 inner iterations adds ~3 min/attempt worst case. Total sweep: maybe 1.5x today's wall time, +$15 LLM.
all_proposals.risk: Distinct from translation_facts because the new context is EXECUTION-DERIVED, not pre-baked YAML. Risk shape: if cslc errors are too cryptic (e.g. cascading errors from a single missing import), the model patches symptoms, not cause, and oscillates. Mitigation: cap at 4 micro-iterations, detect non-converging edit distance, escalate to reviewer.

all_proposals.name: Specialist syntax-fixer model (small/fast) gated by cslc
all_proposals.one_line: After Opus drafts, run cslc; if it fails with a syntax-shaped error (undeclared identifier, wrong arg count, type mismatch), route the file + error to a CHEAP fast model (Haiku 4.5 or Sonnet 4.6) with the sole job of editing the failing lines, NOT to Opus for re-architecting.
all_proposals.mechanism: Add a third role to the 4-role pipeline in cuda2csl.py: a 'syntax_fixer' positioned between implementer and reviewer. Trigger condition: cslc exit != 0 AND error matches a syntax-only regex set (e.g. /undeclared identifier|expected token|wrong number of arguments|no member named/). Route to Haiku via the existing llm_complete wrapper (workflow_common.py) with a stripped prompt: just the failing CSL + 3 error lines + builtin_whitelist_block() from prompt_cuda2csl.py:100. The fixer is forbidden from changing the algorithm — its prompt frames it as 'a CSL syntax linter with edit access, fix only the lines cslc named'. This avoids burning Opus tokens on what are essentially typo-class errors.
all_proposals.why_now: The reviewer's bucket routing today distinguishes A (re-architect) / B (re-implement) / C (contract-fix), but B currently re-runs full Opus on the full prompt for what is often a 2-line typo. The hybrid wrapper run_hybrid_sweep.sh already proves cheap-then-expensive works at the OUTER level (Sonnet then Opus); this is the same idea pushed INSIDE one attempt for the syntax-only subset of failures. The current Sonnet+Opus union ceiling of 6/15 suggests both models leave the same syntax mistakes; a smaller-but-targeted call may actually do better here because it has only one job.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: Eng: 2 days (new role, syntax-error classifier regex, prompt template in prompt_cuda2csl.py, plumbing through cuda2csl.py::translate). Per-call: Haiku is ~$0.005/call vs Opus $0.05; 2-3 fixer invocations per failing attempt = ~$0.015 extra, saves ~$0.05 on the avoided Opus re-implementation. Wall: Haiku is ~2s/call. Sweep cost: roughly flat or slightly cheaper than today.
all_proposals.risk: Shape risk: this LOOKS like more prompting (similar shape to discarded experiments) but differs in two ways — it's gated by execution signal (cslc fired), and it routes to a different model with a narrower task, so it's adding decision branches not prompt context. Real risk: classifier regex misroutes a semantic bug to the fixer, fixer makes the wrong edit, error compounds. Mitigation: limit fixer to 2 invocations; on third, escalate to reviewer.

all_proposals.name: Layout-anchored constrained decoding via skeleton injection
all_proposals.one_line: Instead of letting Opus generate the CSL freely, programmatically build the skeleton (imports, comptime exports/binds, fn stubs with correct signatures) from layout.csl and pass it to Opus as a 'fill in the bodies' template — constraint propagation, not context injection.
all_proposals.mechanism: Add a new module code_translation/layout_to_skeleton.py that statically parses the kernel's layout.csl (which IS shown to the agent per the W1 hiding invariant), extracts: (a) every @export_symbol target name and its inferred type, (b) every @bind_*_task target name, (c) every @set_tile_code-passed compile-time param, (d) every memcpy params struct field referenced. Emit a CSL skeleton: import block + comptime{} blocks with placeholders + empty function stubs with correct signatures and the canonical f_tic/f_toc bodies already filled in (the agent fabricated wrong f_tic bodies often enough that prompt_cuda2csl.py:281-286 had to add a hard requirement). Pass the skeleton to the implementer in a NEW prompt slot: 'Here is the skeleton your file MUST match. Fill in the function bodies. Do not change signatures, names, or comptime declarations.' Use the existing q_translate_cuda_to_csl_bundle template, swap {layout_text} for {layout_text}+{skeleton}.
all_proposals.why_now: Halo_recv_unblock failures are dominated by mismatched names between layout.csl and pe.csl (the model invents `recv_north_task` when layout exports `f_recv_n`); dsr_queue_fabric_init failures are dominated by wrong field names in params structs (`memcpyParams.x_config` vs `memcpyParams.x_in_config`). These are LOOKUP errors that the model commits because it generates from intent rather than from the contract. A skeleton forces the contract to be the starting point. Distinct from translation_facts because the skeleton is structural, executable scaffolding the model fills in — not declarative facts about the language.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: Eng: 3-5 days. Parsing layout.csl is non-trivial but bounded — the 30 kernel layouts in kernels/*/CSL/ are the test corpus, and the parser only needs to handle the patterns these use, not full CSL. Per-attempt LLM: probably -10% (smaller generation target since skeleton is fixed), so saves money. Wall: skeleton extraction is ~1s. Sweep: net cheaper than today, +significant first-time eng investment.
all_proposals.risk: Shape risk: this is the OPPOSITE of translation_facts — translation_facts gave the model declarative facts to remember; skeleton gives it a partially-written program to complete. Constrained-generation patterns are well-validated in code synthesis literature. Real risk: parser fails on a kernel's layout.csl idiom, skeleton is wrong, the model is now forced into the wrong contract. Mitigation: detect parse failures and fall back to today's prompt; add per-kernel skeleton smoke tests.

all_proposals.name: Self-critique against cslc-grounded checklist
all_proposals.one_line: After implementer drafts but BEFORE cslc, ask the SAME model to verify its draft against a 5-item checklist derived from the kernel's cluster, with each checklist item phrased as 'is this thing actually in csl_builtins.yaml / does layout.csl actually export this?' — verifiable yes/no, not free-form review.
all_proposals.mechanism: Add a self_critique() method to cuda2csl.py orchestrator, called inside translate() between line 1410 (extract_code_block) and line 1469 (_benchmark_current_code). Checklist items are auto-generated from: (a) every @import_module path in the draft → check against csl_builtins.yaml; (b) every @export_symbol name → check against layout.csl-extracted exports; (c) every fn name bound via @bind_*_task → check against layout.csl-extracted bindings; (d) every fabric DSD field accessed (.fabin_dsd, .x_config, etc.) → check against layout.csl struct fields. Prompt is structured: 'For each of the following 5 claims, answer YES or NO and a 10-word justification. <list>. If any answer is NO, return a corrected CSL file in a ```csl fence; else return the marker NO_CHANGE.' Critically, the checklist items themselves are GENERATED from static analysis (layout.csl parse + csl_builtins.yaml lookup) — the model only has to AGREE or DISAGREE, not invent the criteria.
all_proposals.why_now: Today the reviewer fires AFTER benchmark, so model burns a compile+simulate cycle before getting feedback on 'you imported a module that doesn't exist'. The self-critique is structurally different from the reviewer because (i) it runs pre-cslc, (ii) its checklist items are derived from machine-checkable sources not free-form rationale, (iii) it has only YES/NO + minimal-edit affordance, not free-form bucket routing. Compared to the discarded semantic_bridge (which was prose-vs-prose review): this is prose-vs-machine-extracted-facts review.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: Eng: 2-3 days (checklist generator + new model call + minimal-diff parsing of the response). Per-attempt: +1 Opus call (~$0.04) but only fires when the draft has at least one checklist mismatch (gate it on the static checker first — if all 5 items pass automatically, skip the LLM call). Saves the wasted cslc+simulator cycle (~90s, no $) on roughly 30% of attempts. Net: +$10/sweep, -20% wall.
all_proposals.risk: Shape risk: this is the closest of the 4 to semantic_bridge / translation_facts (it's still extra prompting). Differs in two ways: (i) the criteria are auto-derived not authored, so they can't drift from reality; (ii) the model output is constrained to YES/NO + minimal patch, not free-form prose. Real risk: model rubber-stamps YES to all 5 to avoid work (a known LLM failure mode in self-critique), in which case the cycle is wasted. Mitigation: monitor the YES/NO distribution; if it's >95% YES across a sweep, kill the experiment fast (this is the same exit criterion that caught translation_facts at 0W/2L/17T).

all_proposals.name: Reference-bundle retrieval for nearest neighbor pe.csl exemplar
all_proposals.one_line: Compute a similarity score between the current kernel's layout.csl + CUDA source and every other kernel in kernels/*/CSL/, retrieve the top-1 nearest neighbor's WORKING pe.csl, and inject it as an exemplar in the implementer prompt — without violating the compute-leak guard.
all_proposals.mechanism: Build an offline index of the 30 kernels in kernels/*/CSL/ (only those whose run.py succeeds), with features extracted from layout.csl: list of imported modules, set of @export_symbol names, set of @bind_*_task IDs, mesh shape (1D/2D), color count, presence of fabric DSDs, collectives_2d usage. At translate() time, score the target kernel against the index, pick top-1 with score > threshold. CRITICAL: the chosen exemplar must NOT be the target kernel (verified by path). Inject the exemplar's full pe.csl into the prompt as 'Here is a working pe.csl from a DIFFERENT kernel that shares this kernel's structural shape (same imports / same task-binding pattern). Use it as a pattern reference for syntax; do not copy its algorithm — your algorithm comes from the CUDA source.' The compute-leak guard at cuda2csl.py:1031 (_assert_no_compute_leak) is keyed to the TARGET kernel's reference compute file via _set_compute_canary; an exemplar from a different kernel will not trigger it. Verify this with a unit test before shipping.
all_proposals.why_now: TF-IDF retrieval over csl-examples gives chunks (functions, paragraphs); whole-file exemplars are what the model actually generalizes from. The 30 working kernels are a higher-quality corpus than csl-examples tutorials (they're real benchmarks, not pedagogical snippets). For halo_recv_unblock specifically: the 7pt-Stencil and Laplacian2D-Halo bundles are already working — but the agent translating 25-point-Stencil never sees a full working halo pe.csl, only TF-IDF chunks. Distinct from translation_facts and semantic_bridge: those were declarative knowledge; this is concrete code the agent can pattern-match against (the same way the existing TF-IDF retrieval works, but at file granularity).
all_proposals.cost_estimate: Eng: 2-3 days (layout.csl feature extractor, similarity scorer, prompt slot, unit test that compute-leak guard does not fire when a non-target exemplar is injected, regression test that exemplar selection is stable across runs). Per-attempt: +0 LLM calls (it's prompt content), +~2k tokens of prompt = +$0.02. Wall: index build is one-shot offline; per-query lookup is ms. Sweep: +$3.
all_proposals.risk: Shape risk: this IS more prompt context, same shape as the discarded experiments at first glance. The structural difference is granularity — translation_facts gave atomic YAML facts (effectively a glossary), semantic_bridge gave CUDA-to-CSL prose mappings (effectively a phrasebook); this gives a complete working program at the same scale as the output (effectively a worked example, the format that's been shown to work for in-context code generation across many studies). Real risk: the wrong exemplar (e.g. retrieving a 1D mesh kernel for a 2D mesh target) actively misleads the model. Mitigation: require similarity score above a hard threshold; if no kernel above threshold, no exemplar (default to today's prompt). Track exemplar-injected vs not in the sweep results so the lift can be measured cleanly.

all_proposals.name: Programmatic compile-error to gotcha-KB feedback (active learning, no LLM)
all_proposals.one_line: When a sweep attempt fails with a cslc error not matched by any existing gotcha regex, log it; once a pattern fires N>=3 times across kernels, AUTO-generate a candidate gotcha entry (no LLM) by templating from the matched error class, then run it through ground_gotcha.py as a smoke test before promotion.
all_proposals.mechanism: Add a new file code_translation/error_pattern_miner.py that tails the final_result.json files in code_translation/results/ (existing artifact, written by write_final_artifacts() at line 2654 of cuda2csl.py). For each failed attempt with a cslc stderr, normalize the error: strip file paths, replace identifiers with <ID>, replace line numbers with <N>. Build a histogram. When a normalized pattern crosses N=3 occurrences across distinct kernels, emit a candidate KNOWN_GOTCHAS entry by templating: 'Compile error <NORMALIZED_PATTERN> seen N times. Trigger pattern: <regex>. Affected kernels: <list>.' Then trigger ground_gotcha.ground_csl_snippet() on a minimal reproducer the miner extracts (the 5 lines before/after the cslc error file:line) using the existing harnesses. Only if a reproducer compiles in clean form and fails as expected in broken form does the candidate get promoted into KNOWN_GOTCHAS_W1_FAILURE_PATTERNS in csl_knowledge_base.py — gated by a human-readable diff for review.
all_proposals.why_now: The hand-curated halo gotchas just shipped (task #65) prove that grounded gotchas DO help when the patterns are real; the failures at workflow rounds r2/r3 (drafters fabricated builtins) and r4 (canonical patterns too composed for minimal harnesses) prove that LLM-DRAFTED gotchas don't work. The unsolved direction is gotchas drafted by mining REAL compile errors from the sweep corpus. The sweep already produces 8 attempts/kernel x 15 kernels = 120 failure traces per sweep — that's a real data corpus, currently discarded after the run. Structurally NOTHING like translation_facts: there is no extra prompt context here (KB is already injected via for_implementer()); the new piece is the automated FEEDBACK LOOP from sweep failures to KB content.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: Eng: 3-4 days (error normalizer, histogram across result trees, reproducer extractor, ground_gotcha integration, diff-based promotion gate). LLM cost per sweep: ZERO additional (the miner is pure Python + cslc). cslc cost: maybe 20 extra cslc runs per sweep for grounding candidate reproducers — ~10 min wall. Ongoing maintenance: the miner becomes a build-time pre-commit that runs on each new sweep's results, so KB compounds rather than staying stuck at hand-curated.
all_proposals.risk: Lowest shape risk of all 6 proposals because it doesn't touch the LLM call at all — it improves the existing KB via a feedback signal that's already being thrown away. The risk it shares with translation_facts: even if the KB grows, if the model isn't acting on KB entries, growth doesn't help. Mitigation is the same as for the existing KB injection — measure pass-rate lift per KB-entry-added (the A/B harness tools/ab_translation_facts.py already exists and can be repurposed). Real risk: the histogram is noisy because cslc errors cascade; the same root cause emits 5 different errors, and the miner sees them as 5 patterns. Mitigation: require the reproducer to compile-fail with the same error class before promotion.

all_proposals.name: Sub-kernel cslc probe gate before bundle assembly
all_proposals.one_line: Slice the implementer's draft pe.csl into compileable sub-snippets and gate the bundle on each sub-snippet's cslc result, surfacing surgical errors instead of one bundle-level failure.
all_proposals.mechanism: Right after the implementer emits pe.csl (in cuda2csl.py's _run_implementer, before benchmark_csl is called), run a new probe module probe_subkernel.py that AST-walks the draft and extracts (a) every top-level @import_module call wrapped in ground_gotcha._HARNESS_SINGLE_PE, (b) every standalone fn body that has no fabric I/O wrapped likewise, (c) each color/DSR/queue declaration block wrapped in send_recv_2x1. Each fragment is compiled via the same _singularity_gate path ground_gotcha.py already uses. The probe emits a structured JSON of {fragment_id, ok, cslc_error_first_line, line_in_draft}. If any required fragment fails, that JSON is fed into the repair prompt (bucket-B path in cuda2csl) as a tight error map — 'fragment_4 (DSR alloc lines 22-28) fails with: error: dsr id 6 already in use'. Halo recv counts, queue 0/1 collisions, and field-name typos all surface here without the full mesh having to compile.
all_proposals.why_now: halo_recv_unblock (6/7 failing) and dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 failing) both manifest as cslc errors deep in a 200-line pe.csl whose top-level errors mask the real cause. ground_gotcha.py already proves we can wrap snippets and get clean cslc verdicts in 10-20s. Reusing the harness on draft fragments turns a single opaque bundle failure into N localized verdicts the repair LLM can act on.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: Eng: ~2 days (extend ground_gotcha harnesses with a fragment-extraction front-end, wire into cuda2csl repair loop). Wall-clock per attempt: +30-90s (parallel-fragment cslc, gated by _singularity_gate). LLM: +0 calls — surfaces structured error map, doesn't ask a model. Per-15-kernel sweep: ~+15-25 min wall-time.
all_proposals.risk: Structurally different from translation_facts (which only added prompt text). Real risk: a passing fragment in isolation may fail in the full mesh because of cross-fragment interactions (e.g. two functions both grab DSR 6). Mitigation: scope to error categories that are intrinsically fragment-local (typos, import field names, builtin arities) — track which error classes the probe is useful for and demote it for the rest. Could fall flat if most failures are mesh-composition bugs, not fragment-local — but the halo gotcha post-mortem said the opposite (canonical patterns 'too composed to fit in minimal harnesses' from the writer's side; the *reader's* job of catching wrong field names is exactly what does fit).

all_proposals.name: Static halo-recv counting linter (compile-time invariant check)
all_proposals.one_line: A Python AST walker over draft pe.csl computes the expected wavelet count per PE from layout topology + send_dsd lengths, compares against the draft's recv_done thresholds and unblock conditions, and rejects mismatches before cslc.
all_proposals.mechanism: Add halo_invariant_lint.py to code_translation/. It takes (draft_pe_csl, layout_csl, kernel_params). It parses (1) every @get_dsd(fabout_dsd, .{.extent = N}) call → per-direction send count, (2) every is_X_edge guard pattern → per-PE neighbor topology, (3) every @block/@unblock + 'expected = N' counter pattern in the draft. It then computes, for each PE coordinate (x,y) in @set_rectangle(W,H): expected_recv[(x,y)] = sum over neighbors of their send extents, accounting for is_edge guards. Compares against constants the draft uses. Emits a verdict 'PE(0,0) is_west_edge expects recv=N but draft sets threshold M' or 'unblock fires before all 4 directions counted'. Routed into the C-bucket (contract-fix) repair prompt as the most prescriptive failure type we have. Crosschecked against the canonical Game of Life pe_program.csl pattern (which already lives at /home/USER/xkernel/kernels/Game of Life/CSL/pe_program.csl:149-156 and is the working idiom).
all_proposals.why_now: halo_recv_unblock is the single biggest unsolved cluster (6/7 fail). The bug class is mechanical (count of recvs doesn't match count of unblocks) and the model's writing of it is mechanical — but cslc doesn't catch it (it's semantic, not type-system-visible) and the runtime symptom is a hang, not a useful error. A textual check that says 'PE(0,1) expects 3 recvs but unblocks at 4' gives the LLM the exact arithmetic correction it needs.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: Eng: 3-4 days (the AST surface is narrow but the topology arithmetic is the hard part — edge cases for corner PEs, axis-major mesh decompositions, c2d_params). Wall-clock per attempt: +1-3s (pure Python). LLM: +0 calls when it passes; rerouted bucket-C repair LLM call when it fails (which is what we want — early routing).
all_proposals.risk: This is the proposal most isomorphic to translation_facts in surface (a regex-style extractor over CSL). Structural distinction: it returns a binary verdict that gates the repair-bucket routing, not extra prompt text. Real risk: real halo idioms are heterogeneous enough that the linter false-positives, causing the orchestrator to reject good drafts. Mitigation: start in advisory mode (log the verdict, don't act), measure false-positive rate against the 84 known-passing bundles, only flip to gating once FP < 5%. If FP stays high (because the topology arithmetic isn't tractable without a full type-checker), the proposal joins translation_facts in the discard pile — but unlike translation_facts, the advisory-mode data is itself useful as a debugger signal.

all_proposals.name: CUDA-vs-CSL property-based equivalence sweep using existing CUDA refs
all_proposals.one_line: For each translated CSL that passes the bundled assert_allclose, run K=8 randomized input matrices through both the kernels/<name>/CUDA/kernel.cu binary and the new CSL, compare element-wise, and fail-route the translation if any input shows divergence beyond the bundled tolerance.
all_proposals.mechanism: Add tools/property_equivalence.py. (a) Generates K random param sets within the kernel's spec.yaml-declared shape range — for GEMM that's (M,N,K) tuples and seeded N(0,1) matrices, for stencils that's (W,H,T) + random init field. (b) Runs each through kernels/<name>/CUDA/kernel.cu via benchmark_cuda.py's existing nvcc+exec wrapper. (c) Runs each through benchmark_csl.run_staged_bundle (with --params=...) against the just-translated CSL. (d) Element-wise compares outputs with a kernel-class-specific tolerance (iterative solvers get larger eps, exact integer kernels get 0). Verdict 'random_inputs_3_of_8_diverged: max_rel_err=0.14 at param=(M=37,N=29,K=11)' routed to bucket-B (re-implement) with the specific param shape the bundled test missed. Crucially: this catches translations that pass the single bundled test case but encode the bug 'off-by-one in tile-boundary' that only triggers on non-power-of-2 sizes — which is a known halo-cluster failure mode.
all_proposals.why_now: We already have kernels/*/CUDA/kernel.cu refs and benchmark_cuda.py wired. Today the W1 verdict is binary on a single bundled testcase; many W1 'passes' may be marginal and many 'fails' may be wrong-on-one-input. K=8 doesn't fix translation directly — but it converts the single-input passing-pile into a stratified pile (robust passes vs flaky passes) and gives the optimizer real signal about which translation to optimize from. It also creates an objective metric to A/B knowledge-injection changes that current binary verdicts mask.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: Eng: ~5 days (generator per kernel-class needs spec.yaml extensions for shape ranges and tolerance class; output comparator needs per-kernel shape mapping). Wall-clock per attempt: +K * (cslc+sim time), so for K=8 and current 30-60s per sim, +4-8 min per kernel. Mitigations: only run on attempts that passed bundled test (skip the 60% bundle-failures); run K=3 by default and K=8 only when bucket-B routing fires. LLM: +0 calls. Sweep cost: turns a 2hr 15-kernel sweep into a 4hr one.
all_proposals.risk: Lowest risk of being shaped like translation_facts (it's an execution gate, not a prompt context). Real risks: (1) CUDA refs may themselves be wrong for adversarial inputs — need to bound generator within the kernel's documented spec, (2) iterative solvers will look 'flaky' due to nondeterministic convergence — handle with a per-kernel-class tolerance and an explicit 'iterative' marker in spec.yaml, (3) this raises the floor (catches bad translations) more than the ceiling (doesn't generate new translations) — so it pairs with the other proposals rather than substituting.

all_proposals.name: Symbolic SMT check of recv/unblock parity from layout
all_proposals.one_line: Encode the draft's per-PE send/recv/unblock graph as Z3 constraints; SMT-solve for any (PE, message-count) combination that violates 'recvs == unblock threshold' — produces a counterexample PE coordinate the repair LLM uses to fix the threshold.
all_proposals.mechanism: Add tools/halo_smt_check.py using python-z3. (a) Parses @set_rectangle(W,H) from layout.csl. (b) Walks the draft pe.csl to build a symbolic graph: for each PE coord (x,y), variables {recv_count_north, recv_count_south, recv_count_east, recv_count_west} bound by the draft's is_edge guards. (c) For each @block/@unblock site, extracts the constant or expression it tests against, encodes 'unblock_fires_at_step_k <=> recv_count == threshold_expr'. (d) Solves for any model where recv_count > 0 and unblock never fires (hang) OR unblock fires before recv_count == expected. If SAT, returns the counterexample {pe=(0,1), recv=3, threshold=4, hang=true} — exactly the input the repair LLM needs. Wired as a bucket-C verdict pre-cslc, parallel to halo_invariant_lint but operating on the *symbolic* graph rather than counting concrete values. Distinct from the lint because it handles parametric expressions (e.g. recv = if (is_corner) 2 else 3).
all_proposals.why_now: The lint proposal handles concrete counts; SMT handles the parametric cases that cause 'works on 4x4 mesh, hangs on 5x3'. Halo bugs that survive small tests but fail on production sizes are a known cluster — this is the verification that catches them without running. Bottleneck doc cites halo as 6/7 fail and 'boundary-hang' as the recurrence; SMT explicitly enumerates boundary conditions.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: Eng: 7-10 days (Z3 encoding of CSL fabric semantics is the deep part; needs a careful subset — not full CSL, just the recv/send/unblock fragment). Wall-clock per attempt: 5-30s solver time (small models). LLM: +0 calls. Risk of solver timeout on complex layouts — add a 60s budget per kernel and fall back to 'inconclusive' which is no-op.
all_proposals.risk: Highest eng-cost proposal; highest risk of getting stuck on CSL semantics that don't cleanly encode (async fabric reordering, microthread arbitration). Most-promising failure mode: the encoding is *wrong* (omits a real CSL semantic) and the SMT result is misleading. Mitigation: ship in advisory mode against the known-passing halo bundles (Game of Life, 7-Point Stencil, Laplacian2D-Halo) and verify the encoding produces 'no violation found' for all of them before letting it gate anything. If it false-positives on real passing code, that's the cliff — but unlike translation_facts, the prototype is testable in a weekend against ground truth.

all_proposals.name: csdb wavelet replay as automatic failure diagnosis
all_proposals.one_line: When a translation cslc-compiles but the sim hangs or asserts, automatically invoke csdb / sdk_debug_shell on the generated artifacts to dump per-PE wavelet trace + task state, parse it for the specific stuck-PE, and feed that to the bucket-B repair prompt — turning runtime hangs into actionable text.
all_proposals.mechanism: Add tools/sim_postmortem.py invoked from benchmark_csl on hang/assert/timeout (not on success). (a) Re-runs the bundle with SDK_TRACE=1 (or equivalent — verify per SDK docs) so cs_python emits wavelet traces. (b) Invokes /home/USER/cs_sdk-1.4.0/csdb on the resulting artifact to dump per-PE task state + last 100 wavelets. (c) Parses the dump with a small Python state machine — finds PEs in 'waiting on recv' state past the sim timeout, extracts (PE coord, task ID, last wavelet received, blocked color). Builds a structured failure-context block: 'PE(2,1) hung at task f_step waiting on color 9, received 2/3 wavelets from west neighbor, last wavelet @ cycle 4032'. (d) This context replaces (or augments) the current stderr_tail in DebuggerInput in debugger_agent.py — giving the debugger sub-agent factual per-PE state instead of stderr fragments.
all_proposals.why_now: Today's debugger_agent sees only stderr_tail + reviewer_rationale. For halo hangs there IS no useful stderr — the sim times out. cs_readelf and csdb already exist in /home/USER/cs_sdk-1.4.0/bin (per DEBUGGER_AGENT_DESIGN.md the v2 plan explicitly cites them but was deferred). Hangs in halo_recv_unblock are exactly the failure mode where 'which PE is stuck' is the diagnosis — and it's recoverable from the artifact, not a property of the LLM's reasoning.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: Eng: 4-6 days, dominated by parsing csdb output (which is opaque and lightly documented). Wall-clock: +30-90s per FAILED attempt (only fires on hangs, ~30% of attempts). Pairs naturally with the existing debugger budget (DEBUGGER_MAX_FIRES_PER_KERNEL=1). LLM: existing debugger call is now ~5-10x more useful; no new LLM call.
all_proposals.risk: Structurally far from translation_facts — this is *failure-time* grounding, not prompt-time context. Risk of overlap with debugger_agent v1 (already shipped, marginal lift per past A/B). Distinction: v1 fed stderr; this feeds simulator ground truth. Real risks: (1) csdb output format may not be machine-parseable without per-version brittleness — mitigate by pinning to SDK 1.4.0 and adding a regression test against a known-hang bundle, (2) the SDK may not allow re-running with trace enabled programmatically — verify before committing to the full design. Failure mode would be 'parses 70% of hangs and silently fails on the rest', which is still net-positive over today's stderr_tail.

all_proposals.name: Template-library retrieval with parameterized lowering
all_proposals.one_line: Reduce CUDA->CSL to 'pick the closest hand-written pe.csl template + replace named holes', not free-form generation.
all_proposals.mechanism: Hand-curate ~15 canonical pe.csl templates (one per shape: halo-1D, halo-2D, collectives_2d-matvec, dsr-queue-async-fabric, tile-local-reduce, broadcast-apply, stencil-fused, etc.) from working bundles under kernels/*/CSL/pe.csl plus /home/USER/xkernel/csl-examples/benchmarks/*/pe.csl. Each template marks PARAM holes (extents, tile dims, reduction op, comptime constants) with sentinel comments like //@HOLE(name=BLOCK_SIZE,type=i16). Add a new pipeline stage in code_translation/cuda2csl.py between analyzer and architect: q_select_template prompt that asks the LLM to pick the template_id matching the CUDA's shape, plus emit a JSON dict of hole values. Then a deterministic Python pass (new templater.py) substitutes holes; the result goes to a SLIM implementer that only handles deviations the template didn't cover, with the template as a hard scaffold (diff-only edits). Run cslc on the post-substitution file before any implementer call; if it compiles, ship it without ever calling the LLM for generation.
all_proposals.why_now: halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail) and dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fail) are exactly the clusters where the SDK has 2-3 canonical patterns and the LLM keeps fabricating variants. The r3/r4 halo-gotcha workflows already proved that LLMs cannot generate these idioms from scratch even with RAG, but they CAN parameterize a known-good one. collectives_2d failures (2/4) are classic 'forgot dest_dsr_ids' bugs that vanish if the template already has them.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: 3-5 eng days to curate 15 templates + write templater.py + new prompt + sub-test harness. ~$0 LLM per template-hit attempt (substitution is deterministic). ~30s wall-clock saved per kernel where it hits. A/B sweep over the 15 W1-failed kernels: 1 hr wall + ~$20 LLM. Adds one ~$0.10 selector call per kernel.
all_proposals.risk: DIFFERENT shape from semantic_bridge/translation_facts (those added prompt context; this REPLACES generation with substitution under cslc gate). The real risk is template coverage: if real kernels don't match any template, the selector either picks a wrong one (worse than baseline) or falls through to current pipeline (neutral). Mitigation: require the selector to output confidence; below threshold, skip templating and fall through. Worst case is baseline performance plus one wasted LLM call.

all_proposals.name: Test-time scaling: 32-candidate parallel sampling with cslc-gated voting
all_proposals.one_line: Stop trying to make ONE attempt smarter; sample 32 cheap Sonnet implementer outputs in parallel, filter by cslc, vote/rank, return best.
all_proposals.mechanism: Add a new mode to code_translation/cuda2csl.py: --sampling-width 32 --temperature 0.9. In translate(), after the analyzer+architect produce design context, fan out 32 implementer calls in parallel (asyncio gather, batched against Argo). Each gets a slightly perturbed prompt (rotate the order of injected gotchas, vary 'show me the canonical pattern for X' phrasing, vary temperature 0.5-1.0). After generation, run cslc on all 32 in parallel under the existing _singularity_gate semaphore from benchmark_csl.py; discard the ~60% that fail to compile. Then rank surviving candidates by: (a) compiles cleanly, (b) passes smoke I/O test, (c) longest agreement run with the architect's DESIGN.md (proxy for fidelity). Return top-1.
all_proposals.why_now: Best-of-N at N=8 is already what 8-attempt repair gives us (40% pass with hybrid). The reason it caps at 40% isn't quality of any single attempt; it's that the 8 attempts are SEQUENTIAL and conditioned on each other's failures, which collapses diversity. Sampling 32 independent shots from a fixed prompt is a different operating point. Recent literature (DeepSeek-R1, AlphaCode2) shows independent sampling + verifier is the dominant scaling law for code gen. Our verifier (cslc + smoke bench) is real, not approximated.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: 1-2 eng days for asyncio fan-out + result ranking. LLM: 32x current per-kernel cost on Sonnet ~= $0.40/kernel instead of $0.05. Wall-clock: dominated by cslc semaphore (4-6 concurrent), so ~32/5 * 30s = 3-4 min vs current 6 attempts * ~45s = 4-5 min. Roughly cost-neutral on time, 8x on tokens. Pilot: $6 across 15 kernels.
all_proposals.risk: DIFFERENT from semantic_bridge/translation_facts (those were extra context per attempt; this is more attempts with the EXISTING prompt). Real risk: if the failure mode is 'no Sonnet sample ever produces a working halo-recv pattern' (which the hybrid sweep ceiling at Sonnet+Opus union 6/15 hints at), then 32 shots get you 32 wrong answers. Mitigation: mix model in the fan-out (24 Sonnet + 8 Opus) so search covers both distributions. If union ceiling holds, this is real - then the conclusion is 'model capability is the bottleneck' and we should redirect to the template-library proposal instead.

all_proposals.name: Profile-guided KB: build the gotcha catalog from real cslc error histograms, not curation
all_proposals.one_line: Replace hand-curated KNOWN_GOTCHAS with auto-extracted (cslc_error_signature -> fix_diff) pairs mined from the 250+ accumulated failed attempts.
all_proposals.mechanism: Write code_translation/build_error_catalog.py that walks /home/USER/xkernel/code_translation/sandbox/cuda2csl/* and the explored/optimization/failures/ tree, extracting (failed_csl, cslc_stderr_lines, next_attempt_csl_if_passed) triples. Normalize cslc errors into signatures (strip line numbers, paths, suggested-fix randomness; cluster by error message template). For each signature with N>=3 examples, compute the minimal diff between fail-csl and the FIRST passing attempt that followed it on the same kernel. Store as JSONL: {signature, n_examples, canonical_fix_diff_snippet, kernels_observed}. Wire into code_translation/csl_knowledge_base.py as a new layer that runs AFTER cslc fails: matches the active error against the catalog and injects the canonical fix-diff into the next repair prompt's context (NOT into translation prompts - only into repair). Gated to the bucket-B repair path in cuda2csl.py.
all_proposals.why_now: We have done 158+ attempts on iterative solvers alone and accumulated huge error logs that are sitting unused under sandbox/. The 11 hand-curated gotchas were built by reading SDK docs; the auto-extracted catalog would be built by reading what the LLM actually does WRONG repeatedly. The halo r3/r4 grounding workflow found that LLMs fabricate error messages - so the source of truth has to be real cslc output. dsr_queue_fabric_init failures (2/3) very likely cluster on 2-3 distinct cslc error signatures that a histogram would surface.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: 3-4 eng days: log parser + diff extractor + signature normalizer + matching layer. Zero LLM cost to build the catalog (pure scan over existing logs). At repair time: one cheap KB lookup, no extra LLM call. Recurring cost: re-build catalog after each sweep (~5 min wall). A/B over 15 W1 kernels: ~$20.
all_proposals.risk: PARTIALLY same shape as translation_facts (extra context to LLM). The structural difference: this only fires when cslc has ALREADY failed and shows a specific signature, so the context is conditioned on hard evidence not on prediction. Mitigation matches what made gotcha curation work vs what made translation_facts fail: tight gating on error signature match, not always-on injection. Real risk: if errors are too diverse (each kernel's failures are unique), catalog has no entries with N>=3. Mitigation: lower threshold to N=2 during pilot; if even that's empty, the conclusion ('failures are idiosyncratic, not patterned') is itself valuable signal.

all_proposals.name: Bench corpus split: separate 'CUDA-shaped' from 'algorithm-shaped' refs and translate from the latter
all_proposals.one_line: Rewrite the failing CUDA references in a CSL-friendly pseudocode (mesh-explicit, message-passing, no shared memory), then measure whether the translator can handle THAT.
all_proposals.mechanism: For the 9 failing kernels, hand-write a sibling reference: kernels/<Name>/PSEUDO/algorithm.py - a numpy-mesh-explicit version where halo exchange is explicit numpy slicing, allreduce is np.sum on a phantom mesh axis, PE id is an explicit loop variable. Add a new --source-style {cuda,pseudo,both} flag to code_translation/cuda2csl.py and a new prompt q_translate_pseudo_to_csl_bundle in prompt_cuda2csl.py that takes the pseudo as input. Run both source styles through the existing pipeline on the same 15-kernel corpus. The DELTA between pseudo-pass-rate and cuda-pass-rate quantifies 'how much of the difficulty is the source-language mismatch'.
all_proposals.why_now: The repivot doc says the agent reproduces references cycle-for-cycle when it succeeds - i.e. when it succeeds, it's barely translating; it's transcribing. The 9 failures cluster around patterns (halo, dsr queue, collectives_2d) that have NO clean CUDA analog: CUDA threading model collapses these into shared memory + __syncthreads, hiding the mesh structure the agent then has to recover. If pseudo-style refs give us 12/15 instead of 6/15, the conclusion 'invest in source preprocessing, not target generation' is the most valuable redirect available.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: 1-2 eng days per kernel to write the pseudo refs (9 kernels = ~2 eng weeks) - this is the expensive part. Pipeline changes: 1 day for prompt + flag wiring. LLM cost matches existing sweep: ~$20 for the diagnostic A/B. The pseudo files become a permanent asset for future re-translation attempts.
all_proposals.risk: Different shape from both discarded experiments: this changes the SOURCE side rather than the prompt context. Real risk: writing the pseudo IS the translation - we've just moved the human-effort goalpost. Mitigation: the pseudo refs are an INSTRUMENT, not a deliverable; they answer the question 'is the bottleneck CUDA-to-CSL or thinking-to-CSL?' Worst case: pseudo also gets 6/15, which proves the framework is the bottleneck and points back at template-library / sampling-width approaches. Either outcome is decision-useful, which is more than translation_facts produced.

all_proposals.name: Drop-the-hard-kernels: declare W1 corpus solved at the 6/15 plateau, redirect to W2/W3 wins
all_proposals.one_line: Strategic exit - admit hybrid Sonnet+Opus union ceiling is 6/15 on this corpus, mark 9 kernels as 'requires human-CSL', invest the budget in W2 cycle reduction where wins ARE happening.
all_proposals.mechanism: Add a 'human_reference_required: true' flag to kernels/<Name>/spec.yaml for the 9 stuck kernels (BiCGSTAB, CG, PCG, Power Method, Cholesky, GEMM_Collectives_2D, 7pt-Stencil_remaining_variants, etc.). Modify code_translation/batch_cuda2csl.py to skip them in W1 mode but include them in W2 mode using the SDK's reference pe.csl as the optimization baseline. Redirect the saved LLM budget (~$30/sweep) into deeper W2 exploration: increase n-rounds from 8 to 24 on the 6 kernels with prior accepts, sample wider angle whitelists, add an 'open-ended angle' that's the LLM freely picking instead of selecting from the 23-entry catalog. Write a brief 'graduated kernel list' policy in /home/USER/xkernel/code_translation/REPIVOT_CYCLES.md.
all_proposals.why_now: The progress doc shows W2 has a real win pipeline: 21 accepts across 6 kernels, biggest single win Game_of_Life -1571 cycles, deepest chain Laplacian2D-Halo 2.55x. The framework's value-per-LLM-dollar is concretely higher in W2 right now. W1 has burned ~$150 of LLM cycles against the same 9 kernels over the last month with no movement. The 'cycle reduction beyond reference' goal in REPIVOT_CYCLES.md is the actual KPI; W1 pass-rate is a means, not an end.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: 0.5 eng day - mostly spec.yaml edits + small batch_cuda2csl.py filter + policy doc. Frees up ~$30/sweep recurring + ~10 eng hours/week of debugging W1 plateau. The redirected W2 sweeps cost the same as current W1 sweeps but produce wins instead of zeroes.
all_proposals.risk: Not the same shape as semantic_bridge/translation_facts (this is a budget reallocation, not a feature). The real risk is 'we declare defeat too early - one more idea would have cracked W1'. Mitigation: keep template-library + sampling-width proposals as periodic re-attempts (quarterly, not weekly). Reframe-risk: if leadership reads W1 pass-rate as the headline metric, this looks like regression. Counter-frame: the same 6/15 with 1/3 the LLM spend, plus deeper W2 wins, is a Pareto improvement.

all_proposals.name: Co-design feedback loop: file actionable cslc/SDK issues from the failure corpus
all_proposals.one_line: Stop working around the SDK; ship a 'top 10 cslc papercuts' report to the Cerebras compiler team based on the 250 logged failures, plus run a fork patch locally.
all_proposals.mechanism: Write code_translation/sdk_issue_extractor.py that mines /home/USER/xkernel/code_translation/sandbox/cuda2csl/*/cslc.stderr for the 10 most-frequent error-message patterns that have a CSL-language fix the LLM struggles with (e.g. silent halo recv-count mismatch, missing dest_dsr_ids gives cryptic 'invalid struct field', async-fabric init order has no warning). For each, write a 1-page reproducer + suggested SDK improvement (cslc warning, error-message wording, new builtin like @recv_count_check). File these as issues on Cerebras's customer portal AND maintain a local sdk-patches/ directory with cslc warning-level patches we apply ourselves via env var. The local patches give immediate signal (LLM sees the better error message NOW); the upstream issues are the long play.
all_proposals.why_now: ground_gotcha.py r4 showed that even Opus + RAG + cslc-grounding can't synthesize correct halo idioms because the SDK error messages are unhelpful: cslc says 'task did not activate' when the real bug is 'halo_count was off by one because south-edge PE has no south neighbor'. The LLM is fighting a tooling deficit, not an intelligence deficit. The framework already has a relationship with the SDK (CSL_SDK_ROOT pinned, internal access) so co-design is feasible.
all_proposals.cost_estimate: 1 eng week for the extractor + 10 issue reports. Local cslc patch effort depends on what's patchable (some warnings might be 50-line additions in the cslc Zig code if source is accessible; some require Cerebras-side commits). Pilot: ship 3 issues + 1 local patch in 2 weeks. The local patches are the high-leverage half - each one improves every future translation attempt for free.
all_proposals.risk: Structurally DIFFERENT from both discarded experiments (this changes the TOOL the LLM is being asked to use, not the prompt). Risk: Cerebras SDK team may not act on issues in any meaningful timeframe, making the upstream-issue half low-yield. Mitigation: prioritize the local-patch half. Second risk: we don't have cslc source access (it's distributed as a binary). Mitigation: even without source, we can wrap cslc with a post-processor that rewrites its error messages based on regex matches - 'translator-friendly cslc' as a 200-line Python wrapper. Cheap to try; either works or proves the tool-improvement angle isn't tractable for us.

all_critiques.name: Skeleton-IR: typed pe.csl scaffold with TODO blocks the LLM fills
all_critiques.critique: The proposal is GENUINELY structurally different from translation_facts on one axis — enforcement-by-codegen instead of enforcement-by-prompt-hope. That distinction is real and credit is due. If the implementer literally never writes the queue-ID line, it literally cannot collide. But the structural-distinction argument only buys what's actually in the scaffold, and inspection of the canonical Laplacian2D-Halo pe.csl (kernels/Laplacian2D-Halo/CSL/pe.csl, 270 lines) shows the scaffold-derivable surface is ~70 lines (params/imports/queue+task IDs/comptime block/f_tic/f_toc) — the remaining ~200 lines (storage shapes, DSD bindings tied to storage, f_send async chain orchestration, num_halos_expected formula with comptime ifs, f_rx_done counter, 5-point stencil with edge guards, copy-back loop) ARE algorithm-dependent and end up as holes. The author's debug-bucket inventory ("wrong task IDs, wrong queue IDs, missing @unblock, fabricated builtins") is the easy half of halo failures; the hard half is mis-wiring the state machine across f_send / f_rx_done / f_compute and getting storage extents to match DSD extents — those are semantic hole problems that survive scaffolding. The author's own escape hatch ("allow a final free edit pass with ≤30 lines diff cap") is the tell: once the LLM needs to add halo_n[Nt] alongside halo_e[Mt] and tweak the rx_done counter logic and add edge-boundary guards, the 30-line budget vanishes, and you're back to free-form generation gated by a brittle scaffold. The composability concern from the author's risk note is also underweighted — "halo cluster" is heterogeneous: Laplacian2D-Halo uses hand-rolled TX/RX with is_*_edge bools, 7pt-Stencil delegates to <stencil_3d_7pts> with no manual fabric code, 25pt-Stencil has different halo widths, Game-of-Life uses block/unblock differently than Laplacian. A stamped 4-cardinal template will straitjacket the kernels it doesn't fit, and the per-template-catalog grows fast: realistic count is 15-20 templates across halo+dsr+collectives variants, not 6. Cost estimate of 3-5 days is light — template authoring and per-hole prompt tuning are the long tail and easily push this to 2 weeks. Prior art is weak: grammar-constrained decoding and Codex-style hole-filling consistently help SYNTACTIC correctness, not SEMANTIC co-design between async control flow and DSD storage shape (which is the actual CSL hard part). Note also that the proposal does nothing for the W2 iterative-solver implementer failures (Power-Method/BiCGSTAB/CG/PCG all 0% W2 improvement) — and the upstream memory note (project_power_method_instrumentation.md) says cycles_send for those is host-RPC-bounded anyway, so even a correct translation can't move the needle until run.py is rewritten. Bottom line: this is plausibly worth a small bet but the expected lift is +1 to +2 kernels on the 15-kernel benchmark (7/15 to 8/15 realistic, 9/15 stretch), nowhere near "4+ passes on 6 currently-failing halo kernels." The win/loss ratio relative to eng cost is mediocre.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: YES, and it should be done first as a 1-day kill-or-confirm test. Concretely: take the existing translation_facts extractor (already shipped in code_translation/translation_facts.py with _IMPORT_FIELD_SCHEMAS — exactly the table the proposal would reuse) and emit a literal CSL prefix for ONE halo kernel — the param block, the @import_module lines with verified handle names, the @get_input_queue(2..5)/@get_output_queue(2..5) lines, the @get_local_task_id(12..15) constants, and the canonical f_tic/f_toc/f_enable_timer/f_memcpy_timestamps fns frozen verbatim. Inject this prefix as a forced-prefix on the implementer's output (or in a system message: "your output MUST begin with the following lines verbatim then continue") for Laplacian2D-Halo + Game-of-Life + 1-2 other failing halo kernels. Run 8 attempts each. If 2+ flip to passing, the structural-enforcement claim is validated and the bigger investment can proceed with confidence. If 0/4 flip, the failures are deeper than scaffold-level and the full proposal will likely return 0-1 wins for 2 weeks of eng. The 1-day test specifically isolates the "codegen-enforced vs prompt-hoped" claim — translation_facts already had the schema in the prompt; this test moves it to forced-output. If even forced-output doesn't fix the cluster, no amount of TODO-hole scaffolding will either.

all_critiques.name: Skeleton-IR: typed pe.csl scaffold with TODO holes
all_critiques.critique:
Structural difference vs translation_facts: YES, the mechanism is different — translation_facts was "tell the model the rules in prompt", skeleton-IR is "emit the rules as code and constrain the model to fill holes". That is a real distinction, and the author flags it correctly. But the structural difference does NOT automatically translate to lift, because the failure mode it claims to address is mis-identified.

Cluster-targeting claim collapses on inspection. The author says the halo cluster is "highly stereotyped, 4-cardinal-neighbor topology". The repo says otherwise. Sampling the halo-shaped kernels:
  - Laplacian2D-Halo: 4 colors {8,9,10,11}, 4 task IDs {12..15}, two staging buffers, num_halos formula based on 4 edge flags
  - Laplacian2D-Reduce: 5 colors (adds NRM=12), plus chained reduction state machine layered on top of the halo state machine
  - LorenzoPredictor-Tile: 2 colors only, directionally-asymmetric tx/rx pairs (forward-only Lorenzo dependency)
  - Residual: 5 .csl files, NOT a halo at all — 3 colors {RXACT_X, PSUM, NRM} with separate axpy/gemv/nrminf/residual modules
  - 25-Point Stencil: 8 .csl files, 16+ task IDs split across data/ctrl/fin phases, channels by direction × stage
The "skeleton emitter from layout.csl + import schema" implicitly assumes a stereotyped target shape. But because the layout.csl IS already authored by hand and given to the implementer verbatim (W1 invariant), all the variance is downstream of layout — the storage declarations, num_halos formula, RX counter, COMPUTE body, EXIT transitions, and per-kernel staging buffers are ALL "fill the holes" territory. So in practice the holes ARE the kernel. The scaffold becomes: param block + imports + sys_mod handle + f_tic/f_toc — which is exactly what the architect's DESIGN.md + cluster-gated gotchas already enforce by prompt. The delta over the existing pipeline is small.

The bottleneck diagnosis is partially right but partially wrong. Halo failures = mis-bind state machine — that includes wrong task IDs (could be scaffolded) AND wrong @unblock plumbing (could be scaffolded) AND missing RX counter logic (algorithm-level, cannot be scaffolded without leaking the answer) AND wrong DSD construction for fabric sends (algorithm-level). Of the 6/7 halo failures, my read is maybe 1-2 are pure scaffold collisions (queue ID, task ID) — those are also the easiest for the gotcha layer to already catch. The remaining 4-5 are state-machine wiring and DSD construction, which the skeleton cannot deterministically emit because they depend on the kernel's iteration structure (single-pass vs iterative-with-counter vs reduce-then-broadcast).

The "free edit pass with ≤30-line diff cap" mitigation is the proposal's own admission of risk, and it's the wrong knob. 30 lines is enough for the LLM to add a wrong queue or misbind a task — i.e. enough to reintroduce every failure mode the skeleton was supposed to prevent. Either you trust the skeleton (no escape hatch) or you don't (escape hatch defeats the constraint). Sketch-synthesis literature (Solar-Lezama, etc.) handles this with a constraint solver verifying the filled sketch — there's no equivalent verification step proposed here; cslc compile-clean is necessary but not sufficient (compiles ≠ converges ≠ matches reference).

Prior art / outside validation: sketch synthesis works in domains with a strong type system + decidable constraint (Sketch DSL → SAT). It does NOT have a proven track record for LLM-based translation to a target with weak documentation, opaque compiler errors, and per-PE state-machine semantics like CSL. The closest analog — typed-hole completion in Haskell/Idris assistants — works because the type system rejects wrong fills. CSL types are looser than that; an LLM can fill a hole with code that typechecks but deadlocks. The prior is weak.

Repo-internal prior art: ground_gotcha.py ALREADY emits typed scaffolds (single_pe, send_recv_2x1, mesh_2x2) to ground gotcha snippets through cslc. That tooling worked for grounding gotchas (workflow r3/r4 grounded snippets) but the gotchas themselves still scored 0/5 on the failing halo kernels because "canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses". This is direct evidence in this repo that the scaffold-instantiation idea hits the composition wall — the same wall this proposal will hit. The author's risk note acknowledges Cholesky/Mandelbrot as out of scope but doesn't engage with the harder fact that even the in-scope halo kernels are not stereotyped.

Composition with existing pipeline: per-hole prompting kills the architect's role. The architect's DESIGN.md is precisely the place where state-machine choice (single-pass vs iterative, reduce-then-broadcast vs interleaved) is decided. If you carve into holes by name (SEND_TASK_BODY, COMPUTE_BODY, EXIT_TASK_BODY), you've baked a state-machine choice into the skeleton. If the kernel needs a different state machine, the skeleton fights the design instead of expressing it. That conflict was the underlying cause of the r4 "canonical patterns too composed" finding.

Expected lift: the high end is +2 W1 passes (one halo scaffold-collision case and one dsr_queue case) = 8/15 = 53%. The low end is 0 (skeleton rigidity blocks the kernels it would have helped while constraining the LLM into worse local minima). My point estimate is +0 to +1 pass, ~5% relative — same magnitude as translation_facts's noise floor, with comparable engineering cost (3-5 days) and similar A/B-discard risk.

Cost-benefit: medium engineering cost, narrow target (only halo + dsr_queue + maybe collectives_2d), and the cluster-gated gotchas + ground_gotcha.py already cover the easy wins inside that target. The marginal lift is competing with already-deployed mitigations on the same bytes.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: 10x smaller version that proves the principle in <1 day: pick ONE failing halo kernel (e.g. Game-of-Life-shaped or Laplacian2D-Halo), HAND-WRITE the skeleton (no emitter), and ask the implementer ONLY to fill the storage + COMPUTE + RX_DONE bodies, with EXIT/SEND/f_tic/f_toc frozen. Run that prompt 8 times under the current 8-attempt budget. If it doesn't pass ≥3/8 times, the principle is dead. If it does, the question becomes: can the deterministic emitter produce the same skeleton from layout.csl alone? That second question is cheap to answer because the skeleton is mostly the layout's set_tile_code field list plus a small fixed table. Cost: half a day. Decision value: high — answers the "scaffolds compose into a working file?" question without building the emitter, and aligns directly with the existing ground_gotcha.py harness pattern that already revealed the composition wall on canonical patterns. If you want a SECOND small version: instead of code-skeleton, ship a "constrained DESIGN.md template" the architect must fill — same idea, no new pipeline path, lower risk; if the architect can't produce a correct state-machine plan when given a typed template, the implementer cannot either.

all_critiques.name: Executable mini-IR: Python reference runner that validates translation semantics pre-cslc
all_critiques.critique:
Structurally distinct from translation_facts/semantic_bridge? Partially. Those were prompt-context injections; this is an executable oracle with a hard gate. That IS a real structural difference and worth crediting. BUT — the gate is on the wrong layer for the documented failure modes.

Failure-mode mismatch (this is the dispositive issue): The 9/15 W1 failures are concentrated in halo_recv_unblock (6/7), dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3), collectives_2d (2/4). Look at what these are: halo_recv_unblock is a CSL-fabric-protocol bug — recv tasks fire before counter reaches the expected value, or @unblock is called against the wrong color, or DSR queues 0/1 are reused after memcpy reserved them. dsr_queue_fabric_init is queue ID / fabric color collision. collectives_2d is wrong field names on import structs. NONE of these are semantic-decomposition errors that an arithmetic Python interpreter would catch. The architect's design "halo width 1, 5-pt stencil, NORTH/SOUTH/EAST/WEST exchange, 2x2 mesh" is almost always CORRECT for the halo kernels. The bug is downstream — in CSL-specific protocol syntax that produces the right algorithm with deadlock/wrong-queue/wrong-builtin. An IR that successfully evaluates the algorithm semantically tells you nothing about whether @get_input_queue(0) collides with memcpy's reservation. The proposal claims "halo width is 1 but design said 2" is a common failure — there is no evidence in PROGRESS.md or the gotchas that this is the actual bottleneck. The author has invented a failure mode that fits their solution.

Prior art that should worry the author: translation_facts spent 19 attempts producing 0W/2L/17T — and that was an easier version of the same idea (structured-fact injection without execution). The reason was that RAG'd gotchas already covered the surface and the IR added perturbation without lift. The exec-IR has the same problem PLUS adds a new failure mode: the architect now has to emit two artifacts (DESIGN.md AND valid JSON IR), and prompt-LLMs degrade non-monotonically when you stack output schemas. The "re-prompt on IR-eval failure" loop is itself an extra LLM round per kernel that could just be additional knowledge in the prompt.

External prior art: AlphaCodium and similar code-gen systems have a "test-driven" oracle loop — but those gate on the TARGET-LANGUAGE compile-and-run, which this framework ALREADY does (cslc + sim). The novel claim is gating on an intermediate semantic check before cslc. The MLIR ecosystem has lit/FileCheck for IR-level validation but those check structural IR conformance, not numerical equivalence — and crucially, MLIR's IR is hand-written by humans, not by an LLM that might get it wrong in a way that masks the real bug. CUDA→assembly compilers like NVCC don't use an "exec IR oracle" — they use static IR transforms. The author's own risk note flags this: "morally similar to MLIR-style multi-level — and Phase 1 of multi-level IR has decades of warnings about who maintains the IR." Correct, and the proposed mitigation ("only build what 8 kernels need") doesn't actually mitigate — every new kernel family will need new opcodes, and the LLM emitting those opcodes will hallucinate them just as it hallucinates CSL builtins.

The new failure mode it introduces: an architect that emits a valid-looking JSON IR for which the Python evaluator returns "matches CUDA" but the design is still wrong at the CSL-protocol level. The 3-way agreement check claim is suspect — if the IR passes and CSL fails, you already know it's CSL-level (you have cslc errors). You didn't need the IR for that diagnosis.

Iterative-solver claim is the strongest part: a numerical oracle for W2 transformations is genuinely useful — but per MEMORY.md, the W2 bottleneck on iterative solvers is that "cycles_send is host-RPC-bounded" — the metric is measuring host↔device sync, not on-device compute. A semantic equivalence oracle does not address this at all. Fix the metric, not add an IR.

10x smaller version: yes. Half a day: skip the IR-emission-by-LLM and instead grep the architect's DESIGN.md for 4 specific facts (halo_width, reduction_axis, tile_dims, mesh_shape) using simple regex; cross-check against the CUDA kernel.cu via separate regex; flag mismatches in the implementer prompt. Tests the "design-vs-CUDA disagreement causes failures" hypothesis in 1 day. If that shows ZERO catches across the 9 failing kernels, you've falsified the proposal cheaply and saved 7 days.

Lift estimate: 2pp (0.3/15) on the optimistic side. Most likely 0/15 lift on W1 — the failures are CSL-protocol bugs, not semantic-design bugs — with some risk of regression from architect-output-schema perturbation, similar to translation_facts' 2L. On W2, zero lift on iterative solvers because the bottleneck is the metric not the transformation correctness.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Half-day falsification test: write a regex extractor that pulls (halo_width, reduction_axis, tile_dims, mesh_shape) from DESIGN.md and from the CUDA kernel.cu, diff them, and log mismatches across the 9 failing W1 kernels. If <2/9 kernels show a mismatch on these fields, the entire "architect-design-is-wrong" premise is falsified and the 5-8 day IR build is cancelled. If 4+/9 kernels mismatch, THEN consider a real fix — but the fix is probably "add halo_width/reduction_axis as explicit DESIGN.md required fields with a regex validator," not a Python interpreter. Even smaller: just add a 1-line check in cuda2csl.py that the architect's DESIGN.md mentions all 4 cardinal halo directions when the CUDA source contains a 5-pt or 9-pt stencil pattern. This is 30 lines of code and addresses the same hypothesis without inventing an IR opcode set.

all_critiques.name: Executable mini-IR: Python reference runner that validates translation semantics pre-cslc
all_critiques.critique:
This proposal misdiagnoses the failure mode and is structurally closer to translation_facts than the author admits.

ON Q1 (STRUCTURAL DISTINCTNESS): The author frames it as "executable oracle that gates the architect, not extra prompt context" - but trace the actual data path: (a) architect emits IR JSON, (b) IR is validated against CUDA reference output, (c) on failure, architect is re-prompted, (d) on pass, the IR is forwarded "alongside the CUDA source" to the implementer. Step (d) is exactly the same shape as translation_facts and semantic_bridge: structured artifact computed by upstream phase, injected into implementer prompt. The added "executable validation" only affects the IR's algorithmic correctness; it cannot affect the CSL-side correctness, which is where the actual failures live. The 3-way agreement check at the END is novel, but at that point you've already paid cslc + sim cost so it gates nothing.

ON Q2 (BOTTLENECK MATCH): This is the killer objection. Look at what's actually failing on the 9 W1 kernels:
  - halo_recv_unblock (6/7): failure is "sys_mod.unblock_cmd_stream() not called from edge PEs," "0-byte D2H stall because recv task never fires," "wrong @block/@unblock pairing on receiver tasks." These are CSL runtime/contract bugs - the algorithm is correct in pseudocode. An exec-IR that says "EXCHANGE_HALO(N, S, E, W, width=1)" can pass numerical equivalence against CUDA reference TRIVIALLY (just do the Python computation), then the implementer still emits wrong cmd-stream unblock logic and the kernel hangs at runtime. The IR adds zero discriminative signal here.
  - dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3): failure is wrong queue IDs collide with memcpy reservations, wrong DSR ids passed to <collectives_2d/pe>, fabric color/route conflicts. None of these have any algorithmic representation that an exec-IR would catch.
  - collectives_2d (2/4): failure is "c2d.get_params takes 3 args not 4," "broadcast takes [*]u32 not [*]f32," ".dim_params = c2d_params.x required." Pure syntactic-surface bugs already covered by the gotchas RAG.

The proposal addresses an imaginary failure cluster ("wrong halo width," "wrong reduction axis") - I see no evidence in PROGRESS.md, the gotchas corpus, or the cluster diagnoses that algorithm-level architect errors are a meaningful fraction of failures. The architect using pseudocode from a clearly-named CUDA kernel rarely flips a reduction axis or picks a wrong halo width when the spec.yaml literally says "halo-1 exchange" and the CUDA file is captioned "5-point Laplacian."

ON PRIOR ART (Q3): IR-based code translation oracles exist (TVM, MLIR, Triton lowering), but they all rely on TYPED, MACHINE-CHECKED IRs that the source language COMPILES INTO - not on the architect LLM emitting JSON that's a freeform claim about kernel semantics. The closest LLM-shaped prior art is the AlphaCode / SWE-bench-style "execute candidate, gate on tests" loop - but that uses the FINAL artifact's behavior, not a phantom intermediate IR. I'm not aware of any published LLM-translation system where a per-task hand-rolled Python interpreter for a 12-op IR moved the needle. The 5-8 day estimate for "Python evaluator for 8 W1-failing kernels" is also wildly optimistic: Cholesky alone (blocked decomposition + back-substitution + cross-PE pivot reduction) is a multi-day implementation if you want it to match CUDA numerically. BiCGSTAB iterates with cross-PE dot products and needs convergence behavior modeling. The "12 ops" list does not include a square-root, a triangular solve, or anything iterative-solver-shaped - the spec needs to grow before day 1 is done.

ON Q4 (SMALLER PROOF): Yes, see below.

ON Q5 (EXPECTED LIFT): The most charitable accounting: of 9 W1 failures, MAYBE 1 has an algorithm-level architect error the IR could catch (Cholesky-class). Even there, the IR-failure → re-prompt → IR-pass loop has to actually produce a CORRECT IR (which is harder than producing correct CSL, since the architect already does prose-level reasoning that's usually algorithmically right). Expected delta: 6/15 → 6/15 most likely, 7/15 in the lucky case. Lift estimate: 2%, possibly negative due to perturbation (longer prompts, extra round-trips, IR-format failures consuming attempt budget). The translation_facts experiment burned 19 attempts to verify 0W/2L/17T on a similar-shape change; this proposal is structurally adjacent enough that the prior is "regression risk roughly equals lift potential."

ADDITIONAL RED FLAGS: (a) The IR has to be re-designed when you add kernel 9, then 10, then 11 - the author's "if >30 ops abandon" stop-loss is appropriate but the 12-op list already misses iterative solvers, sparse formats, and FFT butterflies which collectively cover 5 of the 9 failing kernels. (b) The "Python evaluator runs on CUDA test inputs" assumes CUDA reference outputs are reproducible and the Python eval is byte-equivalent - but the spec.yaml tolerance is 0.0 for Laplacian, and any f32-reordering in the Python eval drifts. (c) Most importantly: if the IR-vs-CUDA equivalence is the gate, then for any kernel where Python can reproduce CUDA output, you've essentially re-implemented the CUDA reference in Python - at which point why not just diff CSL vs the existing CUDA reference (which we already do)? The proposal collapses to "add an extra reference implementation in a third language" which adds maintenance burden, not signal.

VERDICT: The framework has a clear pattern - upstream-injected structured artifacts (semantic_bridge, translation_facts) have failed twice against Sonnet/Opus, both with extensive A/B harness validation. This proposal is the third instance of that shape with extra packaging. The "executable" framing doesn't change the data flow into the implementer. Recommend: do NOT spend 5-8 engineering days here.
all_critiques.smaller_variant:
YES - and it's a forcing function that would falsify the proposal cheaply in <1 day:

Pick the 1-2 kernels where the author's failure-mode hypothesis is most plausible (Cholesky and one of the halo kernels). For each, manually audit the LAST architect DESIGN.md from the most-recent failed sweep and answer: "Did the design contain an ALGORITHMIC error that an exec-IR would have caught (wrong halo width, wrong reduction axis, wrong tile layout)?" If you find <1 such error per 4 failed attempts, the proposal is dead-on-arrival because there's no signal for the IR to capture. If you find ~50%+, then build the SMALLEST possible IR (3 ops: STENCIL_5PT, AXPY, DOT) for ONE kernel (Laplacian2D-Halo), gate ONE attempt with it, and measure: did the IR catch a design that would have failed, OR did it falsely block a design that would have passed? This is a 4-hour experiment, not 5-8 days. If signal exists, escalate; if not, the larger build is fully unjustified.

Alternative smaller variant that targets the ACTUAL bottleneck: skip the IR entirely and instead build a "pre-cslc CSL structural linter" - a Python check that runs on the implementer's output BEFORE invoking cslc, checking for the specific structural-class failures the ab_translation_facts.py harness already enumerates (c2d_params.dim_size misuse, @fmacs arity, queue 0/1 reuse, task-id collision, missing sys_mod.unblock_cmd_stream from edge PEs). This is 1 day of work, addresses the actual failure clusters, and reuses the existing structural checker. That's the experiment worth running.

all_critiques.name: CUDA-side AST IR: tree-sitter parse + structural feature vector for retrieval and gating
all_critiques.critique:
Hard answers to the five questions:

(1) STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCE FROM PRIOR ART. The author claims this is different because "facts drive a decision (cluster + retrieval) not just prompt text." That distinction is real on paper but thin in practice. Look at csl_knowledge_base.py L650-680: the current cluster augmentations already key off CUDA-source terms ("halo", "stencil", "gemv", "broadcast", "neighbor", "border", "is_n_edge"). A tree-sitter AST would replace substring-match with AST-match for the SAME signal. The Single-Tile-Matvec misclustering cited as motivation was fixed in task #42 by tightening string markers, not by needing an AST. Empirically, on the 15-kernel corpus, how many kernels are currently in the wrong cluster? The author doesn't say. If the answer is 0-1 (likely, given task #42), the cluster-detector replacement is a no-op. The retrieval replacement is more substantive but lands in the same prompt-conditioning slot that translation_facts already occupied — the LLM either uses retrieved snippets or doesn't, and the 17T/2L A/B on translation_facts says the implementer ignores syntax-surface context once the obvious gotchas are already in-prompt.

(2) DOES IT ADDRESS THE 9 FAILING KERNELS SPECIFICALLY? No. This is the load-bearing problem with the proposal. halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail) fails because the canonical recv-unblock idiom is COMPOSED (async fabin_dsd + ut_id + activate + per-edge counts + sender-after-receiver-posted ordering) — task #65's hand-curation found that even with cslc-grounded snippets the patterns "too composed to fit in minimal harnesses." A better cluster label and a better-retrieved EXAMPLE don't help if the LLM can't compose the example into a working halo. dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fail) fails on top-level-comptime-only constraints around @initialize_queue / @bind_data_task that are CSL-side, not CUDA-side — knowing more about the CUDA AST tells you nothing about whether the generated CSL has the right comptime structure. collectives_2d (2/4) is closest to a retrieval problem but still mostly an API-arity/structfield problem, which translation_facts directly addressed and lost.

(3) PRIOR ART OUTSIDE REPO. AST-feature retrieval for code IS well-trodden (CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, code2vec, the OpenAI codex-translate work, and Meta's TransCoder). The pattern of "parse source AST + use structural features for example retrieval" produces measured single-digit BLEU/exec lifts on Python<->C++/Java translation. That's the realistic ceiling for the retrieval half. For the gating half there's no real precedent — most translation systems don't have a discrete cluster-of-failures structure to gate against. Yellow flag: nobody has shown AST-keyed retrieval moves the needle on CUDA→target-DSL translation when prose RAG is already present and well-tuned, because the bottleneck shifts to composition, not retrieval.

(4) 10X SMALLER VERSION TO PROVE THE PRINCIPLE. Yes, and it should be REQUIRED before the 6-day spend. Skip tree-sitter entirely; spend 2-4 hours writing a 30-line regex/string-match feature extractor over the CUDA source that emits the 6-8 fields that actually matter (kernel count, __syncthreads count, has_atomics, has_shared_mem, halo_radius if detectable, reduction_axis). Wire it ONLY into the retrieval query (skip the cluster-detector swap — current detector works). A/B against current TF-IDF on the 9 failing kernels. If retrieved-example quality measurably improves AND that produces even 1 new pass, then justify the tree-sitter spend. The author's plan day 1+2 alone is 2 days for something a 1-day regex prototype would test more cleanly. The author's framing implicitly bundles the IR (which is plausibly useful) with cluster-detector replacement (which is a no-op) — the bundle hides which piece does the work.

(5) ACTUAL EXPECTED LIFT. Generous case: 6/15 → 7/15 (one collectives_2d kernel where the right example surfaces and the implementer composes it correctly). Realistic case: 6/15 → 6/15, T-result, indistinguishable from translation_facts A/B. Reason: 6/9 failing kernels are halo, and the failure mode is COMPOSITION not RETRIEVAL — task #65 evidence is the strongest signal you have and it directly contradicts the "better retrieval helps" thesis. Author's risk note is honest about this ("same shape as translation_facts if facts just become extra prompt text") but the proposed mitigation ("facts must drive a decision") only fires if the decisions are load-bearing; the cluster-decision currently works fine and the retrieval-decision lands in a prompt that the implementer already underuses.

Specific concerns with the plan:
- Day 1's "20-field CudaKernelFacts extractor tested on all 15 W1 kernels" — what is the success criterion? The plan doesn't define one. Without a "this field must distinguish kernel X from Y to be worth keeping" gate, you'll ship 20 fields, 6 of which discriminate, and overfit retrieval to the discriminating ones.
- tree-sitter-cuda is real but the CUDA kernels in /home/USER/xkernel/kernels/ are research-grade and mostly clean — libclang would parse them too, with full type information that tree-sitter doesn't have. If the author actually needs typed AST (the proposal says "typed AST"), libclang is the right tool; tree-sitter gives untyped CST. This is a tool choice they haven't actually thought through.
- "Architect verifies DESIGN.md against CudaKernelFacts" — this is a NEW agentic step (an architect-time verifier) glossed as one line. It's actually a significant addition with its own failure mode (architect rejects valid designs, repair-loop thrashes). Should be priced separately.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: YES — and this is the right way to test the idea. Spend half a day, not 6: (a) write a 30-line regex extractor that pulls 6-8 structural features from CUDA source (kernel_count, syncthreads_count, has_atomics, has_shared_mem, suspected_halo_radius, suspected_reduction_axis, grid_dim_2d_vs_1d, host_loop_present). (b) Concatenate those features as a feature-string into the existing TF-IDF query — NO cluster-detector replacement, NO embedding model, NO tree-sitter. (c) A/B on the 9 failing kernels only. If 0/9 turn green, kill the proposal — the bottleneck is composition not retrieval. If 1-2 turn green, you have evidence the AST signal is load-bearing and can justify the tree-sitter spend; specifically inspect WHICH kernels turned green to see if it's halo (the dominant cluster) or peripheral. Hard gate: do NOT touch the cluster-detector — it works, and replacing it adds A/B noise that masks the retrieval signal you're actually testing.
