Also: before any of this, run a 1-hour upper-bound experiment — manually craft the "ideal retrieved example" for the 6 failing halo kernels and inject it directly into the implementer prompt as a forced retrieval. If a hand-picked perfect example doesn't fix them, no retrieval improvement will, and the whole proposal is moot. This upper-bound check costs 1 hour and could kill the 6-day plan before it starts.

all_critiques.name: CUDA-side AST IR: tree-sitter parse + structural feature vector for retrieval and gating
all_critiques.critique:
This proposal fails Q1 honestly when you look at where it touches the pipeline. It claims structural difference from translation_facts because "facts drive a decision (cluster + retrieval), not just prompt text." But both decisions it drives are decisions the framework already makes correctly:

(a) Cluster detection: csl_knowledge_base.py L650-680 already string-matches the CUDA source for halo/stencil/is_n_edge/collectives_2d/dest_dsr_ids markers. The progress log cites ZERO W1 misclassification incidents in the last 6 weeks; the one historical regression (Single-Tile-Matvec) was fixed by gating gotchas to empty-when-no-markers, not by misrouting. There is no evidence current cluster detection is the brittle link.

(b) Retrieval: TF-IDF + cluster augmentation already pins halo queries to pipeline-03-multiple (the canonical halo example). Halo failures are 6/7 WITH the right example retrieved and the canonical hints fed directly into the r4 rewriter (also 0/5). The failure mode is "canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses" per the progress doc — a CSL-side synthesis problem, not a CUDA-side or retrieval problem.

Q2 — does it address ONE OF the 3 failing clusters? No, it addresses none specifically. The 6/7 halo failures are the dominant bucket; they are characterized as synthesis failures (async fabin_dsd + ut_id + unblock discipline + per-PE edge-aware recv counts). None of these are constrained by knowing the CUDA source is a 5-pt stencil — that fact was already trivially identified by substring "halo"/"stencil" and is already on the prompt. The CUDA AST tells the architect what the architect already knows. dsr_queue and collectives_2d are similar: the failure is CSL synthesis of @initialize_queue + DSR plumbing + collectives_2d/pe struct field names, none of which has a CUDA-side counterpart in the AST.

Q3 — prior art: tree-sitter + structural retrieval for code translation has been tried (TransCoder, CodeBERT, Code2Vec). None show structural retrieval as load-bearing for synthesis quality of complex domain-specific lowering. They show small lifts on top of strong neural baselines at MUCH lower target complexity than CUDA→CSL fabric/microthread/queue discipline. This is a yellow flag.

Q4 — yes, a 10x smaller version is the cheapest way to kill this proposal before spending 4-6 days: spend 4 hours hand-labeling the 15 W1 kernels' (memory_pattern, reduction_topology, sync_count, atomic_pattern) and audit (i) is current cluster-detection wrong on any kernel? (ii) does TF-IDF retrieve the wrong top-1 example on any failing halo kernel? If both audits say "current system is right," the proposal cannot lift — because both decisions it would change are already being made correctly. If the audit surfaces ANY misclassification or misretrieval on the 9 failing kernels, then proceed — but only on those specific failure modes, not as a wholesale rewrite.

Q5 — expected lift: 0-1 kernels on the 15-corpus (6/15 → 6/15 or 7/15, i.e. 0-7pt). The IR cannot help the synthesis-bottlenecked halo cluster (6 kernels). It cannot help dsr_queue synthesis (2 kernels). It MIGHT help one collectives_2d kernel if there's a mis-retrieval there, but the cluster augmentation already biases toward c2d examples.

Crucial prior-art match in THIS repo: translation_facts ran 19 attempts, 0W/2L/17T and was discarded. The author calls this out as "the critical mitigation is that facts must drive a decision." But as shown above, the decisions in question are already being made correctly without the IR. So the structural distinction from translation_facts is rhetorical, not load-bearing.

What WOULD plausibly lift: anything that improves CSL synthesis quality on the halo cluster — e.g., few-shot the implementer with a MINIMAL grounded halo skeleton derived from a real cslc-passing micro-kernel (since the r4 finding was "canonical patterns too composed"), or split the halo implementer into a two-step: skeleton-first (fabin_dsd + ut_id + unblock for one direction) then extend-to-4-directions. Those address the actual bottleneck. CUDA-side AST does not.

Secondary concern: tree-sitter-cuda's parse coverage on real CUDA kernels (templated, CUB/thrust-heavy, host launchers with __launch_bounds__, cooperative_groups) is patchy. The "graceful fallback" mitigation means in the worst case the system reduces to current behavior — but then ALSO the lift becomes 0 on the kernels where it would have mattered. The graceful-fallback story makes the proposal safer but cuts its upside.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: A 1-day, 10x smaller version that would actually answer the question: SKIP tree-sitter and SKIP the rewrite. Hand-label the 15 W1 kernels with a 6-field structural record (memory_pattern, reduction_topology, sync_count, atomic_pattern, kernel_count, grid_shape). Then run two audits: (1) Does current marker-based cluster detection match the hand-labels on all 15? (2) For the 9 failing kernels, does TF-IDF+cluster-augmented retrieval put the structurally-most-similar cerebras-csl-skills example in top-3? If (1) and (2) both say "current system is right," kill the proposal — no AST can help, the bottleneck is downstream of retrieval. If either audit surfaces 2+ failures, scope the AST work narrowly to fix THOSE specific failures (one-day patch to the marker list or retrieval weights), and only escalate to tree-sitter if marker-patches can't reach. This audit costs 4 hours of human time and answers the load-bearing question without committing 4-6 engineering days. SECOND smaller variant if the audit somehow says current retrieval IS broken: instead of tree-sitter, just bias the TF-IDF query with hand-extracted CUDA features via regex (halo width = count of [i±k,j±k] index patterns; reduction topology = presence of __shfl_xor/atomicAdd/cooperative_groups). Regex captures 90% of the structural signal for these 15 kernels at 5% of the engineering cost, with the same "drive a decision" property.

all_critiques.name: Local constraint solver: queue/task/color allocator the implementer plugs into
all_critiques.critique:
Empirical evidence from the latest hybrid_sweep_20260614_210137 (the 6/15 baseline) directly contradicts the proposal's premise. I read pe.csl + run.log for the 9 failures and tallied per-attempt verdicts:

THE LLM IS NOT THE PROBLEM IT CLAIMS TO BE. Latest passing Laplacian2D-Halo pe.csl uses queues 4-7, ut_ids 0-3, task IDs 10-15 — all within documented valid ranges, post-r3 gotchas. The cluster's stated trap ('LLM keeps picking queue 1 or task 8') is no longer the failure mode. The cluster failed 6/7 NOT because IDs collide, but because of: blocking @fmovs spin-waits (Cholesky a8), wse3 routing-direction limits (FFT a7), affine DSD expressions referencing non-loop vars (FFT a8), edge-PE never reaching unblock_cmd_stream (Game-of-Life a6), fabric register reads at module scope (Residual a8), pe.csl returned as a 3-line stub (Lap2D-Reduce a6, GEMV-Coll a7), VERIFY=False in run.py (Lorenzo a6), wrong file in commands.sh (Mandelbrot a8). NONE of these are ID-allocation failures.

OF THE 72 FAILING ATTEMPTS ACROSS 9 KERNELS, ID-COLLISION FAILURES TALLY TO ~4: Cholesky a7 (memcpy queue 1 collision), GEMV-Checkerboard a7 (queues 2/3 collide with sys_mod.MEMCPY), GEMV-Coll-2D a6/a8 (mpi_x/mpi_y DSR ID sharing), Residual a7 (queue 1 collision). All 4 are repair-loop attempts, not first-shot; after the linter rejects them the agent still has to fix the deeper bugs to convert kernel-fail→kernel-pass. Catching these earlier saves ~30s cslc time per attempt — that's wall-clock optimization, not pass-rate lift.

Q1 (structurally different from semantic_bridge/translation_facts?): YES, in principle — the linter + repair-gate is a real loop, not a prompt slot. But proposal author admits the kill-switch criterion ('if linter never fires it IS translation_facts'). My read of the evidence says it'll fire on ~5% of attempts and translate to ~0-1 kernel-level conversions. The shape is novel, the leverage isn't.

Q2 (addresses ONE of the 3 clusters?): Claims halo + dsr_queue, but neither cluster's REMAINING failures (post-r3 gotchas) are dominated by ID allocation. dsr_queue_fabric_init cluster's GEMV-Coll-2D failure IS DSR-ID sharing across mpi_x/mpi_y — proposal's strongest case, ~1 kernel of lift if the rest of the design holds. halo cluster: 0 kernels of lift because halo PEs aren't failing on ID allocation anymore.

Q3 (prior art for code translation?): TVM/Halide have schedule constraint solvers but they're for choosing tile sizes / loop orders, not API-symbol allocation. LLVM regalloc is the closest analog but it operates on a typed IR after the frontend has produced valid code — the LLM here is producing the frontend, and the failure modes are semantic (deadlock, wrong export, stub code) not allocation. No directly applicable prior art for 'LLM-emitted DSL with linter-enforced symbol allocator'. Yellow flag confirmed.

Q4 (10x smaller version?): YES — and it's where the real test lives. Just add a regex linter post-generation that checks for `@get_input_queue(0|1)`, `@get_input_queue(8|9|10|11|12|13|14|15)`, and `dest_dsr_ids` duplication across module imports. Wire it into the existing bucket-routed repair. 4 hours of work, no allocator, no resource plan. If THAT catches >20% of failures, build the allocator. My prediction: it'll fire on the ~4 attempts I identified and convert 0-1 kernel.

Q5 (expected lift): 6/15 → 6-7/15. Best case 7/15 if GEMV-Coll-2D's DSR aliasing gets fixed AND the saved repair budget lets the agent get to the real bugs. Likely 6/15 — the deep failures (sync @fmovs hangs, missing unblock, stub pe.csl) consume the budget either way.

FATAL ISSUE: proposal misreads the post-gotchas failure distribution. Author cites the B1 gotchas ('max queue is 7', 'IDs 0-11 reserved') but those gotchas are ALREADY WORKING — the LLM follows them. The remaining failures are NOT 'LLM ignored the gotcha and allocated queue 1'; they're complex semantic bugs (deadlock topology, init ordering, file-naming) that a symbol allocator cannot reach.

PARALLEL TO DISCARDED EXPERIMENTS: closest match is translation_facts. Author's own kill-switch says 'if linter never fires it's translation_facts'. Evidence says it'll fire rarely on the kernels that matter, making it a more-engineered variant of the same idea that already lost A/B 0W/2L/17T.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY THE BOTTLENECK (per evidence): (a) the implementer emits stub/fragment pe.csl files (~5 attempts) — fix with output-shape validator (file must define module, params, exports), this is 1 day and would catch more failures; (b) hangs from missing unblock_cmd_stream on edge PEs — already documented in gotchas, the agent still misses it because the gotcha is text not code — fix with a per-PE control-flow checker on the emitted pe.csl that asserts every branch reaches unblock_cmd_stream; (c) cross-module DSR aliasing in collectives_2d — narrowly fixable. (a) and (b) are the higher-leverage versions of the same 'linter + repair gate' idea but targeting where the LLM actually fails post-gotchas.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Skip the allocator and resource-plan templates entirely. Ship just a post-generation regex linter (4 hours) that checks for: (1) `@get_input_queue(0|1)` calls (memcpy collision); (2) `@get_input_queue(N)` with N>7 on wse3; (3) duplicate dest_dsr_ids/src0_dsr_ids across multiple @import_module calls in the same pe.csl; (4) pe.csl file is <500 chars or has no `comptime {` block (stub detection). Wire into existing bucket-routed repair as a synthetic 'bucket=L' (lint failure) with structured diff. If lint fires >20% of attempts on the failing-9, expand to a real allocator. If lint catches the stub-pe.csl case (it will — that's 3-5 failed attempts in the latest sweep), it pays for itself in saved repair budget even with zero kernel-conversion lift. Higher-EV smaller variant: combine the stub detector + control-flow checker for unblock_cmd_stream coverage on edge PEs — those are the actual remaining failure modes the gotchas can't fix because they're structural, not symbolic.

all_critiques.name: Local constraint solver: queue/task/color allocator the implementer plugs into
all_critiques.critique:
The proposal misdiagnoses the bottleneck. I scanned the most recent hybrid sweep (results/hybrid_sweep_20260614_210137) and tallied the failure rationales across the 15-kernel corpus. Of ~45 failed attempts in the first 3 rounds, only ~6 (~13%) are "ID-out-of-range / hit-a-reserved-pool" failures that a static allocator+linter could catch. The remaining ~85% are: runtime hangs from missing unblock_cmd_stream on edge PEs (Halo att 2, Reduce att 2, GEMV-Cb att 2+3, Mandelbrot att 2+3), layout_mod.get_x_coord() called at module scope (GEMM-Coll, GEMV-Coll, GEMV-Cb, Residual att 3), DSD/tensor_access pointer-typing (Halo att 1), @export_symbol shape (Reduce att 1, Game-of-Life att 1), param i16/u16 (Cholesky att 3), nonexistent builtins like @This() (Residual att 2), and library param shape mismatches (GEMV-Coll att 2+3, GEMM att 3). None of these are ID allocations.

Even within the "ID-collision" subset, the failure shape is "library X already initialized queue Y, you double-init'd it" — NOT "you picked ID 100 which doesn't exist". The allocator would have to model which LIBRARIES (memcpy, collectives_2d/pe, <layout>) implicitly claim which queues/colors per WSE generation per kernel topology, AND model whether the kernel's import shape forwards or shadows that claim. That is exactly the modeling that the LLM already gets wrong even with the gotcha telling it explicitly. Putting that modeling into a static parser duplicates the LLM's brittleness in Python with a smaller training set.

The dead-on-arrival evidence: I read the pe.csl the framework just emitted for Laplacian2D-Halo. It allocated input_queues 4-7 and local_task_ids 10-15. Those are already in the legal free set per the framework's own gotcha block. The LLM is no longer picking colliding raw IDs in the halo cluster; the existing gotcha already moved it into the free pool. The author's own bar — "does the linter fire >20% of attempts?" — would not be met on the halo cluster because the LLM already picks legal IDs. The cluster keeps failing on conditional-init, hang, and fabric-direction bugs that the linter is structurally blind to.

This is structurally the same shape as translation_facts (discarded 0W/2L/17T over 19 attempts). The added "post-generation linter that bounces the output" is real differentiation in principle, but it only matters if the rejected failures are common. They aren't. The 2026-06-04 wrap-up specifically says "RAG'd gotchas already covered the surface, IR added perturbation without lift" — and the surface this proposal covers is a strict subset of that same surface (just IDs, no library/type/syntax facts).

Where the framework actually has lift available: (a) the runtime-hang cluster — needs a deadlock/liveness check, not an ID check; concretely, a static "every fn that gates on halos_done MUST call unblock_cmd_stream on its non-receive branch" linter would hit Halo att 2, Reduce att 2, Mandelbrot att 2+3, GEMV-Cb att 2+3 — easily 5-7 failed attempts in this sweep. (b) the module-scope `layout_mod.get_x_coord()` cluster — needs a per-site call-context check, hits 4+ attempts. Both are syntactic/structural linters but they target failure modes that account for 30-40% of failures, vs IDs at 13%.

Also: the cost estimate is wrong. Parsing layout.csl + commands_wse3.sh for resource claims is not regex-tractable in general — layout.csl uses comptime loops, conditional color assignment (see Laplacian2D-Halo lines 56-89 with px/py loops + is_edge conditionals binding TX/RX per-PE per-direction), and @concat_structs. The Cholesky/GEMM-Coll layouts compose modules whose ID claims live behind library imports. A real allocator either runs cslc to get the resolved binding (slow, same cost as just compiling) or it reimplements a CSL evaluator (large project, indefinite). The "2-4 day" estimate is for a regex prototype that will be defeated by the first kernel with a comptime branch.

No prior art cited because there isn't comparable prior art for ID-allocation static analysis of CSL-or-similar; the analog would be MLIR's register allocation passes, but those run AFTER the LLM has produced semantically valid code, not before, and they don't fix LLM hallucination of library APIs. Treat absence of prior art as the yellow flag.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: 10x smaller version that would prove or kill the principle in <1 day: skip the allocator entirely. Just build the linter. Static post-generation pass that greps the emitted pe.csl for @get_input_queue / @get_output_queue calls and flags any use of IDs 0-1 (memcpy-reserved) or any double-@initialize_queue on the same ID. Wire it to the existing bucket-routed repair loop as a synthetic verdict that fires BEFORE cslc. Cost: 2 hours. A/B on the 15-kernel corpus and count how often the linter fires on attempts that cslc would also have rejected — i.e., is it just trading 30s of cslc time for 1s of regex? If the linter fires on >20% of attempts AND those attempts subsequently pass after repair more often than the baseline, the principle survives and the allocator becomes worth building. My prediction: linter fires on <10% of attempts in halo cluster (LLM already picks 4-7 there), maybe 15-20% in dsr_queue_fabric_init cluster, and the post-linter repair rate is the same as baseline because the LLM was going to fix it from the cslc error on the next round anyway. Net: saves a few minutes of wall time, zero pass-rate lift. Better redirected effort: build a HANG-CLUSTER linter ("every halo recv handler reachable from is_edge branches must call unblock_cmd_stream") — same engineering cost, targets 3x the failure volume.

all_critiques.name: Per-section CSL synthesis with cslc gate on each section
all_critiques.critique:
Six specific problems, ranked by severity.

(1) Wrong failure-mode model. The proposal's premise is "LLM fixes one issue and breaks two others." But the framework already has bucket-routed repair (A/B/C) over 8 attempts, and the marginal pass-rate from attempts 5-8 is 0/14 — meaning more iterations on a near-correct file don't help. The remaining 9 W1 failures are not "LLM thrashing in a 200-line file"; they are kernels where the model never had the right concept for at least one section. Bounding blast radius via sectioning lets the LLM converge faster on a wrong answer in each section.

(2) cslc-passes is a weak oracle for the actual bottlenecks. Per the cluster breakdown: halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail) is about WHEN to call @unblock on recv tasks — wrong placement compiles fine and deadlocks at runtime. dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3) is about queue-ID allocation across `@set_color_config` routes — almost any allocation compiles; wrong ones deadlock or corrupt. collectives_2d (2/4) — pe.csl per kernel often compiles independently; failure is layout.csl/pe.csl coordination on x/y_entrypoints. The proposal's per-section cslc gate is solving the syntactic-error problem (which is mostly already solved by attempts 1-4) while the surviving failures live below the cslc surface. This is the same diagnostic error as translation_facts: shipping more shape-checking infrastructure for problems that aren't shape-violations.

(3) Section coupling is worse than the design admits. The "cumulative compilation" mitigation is honest about the dependency direction but understates the magnitude. CSL pe.csl files have references in ALL directions: section 3's @bind_local_task references section 4's task fn name AND section 1's task ID const. Section 5's f_run references section 2's @export_symbol'd ptrs AND section 4's fn signatures. To get section 1 to compile, you need stub task fns (section 4 shape known) AND placeholder storage ptrs (section 2 shape known). The proposal will degenerate into either (a) generating skeletons of ALL sections up front, then "filling them in" — at which point the LLM is generating the whole file shape anyway in section 1 (defeating the bounded-blast-radius pitch), or (b) the LLM-author of section N pre-declares forward refs that turn out to be wrong, and section N has to be re-emitted when section M's reality lands. Mode (b) reintroduces full-file thrash through the back door.

(4) Prior art is mixed-to-negative for this specific bet. Code-T (NeurIPS 2022, function-test grounded code generation), Self-Edit, Reflexion all add execute-test loops, and the SOTA generally finds 5-15% lift on competition-style coding benchmarks — but that's for problems where the unit-test signal CORRELATES with correctness. For compiler IRs (TVM, MLIR, Triton), the analogue — incrementally generating an IR with type-checker gates — exists in research (e.g. parsel, lemur) but the published deltas on translation tasks are similar magnitude to "just retry with more context," not the qualitative leap the proposal implies. The closest published analogue, AlphaCodium's iterative test-driven flow on competitive programming, gets 12->44% on CodeContests — but its oracle (passing public tests) is end-to-end behavioral, not the per-section structural gate proposed here. There is no published study showing per-section compiler-gate decomposition beats whole-file repair for domain-specific systems languages.

(5) Engineering cost is meaningfully understated. The "5-7 days" budget assumes the decomposer ("split a reference pe.csl into 5 sections programmatically") is straightforward. In reality the 30+ kernels in the corpus already have non-uniform structure — comptime blocks interleaved with fns (Game of Life), multiple comptime blocks (collectives_2d), task fns intermixed with helper fns (halo kernels), some kernels have no entry fns at all (Single-Tile-Matvec uses memcpy-only). Robust round-trip decomposition + reassembly across this corpus is its own week of work, and bugs there silently bias the A/B sweep. Add 3-4 days minimum.

(6) Sweep cost is also understated. 75s × 8 attempts × 9 kernels = 90 min is wall-time-optimistic but per-cslc-invocation is sequential under the singularity_gate (look at ground_gotcha._run_cslc — it serializes through _singularity_gate to avoid the 7-concurrent-runs failure documented in PROGRESS.md §6.2). The parallel-sections mitigation in the design is incompatible with that gate. With realistic per-kernel cslc overhead — including re-tries that the design itself caps at 3-per-section (so 5 sections × up to 3 = 15 cslc calls per attempt, not 5) — you're looking at ~3-4x the current sweep time per A/B cycle. That kills iteration speed during the inevitable debugging phase.

Where it COULD help marginally: 1-2 of the collectives_2d failures and the dsr_queue_fabric_init failures may include literal compile-time errors that survive the current 8-attempt loop because the reviewer keeps re-prompting on the wrong section. Sectioning could plausibly catch these. That's ~1-2 kernels of upside out of 9, hence the 3% expected-lift estimate (≈1 kernel converted, 6→7 of 15, +6.7pp).

Structural distinctness from translation_facts: agree it is structurally different in mechanism (execution-gated vs prompt-context). But the COST/BENEFIT failure mode is the same shape — adding heavy infrastructure for a class of failure that is not the dominant one in the residual. The lesson from translation_facts wasn't "don't add IR" — it was "diagnose the residual failure mode before building infrastructure." This proposal does not diagnose the 9 residual kernels at the level of "what specifically is missing in each failed translation." Without that, both the sectioning decomposition AND the per-section prompt design are guesses.

Specific answer to the 5 hard questions:
1. Structurally different from semantic_bridge/translation_facts — yes, mechanism differs. But same diagnostic failure: targets shape-correctness while residual failures are semantic.
2. Addresses NONE of the three clusters specifically. dsr_queue_fabric_init partly (queue ID conflicts may surface in cslc); halo_recv_unblock and collectives_2d are runtime/coordination failures invisible to cslc.
3. AlphaCodium / Reflexion-style iterative refinement is published; per-section compiler-gated synthesis for DSL translation is not. Yellow flag confirmed.
4. Yes — see smaller_variant.
5. +1 kernel (6→7/15, +6.7pp) realistic upper bound; coin-flip whether even that lands given (2)-(3) above.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: YES, and the smaller variant is the only version worth running. Skip the decomposer and the per-section synthesis entirely. Instead: take the existing 8-attempt full-file repair loop and add ONE cslc gate after each attempt that, on compile failure, extracts the specific cslc error and the +/-10 lines around it, and re-prompts the LLM with ONLY that error and that slice (not the whole file, not the whole error log). This is a 1-day change, reuses ground_gotcha's _run_cslc directly, and tests the hypothesis "tighter error-focused re-prompts beat full-file repair" without the section-decomposition infrastructure tax. If THAT shows lift on the 9 failing kernels, then the per-section proposal is worth considering as the next step. If it doesn't show lift (which I expect — the 8-attempt budget already exhausts the LLM's ability to fix surface errors), then the whole per-section bet is dead-on-arrival and you saved a week. CRITICAL: before either, spend 0.5 day classifying the 9 residual failures into "fails-to-compile" vs "compiles-but-deadlocks" vs "compiles-runs-wrong-output." If <3 are in the first bucket, do not build either variant — the IR direction is wrong and the next experiment should be runtime-trace-based (e.g. record fabric state on deadlock, feed back as gotcha) rather than compile-time.

all_critiques.name: Per-section CSL synthesis with cslc gate on each section
all_critiques.critique:
Hard-questions answers:

Q1 (structurally different from semantic_bridge / translation_facts?): YES, genuinely different in shape — this is execution-gated incremental construction, not prompt-context dressing. The author's "fundamentally different" claim is fair on the *mechanism* axis. But it's NOT different on the dimension that mattered for those failures: those proposals failed because they did not move on the *load-bearing* failure (per-cluster syntactic/semantic mistakes in the LLM's CSL output). The relevant similarity-of-shape risk is "ceremony around the same LLM" — and on that axis, this proposal still has it: the LLM still writes the section, the LLM still has to know what `@bind_local_task` and `fabin_dsd` look like. Sectioning only buys you something if the LLM's per-section error rate is much lower than per-file error rate AT THE SAME spec. That is empirically untested.

Q2 (does it address one of the 3 stuck clusters?): NO — it's a generic structural intervention. Worse, the specific failure mode for halo_recv_unblock is NOT "the LLM emitted code that fails to cslc-compile" — based on PROGRESS.md and the 269-line Laplacian2D-Halo reference, halo failures are *runtime* / *behavioral* (RX_DONE counter wrong, num_halos_expected miscomputed at comptime for edge PEs, async-recv posted after sends, queue/color binding inconsistent across layout↔pe, halos that arrive before recv is posted → stall). cslc happily compiles all of those. A per-section cslc gate cannot catch any of them. The proposal optimizes for the wrong oracle. Confirm this against the failing runs before building — if the actual W1 failure mode for the 6/7 halo kernels is "cslc passes but sim deadlocks / numerics wrong", the entire premise dies. r4 grounded gotchas already showed cslc-clean snippets that didn't run correctly in real harnesses (per the 0/5 result). This proposal scales that same blind spot up to whole files.

Q3 (prior art for sectioned/gated codegen at this complexity?): Partial. Self-Debugging / Reflexion (Chen et al. 2024) and execution-feedback codegen variants improve simple synthesis but the sectioning-with-typecheck-gate pattern is closer to *interactive theorem-prover tactics* (Coq/Lean) or *structured editor codegen* — and those work on small leaves, not 269-line systems-code files with non-local invariants. For CUDA→PTX / MLIR lowering: lowering passes are deterministic and rule-based, they do not LLM-generate-then-typecheck per section. The closest plausible prior art is Microsoft's CodeAct / iterative SMT-guided synthesis, which has not been demonstrated to lift pass-rate on non-trivial systems code where cross-section invariants (a color is declared in §1, used in a DSD in §3, bound to a queue in §4, routed in layout.csl which the agent does see) dominate. Yellow flag is real.

Q4 (10x smaller proof?): YES, and you should require it before the 5-7 day build. The cheap version: pick 2 halo kernels (e.g. Laplacian2D-Halo and 7pt-Stencil, both have hand-references), take the current best failing LLM output, split it into the 5 sections by hand, and for each section ask "does cslc on this section's harness substitution produce a useful error that would have steered the LLM differently than the current full-file reviewer error?" If for the actual halo failures cslc emits the same generic "fabric_color expected" or compiles clean (because the bug is runtime), then the gate adds no signal. Half-day experiment, no LLM in the loop, kills the proposal cheaply.

Q5 (expected lift): I'd put it at -2pt to +1pt on the 15-kernel W1 benchmark, with mode around 0pt. Reasoning: (a) the cluster that this most plausibly helps — dsr_queue_fabric_init — has only 2 failing kernels, so even a generous 50% conversion is +1 (6→7). (b) halo's failure mode is largely post-compile (cslc gate adds nothing). (c) collectives_2d failures: the existing mesh_2x2 harness is 2x2 but real collectives_2d kernels use larger meshes with the kernel-specific c2d entry-point bindings — substituting a section into mesh_2x2 will compile-clean for code that fails in the real layout (false negative on the gate). (d) realistic risk of -1 to -3 from latency-induced reduction in attempts per kernel under budget (75s × 5 sections × 1-3 retries × N kernels seriously crowds the wall-clock budget) plus section-decomposition bugs creating new failure modes the existing 8-attempt full-file path doesn't have.

Specific technical objections grounded in the code:
1. The harness `pe_template_csl` in ground_gotcha.py declares zero params and a `f_run` stub. To compile-gate §1 (params + colors + queue/task ID decls) of a halo pe.csl, you need a HARNESS THAT DECLARES MATCHING colors at the layout side and supplies the params at the @set_tile_code site. The current harnesses (single_pe / send_recv_2x1 / mesh_2x2) hard-code their own param surface. You'd need a per-cluster harness GENERATOR that parses the in-progress layout.csl the agent has and synthesizes a matching scaffold. That is the bulk of the work; the proposal underestimates it as "Day 1-2: section decomposer". Building harnesses that faithfully mirror an arbitrary in-progress layout.csl param surface is its own translation problem.

2. The author's mitigation "cumulative compilation: §4 compiles all of 1+2+3+4" means by §4 you ARE compiling close to the full file — the per-section blast-radius bound the proposal sells degrades to "the cslc error pointer is closer to the new code". That's a reviewer-feedback improvement, not a gating improvement. And we already feed cslc errors back to the reviewer.

3. Non-local invariants the cslc gate cannot enforce that ARE the halo failure mode: queue ID matches between layout's `@set_color_config` route and pe.csl's `@get_input_queue`; num_halos_expected computed correctly for all 4 corner PEs at comptime; RX_DONE counter reset *before* the recv is posted; output queues for memcpy reserved 0-1, code uses 2+. cslc catches none of these even on the FULL FILE, let alone per section.

4. The 8-attempt budget claim ("burned on round-trips where LLM fixes one issue and breaks two others") is plausible but unverified in the proposal. Before adopting sectioning as the fix, instrument the existing 8-attempt repair loop to count "reviewer/debugger fix re-introduces a previously-fixed bug". If that's not the dominant failure pattern (vs. "never produces correct halo-recv ordering even on attempt 1"), sectioning solves the wrong problem.

5. "Halo skips Opus per empirical evidence" (from the framework state). Whatever is going wrong on halo, it's a class of bug the strongest model also can't fix when handed the whole context. That suggests the bottleneck is knowledge/understanding, not LLM-stamina-across-200-lines. Sectioning improves stamina, not knowledge.

Bottom line: structurally novel relative to the discarded experiments — fair. Likely to lift the pass-rate on the actual stuck kernels — no, because the oracle (cslc) is blind to the dominant failure mode (runtime fabric stalls). The 5-7 day cost is non-trivial relative to its expected lift; do the 1-day proof first or pick a different intervention.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Half-day proof, no engineering: For each of the 6 failing halo kernels, take the best failing LLM-produced pe.csl from logs and (a) run it through cslc as a whole to get the full error, (b) hand-split it into the 5 proposed sections and run cslc on the cumulative harness substitution at each section boundary. Three measurable questions: (1) Does any section's cslc error point at the actual root-cause bug more usefully than the full-file error? (2) For halo runs that compile-clean but fail at runtime (likely the majority), does ANY per-section gate flag anything? (3) Could the per-section error have plausibly steered an LLM to a different output? If (1) and (3) are no on >=4/6 halo kernels OR (2) confirms the runtime-only failure mode dominates, kill the proposal before building. If results are mixed, build a much narrower version: keep the full-file generation path, add a SINGLE post-generation pass that runs cslc on the comptime block in isolation (the highest-error-density section per the existing reviewer logs) and feeds that as an extra reviewer hint — 1 day of work, captures most of any real signal, and doesn't restructure the orchestrator.

all_critiques.name: Reference-CSL retrieval via structural similarity over ground-truth pe.csl corpus
all_critiques.critique:
Three concrete problems, in order of severity.

(1) W1 INVARIANT VIOLATION IS NEAR-CERTAIN, NOT HYPOTHETICAL. The proposal's corpus is /home/USER/csl-examples/benchmarks/*/src/*.csl. I verified: that glob includes power-method/src/kernel.csl (196 LOC), bicgstab/src/kernel.csl (349 LOC), conjugate-gradient/src/kernel.csl (291 LOC), preconditioned-conjugate-gradient/src/kernel.csl, 7pt-stencil-spmv/src/kernel.csl. These ARE the ground-truth pe.csl files for 5+ of the 15 W1 benchmark kernels. The W1 invariant exists precisely to prevent the agent from cribbing these. Retrieval via embedding similarity over CudaKernelFacts will, by construction, return the matching ground-truth file as top-1 for every iterative-solver query — that's how embedding similarity works on a small same-domain corpus. "Anonymization" is doing all the load-bearing work, and regex-scrubbing symbol names from a 300-line halo state machine leaves the dataflow shape (which task fires which, on which RX_DONE_TID, with which counter increment) FULLY INTACT. The dataflow shape IS the answer the agent is supposed to derive. The compute-leak canary is keyword-based — it won't catch structural leakage. This is not a "secondary risk"; it's the primary mode of action of the proposal, dressed up as a feature. If the patterns DON'T leak the answer, they're too abstract to help; if they DO help, they leak the answer. The author's own mitigation rule ("hand-inspect 5, ask is this already in knowledge_base") doesn't test the right thing — the right test is "does the implementer produce code that would not differ if it had seen the ground-truth pe.csl directly?"

(2) STRUCTURALLY ISOMORPHIC TO translation_facts, JUST WITH MORE TOKENS. translation_facts was 0W/2L/17T over 19 attempts. Its failure mode was "RAG'd gotchas already cover the surface; the additional structured payload adds perturbation without lift." This proposal injects 200-500 additional tokens of structural pattern into the SAME implementer prompt slot ({worked_patterns} added to q_translate_cuda_to_csl_bundle). The shape is identical: pre-implementer payload of distilled structure, cluster-keyed. The differentiator the author proposes ("dataflow shapes, not lists of rules") is rhetorical — anonymized halo skeletons rendered as text ARE lists of rules with arrows in them. The implementer is a single-shot generator; whether you give it "rule: drain RX before re-arming" or "pattern: stage→fmovs(.activate=RX_DONE_TID)→counter--→fire COMPUTE@expected" is the same intervention dressed differently. The 17 ties on translation_facts predict the same outcome here.

(3) DOESN'T ATTACK THE ACTUAL BOTTLENECK. The 9 W1 failures are not "the model doesn't know the halo skeleton." Today's halo gotchas (3 just shipped, cslc-grounded) already encode the skeleton. The failures per the progress doc are at the COMPOSITION layer: halo state machine + DSR queue init + collectives_2d interact, and the implementer's single-shot generation gets one of the three coordinated correctly while breaking the other two. Adding another instance of "here's the skeleton" doesn't fix composition — only multi-pass implementation, contract verification between passes, or a constrained-decoding harness does. The author's hard-question 2 answer would have to be "it addresses halo_recv_unblock generically" which is just "more context for the cluster that already has the most context."

PRIOR ART CHECK: nearest external analog is retrieval-augmented code translation (e.g., kNM-style retrieval for code completion, AlphaCodium's example retrieval). Those operate on corpora of 1000s-100Ks of examples where similarity is meaningful. A 30-file corpus where 5 files are ground truth for 5 of the 15 eval kernels is not retrieval — it's lookup-with-extra-steps. No published precedent for "anonymized pattern templates from same-domain corpus beating direct prose RAG" at this corpus size that I'm aware of.

FAILED HARD-QUESTION SCORECARD: Q1 same-shape-as-translation_facts: yes. Q2 addresses a specific failure cluster: no, generic. Q3 external precedent: weak. Q4 1-day proof: possible but see smaller_variant. Q5 expected lift: most likely 0/15 delta with non-zero regression risk from new perturbation on the 6 passing kernels (Single-Tile-Matvec already regressed once under always-on context).
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Yes, and the smaller version is also the correct diagnostic. Skip the corpus, skip the embedding index, skip the anonymizer. Day 1 only: take the 3 hardest failing kernels (power-method, bicgstab, CG), MANUALLY extract the halo skeleton + DSR init + collectives pattern from their ground-truth kernel.csl by hand (you the developer, not the LLM, doing the anonymization properly), inject DIRECTLY into the implementer prompt with the W1 invariant temporarily lifted for those 3 kernels only. Run A/B. If even with hand-curated, hand-anonymized, manually-perfect "patterns" the implementer still fails 2/3, the proposal is dead — the bottleneck is composition, not retrieval. If it passes 3/3, then you've proven the patterns CAN teach but you've also proven they constitute a W1 leak (because you used the actual ground truth). At that point the question is "can anonymization preserve enough signal to help without leaking" — which is a much harder research question than the proposal acknowledges, and should be tested with that 3-kernel oracle before any embedding infrastructure is built. Expected outcome of the smaller variant: 1/3 or 2/3 with hand-curated patterns, confirming the proposal is bottlenecked by composition not retrieval, and saving 4 of the 5 proposed engineering days.

all_critiques.name: Reference-CSL retrieval via structural similarity over ground-truth pe.csl corpus
all_critiques.critique:
Three specific problems, not generic skepticism.

(1) CORPUS-IS-ANSWER-KEY. I verified `diff /home/USER/csl-examples/benchmarks/gemv-collectives_2d/pe.csl /home/USER/xkernel/kernels/GEMV\ Collectives\ 2D/CSL/pe.csl` returns empty — the xkernel reference pe.csl files ARE the csl-examples benchmark pe.csl files (Cerebras seeded xkernel from upstream). So "Build an index over the 30 working pe.csl files in csl-examples" means building an index over the exact files the W1 invariant exists to hide. The author thinks the compute-leak canary catches this; it doesn't, because the canary is set from the SPECIFIC kernel's reference (cuda2csl._set_compute_canary takes the per-kernel `reference_compute` and extracts ONE distinctive line). When the implementer is solving Game-of-Life and the retriever returns "anonymized patterns from 25-pt-stencil/task.csl + gemv-collectives_2d/pe.csl + bicgstab/kernel.csl," the canary is looking for the Game-of-Life canary line, not those three. The author's tertiary risk mitigation ("cluster-bucket-filter before similarity ranking — only retrieve from the halo bucket if the query is halo") makes this WORSE: for the 6/7 failing halo kernels, the halo bucket in csl-examples contains 25-pt-stencil, 7pt-stencil-spmv, stencil_3d_7pts, game-of-life — i.e., the exact ground truths for 4 of those 7 failures. You're then proposing to anonymize them and feed them back. That's an answer-key with the variable names renamed. Either the test suite is now meaningless (the score goes up but doesn't reflect translation capability), or "anonymization" is so aggressive it's just the prose summary RAG already has.

(2) SAME-SHAPE-AS-TRANSLATION_FACTS. The author flags this risk but waves it away with "patterns must be structurally different from prose." Look at what their own anonymized halo example would emit: "for direction in {N,S,E,W}: stage column → @fmovs async with .activate=RX_DONE_TID, decrement counter on RX_DONE, fire COMPUTE when counter==expected." That is prose. It is the same shape as a KNOWN_GOTCHAS_W1_FAILURE_PATTERNS entry. Worse: this exact halo state-machine pattern is what 5 hand-curated halo gotchas (shipped today) already encode, after grounding through cslc (G1/G2/G3 in the task log). The translation_facts A/B was 0W/2L/17T across 19 attempts — the lesson was NOT "the YAML format was wrong" but "the model already had the surface knowledge, repackaging it didn't help." A retrieved-pattern injection has the same structural failure mode. The author's own validation rule ("hand-inspect 5 retrieved patterns and ask: is this in csl_knowledge_base?") will, by my reading of csl-examples vs the shipped halo gotchas, return yes on 4/5 — meaning by the author's own kill-criterion this should not ship.

(3) WRONG-BOTTLENECK-DIAGNOSIS. The W1 failures are not "agent doesn't know what halo state-machines look like." The r4 grounded+rewriter halo workflow showed the agent CAN draft plausible halo code that ALMOST compiles — it fails on specific cslc semantics (RX_DONE color routing, queue conflicts with memcpy reservations, microthread activation ordering on WSE-3). 4 rounds of halo-gotcha drafting + 8-attempt budget bump + per-cluster RAG haven't fixed it. The bottleneck is RUN-AND-FIX (toolchain feedback loop quality), not pattern-context-at-translate-time. The 6/15 ceiling has been hit by every "more context for the implementer" experiment. The proposal is the fifth attempt to push past that ceiling by enriching context, and it has no mechanism that explains why iteration 5 succeeds where iterations 1-4 (semantic_bridge, translation_facts, cluster-gated gotchas, halo-gotcha workflows r2/r3/r4) all stalled.

PRIOR ART. Code-pattern retrieval for code generation (CodeT5+, ReACC, kNN-LM for code, RepoCoder) does work for languages with huge corpora (Python/Java/JS at GitHub-scale). The retrieval gain shrinks dramatically when (a) the corpus is <100 files, (b) the LM already saw the corpus in its training data (Cerebras csl-examples is public on GitHub — Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7 almost certainly trained on it), and (c) the failure mode is semantic compile errors, not "unfamiliar idiom." All three apply here. No published evidence that 30-file-corpus retrieval moves the needle on translation accuracy for a DSL the LM has already seen.

QUESTION-BY-QUESTION:
Q1 (structurally different from semantic_bridge/translation_facts?): No. Same shape: orchestrator-side preprocessing → text injected into implementer prompt. The "embedding-based" retrieval substrate is novel relative to TF-IDF, but the SLOT (extra context block before the implementer fires) is identical, and the failure mode of context-block experiments is now well-established in this repo: 0W when the slot's content is already in another slot.
Q2 (addresses ONE of the 3 failing clusters specifically?): Tries to address all three generically. That's a tell — every successful intervention has been cluster-specific (cluster-gated gotchas, halo-skips-Opus promotion gate).
Q3 (outside-repo evidence?): No citation. RepoCoder-style retrieval for code generation works at scale, not at the 30-file scale proposed, and not for a DSL already in LM training data.
Q4 (10x smaller version?): Yes — see `smaller_variant`. It's a strictly better probe.
Q5 (actual expected lift from 6/15 baseline?): 0 ± 1 kernel. Non-trivial regression risk on Single-Tile-Matvec-class kernels if anonymized patterns leak halo-ish noise into trivial-kernel prompts (same mechanism that caused the resweep w1lo0sycr regression before cluster-gating).

SHIP RECOMMENDATION: Do not ship as proposed. If anything from this idea survives, it's a tiny probe (see smaller_variant) that REPLACES, not augments, the existing halo gotchas — and only after running through the same cslc-grounding gate that killed halo-workflow rounds r2/r3.
all_critiques.smaller_variant:
10x smaller probe, 1 day, falsifies the hypothesis cheaply, avoids the leak problem:

PROBE: "ablation 1-of-3" — for 3 currently-shipped grounded halo gotchas, replace them with retrieved-pattern equivalents (anonymized snippets from one held-out csl-examples halo file, picked by hand not embedding similarity) and re-run the 7-kernel halo subset. If the retrieved-pattern version matches or beats the hand-curated gotchas on the same 7 kernels, the structural-pattern hypothesis has signal. If it loses or ties, kill the full proposal.

Why this beats the full 5-day plan:
- 0 new infrastructure (no MiniLM index, no anonymizer module). Reuses the existing gotcha-injection slot.
- Tests the load-bearing claim ("retrieved patterns teach more than hand-curated prose") directly, not bundled with retrieval-stack engineering.
- Leak risk bounded: held-out file is one chosen file scrubbed once by hand.
- Falsifiable in <1 day, ~$5 in LLM spend.
- If it works, you've found signal that informs whether the full proposal is worth doing. If it fails, you've saved 4 days and avoided polluting W1 with answer-key leakage.

SECOND, ORTHOGONAL, GENUINELY NON-IR probe addressing the actual diagnosed bottleneck: instead of "more context before translate," tighten the FEEDBACK LOOP. Add a single-shot cslc dry-run on a stub harness BEFORE the implementer's output reaches the reviewer — catch the "I invented a builtin" / "I referenced .dim_size" class of error with a real toolchain signal, not a reviewer prompt trying to predict cslc's verdict. Reuses the grounding helper from G1 (ground_gotcha.py). Likely lift: 1-3 kernels on the 9 failing, primarily in the dsr_queue_fabric_init and collectives_2d clusters where errors are mechanical. This is what the proposal-author should be brainstorming if "better IR" keeps failing — the bottleneck is at the OUTPUT side (verify-then-repair), not the input side (more-context-then-generate).

all_critiques.name: Nearest-neighbor skeleton seeding from passing kernels
all_critiques.critique:
Q1 (structurally different from semantic_bridge / translation_facts?). PARTIALLY. The author's framing — "constraint surface, not free-floating text" — is real but oversold. semantic_bridge and translation_facts were prose/YAML the implementer could ignore; a skeleton with `// TODO` markers is harder to ignore because the model defaults to filling holes rather than restructuring. BUT the implementer is a single-shot LLM that already gets a layout.csl plus 4KB of tutorial_context and is perfectly capable of "improving" the skeleton (renaming colors, re-numbering queues, adding "missing" tasks). Unless cuda2csl.py adds a post-hoc diff that REJECTS attempts that mutated the wiring block, this is still soft injection. The author claims forced compliance but the mechanism doesn't enforce it — that's the same overclaim that sank translation_facts. The "skeleton is a constraint surface" intuition is right only if you add a verifier; without one, it degrades to "more context, with TODO markers."

Q2 (does it address ONE failing cluster specifically?). YES for halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail) — wiring density check confirms it (Laplacian2D-Halo pe.csl has 28 wiring decls vs GEMV's 12 and Cholesky's 11), and the failure cluster name itself ("halo_recv_unblock") is exactly the wiring surface this proposal preserves. PARTIALLY for dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fail) — DSR/queue/fabric-init is wiring too, but the 3 kernels in that cluster may not share a single skeleton donor (need to actually check signature distances; the proposal assumes neighbors exist but doesn't enumerate them). NO for collectives_2d (2/4 fail) — GEMM-Collectives-2D and GEMV-Collectives-2D pass in the existing index, so for the 2 failing ones this is just retrieving the passing sibling, which is essentially leaking the answer (see Q5 risk).

Q3 (prior art). Weak. "Skeleton-based program synthesis" is real (Sketch, SyGuS, Solar-Lezama 2008) but those are for tiny constraint-solved holes, not LLM body-fill at the scale of a CSL compute loop. The closest LLM-era analog is repo-level retrieval-augmented code completion (RepoCoder, CoCoMIC, 2023-24), which DOES show measurable lift on cross-file completion — BUT those benchmarks use natural-language docstring + signature as the hole spec, not "TODO" markers in a wired-up scaffold. AlphaCodium-style structured iterative fix on code-contests is more relevant and shows real gains, but it's iterative + test-driven, not single-shot skeleton-fill. I have not seen published evidence for "structurally-keyed neighbor skeleton with body-holes → LLM body-fill" working on a translation task where the wiring grammar is unfamiliar to the model. The CSL wiring grammar IS unfamiliar (cslc-grounded halo-gotchas r3/r4 showed the model fabricates builtins). Yellow flag.

Q4 (10x smaller version that proves it in <1 day?). YES — and the author should be required to do this before the 2-3 day build. Specifically: hand-author ONE skeleton from Laplacian2D-Halo pe.csl (delete bodies of SEND/COMPUTE/RX_DONE/EXIT, keep all param/const/queue decls), inject into ONE failing halo kernel's implementer prompt as a static string (no index, no signature matching, no abstractor), run 8 attempts. If that kernel doesn't pass, the full version won't either, because the full version adds noise (wrong neighbor choice, abstraction loss) on top of the same core hypothesis. This is a 2-hour test, not a 1-day test. If the author skips it, that's a process red flag — the discarded experiments (semantic_bridge, translation_facts, halo r2/r3/r4) all could have been killed by a similar single-instance probe.

Q5 (expected lift on 6/15 baseline). I estimate +1 kernel, possibly +2, with non-trivial chance of 0. Reasoning: (a) of the 6 halo failures, several likely have unique CUDA-side shapes (e.g., 7pt vs 5pt stencil, different boundary handling) that the body-fill will get wrong even with perfect wiring — the failures aren't ONLY wiring, they're wiring + body together; (b) the 2 collectives_2d failures, if the donor is the passing sibling, this is closer to leakage than translation — the moment the proposal works there, you have to ask whether you've just memorized the answer; (c) the dsr_queue_fabric_init cluster (2/3 fail) only has 3 members, so neighbor selection is fragile. Author's "STRUCTURALLY DIFFERENT" framing implies this should be a category-killer; if it lands at +1 it's the same magnitude as several discarded experiments and should be killed with the same discipline. Bottleneck-of-the-bottleneck concern: even granting perfect wiring injection, the halo cluster's 6/7 failure rate is partially a model-capability ceiling (Sonnet/Opus union is already 6/15) — moving wiring from "model generates" to "scaffolded" only helps the subset where wiring was the LAST mile. Per memory note on iterative solvers being host-RPC-bounded (irrelevant to W1 pass-rate but symptomatic of how often "the bottleneck" turns out to be elsewhere), I'd bet against >2-kernel lift.

Additional concerns not in the 5 questions: (i) The author says "reuse knowledge_persistence.bundle_identifier_set + tutorial_leak_check" — verified those exist (knowledge_persistence.py:745, 773), but tutorial_leak_check was designed for tutorial snippets, not a near-complete pe.csl with bodies stripped. Leak detection by identifier-set will catch verbatim variable names but NOT structural leakage (e.g., the agent gets the donor's exact 4-task graph for a kernel where the CUDA reference uses 2 tasks). The canary needs to be structural, not lexical. (ii) "Replaces some of the ~4KB tutorial_context block" — this is a hidden A/B confound. If the skeleton replaces tutorial context and pass rate stays at 6/15, you can't tell whether the skeleton helped and tutorial-context hurt, or both were neutral. The experiment must add the skeleton alongside, then ablate. (iii) Free real estate this proposal ignores: the skeleton could also seed the architect step (DESIGN.md) with the donor's task-graph, which is upstream of wiring fabrication. Doing only implementer-side seeding ignores that the architect's prose plan is what later wiring follows from.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Hand-author ONE skeleton from Laplacian2D-Halo pe.csl. Strip the bodies of SEND/COMPUTE/RX_DONE/EXIT tasks, keep all params/colors/queues/task-ids/DSDs intact, insert `// TODO: implement` in each body. Inject as a static string into the implementer prompt for ONE failing halo kernel (pick the closest CUDA-shape match, e.g., a 5-point stencil variant if one is in the failing set; else 7pt-Stencil). Run 8 attempts. Total time: 2 hours, zero infra. Decision rule: if that kernel passes when it didn't before, build the index + abstractor + signature matcher. If it doesn't pass, the full proposal is dead — don't spend 2-3 days. Bonus: also inject the same skeleton's task-graph (just the comment-block summary at the top of Laplacian2D-Halo pe.csl, lines 16-30) into the architect prompt for the same kernel. This tests whether seeding the design step is upstream-cheaper than seeding the implementation.

all_critiques.name: Nearest-neighbor skeleton seeding from passing kernels
all_critiques.critique:
Q1 (structural difference): YES, genuinely different — and this is the strongest leg of the proposal. semantic_bridge and translation_facts were both injected as DESCRIPTIVE side-channels that the implementer was free to ignore (and per the 19-attempt A/B on facts, did ignore). A hole-punched pe.csl is a STARTING STATE, not a description. When you tell a frontier LLM "here is your starting file, replace the TODO bodies, do not touch wiring," compliance is high because the model is now in patch-mode rather than synthesis-mode. The "constraint surface vs descriptive surface" framing the author proposes is real. Caveat: I have seen models silently rewrite "do not touch" wiring when their compute body needs a different shape (e.g. they wanted 6 queues but the skeleton declares 4); the reviewer/repair loop must specifically check skeleton-conformance, not just compilation, or you'll lose the wiring fidelity that justifies the whole intervention.

Q2 (bottleneck specificity): PARTIAL match, and this is the proposal's weakest leg. Verified on disk: halo_recv_unblock has a clear donor (Laplacian2D-Halo/CSL/pe.csl, 269 lines, exactly the 4-direction TX/RX_oq/iq + RX_DONE_TID + num_halos_received counter + edge-aware @initialize_queue WSE-3 block that the failing kernels need to rebuild from scratch). So 6/7 halo failures have a real, high-fidelity neighbor. BUT dsr_queue_fabric_init failures are dominated by the iterative-solver family (BiCGSTAB, CG, PCG, Power-Method per the memory note), and these use MULTI-FILE CSL (blas.csl + kernel.csl + layout.csl, verified — Conjugate Gradient has 5 .csl files, BiCGSTAB has 5). A single hole-punched pe.csl skeleton does NOT model that file decomposition; the donor for an iterative solver is "Residual," which is also multi-file. The proposal as written would either need to skip iterative solvers entirely, or be extended to multi-file skeletons (significantly more abstractor logic — replace_function_bodies must be aware of cross-file symbol export/import). collectives_2d (2/4 fail) similarly often involves stitched compute files. Honest re-scope: the proposal is really a halo-only intervention dressed as a general scheme.

Q3 (prior art): Code-fragment / hole-filling code synthesis IS well-established (Codex hole-filling, GitHub Copilot, GraphCodeBERT, even classical sketch-based synthesis like Sketch/Rosette). For low-level / HW-targeted DSL translation specifically, retrieval-augmented patch generation has shown real lift in MLIR and Triton work, and Halide's autoscheduler community has used "seed schedule" injection effectively. So it's not unprecedented. What I can't cite: a clean published result that says "structural skeleton seeding beat descriptive RAG by N% on a fabric-DSL translation task." Yellow flag rather than red — but not green.

Q4 (10x smaller version): YES, and you should absolutely do this first before the full 2-3 day build. Smallest viable spike: take ONE failing halo kernel (pick the one closest to Laplacian2D-Halo, probably 25-Point Stencil or 7-Point Stencil), hand-strip Laplacian2D-Halo/CSL/pe.csl into a TODO-skeleton (literally vim, 30 minutes), prepend it to the implementer prompt with the "do not touch wiring" rubric, and run 3-5 attempts. If even hand-crafted, hand-targeted skeleton seeding fails to move the needle on the best-matched halo kernel, the automated version with worse neighbor selection won't either. This is a half-day spike, not 2-3 days, and it gates the rest of the work. I would refuse to fund the full build without this signal.

Q5 (realistic lift): Best-case 2-3/15 lift (40% → 53-60%), more likely 1-2/15 (40% → 47-53%). Reasoning: halo_recv_unblock cluster is 6/7 failing and is the only cluster with a confirmed clean donor — even if skeleton seeding solves HALF of that cluster (3 wins, which is optimistic given that "wiring rebuilt correctly" doesn't guarantee the compute body lands), that's 3/15 = 20pt lift. But three confounders pull it down: (a) the BEST current sweep is already a Sonnet+Opus union, so the wins go to whichever model the skeleton helps less for, narrowing marginal lift; (b) for some failing halo kernels the failure is the COMPUTE body (boundary conditions, stencil shape) not the wiring, and the skeleton doesn't help there; (c) implementer may discard or distort the skeleton on hard cases — empirically Sonnet 4.6 is variable about respecting "do not touch" constraints in long contexts. Set expectation at +1 to +2 kernels, single-digit-percent lift; treat +3 as a great outcome.

Additional concerns the author didn't list: (i) the abstractor is non-trivial — "strip identifiers, keep wiring" requires parsing CSL well enough to distinguish a queue-id literal (KEEP) from a stencil-radius literal (STRIP). A regex/AST pass over CSL is finicky; donor-file count is 25 but only ~5-7 cleanly match the halo signature. Plan for the abstractor to be the longest part of the eng work, not the indexing. (ii) Signature-distance metric needs validation — "≥3 of {colors, queues, microthreads, rectangle-shape}" sounds reasonable but Laplacian2D-Halo and Residual have very different shapes despite both being "halo-like"; you may need per-cluster donor pinning rather than learned distance. (iii) Leak surface is real and the author's mitigation (bundle_identifier_set + tutorial_leak_check) is correct but needs to also strip the LICENSE header / file-level comments that name the donor kernel — verified the Laplacian2D-Halo pe.csl has explicit "5-point 2D Laplacian compute file" comment in the header that would tell the model exactly what it's being seeded from.

Bottom line: structurally novel relative to prior failed experiments, addresses a real failure mode with a real donor, but scope is narrower than pitched (halo cluster mainly; iterative-solver cluster needs multi-file extension that doubles the eng cost). Worth doing as a small spike first, then expanding only if the spike moves the needle on the targeted halo kernel.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Half-day spike: hand-craft ONE skeleton from Laplacian2D-Halo/CSL/pe.csl (manually replace tile sizes, boundary-condition body, and identifiers with TODOs while preserving all queue/color/task-graph declarations verbatim). Inject it as a literal string into prompt_cuda2csl.py's implementer slot ONLY for the closest-matched failing halo kernel (probably 7-Point Stencil or 25-Point Stencil — verify via signature match). Run 5 attempts on that one kernel. If 0/5 pass even with the highest-fidelity hand-crafted, hand-targeted skeleton, the automated full version definitely won't — kill the proposal. If 2+/5 pass, proceed to (a) hand-craft 2-3 more skeletons (one per donor pattern), (b) write a coarse signature-match dispatcher (not the full feature-distance index — just a hand-coded "if layout looks halo-shaped, use halo skeleton" rule), and run the targeted halo cluster again. Skip the full 25-kernel automated index / multi-file extension until you have evidence the targeted single-file version works on at least 2 kernels. Total: 0.5 day for the spike, 1-1.5 days for the targeted version, defer the general automated version. Critically, treat the spike as a kill-gate, not a green-light: a 0/5 result on the best-matched case should kill the whole proposal, not motivate "let's try harder."

all_critiques.name: Compile-validated few-shot construction
all_critiques.critique:
Hard answers to your five questions:

(1) STRUCTURALLY DIFFERENT FROM PRIOR ART? Partially. Same delivery vector as translation_facts and semantic_bridge (extra block injected into implementer prompt, cluster-gated). The author's distinction — "executable artifacts, not facts about the language" — is half-true and half-misleading:
 - Half-true: a verbatim minimal compiling .csl is closer to copyable substrate than a YAML manifest of facts. The implementer can lift wiring with high fidelity.
 - Misleading: the existing TF-IDF corpus ALREADY includes the real compiling artifacts (/home/USER/csl-examples/benchmarks/25-pt-stencil/{oned_exch,task,layout}.csl, gemv-collectives_2d/*, 7pt-stencil-spmv/*). These are executable, compile to ELF, and are surfaced to the implementer at max_chars=4000 via tutorial_context with cluster-augmented queries. So the differentiator isn't "executable" — it's "minimal + whole-unit + curated to the cluster". That is a real but narrower delta than the proposal claims.

(2) DOES IT TARGET THE 9 FAILURES SPECIFICALLY? Halo_recv_unblock (6 failures) plausibly yes — wiring boilerplate is the named failure mode and a single 60-line halo_recv_unblock_4color.csl card would let the LLM template-copy the queue ids / unblock_cmd_stream / fabin_dsd order it currently rederives wrong. Dsr_queue_fabric_init (2 failures) plausibly yes for the same reason. Collectives_2d (2 failures): less promising — the existing collectives_2d gotcha already prescribes the exact import signature and the kernels still fail; that suggests the failure isn't "doesn't know the wiring" but "knows the wiring, fails to compose it with the algorithm". A card won't fix composition.

(3) PRIOR ART ELSEWHERE? Yellow flag. Few-shot exemplar selection for code gen is well-studied (CodeT, DocPrompting, REDCODER, Self-Edit) and consistently shows ~3-8pt on small-DSL benches like CodeContests/MBPP. For novel-DSL translation specifically (Triton kernel synthesis papers, MLIR-lowering work like 2024 LLM4HLS), retrieved-exemplar approaches show 2-5pt lift, occasionally more when the exemplar is near-isomorphic to the target. NO published result I'm aware of for "minimal verified compiling idiom card" for CUDA->novel-ISA translation specifically — that's both the opportunity (untested) and the risk (untested). The closest negative is your own halo r4 result: "canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses." That is the exact failure mode this proposal must avoid by construction.

(4) 10X SMALLER PROOF: yes, cheap. Hand-author ONE halo_recv_unblock card (the 4-color queue/unblock pattern). Inject verbatim into implementer prompt for the 6 failing halo kernels only. ~4 hours of work. If 0/6 still pass, kill it. If 1-2/6 pass, the principle holds and the 8-card build is justified. This is the right next step — and you should run it BEFORE committing 4-5 eng-days.

(5) EXPECTED LIFT: I'd estimate +1 to +2 kernels (6/15 -> 7-8/15, so +7-13pt). NOT the +3-4 the proposal implicitly promises. Reasons to discount:
 - collectives_2d cluster is composition-bound, not wiring-bound (see #2)
 - dsr_queue_fabric_init is only 3 kernels total; even a perfect fix is +2/15
 - On halo_recv_unblock, the post-mortem from r4 says canonical halo patterns are "too composed to fit in minimal harnesses" — minimal cards may not be enough; the failing kernels need the wiring AND the edge/corner branching AND the per-PE role logic to coexist. If the card omits any of these, the LLM still composes wrong.
 - Single-Tile-Matvec regression precedent: even cluster-gated extra context regressed a passing kernel once. Cards need the same firewall.

KEY RISKS THE PROPOSAL UNDERWEIGHTS:
 - Contamination is harder to guard than the proposal admits. tutorial_leak_check uses substring/identifier matching against benchmarks/*/pe.csl, but a generic "send/recv with unblock" card will share many tokens with any halo kernel's pe.csl. The proposed ">3 token overlap" threshold will either be too strict (rejects useful cards) or too loose (leaks structure). Need a semantic-not-lexical leak check.
 - The "minimal" constraint fights the "covers the failing pattern" constraint. r4 showed this directly. If your halo card has to include edge/corner branching to be useful, it's no longer a 60-line minimal card.
 - Cluster classifier accuracy is unmeasured. If a kernel is mis-classified, you inject the wrong card and may distract more than help (Single-Tile-Matvec regression analog).
 - Token displacement: 3 cards * ~1KB displaces ~3KB from tutorial_context. The displaced chunks may have been carrying load you don't know about. Need to A/B with card-on vs card-off, NOT card-on vs no-context.

VERDICT: Not dead-on-arrival. Plausibly worth a one-card pilot on the 6 halo kernels in <1 day before committing to the full build. If pilot shows 0 wins, kill — translation_facts also looked plausible and ran 19 attempts at 0W/2L/17T. If pilot shows >=1 win, the 8-card build is justified, but expect modest lift (1-2 kernels), not a step change.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: One-card pilot: hand-author halo_recv_unblock_4color.csl (60 lines, cslc-verified), inject verbatim into implementer prompt for just the 6 failing halo_recv_unblock kernels, run 2 attempts each, compare pass rate vs baseline. Total cost: ~4 hours authoring + 1 sweep. Kill criterion: 0/6 pass. Promote criterion: >=1/6 pass that wasn't passing before. This is strictly better than the full 8-card build as a first move because (a) it tests the riskiest cluster directly, (b) it costs 10x less, (c) it answers the r4 "canonical patterns too composed" objection head-on.

all_critiques.name: Compile-validated few-shot construction (idiom cards)
all_critiques.critique:
Hard critique, grounded in what's already in the repo:

1) STRUCTURAL NOVELTY: weak. The baseline already injects cslc-compiling code, not just prose. `tutorial_context()` (csl_knowledge_base.py:1068) retrieves TF-IDF-ranked chunks from `csl-examples/benchmarks/**/pe.csl` and `cerebras-csl-skills`, both of which compile. The 11 cluster-gated gotchas (_GOTCHA_SECTIONS_BY_CLUSTER) already cite specific compiling files like `csl-examples/benchmarks/game-of-life/pe_program.csl` for halo, `gemv-collectives_2d` for c2d, etc. The cluster classifier `_augment_query_for_w1_clusters` already biases retrieval into the right corpus. So the delta isn't "verified compiling code vs prose," it's "hand-curated minimal compiling snippet vs TF-IDF-retrieved fragment of a real compiling kernel." That's the same shape as translation_facts (extra cluster-gated context inserted pre-implementer with the same insertion point) — translation_facts was 0W/2L/17T over 19 attempts. The author's "executable vs YAML" distinction is real but small; both are 0.5-1KB of structured grounding consumed by the implementer.

2) CLUSTER ADDRESSING: the proposal's own framing collides with the strongest prior-art lesson in the repo. Halo-gotcha r4 (cslc-grounded + canonical hints) was explicitly killed because "canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses" (DISCARDED list). A 4-color halo-recv with edge-dependent expected_recv, ut_id pools, async fabin_dsd posting BEFORE sends, AND boundary-PE unblock_cmd_stream coverage — that's the canonical halo idiom, and it does not fit in <60 lines as a compiling harness. If you abstract enough to fit, you lose the very wiring that the agent keeps fabricating wrong (per-PE recv-count plumbed from layout edge bools). The harness templates in ground_gotcha.py already have `send_recv_2x1` and `mesh_2x2`; the r4 workflow already used them and produced 0/5 wins. This proposal is r4 with the "rewriter" replaced by hand-authoring, but the binding constraint was the harness's composability ceiling, not the rewriter's quality.

3) CONTAMINATION GUARD KILLS UTILITY: the proposal's own mitigation — reject any card sharing >3 tokens with any `benchmarks/*/pe.csl` (tutorial_leak_check) — is fatal in practice for halo. The W1 halo failure corpus IS game-of-life / 7-point-stencil / Laplacian2D-Halo variants, and the only known-correct minimal halo template lives at `csl-examples/benchmarks/game-of-life/pe_program.csl`. A "minimal halo card" that doesn't share substantial tokens with that file is either (a) the wrong wiring, or (b) so abstracted (placeholder names, stub bodies) that it stops being the executable artifact the proposal claims to value. The collectives_2d case is even worse: the gotchas already cite `gemv-collectives_2d/pe.csl` line-by-line; a card that copies that pattern fails the leak gate, and one that doesn't is back to being prose.

4) PRIOR ART OUTSIDE THE REPO: I don't have evidence of "compile-validated minimal idiom cards beat compile-validated retrieved tutorial chunks" being demonstrated for code translation. The closest is generic few-shot, where retrieved few-shots tend to dominate hand-authored when the corpus is non-trivial — and this repo's corpus (csl-examples + cerebras-csl-skills) is large enough that retrieval is the stronger baseline.

5) BOTTLENECK DIAGNOSIS MISMATCH: halo 6/7 fail; dsr 2/3 fail. The known failure mode (per the iterative-solvers memory note and the cluster gotchas) is that the model emits a hardcoded `expected_recv = 4` instead of plumbing edge bools — a SEMANTIC error of "didn't realize recv-count is per-PE," not a syntactic error of "didn't know which builtin." A minimal compiling card that uses the right pattern with `expected_recv = 4` for a 1x2 mesh will reinforce the wrong instinct (since 4 is the literal count there), not correct it. The gotchas already include the literal phrase "Halo recv-count is per-PE and edge-dependent — hardcoded 4-neighbor counts deadlock boundary PEs," and the agent still ships hardcoded 4s. Adding a compiling 2x1 card next to that prose doesn't unblock the failure mode.

6) EXPECTED LIFT: low. Generous case: 1 of the 9 failing kernels flips because the implementer literally pastes a wiring fragment. Realistic case: 0. The strongest evidence against is that r4 specifically tried "hand-curate canonical halo patterns as compile-grounded references injected to the rewriter" and got 0/5. The proposal is r4 minus the rewriter step; that's not obviously stronger.

7) WHAT THE PROPOSAL DOES NOT EXAMINE: the actual failure mode on the iterative-solvers W2 (0% improvement) is documented in MEMORY.md — run.py runs the iteration loop on the host with blocking RPCs, so cycles_send measures host-device sync, not on-device compute. No amount of pe.csl-side few-shot fixes that; the fix is host-side. The W1 halo failures fail at runtime / contract-mismatch, not syntax. Both bottlenecks are upstream of "give the implementer better wiring snippets."

The only place this might earn its keep is dsr_queue_fabric_init, where the failure does look more like "wrong builtin signature" than "wrong algorithm" — and dsr is 1 PE, so the harness composability ceiling is lower. But that's 2 kernels of upside, gated through the same contamination filter that kills the halo case.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Yes, materially smaller and worth doing instead: ship ONE card for dsr_queue_fabric_init only — the cluster where (a) the failure mode is "wrong builtin signature/order" not "wrong algorithm," (b) the canonical pattern fits in <40 lines of single-PE harness without composability blowup, and (c) the leak-gate is easier to satisfy because the dsr setup is mostly boilerplate that's identical across benchmarks. One card, one A/B over the 3 dsr W1 kernels, half a day of work. If that doesn't move 1/3 to 2/3, no other card will. Do NOT attempt the halo card first — r4 has already established that road is closed. An even smaller test: take the existing halo gotcha text (the prose form already in _GOTCHA_SECTIONS_BY_CLUSTER) and just append a known-good 25-line snippet inline AS PART OF THE GOTCHA, no new file, no new index, no new compile gate — same hypothesis at near-zero engineering cost. If that doesn't move 6/7→5/7 on halo in one resweep, the full proposal won't either.

all_critiques.name: Retrieval over our own version_trace.json (success ICL)
all_critiques.critique:
This is semantic_bridge/translation_facts in a new wrapper, and it fails the same way they failed. Specific objections:

1. SHAPE: This is "more structured text injected into the implementer prompt before generation" — the exact prompt-engineering shape both discarded experiments occupied. The author's claim of structural difference (i) executable code not facts, (ii) similarity-gated not always-on, (iii) scales with success — none of these address WHY semantic_bridge/translation_facts lost. The discard notes say "algorithm-level prose didn't address syntax-level failures" and "RAG'd gotchas already covered the surface, IR added perturbation without lift." Executable precedent is still algorithm-level, and it's still subject to RAG overlap. The implementer already gets cluster-gated tutorial examples from cerebras-csl-skills via TF-IDF — those ARE working CSL programs of similar shape. Adding our own (lower-quality, less idiomatic) wins on top is more of the same signal.

2. INDEX IS NEARLY EMPTY AND BIASED. I walked results/cuda2csl: ~29 version_trace.json files across ~18 kernels. Only 5-6 distinct kernels have ANY PASS attempt (7pt-Stencil x10 runs, BiCGSTAB, CG, Power-Method, PCG, plus Wide-Mult/Single-Tile-Matvec in scattered runs). And per MEMORY.md, the iterative-solver passes (BiCGSTAB/CG/PCG/Power-Method) are exactly the family where cycles_send is host-RPC-bounded — those "wins" are run.py shape, not on-device translation quality. So the usable index is effectively {7pt-Stencil, maybe 2-3 trivial kernels}. The claim of "6 fresh ship-quality pairs the framework has never used" is misleading: most of the 6 are either RPC-loop artifacts or near-duplicates of 7pt-Stencil.

3. CLUSTER MISMATCH (FATAL). The 9 failing kernels live in clusters {halo_recv_unblock, dsr_queue_fabric_init, collectives_2d}. The PASS set lives in clusters {trivial-elementwise, host-RPC-loop solver, single-stencil-halo}. Structural-similarity retrieval over CUDA AST features (loop nest, atomicCAS, blockDim) will NEVER match a failing halo kernel to a passing trivial kernel — and even if you force a match by lowering the 0.7 threshold, the retrieved CSL has none of the halo_recv_unblock idioms the target needs. The proposal cannot lift the clusters that are actually failing because the index is empty for those clusters. This is the precise definition of "doesn't address the bottleneck."

4. NO PRIOR ART. The author asked themselves the question; the answer is no. Few-shot retrieval from past successes is well-trodden for high-level code generation (Codex, SWE-bench retrieval baselines) but I'm not aware of evidence it works for hardware-DSL lowering where the failing surface is fabric-config syntax + initialization ordering, not algorithm choice. CUDA→PTX/SASS lowering doesn't use this because the IR is the precedent. MLIR conversion patterns are hand-written rewrite rules, not retrieved examples. Yellow flag confirmed.

5. CONTAMINATION RISK IS UNDERESTIMATED. The author flags it but the mitigation (kernel-name blacklist + spec.yaml hash) doesn't address the real risk: many of our 15 benchmark kernels are NEAR-DUPLICATES (GEMV / GEMV-Checkerboard / GEMV-Collectives-2D / GEMM / GEMM-Collectives-2D / CG / PCG / BiCGSTAB / Power-Method). If GEMV passes once, GEMV-Collectives-2D will retrieve it as the top precedent and copy its non-collective pe.csl, which will score as a "pass" by structural similarity but fail the actual benchmark because collectives_2d needs teamlib code the precedent doesn't have. You'd inflate apparent index hit-rate without lift, and risk REGRESSING the variant kernels by anchoring them to wrong precedent.

6. THE BIT THE PROPOSAL DOESN'T ANSWER: why does the implementer "re-derive architectures it has previously gotten right" — when it gets the cerebras-csl-skills examples via TF-IDF already? If the answer is "those examples are too generic" then adding our own (less idiomatic, less canonical) examples is worse, not better. If the answer is "implementer ignores them," that's a prompt-attention problem, not a retrieval problem, and shipping more text makes it worse.

EXPECTED LIFT: 0/15 most likely. Possible -1/15 from variant-kernel cross-contamination.
