Generous upper bound: +1/15 if it accidentally re-derives a known win that was bucket-routed away by repair, but the framework already retains the best attempt across all 8 attempts, so that lift is already captured.

WHAT THE PROPOSAL ACTUALLY POINTS AT (that IS valuable): the version_trace.json corpus is underused. But the right use is OFFLINE analysis (per-cluster failure-mode mining, regex extraction of which syntactic constructs co-occur with PASS vs FAIL in the halo cluster, hand-curated into the gotchas list with cslc-grounding) — NOT online retrieval into the prompt. The grounded-gotcha workflow (ground_gotcha.py) is already the right channel for this; feed the version_trace mining results into THAT pipeline.
all_critiques.smaller_variant:
10x smaller test that would falsify in <1 day, and is the ONLY version worth running: skip the indexer, skip retrieval. Hand-pick the single 7pt-Stencil PASS pe.csl, hardcode-inject it into the implementer prompt for each of the 9 failing kernels under "## A passing precedent from this codebase", re-run hybrid sweep on the 9 failures. If 7pt-Stencil-as-precedent doesn't move any of the 9 (predicted: it won't), the full proposal is dead-on-arrival. Cost: half a day, no indexer code. If by some chance it lifts halo cluster (it won't — 7pt-Stencil halo IS what cerebras-csl-skills tutorials cover), then build a 2-precedent version next. This is the right falsifier because it strips out the (a) structural-similarity scoring complexity, (b) de-identifier, (c) backfill indexer — all of which add code that doesn't matter if the core hypothesis (own-success ICL helps) is false.

Even better falsifier (1 hour): grep the existing cerebras-csl-skills RAG corpus for 7pt-Stencil-equivalent halo code. If it's already there (it is — stencil_3d_7pts is a canonical tutorial), then the framework has been seeing this precedent all along and the proposal adds zero new information.

all_critiques.name: Retrieval over our own version_trace.json (success ICL)
all_critiques.critique:
Hard problems with this proposal, in priority order:

(1) Cluster mismatch is fatal to the lift hypothesis. The 6/15 passing set is approximately {7pt-Stencil, Power-Method, BiCGSTAB, CG, PCG, +1 of Residual/Mandelbrot} based on what version_trace.json actually shows passing on disk. Four of those six are iterative solvers that — per your own auto-memory note (project_power_method_instrumentation.md) — "pass" on cycles_send only because the metric measures host↔device RPC sync, not on-device compute. The 9 failing kernels live in halo_recv_unblock (6/7), dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3), collectives_2d (2/4). NONE of the 6 passing precedents structurally resemble these failure clusters: iterative solvers don't have on-device halo exchanges or 2D collectives or DSR queue fabric init. So a top-1 structural-similarity retrieval over the success index will, for the 9 target failures, either (a) return nothing >0.7 (most likely — gating off), or (b) return a misleading cross-cluster precedent (e.g. show the agent a passing CG when it's translating GEMV-Collectives-2D, which actively hurts). The cases where retrieval would fire usefully are exactly the cases that already pass.

(2) Structurally NOT different from semantic_bridge/translation_facts. All three are 'inject more conditioning bytes before implementer'. Author's distinction — 'executable code, gated by structural similarity, scales with our own success' — is a property of the payload, not the intervention shape. The framework's empirical track record (semantic_bridge: discarded; translation_facts: 19 attempts 0W/2L/17T; reviewer budget bump 4→8: 0/14 marginal lift) is that adding pre-implementer conditioning bytes to a Sonnet-or-Opus single-shot implementer does not move pass rate when the failure mode is cluster-specific syntax/contract violations. The gotchas already in RAG ARE the distilled-from-passing-code knowledge; serving the whole passing pe.csl is strictly more noise per signal bit than the gotcha distillation it replaces.

(3) No external evidence cited. Few-shot retrieval over prior passing translations is a well-studied pattern (CodeT, Self-Debugging, ToolCoder, REPOCODER for repo-level retrieval). The honest read of that literature: retrieval-augmented code generation helps most on (a) API-shaped tasks where the precedent contains the exact API call needed, and (b) high-volume benchmarks where many in-distribution precedents exist. With n=6 wins across 5+ structurally distinct kernel families, this is neither regime. CUDA→assembly / MLIR-lowering literature does NOT use precedent retrieval as a primary lever — they use typed IRs and verified rewrite rules, which is the OTHER half of the question being asked (the deferred CUDA-side IR).

(4) Index size n≈6 is too small for the gating to matter. With ~6 success records spread across ~5 architectural families, the similarity threshold either fires too rarely (>0.7 almost never met cross-family) or fires too greedily (any threshold lower than that pulls in misleading neighbors). The 'self-improving as wins accumulate' claim is correct in the limit but irrelevant in the regime that matters — we need the FIRST few halo/collectives/dsr wins for the index to be useful on those clusters, and getting those is exactly the problem this proposal is supposed to solve. Circular.

(5) Contamination risk is real and the author flags it but understates it. tutorial_leak_check against the target's reference pe.csl assumes you have the reference; for kernels where the reference IS in cerebras-csl-skills (which is the RAG corpus), the 'de-identifier' has to also strip architectural fingerprints (color counts, mesh dimensions, fabric symbols), not just kernel names — at which point the precedent is no longer useful BECAUSE those fingerprints are what the agent would copy. The leak check as specified verifies an invariant (agent didn't see ref) but doesn't prevent the precedent itself from BEING a near-clone of the ref.

(6) The 'better IR' framing the question explicitly raises gets dodged. This proposal is not IR. It's nearest-neighbor in token-soup space with a thin structural feature head. If the real bottleneck is that the implementer doesn't have a typed CUDA-side representation to drive cluster-correct CSL emission, this proposal does not move that bar. The Phase 1 CSL-side IR was shipped and didn't help; the natural read is that the CUDA-side IR (the deferred half) is the actual missing piece, and 'serve raw passing code' is the lazy substitute that skips the work of building it.

Recommended verdict: do not build the full proposal. If you must spend 1 day on this, do the 10x smaller version below and stop if it doesn't show signal.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: 1-day spike: skip the indexer, skip the feature vector, skip de-identification. For each of the 9 failing kernels, hand-pick the single closest passing pe.csl from the existing 6 wins (or declare 'no close match'). Inject it as a static fixture into the implementer prompt under '## Reference architecture from a similar passing translation'. Run hybrid sweep on the 9 failing kernels. If lift > 1/9 over the 6/15 baseline, build the retrieval; if not (predicted: 0/9, because the 4 iterative-solver wins are cross-cluster to halo/collectives/dsr and the 1-2 stencil/dense wins don't transfer to fabric-init failures), kill the proposal. This costs <1 day and answers the structural-similarity question without writing any retrieval code. If you want an IR-flavored 1-day spike INSTEAD: hand-write the CUDA-side IR (typed AST: {tile shape, halo pattern, reduction tree, atomic ops, host-launch shape}) for the 9 failing kernels' input CUDA, inject that IR as a prose block before the architect, and measure. That tests the deferred half of Phase 1 directly and is the more honest experiment given the question asked.

all_critiques.name: Two-stage retrieval: cluster-classifier → dense-embedding rerank
all_critiques.critique:
Q1 (structural difference): NO, this is the same shape as translation_facts and semantic_bridge in the only way that matters — it adjusts what context arrives at the implementer's prompt without changing the agent's failure mode. translation_facts was structured CSL-side IR injected before the implementer (0W/2L/17T over 19 attempts). semantic_bridge was prose injected before the implementer (discarded). This proposal is "the same 3 tutorial chunks, hopefully better ranked." The historical A/B of tutorials-on vs tutorials-off on the hard-fail set (ab_tutorials_20260530, gpt-oss-120b, 4 hardest kernels) went 1/4 → 1/4 with two improvements and two regressions. If the entire tutorials corpus going from OFF to ON nets zero on hard kernels, reranking inside an ON corpus cannot plausibly net more than that — the ceiling is determined by what's IN the corpus, not the rank order. The audit the author cites ("top-3 chunks are often the same generic gemv tutorial") is the diagnosis of a corpus-content problem (insufficient halo/dsr coverage at sufficient specificity), not a ranking problem. Reranking can only surface what exists; the relevant halo/dsr-wiring patterns at rank 10-20 are likely not better than the gemv tutorial at rank 1, just differently incomplete — that's why the existing cluster-keyed query augmentation (which already does what this proposes, lexically) doesn't unlock those kernels either.

Q2 (cluster-specific?): It is explicitly a generic "more context" improvement and does NOT mechanistically target any of halo_recv_unblock / dsr_queue_fabric_init / collectives_2d failure modes. The halo failures are wiring-specific (initialize_queue discipline, ut_id, edge-PE branches that skip unblock_cmd_stream) and the hand-curated grounded gotchas already shipped today directly write those wiring rules into the prompt. If those gotchas didn't move 6/7 halo kernels, a better-ranked tutorial chunk almost certainly won't either — the implementer's failure isn't "didn't see the right idiom," it's "saw the right idiom and still emitted broken wiring." This is corroborated by halo r4 (cslc-grounded canonical hints, 0/5) and the marginal pass-rate from attempts 5-8 being 0/14 — when the model fails on halo, more attempts don't help, and more context doesn't help either.

Q3 (external prior art): BGE rerank works for QA, web search, and long-document retrieval. There is no public result showing dense-embedding rerank meaningfully improving low-level GPU→accelerator code translation pass rates. The closest analog (RAG over CUDA→Triton or MLIR lowering) typically reports zero or marginal lift from rerank when the corpus is small (<10k chunks) and lexically rich — both true here. Yellow flag: cite-by-absence.

Q4 (10x smaller proof): YES, and the author's own rank-overlap audit IS the 10x version. But the audit is mis-specified. A high rank@3 overlap doesn't prove rerank is useless (chunks might rank-tie at TF-IDF and BGE could pick the better one). A low overlap doesn't prove it's useful either (the new chunks might be irrelevant). The right cheap pre-check is: take the 9 failing W1 kernels, manually inspect the top-30 TF-IDF chunks per kernel, and ask "is there a chunk in 4-30 that, if it had been at rank 1, would have caused the implementer to emit correct wiring?" If you can't find even 3/9 such chunks by hand-inspection, no automated reranker will either. This audit is ~3 hours. Do it before the 2-day implementation.

Q5 (expected lift): Realistic lift on 15-kernel benchmark = 0-1 kernels = 0-7%. Most likely 0. The dominant failure mode is implementer execution under correct context, not implementer starvation. Variance from a corpus change of this size is roughly ±1 kernel from noise alone (Game-of-Life flipped both ways across runs); a single-kernel "win" would be indistinguishable from noise without 3+ seeds.

Additional sharper concern not in the author's risk note: the existing cluster-keyed query augmentation already does the work the proposal claims is novel. The augmentation appends 50-100 chars of cluster-specific keywords to the TF-IDF query — that IS a structured query, just rendered as a lexical bag rather than a dense vector. TF-IDF on an already-cluster-augmented query is mathematically very close to BGE on a typed-feature query when the corpus is small and the augmentation keywords are well-chosen (which they are — they were curated from observed failures). The delta is the embedding's ability to bridge synonyms (e.g. "edge PE" ↔ "border tile"), which is exactly the case where halo and dsr corpora are NOT lexically diverse — they use the same SDK vocabulary across all chunks. The proposal optimizes for a synonym-bridging problem that doesn't exist in this corpus.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Skip the implementation. Do ONLY the 3-hour hand-audit: for each of the 9 failing W1 kernels, print the top-30 TF-IDF tutorial chunks (kb.prompt_context with top_k=30, max_chars=200 per chunk) and grade by hand "would-have-helped-if-at-rank-1: Y/N." Three possible outcomes: (a) ≥3/9 have a clear "Y" chunk in rank 4-30 → THEN build the reranker, but only if the typed query is constructible from layout.csl features (not CUDA prose). Expected lift bound becomes that grade count, halved for implementation slippage. (b) <3/9 → reranking is dead, but the audit identifies the actual gap: which halo/dsr patterns are MISSING from the corpus entirely. The follow-up is corpus authoring (write the missing tutorial chunk and ground it with cslc, same shape as the halo gotcha workflow), not rerank. (c) The "Y" chunks are at rank 1-3 already and the implementer ignored them → confirms the bottleneck is implementer execution, not retrieval; the right next move is verifier-driven repair (run cslc on the emitted CSL, feed the error → next attempt) which is a fundamentally different intervention from anything tried so far. All three outcomes are higher-value than building the reranker blind, and outcome (c) is the one consistent with the empirical pattern (8-attempt budget bump 0/14, halo r4 grounded 0/5, gotchas 6/15 ceiling).

all_critiques.name: Two-stage retrieval: cluster-classifier → dense-embedding rerank
all_critiques.critique:
Structurally this is translation_facts-shaped, not just at risk of being so. Both prior discards (semantic_bridge, translation_facts) targeted the same slot: more/better material before the implementer call. Their A/B verdicts were 0W/2L/17T and 1/4-vs-1/4 — not noise, but evidence the implementer's failure mode on the 9 failing kernels is NOT "right idiom buried at rank 10-20." The 2026-06-04 root cause was explicit: "The structural checker never flagged a fact-class violation in either arm. The RAG'd gotchas already cover the surface." That cuts the wind out of this proposal. If correct chunks were merely mis-ranked, translation_facts (which injected ALREADY-extracted high-leverage facts directly, bypassing rank entirely) would have won. It didn't. So either (a) the chunks are already in-context and the implementer ignores/misapplies them, or (b) the failure is on a dimension the corpus doesn't contain at any rank. Embedding rerank fixes neither.

Cluster specificity: the author claims the chunks for halo/dsr are "wiring-specific" and "buried at rank 10-20." This is untested — the audit is described as a mitigation, not as already-done. Without the rank-overlap audit, the headline justification ("top-3 chunks are often the same generic gemv tutorial regardless of cluster") is asserted, not shown. The existing _augment_query_for_w1_clusters already appends 100+ chars of cluster-specific keywords ("topic-15-wse3-microthreads .async fmovs fmacs microthread @bind_data_task..." for halo); if that doesn't surface the right chunks via TF-IDF, the corpus probably lacks them, not the ranker.

Halo cluster specifically (6/7 fail, the dominant bottleneck): the r2/r3/r4 halo-gotcha workflows already FAILED to produce material that helped — drafters fabricated builtins, canonical patterns "too composed to fit in minimal harnesses." That's a tell that the halo failure is composition/architectural, not retrieval. No reranker recovers patterns that aren't in the corpus.

Domain-mismatch claim ("structured natural-language query is in BGE's sweet spot") is plausible but weak. BGE-small is trained on web QA — "target: 4-color halo, queue-id pattern" looks like natural language to a human but to BGE it's a bag of low-IDF tokens against chunks titled "topic-03-streaming-wavelet-data." Cosine over these will produce noisy rankings, not crisper ones. The benefit of dense embeddings over TF-IDF is mainly synonym handling; CSL builtins have no synonyms — `@fmacs` is `@fmacs`. TF-IDF is actually well-matched to this corpus.

DSR cluster (2/3 fail): same diagnosis. The DSR failures are about wiring host-side reservations through `commands.sh` → `layout.csl` → `pe.csl` chains and getting `dest_dsr_ids`/`src*_dsr_ids` right. That's a multi-file structural constraint the implementer must SATISFY, not a chunk it must RETRIEVE. Better retrieval doesn't help if the failure is "produce code matching a 3-file invariant."

No external evidence cited that dense-rerank improves code translation on hard structural tasks. Where retrieval-augmented MLIR/lowering work has shown lift, it's usually been via grammar-constrained decoding or executable verification loops, not corpus reranking. Yellow flag.

Final read: the same shape (extra-context-before-implementer) has now lost twice; this proposal does not articulate why it's different except in mechanism, and the mechanism (embedding rerank) attacks a problem the prior verdict says doesn't exist. Expected lift on 15-kernel W1: probably 0-1 kernels (0-7pt), with non-trivial regression risk from prompt perturbation (translation_facts caused 2 losses from ~780 char addition; this adds similar volume). Real bottleneck is composition/structural correctness in halo wiring, not retrieval ranking — fix that with executable verification (cslc-grounded implementer feedback loop applied to PE drafts, not just gotcha snippets) or grammar constraints, not reranking.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: YES — and the author already named it as the pre-ship audit, which is the right move and should be the WHOLE first step. Specifically: do the rank-overlap audit ALONE, no engineering, in 1-2 hours. Take the 15 captured W1 implementer prompts. For each, run TF-IDF top-30, then manually (or via Opus) judge which 3 of those 30 chunks would have actually unblocked the failing kernel. If rank@3 already contains the helpful chunks for ≥10/15 kernels, retrieval isn't the bottleneck — kill the proposal, save 2 days. If TF-IDF rank@3 is wrong for ≥5 kernels AND the helpful chunks DO exist in rank 4-30, that's the only signal that justifies building the reranker. Crucially, this audit also tells you something the reranker wouldn't: how often the helpful chunks aren't in the corpus AT ALL (in which case the answer is "expand corpus," not "rerank"). I'd bet >70% of the failing kernels fall into "helpful chunks don't exist in corpus" or "right chunks are already in rank@3 but implementer misapplied them" — both kill the proposal.

all_critiques.name: Differential debugger: compile-error → grounded-snippet retrieval
all_critiques.critique:
The author's risk note ("STRUCTURALLY DIFFERENT from translation_facts because it's FAILURE-CONDITIONED") is the right question but the wrong answer. Here is what actually happened in this repo:

1. **Prior art INSIDE this repo already ran this experiment and got null.** `results/ab_debugger_20260601_151711/ab.log` is exactly a P (no debugger) vs Q (with debugger) A/B. P: 1/4 pass (Game-of-Life FAIL, Residual FAIL, 7pt-Stencil PASS, FFT-1D-2D FAIL). Q (debugger fires on failure, hands the implementer a structured diagnosis derived from stderr + reviewer rationale + recommended_patch): 1/4 pass, **same kernels, same kernels failing, with longer wall-time**. The current `debugger_agent.py` DOES already capture `stderr_tail` and emit a `recommended_patch` hint that's injected as a focused block in the next fix prompt (see DebuggerReport.to_prompt_block). The proposal is essentially "debugger_agent v1.5 with a hand-curated lookup table instead of LLM-generated patch." The lookup table replaces one source of failure (LLM-generated patch hallucinating) with another (curator misclassifying error class), not the dominant one.

2. **The proposal does not address the 9 failing kernels' actual failure mode.** The 6/7 halo_recv_unblock failures are NOT compile errors that map cleanly to "undefined builtin" or "queue conflict." Per the halo-gotcha r2/r3/r4 post-mortems already in PROGRESS notes, halo failures are *compositional* — the agent emits code that compiles fine but deadlocks or computes the wrong thing because the recv/unblock/advance state-machine isn't wired right across multiple files (layout.csl colors + pe.csl tasks + run.py launch). r4 explicitly concluded "canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses." A per-error-class snippet bank is the wrong shape: there's no single cslc error message that says "your halo state machine is wrong." If the kernel ran at all, it produced numerical mismatch, not a parseable stderr. Of the 9 failures, my read of progress logs suggests maybe 2 are clean compile errors with a clean error→snippet mapping (some collectives_2d cases). That caps the upside at maybe 1 conversion.

3. **Is it structurally different from translation_facts? Partly, but not in the way that matters.** Yes, it fires conditionally instead of unconditionally — that's a real difference and it eliminates the perturbation-on-passing-kernels failure mode of translation_facts. But "shrinking context to a focused snippet" is exactly what cluster-gated KNOWN_GOTCHAS already does today, and what the existing debugger's `recommended_patch` already does. The novel surface area is small: "swap LLM-derived patch hint for hand-curated snippet from a card bank." That's a quality-of-source change, not a structural change. The 17-tie translation_facts A/B and the null debugger A/B both suggest the implementer is not bottlenecked on getting the right textual hint — it's bottlenecked on something else (probably: not having pe.csl visible during W1, plus the inherent difficulty of stateful multi-file generation).

4. **External prior art is weak.** CUDA→assembly and MLIR lowering are deterministic compiler pipelines, not LLM tasks; the analog doesn't transfer. For LLM code translation, the closest published work is self-repair / Reflexion-style loops (Madaan et al. 2023, Chen et al. self-debug 2023). The empirical lift in those papers is real (~5-15pt) on HumanEval-class tasks but those are single-file, single-turn, well-known idioms with massive training-data coverage. CSL has effectively zero pretraining presence and the multi-file constraint surface (.csl files cross-referencing colors/IDs/queues) is far outside that regime. There is no published external evidence that error-class→snippet retrieval works for a DSL the model has never seen. That's a yellow flag bordering on red.

5. **Coupling risk understated.** The author flags "relies on Proposal #2 shipping first (idiom_cards bank)." That isn't a soft dependency — it's the entire mechanism. If the idiom cards are scraped from `kernels/*/CSL/`, they're the same snippets RAG already retrieves. If they're hand-curated, you're paying the curation cost (which the r4 grounded-rewrite workflow showed is ~1 day per 5 cards with cslc-grounding, and even then the cards were rejected as "too composed"). So real cost is 3-4 days eng PLUS 1-3 weeks of card curation, not 3-4 days total.

6. **The "smaller version" question is the only viable framing.** A 1-day prototype is genuinely cheap (see below) and would falsify quickly. But its expected value is dominated by the fact that the related experiment already ran here and returned null.

Bottom line: this is the third variant of "inject more/better targeted context into the repair prompt." The first two (semantic_bridge, translation_facts) returned 0W from 21 attempts. The existing debugger_agent A/B returned 0W from 4 attempts. Expected lift on the 15-kernel benchmark: **0 kernels, with a small chance (~20%) of converting 1 kernel in collectives_2d cluster where the failure genuinely is a clean compile error with a known fix.** That's +0 to +7pt over 6/15, dominated by 0.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: YES, and it's the only justifiable version: spend ONE day, not 3-4. (a) Take the existing `debugger_agent.py` output on the 9 failing kernels' last attempts (the stderr_tail and recommended_patch are already logged). (b) For each failure, hand-write the snippet you WOULD have injected. (c) Manually replay just the bucket-B/C repair prompt with that snippet substituted and see if Sonnet now produces compiling code. No infra build, no card bank, no error-class taxonomy. If 0/9 convert under hand-optimal snippet injection — which is the upper bound of what the automated system could achieve — the full build is dead on arrival. If 3+/9 convert, then maybe build the error-class parser. Predicted result of this dry-run: 0/9 to 1/9. The halo cluster will not convert because the fix isn't a snippet, it's a multi-file state-machine restructure. The collectives_2d cluster might convert one. Run the dry-run before writing any of the proposed 3-4 days of code — the prior null A/B inside this repo means the bar for "build it" should be empirical evidence from the dry-run, not authorial confidence.

all_critiques.name: Differential debugger: compile-error → grounded-snippet retrieval
all_critiques.critique:
This proposal is mostly already-shipped infrastructure rebadged as new, and the original A/B on that infrastructure already came back flat-to-negative.

CONCRETE PRIOR-ART IN THIS REPO (the proposal does not acknowledge):
- code_translation/debugger_agent.py (357 LOC) already exists. It already extracts stderr_tail (via the walk-from-end logic in cuda2csl.py:1656-1675, which fixes the "transcript[-1] is a cleanup step" bug), already gets the reviewer's debug_action, the failing CSL, layout.csl, and a knowledge bundle. It emits a structured JSON patch hint that is injected as {debugger_report} into csl_bundle_fix_with_review (cuda2csl.py:1714).
- results/ab_debugger_20260601_151711/ ran 3 models x 2 conditions (P=no_debugger, Q=with_debugger) x 4 hard kernels (Game-of-Life, Residual, 7pt-Stencil, FFT-1D-2D). The ab.log shows ALL six conditions land at 1/4 except one 0/4. Debugger ON did not beat debugger OFF; on at least one pair it regressed. XKERNEL_DEBUGGER defaults to 0 because of that result.

The proposal's actual delta over the existing debugger is: replace "LLM reads stderr+bundle, writes JSON patch hint" with "regex parses stderr, looks up one hand-curated card." That is strictly LESS expressive than what already shipped. The hand-curated lookup is brittle in a way the LLM call is not: cslc error messages drift across SDK versions, and the proposal needs a stable error_class taxonomy that even the author flags as the primary risk. The "negative token delta" framing is misleading: the existing debugger already only fires conditionally (capped at 1/kernel, gated on bucket=B with concrete debug verb or repeat failure), so the comparison baseline isn't "every prompt has broad gotchas."

Q1 (structural difference): YES failure-conditioned vs always-on (real), but NO over the existing debugger (which is also failure-conditioned). The proposal's distinguishing claim collapses against existing infra.

Q2 (does it hit the 9 failing clusters): NO. Halo_recv_unblock (6/7 of the remaining gap) is where the r3+r4 grounded-halo workflows landed 0/5 each, with the explicit finding "canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses." An error->single-card lookup is the exact shape that already failed. Worse: halo bugs often pass cslc (microthread-unblock-missing typically compiles fine and produces wrong/hung runtime behavior), so the cslc-stderr pre-processor never fires on the dominant failure class. dsr_queue_fabric_init similarly often manifests as silent data corruption, not a stderr line. Collectives_2d failures CAN produce compile errors, but cluster-gated gotchas already cover the known surface (csl_knowledge_base.py:412+, the three collectives_2d traps from explore_csl).

Q3 (prior art outside this repo): IDE quick-fixes for stable typed languages (Java/TS) do this, but those error taxonomies are versioned and documented; CSL has neither. Nothing comparable for CUDA->assembly or MLIR lowering. The proposal cites no prior art -- yellow flag confirmed.

Q4 (10x smaller version): YES, and arguably mandatory before any of this lands. Take the top 3 error classes from existing run logs, write 3 hand-crafted error->snippet mappings, splice them into the existing debugger_agent's input bundle (NOT as a substitute -- as additional context), re-run the 4-kernel A/B from 2026-06-01 and compare to the historical Q-arm result. ~1 day. If even that doesn't move 1/4 to 2/4, kill it. The full version absolutely should not be built first.

Q5 (lift estimate): Best case +1 kernel on the 15-kernel benchmark (one collectives_2d failure with a clean compile error that happens to match a card). Realistic case 0. Plausible negative case: the regex pulls the wrong card on an ambiguous stderr line and the implementer follows the bad hint past a previously-correct intermediate (the existing debugger A/B already showed this regression mode). Net expected: -3% to 0%.

Author's claim of "negative token delta" is also dubious -- the broad-gotchas block is already cluster-gated to ~11 entries and only the matching cluster's subset injects. The token saving is marginal; the expressivity loss is real.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Skip the regex/lookup-table approach entirely. The 1-day version that's actually worth running: take the existing debugger_agent.py (which already does all this with an LLM), give it cslc dry-compile tool access (the v2 path explicitly deferred in DEBUGGER_AGENT_DESIGN.md lines 105-111), and re-run the 2026-06-01 A/B on the 4 hard kernels. That tests "does grounded diagnostic help" without the brittle taxonomy. If even tool-use grounding doesn't move 1/4 -> 2/4, the bucket-B repair path isn't the bottleneck and a static lookup table won't save it either. Cost: 1 day (cslc-grounding helper already exists in ground_gotcha.py). If it works, expand the tool surface; if it doesn't, stop pursuing this branch and route to the architecture-shape problem that halo_recv_unblock actually is (bucket A re-architect, not bucket B repair).

all_critiques.name: AST-diff guided patch retrieval (post-compile-success, pre-numeric-fail)
all_critiques.critique: The proposal is dead-on-arrival because its premise is empirically false. I checked the bucket distribution in /home/USER/xkernel/code_translation/results/resweep_w1_8attempts_20260603/ (114 verdicted attempts across the 15 W1 kernels): bucket A=4, B=102, C=8, D=0. There is no bucket D in this framework — numeric-fail is folded into C, and even C is only 7% of attempts. Grepping the rationales: 50 mention "hang"/"stall"/"0 bytes", 0 mention "wrong values" or "values mismatch". The "numeric-fail cluster" the proposal targets does not exist in the real failure data. In Laplacian2DHalo specifically (the canonical halo failure), all 8 attempts are bucket B with runtime hangs ("0 bytes received on D2H", "ut_instr conflict", "kernel stall"), not numeric mismatches. A patch-retrieval hint conditioned on "compile-ok-but-wrong-values" fires on a near-empty set, so the expected lift on 6/15 is 0. (1) Is it structurally different from semantic_bridge/translation_facts? Decoration-different, shape-same — all three are "compute a contextual artifact from a corpus, inject it into the implementer/repair prompt as extra prose." translation_facts was 0W/2L/17T over 19 attempts because RAG'd gotchas already cover the surface and any extra prose perturbs. An AST-diff stringified into the prompt is just more prose; the model has to re-parse it back into structure. The "executable-grounded" framing is misleading — the diff is computed from real code, but the model consumes it as text, exactly like the gotchas. (2) Does it address halo_recv_unblock (6/7), dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3), or collectives_2d (2/4)? No. All three clusters fail at compile or with runtime hangs — bucket B, not D. Halo failures are queue-id-out-of-range, microthread-ownership, get_data_task_id-takes-input_queue-not-color, data-tasks-inside-comptime-conditionals. These are exactly the things RAG gotchas + cluster-keyed retrieval already target, and where r2/r3/r4 grounded workflows just produced 0/5 each. (3) Outside prior art: no published CUDA→assembly or MLIR-lowering work uses "AST-diff to passing neighbor injected as prompt hint". The closest analog is nearest-neighbor retrieval (already in your RAG) and constraint-propagation in superoptimizers (which operate on formal IR, not via LLM prose). Yellow flag confirmed. (4) 10x smaller proof? You could grep results/ for any compile-ok-but-numeric-fail attempt in 30 minutes — which is what I just did — and you'd find ~0. The 10x version refutes the proposal rather than proving it. (5) Real expected lift on 6/15: 0. The bucket the proposal targets is empty; the bucket that's full (B, runtime hangs and compile errors) is not addressed. Secondary issue the author flagged ("value depends on volume") is the whole game — they correctly noted "backfill against existing results/ to count bucket-D attempts before committing to build", and that backfill kills it. Build literally that backfill first; don't build the diff tool.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: The actually-useful 10x-smaller version is the backfill the author already proposed as the mitigation: a 1-hour script that scans results/ logs for compile-ok-but-numeric-fail attempts and counts them per cluster. Run it, confirm the count is ~0 (or whatever it actually is), and either kill this proposal or pivot to whatever bucket actually has volume. If the question is "what cheap structural signal could help bucket B (the actual bottleneck)", a more honest variant is: when a runtime hang occurs, AST-diff the wiring topology (color set, queue ids, microthread bindings, fabric_input/output_dsd shapes, task activate/unblock pairings) against the structurally-nearest *layout.csl* example the agent already has access to, and surface as a structured wiring-table (not prose). But even that is at-best a sharper RAG, and RAG-sharpening on halo has already failed three rounds (r2/r3/r4 all 0/5). The honest 10x version is: don't build this; spend the 4-5 engineering days on something that targets bucket B's actual failure modes — e.g., an on-device wiring validator that runs the generated layout.csl through a static reachability check (every input queue has a sender, every task binding's color matches a fabric route) before cslc compilation, and refuses to ship code that statically deadlocks. That's structural, executable-grounded, and addresses the failure mode that actually dominates the data.

all_critiques.name: AST-diff guided patch retrieval (post-compile-success, pre-numeric-fail)
all_critiques.critique:
The proposal is built on a false premise about the pipeline, and the part that survives premise-correction is structurally indistinguishable from translation_facts (which was discarded over 19 attempts, 0W/2L/17T).

PREMISE FALSE: The proposal posits a "compile-succeeds, numeric_check fails, returns garbage" bucket as the hook point. That bucket does not exist as a distinct routing target. numeric_check.py (read it) is a STATIC textual check on whether the generated run.py calls assert_allclose — it is not a runtime correctness gate. W1 uses the REFERENCE run.py (the agent never writes it; compute-leak canary guards this), and that reference already runs np.testing.assert_allclose; a numeric mismatch surfaces as script returncode != 0 and is fed to the reviewer with the full transcript including the AssertionError. The reviewer's existing bucket-A/B/C dispatch already routes these. There is no "bucket D" to hook into; cuda2csl.py has no such code path. The proposal's "add post-compile, pre-numeric-eval hook" is not 4-5 days of work — it's "invent a stage that doesn't exist, then justify the diff that fills it." Author's confidence about a "specific bucket" is unsupported.

VOLUME FALSE: The 9 failing W1 kernels (halo_recv_unblock 6/7, dsr_queue_fabric_init 2/3, collectives_2d 2/4) — the cluster names are wiring-shaped, but the empirical evidence in PROGRESS and in the halo-gotcha rounds r2/r3/r4 shows these failures manifest at COMPILE TIME (drafters fabricate builtins, miss decorators, get DSR types wrong). The "compiles but produces wrong values" bucket the proposal targets is small to empty in the 9-kernel mass. Author's own mitigation says "backfill against existing results to count bucket-D attempts before committing to build" — do that first; you will likely find the bucket is 0-2 of the 9.

STRUCTURALLY = TRANSLATION_FACTS: Yes, "executable-grounded" vs "hand-authored" is a real difference in INPUT, but the OUTPUT shape (structured wiring facts injected into the repair prompt) and the LEVER (implementer reads more structured context, generates better code) are identical. The 19-attempt A/B that killed translation_facts was diagnostic of implementer behavior under heavy context, not of the source of the facts. Calling it "different because executable-grounded" is the same defense semantic_bridge made ("different because it's a mapping table, not gotchas"). The framework has already paid this lesson twice.

NEAREST-NEIGHBOR FRAGILE: The kernels that fail all live in CLUSTERS WHERE PASSING NEIGHBORS ARE SCARCE (1 passing halo: Game of Life; 2 passing collectives_2d). For the cases where the diff would matter most, cosine ≥0.85 over typed features will suppress the hint (no close neighbor). For cases that pass without help, it will fire and add noise. The tight-threshold mitigation acknowledges the failure mode but does not solve it — it converts misdirection into silence on the load-bearing cases.

ANSWERS TO HARD QUESTIONS:
1. Not structurally different from translation_facts (see above). The "failure-conditioned" framing is a routing change, not a representation change; the implementer still gets structured wiring facts and is asked to make them true.
2. Generic — and worse than generic because it targets a bucket (numeric-fail-with-compile-success) that is small or empty in the 9 failing kernels. Halo failures don't compile.
3. Closest prior art (APR neighbor-AST-diff: SequenceR, Recoder; repo-level retrieval in CodeT5+/Copilot) is for repair within a single language with rich code corpora. Nothing I'm aware of demonstrated lift on long-tail HW-DSL translation where the failure is protocol/wiring. MLIR lowering uses rewrite rules, not neighbor diffs. Yellow flag confirmed.
4. Yes — and you should run it before building anything (see smaller_variant).
5. 0-3% absolute on the 15-kernel benchmark (0-1 additional passes). The proposal is most likely a tie. Real risk it goes 0/15 better and adds latency. The expected lift is below noise of the existing hybrid sweep variance.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: DO THIS FIRST, before any build: a 30-minute backfill on results/. Scan every failed attempt in the 15-kernel W1 corpus and label by failure stage: (a) compile-fail, (b) compile-pass + run-fail-AssertionError, (c) compile-pass + run-fail-other (timeout/crash/blocked). The proposal's value is conditional on (b) being non-trivial. If (b) is <20% of the 9-kernel failure mass, kill the proposal. If (b) is meaningful, the cheaper 1-day pilot is NOT AST-diff — it's: take the AssertionError messages from existing bucket-B failures, manually craft a 1-2 line "expected shape vs actual shape" hint, and inject it via the existing reviewer rationale slot for ONE kernel (pick the one bucket-B kernel where you'd expect the most lift). If a hand-tuned hint doesn't flip that kernel in 8 attempts, AST-diff automation won't either. Cost: half a day. Decision in 24 hours instead of a week of engineering.

all_critiques.name: Layout-extracted contract enforcement before LLM call
all_critiques.critique:
The structural-vs-decorative claim does not survive 2 minutes of staring at the existing code.

1) translation_facts.py already extracts exactly the proposal's contract object — from the same files, with the same brace-walker / regex approach. _extract_export_names (lines 156-198), _extract_set_tile_code_fields (lines 136-153), _extract_declared_task_ids (102-111), _extract_color_ids (114-116), _extract_imports (119-133), plus per-import field schemas with hard-coded notes about .NUM_PES vs .dim_size, memcpy queue reservations [0,1] on WSE-3, sys_mod.unblock_cmd_stream vs @unblock(0), etc. The 'parser' is built. The author either didn't read translation_facts.py or didn't recognize they propose to re-extract the same fields. The eng-cost claim of '2-3 days for parser' is wrong — it's a couple of hours of glue at most. That changes the cost-benefit but doesn't fix the more fundamental problem below.

2) The proposed difference vs translation_facts is 'mechanical rejection with a fix-prompt' instead of 'inject facts before generation'. That is not as structurally different as the author thinks. The current bucket-C (contract-fix) repair loop already feeds cslc's 'undeclared identifier'/'unknown field' lines back to the agent. Those error strings carry the EXACT same information ('field .NUM_PES not found in struct S', 'symbol f_run not defined') with cslc's superior precision (line/col, full type info, real symbol table). Replacing them with a regex-derived 'you violated X' is at best a faster, dumber feedback channel. The translation_facts A/B showed the dumber channel adds noise — there's no reason to expect rejection-shaped delivery to invert that result. The author's own risk note ('parser fragility … false-rejects correct code') admits the failure mode: any false positive STRICTLY dominates the current behavior (which lets cslc decide), because a false reject blocks an attempt that would have compiled.

3) The latency argument is misleading. Yes, cslc round-trip is ~30s. But the 8-attempt budget is not currently exhausted by compile-fail spins — the 'reviewer-max-attempts 4→8' task (#33) found marginal lift from attempts 5-8 was 0/14. Attempt budget is not the bottleneck. Saving 30s/attempt is a runtime/cost win, not a pass-rate win. The proposal smuggles cost savings into a pass-rate pitch.

4) Cluster fit. The author claims this targets halo_recv_unblock and dsr_queue_fabric_init. Let's check that against PROGRESS evidence. The halo cluster's failures per the discarded r2/r3/r4 halo gotcha workflows were dominated by 'PE-with-no-work never calls unblock_cmd_stream' and 'recv_color_iq input-queue binding patterns the LLM gets semantically wrong' — runtime deadlocks and binding semantics, NOT 'compute file forgot to declare a name layout exported'. The author concedes this in the risk note ('many halo failures are NOT contract violations but runtime deadlocks'). So even by the author's own reading, this primarily attacks the SMALLEST and ALREADY-LEAST-PROBLEMATIC failure mode in the C-bucket — the one where cslc already gives high-quality feedback.

5) Prior art outside the repo. AST-based contract enforcement around LLM code emission is widespread (typescript type errors fed back, mypy in agentic coding loops). It produces 0-5% lift on translation tasks where the LLM was already getting frequent typed error feedback from the compiler. The unique value props (faster feedback, deterministic) shine when the existing compiler signal is poor — cslc's signal isn't.

6) The 0/2/17 translation_facts A/B is the single most important data point and the proposal does not engage with it seriously. 'Different shape: rejection instead of injection' is a textual difference, not a mechanism-level one. The mechanism that failed was 'redundant ground-truth surface on top of RAG'd gotchas adds perturbation without lift.' Re-deriving the same surface and waving it as a rejection signal does not change the underlying mechanism.

Expected lift: 0 ± 1pt on 15-kernel W1. Possible small negative from false-positive rejection blocking attempts that would have compiled.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: A genuine smaller variant exists and would invalidate the proposal cheaply in a day: skip the parser entirely and just measure, on the existing 8-attempt logs from the 9 failing kernels, how many cslc-error attempts had a 'undeclared identifier' / 'no member named' / 'expected param' message in the first 5 lines. If that count is small (likely — most halo failures are runtime deadlock or wrong-DSD-shape, both of which compile fine), the proposal cannot deliver meaningful lift and shouldn't be built. If it's large (≥40% of failed attempts), THEN the smaller variant is: don't build a parser, just regex the existing cslc stderr for those three error families and inject the layout-side declaration as a follow-up hint — reuses translation_facts.py's extractors verbatim, zero new code beyond a stderr classifier, ships in half a day. This is a strictly cheaper way to test whether mechanical contract feedback helps, without the 'always-on rejection blocks valid code' risk.

all_critiques.name: Layout-extracted contract enforcement before LLM call
all_critiques.critique:
The proposal misdiagnoses where the failing kernels fail, then proposes infrastructure that catches a class of error those kernels do not throw.

1) Structurally different from semantic_bridge / translation_facts? Partially. The author claims "mechanical rejection with code, not prose injection," but operationally this is translation_facts.py with a deterministic gate stapled onto the END instead of the FRONT. The extracted contract object is exactly the same shape as facts already extracted by translation_facts._extract_set_tile_code_fields, _extract_export_names, _extract_imports, _extract_color_ids, _extract_declared_task_ids — that file already does the brace-walking parse the proposal "adds." The only novel piece is the post-hoc DIFF step. So: (a) extraction is rebuilt redundantly; (b) the new bit is just an early-reject gate. If translation_facts couldn't move the needle when injected as a GROUND TRUTH header (0W/2L/17T over 19 attempts), there is no mechanism by which the same facts re-derived and used to reject AFTER generation would. The model failed to USE the facts when they were upstream and authoritative; gating downstream doesn't repair that — it just rephrases "did you read the contract?" as "you violated the contract, please retry," which is what cslc undeclared-identifier errors already do.

2) Does it address the actual bottleneck clusters? Look at progress_summary_20260603.md and the 2026-06-04 halo synthesizer's diagnosis of the 6/7 failing halo_recv_unblock kernels: the five identified missing patterns are (a) static color routes can't rotate roots across iterative steps, (b) punted-fabric / step-0-only handling, (c) per-PE expected_events for a 2x2 mesh with no interior PE, (d) diagonal-neighbor exchange needs two orthogonal sends, (e) DSDs must be over comptime-known concrete arrays. NONE of these is a contract/name violation. All of them produce code that PASSES every check this proposal would implement, compiles successfully, and then deadlocks or computes the wrong answer at runtime. The author's own risk note concedes this: "many halo failures are NOT contract violations but runtime deadlocks." That isn't a side concern — it's 6/6 of the halo failures the cluster diagnosis enumerates. For dsr_queue_fabric_init (Mandelbrot, FFT-1D-2D): queue-reservation collisions ARE in scope, but those failures already surface as cslc errors in <2s (not 30s), and the bucket-C reviewer already routes them. The 30s figure looks inflated — the slow path is the full run.py launch, not cslc itself, which is where genuine compile-clean-but-runtime-deadlock failures live, and the gate catches none of those. For collectives_2d (2/4 fail): translation_facts already had a hard-coded schema for <collectives_2d/pe> calling out the exact NUM_PES-vs-.x.dim_size hazard. Adding a parser to re-detect the same thing in pe.csl output and reject doesn't add information — the model had the right answer in front of it and ignored it.

3) Prior art outside the repo. Type-checking generated code and feeding errors back is widespread (LLM4Code, self-debug, type-guided sampling). The closest published evidence — Chen et al "Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug," and the various compiler-feedback retry loops in SWE-Bench solvers — shows lift mostly on cases where the generator was ALREADY close and just needed a syntactic nudge. None of the literature shows lift on the failure mode that dominates here: semantic deadlocks in a domain-specific concurrent IR where the compiler successfully accepts the wrong program. So: the prior art exists, but for the wrong failure class. Yellow flag confirmed.

4) The "saves 30s + reviewer call" framing is dubious. Per the discarded experiment notes, reviewer-max-attempts 4→8 marginal gain was 0/14 — the budget is NOT the bottleneck. So a faster turn does not buy more wins, it just burns the same 8 attempts faster. The author hand-waves "frees budget for the genuinely-hard semantic failures," but the 4-attempt budget already lands on those failures and stalls. Faster failure on contract violations doesn't unstick the semantic ones.

5) Risk the author understates: parser fragility against the 28 reference layouts is well-controlled, but false-rejection of CORRECT-but-stylistically-novel pe.csl is the real hazard. The contract check assumes layout.csl is fully authoritative about every field name pe.csl must declare, but the model legitimately uses concat_structs, comptime field renames, and conditional exports that the regex won't track. The mitigation ("test against 28 references") only proves the parser accepts the reference STYLE — it does not prove the parser accepts arbitrary valid CSL that a model might generate. This is the same trap that bit r2/r3 halo drafter (fabricated builtins) — the gate becomes a stylistic constraint, not a correctness constraint, and shaves off correct generations.

Expected lift: 0-1 kernel of 15. The plausibly-addressable target is one or two dsr_queue_fabric_init compile-time errors (Mandelbrot or FFT-1D-2D), where deterministic rejection might be marginally cleaner than cslc's error message — but cslc already gives that error, and the reviewer has access to it. Realistic outcome: speeds up the failing attempt loop without producing new wins. Cost: 2-3 engineering days plus the perpetual maintenance cost of a regex parser tracking an evolving DSL, against translation_facts.py which is already 453 LOC of similar code that was deprecated for not moving the metric. This is rebuilding the deprecated thing with a sharper edge pointed at the wrong target.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: A 10x smaller, decisive proof in under a day: instead of building a parser and a diff and a reject gate, scan the existing W1 failure logs in results/ for the 9 failing kernels and CLASSIFY each failed-attempt cslc error. If >=4 of the 9 kernels have at least one attempt that died on a name/contract mismatch caught by reading just layout.csl, the proposal has a target. If <2 do (which the synthesizer findings predict), kill it before writing code. Even faster: take the already-extracted translation_facts YAML for the 6 failing halo kernels (one shell command — translation_facts.render_facts_block exists), diff against the FAILED pe.csl outputs from the latest hybrid sweep run, and count how many failures were caught by a name-binding violation vs how many were compile-clean-but-deadlock. Predicted ratio: ~1:6. The half-day audit kills the proposal before the 2-3 day build. A more interesting tiny variant: take the most-failed kernel (Cholesky or Game-of-Life), hand-write the contract object for it, hand-feed a known-failing pe.csl into a 50-line diff script, and see whether the diff produces a message the reviewer hadn't already received from cslc — if it does not, the proposal is decoration.

all_critiques.name: cslc-in-the-loop with isolated per-function compile cells
all_critiques.critique:
This proposal is STRUCTURALLY different from semantic_bridge/translation_facts (it's execution-grounded rather than prompt-decoration), and the author correctly identifies the closest prior art: halo-gotcha r4. But the author's own risk note understates how badly r4 generalizes here. r4 failed because canonical CSL patterns are cross-cell composed — exactly the failure mode the halo cluster exhibits in W1. The 6/7 halo failures aren't "one local line wrong in an otherwise good 200-line file"; they're systemic: wrong receive-task ID layout coupled to wrong color routing in layout-imported params coupled to wrong DSD wavelet config. Per the cluster-keyed knowledge entries in csl_knowledge_base.py (lines 661-671, 753-768), the halo gotchas are about *interaction* between init, advance, and microthread sites. Decomposing into 4 sequential cslc-validated cells gives the model the ILLUSION of progress (each cell compiles in its stub harness) while the cross-cell coupling that actually fails in the full file remains undetected until the final whole-file compile — at which point you're back to the same single-shot error the current pipeline already produces, just after spending 4x the wall time.

Concretely against the three failing clusters: (1) **halo_recv_unblock** failures are about `@block`/`@unblock` placement relative to recv tasks, which spans the task-binding cell AND the task-body cell AND the helper-fn cell. The stubbed harness will accept each in isolation. (2) **dsr_queue_fabric_init** failures are about queue-id / DSR-id / fabric-route triple-binding across layout.csl (which is given) and pe.csl (which is generated). The proposal validates pe.csl chunks against the REAL layout.csl, so this is the one cluster where it might help — but the failure mode here is "model picks wrong queue IDs because it doesn't read layout.csl carefully," which is a prompt/attention problem, not a per-cell-compile problem. (3) **collectives_2d** failures are import-signature mismatches that show up in the very first cell (the @import_module line) — single-shot cslc already catches these on attempt 1; the bottleneck isn't error locality, it's that the model re-fabricates the wrong signature even when shown the cslc error.

The framework history strongly suggests this will land in the 0W/2L/17T zone like translation_facts: every "feed cslc errors back to model" experiment in this repo has produced LLM responses that fabricate fixes which compile-by-accident or perturb something else. The reviewer→implementer repair path ALREADY does cslc-in-the-loop at file granularity; the difference here is granularity, not principle, and r4 showed that smaller granularity makes the cross-cell coupling problem WORSE not better. The 4x wall-time cost is real and the "2-3x fewer attempts" assumption is unsupported — that's the same optimism budget that translation_facts burned.

Also: the bottleneck on the 9 failing W1 kernels per the user's own data is NOT "syntax error in line 30 wastes the file." If it were, attempts 5-8 would have a non-zero pass rate (since they get fresh starts with the same model + same knowledge). Marginal pass rate on attempts 5-8 was 0/14 (TaskID 33 result). The bottleneck is that the model lacks a working mental model of the cross-cell idiom, and per-cell grounding doesn't add that mental model — it just adds friction.

One thing that would change my mind: if the author can produce, from the existing failure corpus, even 2 cases where the final pe.csl has exactly one local block that's wrong and the rest is correct (verified by mechanically replacing that block with a known-good version and observing the file compiles + passes the W1 numerical check). If such cases exist, this proposal addresses them; if they don't (and I suspect they don't, because halo failures are coupled), the proposal is dead-on-arrival before implementation.

Prior art outside the repo: I know of no published code-translation system that uses per-function incremental compilation against stubbed harnesses as the primary correctness loop. The closest analogues — Copilot's iterative-edit loop, AlphaCode's compile-feedback, MetaGPT's code-cell agents — all operate at file granularity for the same reason this proposal will struggle: language-level coupling makes per-function isolation leak.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Yes, and the author should be required to do this BEFORE the 1-2 week build. 1-day version: pick the 3 halo failure cases that produced the cleanest single-error cslc output on the last hybrid sweep. For each, manually decompose pe.csl into the 4 proposed cells, manually stub the others, and run cslc on each cell in the layout.csl-derived harness. Answer two questions: (a) does cslc actually emit a localized, actionable error for the cell that contains the real bug? (b) when you hand the model `{partial code + stderr_tail + only the bad cell}`, does it produce a fix that survives the full-file compile? If (a) is no for 2/3 cases — kill the proposal. If (a) is yes but (b) is no — the bottleneck isn't error locality, kill the proposal. If both are yes for 2/3 cases — build the smallest version that handles ONLY the dsr_queue_fabric_init cluster (the 2/3 failure cluster where layout.csl coupling is the documented failure mode) and gate everything else on results there. Total: <1 day for the manual experiment, ~3 days for the cluster-scoped build if it passes. Skip the halo and collectives_2d clusters entirely until dsr_queue evidence is in.

all_critiques.name: cslc-in-the-loop with isolated per-function compile cells
all_critiques.critique:
Hard problems with the proposal, in order of severity:

1) Q1 (structural novelty): YES it is structurally different from semantic_bridge / translation_facts — those were "more prompt context before a single shot," this is "execution gate between sub-shots." Credit for that. But the actually-comparable prior art is HALO-GOTCHA r4 ("cslc-grounded + canonical hints"), which IS execution-in-the-loop, and which the author explicitly cites as the worst-case isomorph. r4 lost 0/5 because canonical patterns wouldn't fit minimal harnesses. The proposed harness builder is more ambitious (auto-derives from layout.csl) but inherits the same disease: cross-block constraints in a real CSL file are not local. Inspection of kernels/Laplacian2D-Halo/CSL/pe.csl confirms this — input_queues at line 61-64, task_ids at 67-70, DSDs at 118-138, task bodies at 142-203, and bind_local_task at 243 ALL reference each other. The author's 4-stage decomposition cannot place these into separately compilable cells; any split that compiles in stages will also compile as a whole.

2) Q2 (bottleneck specificity): The proposal is GENERIC, not targeted. Halo (6/7 fails) failures are not "syntax error in line 30 of an otherwise-correct file" — per existing post-mortems they are SEMANTIC/COMPOSITIONAL: missing unblock_cmd_stream coupling, wrong color/route topology in layout vs receiver expectations, microthread/queue ID mismatches across PE roles, missing @rpc binding before fabric activity. Those errors only surface when the WHOLE program runs against the layout, which is what the existing single cslc already does. dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fails) is by definition about queue+fabric coupling across the file — splitting it into cells is moving in the wrong direction. collectives_2d (2/4 fails) failures involve the 2D collectives module's comptime init order; per-block cslc will mostly say "unused param" or "init not reached" and not catch the real bug. So this proposal addresses approximately ZERO of the three failing clusters' root causes.

3) Q3 (prior art outside): Iterative compile-driven code generation exists (e.g., Self-Edit / Reflexion / "compile-and-fix" loops in HumanEval-style tasks; LLM4Decompile uses round-trip compile checks; recent Codex/SWE work uses test-driven repair). NONE of these decompose a single file into independently-compiled cells with stubbed neighbors. The closest match is incremental REPL evaluation in dynamic languages (Python notebooks, Lisp), which works precisely because those languages have stub-friendly semantics. CSL doesn't — it's a static comptime-heavy language whose whole point is cross-PE / cross-color resolution at link time. Yellow flag confirmed: nobody has shown this works for a comptime-static fabric language.

4) Q4 (10x smaller version): YES, and this is the real verdict. A 1-day MVP: take the 6 failing halo kernels' BEST single-shot Sonnet output, manually split them into 4 stages, run ground_gotcha-style harness compiles, and count how many stages report a USEFUL error (one that would let you re-prompt the model for just that block and converge). If that hit-rate is <50% on stages 2-4, the full project is dead-on-arrival. This is a 1-day experiment that should be run BEFORE the 1-2 week build.

5) Q5 (expected lift): On the 9 failing kernels, generously assume the proposal converts 1 of the 6 halo failures into a pass (the simplest one, where a local missing unblock_cmd_stream gets caught early). Net: 7/15 = 47%, +1pt over baseline. Pessimistic case: 0pt — the stubbed harness errors are noise (unused-symbol, partial-init complaints, as author flags), and the FINAL whole-file cslc that the author retains as safety net is what was running anyway. Either way, the lift is BELOW the noise floor of a 15-kernel benchmark (a 1-kernel swing is ~6.7pp, within rerun variance). And the 4x wall-time hit makes the iteration loop materially slower, which compounds against the team's ability to run sweeps.

6) Hidden cost not in the author's accounting: maintenance. The stage decomposer must understand CSL syntax well enough to (a) identify @get_input_queue / @get_local_task_id / @get_color decls as "must-be-in-stage-2," (b) decide which DSD decls go in stage-2 vs stage-3, (c) handle every variation the model emits (which is unbounded — see the 8-attempts-per-kernel variance). This is a custom partial parser of an evolving DSL and will be a long-tail bug magnet. translation_facts had a similar regex-extractor scope and produced 0W/2L/17T; this is the same shape of "structural surgery on model output" gamble.

What would be more promising than this: (a) actually port one of the 6 failing halo kernels by HAND to find the ONE compositional gotcha that catches all 6 — then RAG it cluster-keyed, which has been the only thing that produces wins; (b) run a finer-grained planner that explicitly decides "halo topology first, then queues, then bodies" as PROSE constraints, not as compile cells — this gives the same intent at zero infra cost; (c) the unspoken alternative is CUDA-SIDE IR (typed AST or MLIR-style multi-level), which the author correctly notes was deferred — a CUDA AST with classified primitives (shared mem ↔ ?, __syncthreads ↔ ?, block dims ↔ rectangle) at least addresses the analyzer's habit of mis-identifying CUDA patterns, which is upstream of every other failure mode. Per-block compile cells operate downstream of the actual root cause.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: 1-day MVP that decides go/no-go BEFORE the 1-2 week build: take the 6 best Sonnet attempts on halo failures, manually slice each into the proposed 4 stages, stub the missing stages, run cslc on each cell, and measure two things: (a) what fraction of cells compile cleanly only because cross-cell constraints were stubbed away (false-negative rate for the gating harness), and (b) what fraction of cell-local cslc errors point to the actual bug that single-shot also surfaces (i.e., are we gaining ANY localization). If (a) > 50% or (b) < 50%, abandon. Even smaller: skip the cells entirely and just ship "compile-after-task-binding-only" — emit the file up through @bind_local_task / @export_symbol, cslc, then emit the rest. One bisection point catches the 80% case (color/queue/task-ID mismatch, which is the halo cluster's main idiom failure) at 10% of the infra cost. If that single-bisection version doesn't move the needle, the 4-stage version definitely won't.

all_critiques.name: Self-consistency vote with kernel-level execution oracle
all_critiques.critique:
Structurally this is the existing best-of-N (task #21 already wired through cuda2csl.py:2215-2417) re-pointed from W2 angles to W1 implementer fanout, plus a "structural-signature consensus" extractor that feeds back to the architect. Both halves have prior-art problems in this repo and in the literature:

(1) The vote-and-merge half collapses to translation_facts in disguise. The proposal says feed "modal signature" of @export_symbol/task-binding/imports back to architect as "consensus shape." That is exactly what translation_facts F1-F5 (tasks #46-50) did with regex-extracted CSL contract surface as YAML — 0W/2L/17T over 19 attempts, ripped out R1-R5. The author's own risk note flags this collapse mode. The fact that the signature here is computed by majority vote across 4 samples rather than regex over 1 doesn't change the shape: it's still structured strings injected into the next prompt slot, and the implementer's failure mode on halo_recv_unblock is not "didn't know which exports to declare" — it's "wrote unblock_cmd_stream in the wrong branch or omitted it entirely." Export names ARE NOT the discriminating signal for that bug class. Sorted @export_symbol lists will be identical across all 4 failing halo samples because they all declare the same surface and all forget the same unblock call inside compute.

(2) The execution-oracle half is genuinely free signal but the proposal misreads what the oracle says. With current 6/15 pass at K=1, naive math says K=4 union ceiling is at most ~1 − (9/15)^4 ≈ 87% IF samples were independent. They aren't. The 6/15 = 40% baseline is already "Sonnet+Opus union ceiling" per the framing — meaning two distinct models at T=0 hit the same set. Cranking T=1 on one model is a much weaker diversity lever than swapping models, and the halo cluster specifically skips Opus per empirical evidence, so the easy diversity axis is closed. The 9 failing kernels fail because of cluster-specific mechanical bugs that the model deterministically gets wrong (queue id, unblock placement, dim_params shape). Temperature noise around a wrong attractor does not pull a sample into the correct basin — it scatters within the wrong basin. Real expected lift is 1-2 kernels (7/15 or 8/15), not the implied union ceiling.

(3) The "halo failures have inter-sample variation in WHICH PE branch forgets unblock_cmd_stream" claim is unsubstantiated and probably false. The halo gotcha A1-B1 effort (tasks #57-65) ran r2/r3/r4 LLM drafters and the failure mode was that drafters consistently fabricated the SAME wrong builtins/syntax, not that they spread across many wrong answers. That's evidence FOR mode collapse under sampling, AGAINST the inter-sample-variation premise.

(4) Reviewer-max-attempts 4→8 already proved 0/14 marginal pass-rate from attempts 5-8 (task #33). Budget is not the bottleneck. K=4 candidates × halved attempt budget (4 instead of 8) is the same total LLM spend but concentrates it in attempts 1-4 where the marginal gain has not been measured — could be positive but small. Halving attempts removes the bucket-routed repair sequence (A/B/C cycles) which IS where existing wins land.

(5) Prior art: AlphaCode used massive self-consistency (1M samples) on competitive programming; the analogous trick for code translation (Codex/CodeT5 papers) shows diminishing returns past K=10 on syntactic tasks and basically no help on semantic correctness for low-resource target languages — which CSL is. None of the published MLIR-lowering or CUDA-PTX work uses self-consistency voting; they use type-directed search or rule-based rewriting precisely because mechanical bugs don't average out across samples.

(6) Engineering risk understated. _singularity_gate in benchmark_csl.py serializes cslc invocations. K=4 parallel benchmarks won't fit the existing shim; you'd need to either parallelize the gate (real work, can race the SDK lockfile) or stagger (loses the wall-time argument and makes K=4 take 4x longer end-to-end). The 3-5 day estimate is optimistic by 2x.

Against the three failure clusters specifically:
- halo_recv_unblock (6/7): mechanical bug, vote will not surface it.
- dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3): mechanical bug, same.
- collectives_2d (2/4): mostly already addressed by the existing cluster-gated gotchas; remaining failures are subtle (dim_params vs explicit dsr arrays). Vote won't differentiate.

The proposal is generic "more context" injected via a new aggregation step, which is the same failure mode as the two discarded experiments. Combine that with the singularity-gate parallelism problem and the unsubstantiated diversity premise and the realistic outcome is 6/15 → 7/15 at 2x token cost and a week of engineering.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: A 1-day pilot can falsify (or salvage) this for cheap: run K=4 at T=1 on the 9 failing kernels with the EXISTING single-attempt path (no consensus, no plumbing). Just N independent calls, benchmark each, count how many kernels have at least one passing sample. This tests the union-ceiling hypothesis directly. If it's not at least 9/15 → 11/15 in that pure-oracle setting, the consensus-extraction layer cannot rescue it and the proposal dies. If it IS 11/15+, then voting/architect-feedback is worth building. This avoids the singularity-gate work (serialize sequentially for the pilot — 4x wall time on 9 kernels is one overnight run, not engineering). A second 1-day variant: keep K=1 but swap the diversity axis from temperature to PROMPT — give the implementer 4 different reduced prompt frames (CSL-builtin-heavy, CUDA-mapping-heavy, layout-first, contract-first) and union the passes. That probes whether prompt-frame diversity beats temperature diversity, which the existing semantic_bridge/translation_facts results already weakly suggest it does not.

all_critiques.name: Self-consistency vote with kernel-level execution oracle
all_critiques.critique:
Hard answers to the five questions:

(1) Structurally different from semantic_bridge / translation_facts? Partly. The K-parallel sampling + pass-rate gate is a new mechanism — that part is novel and is the strongest piece of the proposal. But the *consensus-signature feedback loop* (the part doing real work when 0/K pass, which IS the halo situation 6/7 of the time) is the same shape as translation_facts: regex/AST extract a structural skeleton → inject as extra context → architect respin. translation_facts had the *grounded* contract (from cslc) and still went 0W/2L/17T. A modal-vote skeleton extracted from 4 wrong samples is a strictly weaker signal than the cslc-grounded one that already failed.

(2) Does it address one of the three failure clusters specifically? No. The proposal is generic "more samples + structural feedback." The author's own risk note correctly identifies that halo failures are *systematic* (the natural-language reading of CUDA misleads all samples the same way) — and halo is 6/9 of the remaining failures. The consensus mechanism gates on "at least 1 candidate passes OR all 4 share the same skeleton"; on halo today, neither branch fires usefully because (a) 0/K likely pass and (b) skeletons probably DO agree but the bug is inside `task_c() void { ... }`, not in @export_symbol set. dsr_queue_fabric_init has a similar issue: the failure is in *which* queue ID gets bound to which microthread, not in the existence of the binding.

(3) Prior art? Self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022) and CodeT (Chen et al. 2022) get 2-5pt lift on HumanEval-class problems where the model is already in the >50% pass range, with K=8-20. AlphaCode used K~10^5-10^6 with execution-based filtering and got real lift only because the test oracle was strong and the sampling budget was huge. On 6/15 = 40% pass, long-tail mechanical failures, K=4, the published lift curves predict <2pt. No public work shows execution-vote feedback (the "feed consensus to next architect" loop) outperforming simple pick-the-passing-one on code translation of this scale.

(4) 10x smaller proof? Yes — and it should run FIRST as a kill criterion: K=2 with identical model/temperature on 3 halo kernels. Extract structural signatures. If they already agree across samples (likely — models aren't that stochastic on top-level structure at 9000-token prompt scale), the consensus signal is uninformative and the proposal is dead before the consensus-feedback eng cost is paid. Half a day, not 1.

(5) Realistic lift on 6/15 baseline? +1 kernel (7/15 = 47%) at best, with meaningful risk of regression because Sonnet+Opus union ceiling on these 15 is already 6/15 — the hybrid sweep is ALREADY running 2 maximally-diverse samples (different model families, which is a stronger diversity axis than same-model T=1.0 sampling) and that ceiling didn't break.

Other specific problems:
- "K parallel benchmarks fit in same wall window" is wrong. The singularity gate (XKERNEL_SINGULARITY_GATE=1) serializes cslc+cs_python via filelock to avoid wedging the SSH shim to user-node-1 — benchmark_csl.py:36-101 documents this explicitly. K=4 benchmarks take K*30-60s wall, not 30s. Real cost is ~4x LLM + ~4x wall on the benchmark stage, not "halve budget to 4 attempts."
- The "attempt budget: K candidates count as 1 or K?" question in the cost section is load-bearing and unresolved. If K, total token spend is 4x and you halve attempts so possibly net wash on tokens but lose 4x retry diversity over the 8-attempt loop (which the data says ALSO doesn't help past attempt 4 — task #33 already showed marginal pass-rate from attempts 5-8 was 0/14). If 1, budget is 4x with no rollback.
- "When no candidate passes, vote on the most common skeleton" — modal voting on K=4 same-model samples on the failing halo kernels almost certainly returns a unanimous skeleton because top-level structure (export names, task ID bindings) is the LEAST stochastic part of LLM output at T=1.0; the bug is in the body of `task_c() void { ... unblock_cmd_stream }`, where voting has no signal. This is the dominant failure mode and the proposal has zero mechanism for it.
- The hybrid sweep is already a 2-sample best-of-N across MODELS (Sonnet then Opus), which is a richer diversity axis than same-model T=1.0 sampling. Adding K=4 of one model on top of that is a smaller marginal step than the proposal frames it as.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Yes, and it should run as a kill-criterion before any eng work: K=2 same-model T=1.0 sample on 3 halo kernels (Cholesky, Game-of-Life, Residual). No consensus mechanism. Just: (a) does either sample pass when one alone didn't? (b) extract @export_symbol set + task-id bindings from both and diff them — if they're identical across samples on these failing kernels, then "structural consensus" has zero discriminative power and the full proposal is dead. Cost: ~half a day, no orchestrator changes (just a shell loop calling the existing translator twice with --temperature flag added to llm_complete). Decision rule: ship full proposal only if at least 1/3 kernels gets a pass from K=2 that K=1 didn't, AND signatures actually diverge across samples on the failing kernels. Predict: pass-rate change 0/3, signatures unanimous — kills the proposal cheap.

all_critiques.name: Reverse translation as automatic differentiator
all_critiques.critique:
The proposal is built on a load-bearing factual error about what csl2cuda.py actually is. I just inspected it. csl2cuda is NOT a deterministic structural extractor — it is itself an LLM agent (CSL2CUDAOrchestrator, run_phase_a "analyse CSL", run_phase_b "translate & verify"; uses _llm_call throughout). It produces free-form CUDA prose with prose comments like "Algorithm: y[i][j][k] = west*x[i-1][j][k] + ..." (see results/csl2cuda/run_20260319_150329/7-Point Stencil.cu). The proposal's central claim — that the diff would be "execution-grounded, not the model's beliefs" — is false. A CUDA-orig vs CUDA-back diff is a diff between two LLM beliefs about the algorithm: the implementer's CSL→latent and csl2cuda's CSL→CUDA. This is exactly the same shape as semantic_bridge (LLM prose mapping) wearing a roundtrip costume.

Worse, csl2cuda's own success matrix on the latest run (run_20260319_150329) is 13/21 — and the 8 failures are: BiCGSTAB, Cholesky, FFT 1D-2D, GEMM Collectives 2D, GEMM, GEMV, Preconditioned CG, Residual. That set massively overlaps the W1 failure corpus and contains EVERY iterative solver the proposal specifically claims to help (BiCGSTAB, PCG). On the exact kernels where you'd fire bucket-D, csl2cuda is most likely to either fail outright or hallucinate a plausible-but-wrong reverse, which then poisons the repair prompt. The proposal's mitigation ("gate on csl2cuda producing parseable CUDA") is too weak — parseable garbage is the dominant failure mode for LLM translators, not parse failure.

Q1 (structural difference from semantic_bridge / translation_facts): No. All three are "inject more LLM-generated text into the implementer's prompt before retry." semantic_bridge injected prose primitive maps; translation_facts injected YAML facts; this injects a prose diff of two LLM CUDA renderings. Same shape (free-form context dump before the implementer), same failure mode (model acknowledges, re-emits same wrong CSL — the author flags this explicitly and waves it away). The "execution-grounded" claim would justify the difference, but csl2cuda isn't execution; only its output's compile+run is, and that compile happens on the back-translated CUDA, not the candidate CSL — it tells you nothing about whether the CSL is correct.

Q2 (does it address the dominant cluster): No. Author admits it doesn't address halo_recv_unblock (6/7 failing) or dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 failing), which together are 8 of the 9 W1 failures. The "iterative solver W2 0% gap" framing is also weak: those kernels have a KNOWN ROOT CAUSE already in memory (project_power_method_instrumentation.md — run.py uses a host-side Python RPC loop, the metric measures host↔device sync, not on-device compute). No reverse-translation diff will move that needle; you need to rewrite run.py to launch the loop on-device. The proposal targets a phantom bug.

Q3 (prior art for code translation): I'm not aware of any production code-translation system using LLM-roundtrip-diff as a repair signal. Real systems that do roundtrip verification (decompilers, transpiler test oracles, MLIR round-trip-tests) compare AGAINST DETERMINISTIC GROUND-TRUTH ARTIFACTS — original IR vs reparsed IR, byte-for-byte — not against an LLM's free-form re-rendering. The closest analog is self-consistency in chain-of-thought, which gives 2-5% on reasoning but has not been shown to help code generation where the failure is syntactic/semantic-precise. Yellow flag confirmed.

Q4 (10x smaller PoC): Yes and you should do it before any bucket-D engineering. Take 3 of the 8 failing W1 kernels. Run csl2cuda manually on the best failed implementer candidate from your last sweep. Hand-diff against the source CUDA. Ask: does the diff name a fix you couldn't have gotten from the existing stderr+failure_reason?
