My prediction: on halo kernels, csl2cuda will fail or produce CUDA that doesn't even encode the fabric routing concept, so the diff will be noise. On iterative solvers, the diff will say "loop bounds differ" or similar surface-level things you already know. Cost: 4 hours, not 1 week.

Q5 (expected lift): On the 15-kernel benchmark from 6/15: I estimate +0 to +1 (0–7pt), with non-trivial risk of -1 if the noisy diff misroutes a previously-borderline-passing bucket-B repair. Author's "addresses W2 iterative gap" claim is undermined by the memory note that the iterative gap is a host-RPC measurement artifact, not a translation bug.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: The 1-day PoC described in Q4 above is the right next step before any bucket-D engineering: manually run csl2cuda on 3 failed W1 candidates (one halo, one DSR, one collectives_2d), hand-diff against source CUDA, ask whether the diff names a fix you couldn't get from existing signals. If even 1 of 3 yields actionable text, escalate to a minimal bucket-D wired only for the runtime-pass-but-wrong-values case (not generic compile-fail). If 0 of 3, kill it. A smaller-but-different angle that captures the actual intent: instead of csl2cuda roundtrip, use the existing CUDA reference as a structural skeleton — extract loop nests / reductions / array-access patterns from the CUDA via tree-sitter (deterministic, not LLM) and present them as a structural CONSTRAINT to the implementer ("your CSL must implement N reductions over dim 1; the candidate implements 1"). That's execution-grounded in a way the proposal claims but doesn't deliver, since the CUDA AST is ground truth, not an LLM rendering. Two days of work, no new LLM provider, no dependency on csl2cuda's flaky output.

all_critiques.name: Reverse translation as automatic differentiator
all_critiques.critique:
Going through the five hard questions:

(1) Structurally different from semantic_bridge / translation_facts? Only partially. All three inject extra text into the implementer's repair prompt. The author argues the diff is "execution-grounded" because it comes from a real reverse pass, but the consumer is still an LLM reading prose and choosing what to act on. translation_facts also injected real, machine-extracted, structurally-grounded data (regex'd from the actual CSL builtins list) and still went 0W/2L/17T because the implementer didn't need a new substrate — it needed the missing idiom. The shape mismatch isn't "prose vs structured", it's "knowledge vs perturbation". CUDA-back diffs are knowledge of a different sort but they're still arriving as token-stream context to a model that already has the original CUDA, the design.md, and the failure transcript in scope. The new signal has to outcompete those for attention. That is exactly the failure mode the bridge/facts experiments hit.

(2) Does it address one of the 9 failing W1 kernels' clusters? The author admits no — halo_recv_unblock (6 fails), dsr_queue_fabric_init (2 fails), collectives_2d (2 fails) are all idiom/contract failures, not semantic-arithmetic gaps. Reverse-CUDA diff cannot say "you forgot @unblock on the recv task" because the original CUDA also doesn't have @unblock — that's a CSL-only concept that disappears in csl2cuda. So the proposal targets at most the W2 iterative-solver gap (CG/PCG/BiCGSTAB/Power_Method, all 0% improvement) plus an unknown small slice of W1. But MEMORY.md flags that the iterative-solver W2 gap is host-RPC-bounded — cycles_send measures host↔device sync, NOT on-device compute. No semantic-diff signal will change that; the fix is rewriting run.py to launch the loop on-device. So this proposal addresses a phantom: the iterative-solver failures aren't semantic translation bugs at all.

(3) Prior art? Back-translation as a training signal exists in NMT (Sennrich 2016) and in some code-translation literature (TransCoder used back-translation in training, not as a per-attempt repair signal). I'm not aware of anyone using single-shot reverse-pass diffing as an inference-time repair channel for low-level systems code (CUDA→SASS, MLIR lowering, etc.). The absence of cited prior art at this complexity tier is exactly the yellow flag the author asked us to note.

(4) 10x smaller proof? Yes, and the author should be required to run it first: on the 4 iterative-solver kernels and the 2 collectives_2d failures, manually run csl2cuda on the last failed attempt of each, diff against the original CUDA, and check whether the diff actually names a fix-shaped gap. This is a half-day of work with zero new code. If 0/6 of those diffs would have plausibly fixed the bug, kill the proposal. I strongly suspect the result will be 0/6 or 1/6 — csl2cuda is a noisy translator (it has its own LLM call, its own failure modes) and the diff between "two LLM-generated CUDA versions of the same algorithm" will be dominated by stylistic variance, not the load-bearing semantic gap.

(5) Realistic lift on 6/15 baseline? Halo cluster (6 fails) and DSR cluster (2 fails) get zero benefit by construction. The 2 collectives_2d fails might catch a benefit if the gap is genuinely loop-bound or reduction-op mismatch (rare in this corpus). Most plausible outcome: +0 or +1 wins, with non-trivial risk of regressions on currently-passing kernels via prompt bloat. Net estimated lift: 0-2pp (i.e., 6/15 → 6/15 or 7/15 in expectation). The "+1 medium LLM call per repair" cost is the lesser concern; the dominant cost is engineering time being spent on the wrong bottleneck while the actual halo/DSR cluster gap goes unaddressed.

Additional load-bearing concern the author undersells: csl2cuda.py was built for CSL→CUDA forward translation as a separate project, not as a verifier. It uses its own LLM call, which means a malformed CSL candidate will produce malformed CUDA, and the diff will hallucinate gaps that don't exist. The author's "gate on parseable CUDA" mitigation doesn't help — parseable garbage CUDA is the failure mode, not unparseable. You'd need a near-deterministic CSL→CUDA pass (clang-style AST lowering) for the diff to mean anything, and that doesn't exist in this repo.

Pattern-match to prior failures: this is shape-isomorphic to translation_facts. Both said "we have structured information the implementer doesn't have; inject it as a prompt block." Both reasoned about the mechanism plausibly. translation_facts went 0W/2L/17T. The author's own risk note acknowledges the "same-shape-as-semantic_bridge risk." That should be disqualifying absent a sharper differentiator than "the diff is more specific."
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Half-day manual study, no code: take the last failed candidate from each of the 4 iterative-solver kernels + 2 collectives_2d fails + 1 representative halo fail (7 cases). Run csl2cuda on each by hand. Diff against the original CUDA. For each diff, ask: (a) does the diff actually name the bug? (b) would it have been an effective repair signal? Decision rule: ship only if ≥4/7 diffs name a fix-shaped gap AND ≥1 names the halo bug (because halo is the dominant cluster). Cost: half a day of human time, zero LLM spend, zero new code. I predict 0/7 or 1/7 and a kill decision. If by some chance it hits 4/7, the engineering investment is justified — but do the cheap experiment first. The author should never get to the "1 week engineering" line without this gate.

all_critiques.name: Iterative deepening: 1-PE prototype, then scale
all_critiques.critique:
This proposal is structurally a variant of "give the implementer another artifact before the hard step," which is the exact shape of the discarded semantic_bridge and translation_facts experiments. The novel twist — the artifact is generated by an earlier LLM phase rather than curated — is strictly WEAKER, not stronger: the model now conditions on its own (possibly idiosyncratic) prior output instead of canonical material like csl_builtins.yaml. translation_facts went 0W/2L/17T over 19 attempts and was killed; expect similar.

Three concrete failure-mode mismatches with the documented bottlenecks:

1) Halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail) failure surface is **inside the 1-PE→multi-PE delta**, not inside the compute. The cluster name is literal: failures are about `@block`/`@unblock` on recv tasks, expected-count tracking, color routing in layout.csl, and the queue/fabric init sequence. None of this exists in a 1x1 rectangle. A passing 1-PE compute file teaches the model nothing about the canonical halo idiom — which is exactly what halo gotcha r4 (cslc-grounded + canonical hints) tried to inject directly and got 0/5 on. If feeding canonical patterns through the prompt didn't land, feeding a passing-but-unrelated 1-PE compute file as "context" will land less. The author's own risk note flags this; it should be the headline, not the footnote.

2) The 1-PE shim generator reads layout.csl to derive the stripped version. But layout.csl is **already in the agent's window** under the W1 firewall (pe.csl is hidden, layout.csl + run.py + commands.sh are visible). The proposal does not add information; it removes information (the fabric colors) for one phase, then restores it for the next. Removing information then re-adding it is not the same as injecting new information.

3) The 7pt-Stencil and Single-Tile-Matvec precedents cited as "compute-only works" are existence proofs the agent can do compute-only kernels — NOT evidence that a 1-PE warmup helps with multi-PE kernels. The cited 7pt-Stencil 2129→1076 win is a W2 OPTIMIZATION on already-translated CSL, not a W1 translation success enabled by a compute-first decomposition. Conflating these is the same shape of evidence misuse the framework has been bitten by before.

Question-by-question:
Q1: NOT structurally different from semantic_bridge / translation_facts. All three say "stuff more relevant context in front of the implementer." This one's context is dynamic (generated) instead of static, but dynamic-from-LLM is the weakest form of context (max risk of perturbation, min ground truth). Score same shape, lower content.
Q2: Targets halo_recv_unblock and collectives_2d nominally. In practice addresses neither — the failures are in the connective tissue this proposal explicitly strips out for the 1-PE phase. dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fail) is even worse: that's about queue ID allocation across PEs, has no 1-PE form at all.
Q3: No prior art cited in proposal. Multi-stage code lowering (MLIR, CUDA→PTX) does NOT use "translate to simpler target first, then scale" — it uses progressive lowering where each stage is a strict subset of the next. The 1-PE→multi-PE relation is NOT subset; it's a different program (different colors, different tasks, different control flow). The analogy doesn't hold. Yellow flag confirmed.
Q4: Yes — pick one halo kernel (Residual or Laplacian2D-Halo), hand-author a 1-PE shim in 1 hour, run the existing translate loop against it, then prompt for scale-up with the working compute as context. If even 1/2 hand-tested halo kernels don't pass scale-up, the full investment is wasted. The author proposes "2-3 halo kernels" — go smaller: 1 kernel, manual shim, 1 day, kill/proceed decision.
Q5: Best-case +1/15 (one collectives_2d kernel where the compute really IS the bottleneck and the fabric is boilerplate). Realistic 0/15. Worst case -1/15 (regression on a kernel that currently passes via a different decomposition because the model anchored to its 1-PE solution and can't restructure for multi-PE). Net expected: +0 to +1, with non-trivial downside on currently-passing kernels if accidentally enabled. The "opt-in via spec.yaml" mitigates the regression risk but also caps the upside.

One non-trivial value the proposal does not claim: a passing 1-PE compute file is a **correctness oracle for the debugger sub-agent**, not a scaffold for the implementer. The debugger could diff the failed multi-PE output against the 1-PE output to localize whether the bug is in compute or in fabric. That's a different and more defensible use — and it's a smaller engineering scope than the two-phase orchestrator. If the framework wants to extract any value from this idea, that's the version to build.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Drop the orchestrator entirely. Instead: for ONE halo kernel (Residual is simplest), hand-author a 1-PE shim layout.csl + bench harness in a single afternoon. Run the existing translate loop 4 attempts against it. If it doesn't pass at all, kill the idea — the framework can't even do compute on these kernels, so the "compute is easy, fabric is hard" premise is false. If it does pass, manually paste the working compute into the scale-up prompt for the same kernel's multi-PE bundle and run 4 more attempts. Total cost: 1 day, 1 kernel, no spec.yaml field, no orchestrator wrapper, no LLM-driven shim generator. If 1/1 scales up, then invest in the orchestrator. If 0/1, abandon and re-invest the saved week into either (a) building the CUDA-side IR half that was deferred (the actual open question the prompt raised), or (b) the debugger-oracle reframe (use the 1-PE pass as a diff target for failed multi-PE attempts, not as implementer context).

all_critiques.name: Iterative deepening: 1-PE prototype, then scale
all_critiques.critique:
Structurally this IS different from semantic_bridge/translation_facts — those inject context into a single-shot synthesis, while this decomposes synthesis into two phases with an empirical pass-checkpoint between them. Credit for that. But the diagnosis is wrong about where the bottleneck lives, which kills most of the expected lift.

The author's own evidence undermines the proposal: Single-Tile-Matvec (compute-only, no fabric) already passes. That tells you the compute layer is NOT the failure mode — the fabric layer is. The 1-PE phase will therefore validate the easy part of the problem. The scale-up phase then has to do exactly what the current pipeline already fails at: produce the canonical halo_recv_unblock / dsr_queue_fabric_init / collectives_2d wiring. Halo r4's finding ("canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses") explicitly identified canonical-pattern recall on the fabric layer as the bottleneck. Handing the model a working compute kernel does nothing to address recall on the fabric side.

Cluster-specific analysis:
- halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail): scale-up phase still has to invent the recv unblock dance from scratch. 1-PE checkpoint teaches zero halo semantics. Maybe +1 kernel from reduced cognitive load.
- dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fail): entirely fabric. 1-PE phase contributes nothing. Expected lift: 0.
- collectives_2d (2/4 fail): c2d.get_params + scatter/broadcast/gather pattern is exactly the "composed canonical pattern" that halo r4 couldn't fit. Same story.

Prior art is thin. Curriculum/draft-refine has worked for math reasoning and competitive programming, but I'm not aware of a published result showing "stub-out-distributed-then-scale-up" works for HW kernel translation at this composition complexity. The author's own risk note is the strongest critique in the proposal: "the model might rewrite from scratch and ignore the 1-PE solution." The proposed mitigation (force diff justification) is plausible-sounding but adds prompt-engineering surface area without addressing the recall problem.

Also note: the architect role already produces DESIGN.md prose that decomposes compute vs communication. This proposal partially reimplements that decomposition with an empirical checkpoint. If the architect's logical decomposition isn't biting, an empirical one might do slightly better, but not 3x better. Probably 1 kernel of lift.

Cost is real: opt-in spec.yaml flag means hand-curating which kernels qualify (and on a 15-kernel benchmark, that's most of the engineering work). The "1-PE shim generator from layout.csl" is non-trivial — auto-deriving a sensible 1x1 layout requires stripping c2d_params, halo color decls, and rewiring memcpy_params, while keeping enough structure for the compute to still type-check. This is a ~1-week ask for an expected 1-kernel lift on a benchmark of 15.

Yellow flag, not red: not dead-on-arrival, but the cost/benefit is poor given prior-art weakness and the diagnosis mismatch.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Skip the orchestrator entirely. Hand-write 1-PE reductions for 3 halo kernels (the easy ones to reduce — pick kernels where the compute has an obvious 1x1 form). Construct ONE prompt manually: "here is known-good single-PE compute kernel; here is the multi-PE layout.csl exposing colors X/Y/Z; produce multi-PE pe.csl." Run on Opus 4.7. If 0/3 scale up to passing, kill the proposal — the 1-PE checkpoint isn't the missing constraint. If 2-3/3 pass, that's strong evidence and worth building the orchestrator. ~4-6 hours of work. This avoids the spec.yaml curation overhead, the shim generator, and the two-phase orchestrator, all of which are sunk cost if the principle doesn't hold. Critical: do this test BEFORE writing any of the proposed 200 LOC, because the proposal's value depends entirely on a hypothesis that has not been tested and conflicts with the halo r4 finding.

all_critiques.name: Plan-then-verify: architect emits a checkable structural spec before implementation
all_critiques.critique:
Q1 (structural difference vs translation_facts / semantic_bridge): The proposal claims three discriminators — (a) validated against real layout.csl, (b) LLM-authored not regex, (c) blocks downstream when invalid. Of these, only (c) is genuinely new behavior; (a) is also true of translation_facts (translation_facts.py reads real layout.csl via _extract_imports/_extract_set_tile_code_fields/_extract_export_names — see lines 119-198), and (b) is a choice the prior experiment could also have made. So the actual delta over translation_facts is a fail-fast gate, not a richer artifact. The question becomes: does the gate fire on bugs the implementer would have made anyway? Which leads to Q2.

Q2 (does it address the 9 failing kernels' specific bottlenecks?): No, not really, and this is the load-bearing weakness. Walk through the failure clusters:
- halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail): the failure mode per the discarded r2/r3/r4 work is the implementer producing semantically wrong recv/unblock ordering INSIDE handler bodies, with correct top-level imports/exports/task IDs. A structural spec saying {fabric_ops: [{role: recv, color: C1, queue_id: 0, async: true, ut_id: 4}]} is exactly the kind of thing the LLM is good at writing syntactically — and that won't catch "you forgot to advance the DSD after the unblock fired" or "your handler reactivates before the next phase's data lands." The validator-against-layout.csl check passes for almost any plausible YAML because layout.csl declares the color and queue, but says nothing about handler-body semantics.
- dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fail): the canonical failure is init-order inside @comptime — DSR reservations done after a queue is used, etc. A spec like {imports: [...], task_bindings: [...]} doesn't represent ordering of comptime statements. The proposal's own risk note admits CSL has "recursive layout loops, conditional struct fields" the schema can't express, and these are exactly the constructs the dsr_queue cluster fails on.
- collectives_2d (2/4 fail): the surviving failures (after the targeted gotchas shipped) are around c2d_params struct construction inside layout.csl AND the matching pe.csl @param shapes. translation_facts already lists set_tile_code field names AND has hard-coded _IMPORT_FIELD_SCHEMAS entries for <collectives_2d/pe> and <collectives_2d/params> (lines 59-72). The 17 ties in the translation_facts A/B say those facts being PRESENT didn't translate to wins on these failures. Putting the same surface inside a "validated spec" doesn't make the implementer more likely to USE it correctly — it just makes the architect more likely to copy it.

So the proposal addresses the easy half of each cluster (imports, exports, task IDs, color literals — all the things translation_facts already covered) and leaves the hard half (handler-body semantics, comptime ordering, async fabric protocol) untouched. The author's own gate criterion — "validator rejects >=1 plan per kernel on average" — is misframed: the validator will reject plans whose IMPORTS or EXPORTS are wrong, but those are not the implementer's failure mode on the 9 stuck kernels. Most rejections will be on the trivial surface the existing gotchas+facts already taught the architect to write correctly; the rejections won't correlate with kernels that ultimately pass.

Q3 (prior art): MLIR's progressive lowering and TVM's relay-to-TIR pipeline use validated structural IRs, and those work — but they work because the lowering steps are deterministic, not LLM-authored, and the validation catches type/shape errors that propagate predictably. The closest LLM analog is "spec-then-code" prompting (Park et al. on program synthesis with spec verification, plus Self-Debug variants), and the consistent finding there is that spec-first helps when the bug class is "wrong API surface" and DOESN'T help when the bug class is "wrong control flow / async semantics." That maps directly onto: helped translation_facts already covered the API surface, didn't help on the halo/DSR ordering bugs that remain. No published result I'd cite for "LLM-authored validated IR beats prose plan on a hard translation benchmark of comparable shape."

Q4 (10x smaller version, <1 day): YES, and the team should do this before building anything. Concretely: write a 50-line tool that takes the existing free-form DESIGN.md emitted by today's architect, extracts {imports, exports, task_bindings, fabric_ops} via the same regex layer translation_facts already has (or a quick LLM extraction call), validates against layout.csl, and reports DISAGREEMENTS. Run it on the saved architect outputs from the last hybrid sweep's 15 W1 kernels. If the disagreement rate on the 9 FAILING kernels is high AND the disagreements cluster on imports/exports/task-IDs, the proposal might be worth building. If the disagreement rate on failing kernels matches the rate on passing kernels — or if the disagreements are in handler-body prose the schema can't capture — kill it. This costs half a day and answers the central question.

Q5 (expected lift): 0-1 of 15. The honest argument for >0: maybe one kernel currently fails because the architect prose contradicts itself about queue assignments, and the implementer picks the wrong half; a validated spec would force consistency. That's a real failure mode but it's not the dominant one. The honest argument for 0: translation_facts shipped 17 ties out of 19, the validation step doesn't address handler-body bugs, and "more structure earlier" has been the failed hypothesis behind the last three discarded experiments (semantic_bridge, translation_facts, reviewer budget bump). The base rate on "plausible-sounding pipeline addition" in this repo is ~0% lift over the last three swings.

One genuine risk the author named but underweighted: when the schema can't express something (comptime, recursive layout), the architect escape-hatches to prose and the validation is bypassed for the hard cases. This means the validator catches ONLY the easy cases — which are also the cases where the implementer already gets it right. Selection bias makes the gate look useful when it isn't.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: The 1-day diagnostic above (extract-and-disagree over saved architect outputs) IS the smaller variant — and it's a precondition, not a stepping stone. If the disagreement signal isn't there, don't build the spec. If it is, the next smaller variant is to ship JUST the validator as a reviewer-side checker: when an attempt fails, run the validator on the produced pe.csl + layout.csl and route the bucket (A/B/C) using its output, with no architect-side YAML at all. That keeps the architect free-form, adds zero LLM calls, and tests whether structural disagreement is even a useful signal for repair routing. Only if that lifts repair effectiveness should you invest in the architect-side schema. The full proposal as written is ~10x too large for the evidence behind it; the validator-as-router variant is the right minimal probe.

all_critiques.name: Plan-then-verify: architect emits a checkable structural spec before implementation
all_critiques.critique:
Q1 (structurally different from semantic_bridge / translation_facts?): Partially yes, but the difference cuts the wrong way. The novelty claim is "validated before reaching implementer, not just decorated." That IS a real shape difference. But what does the validator actually check? Per the schema: imports exist in layout.csl, exports satisfy layout references, task_id_vars and fabric colors are declared in layout. Look at translation_facts.py — it already extracts ALL of that (lines 102-201: declared_task_ids, color_ids, imports, set_tile_code_fields, exports). The validator's checkable surface is EXACTLY the surface translation_facts already extracts and inlines. translation_facts handed those facts to the implementer as "ground truth"; this proposal hands them to the architect with a reject loop. The implementer in the failing 19-attempt A/B already had the facts and the failures weren't of the "wrong task_id" or "wrong color id" shape — they were halo-protocol semantics (missing unblock_cmd_stream on a boundary branch, sync @fmovs on fabric DSD, queue-ID-pool collisions). A typed plan that lists "task_bindings: [{id, handler, fired_from}]" passes the validator while still encoding the buggy semantics. The discriminator the author proposes ("does validator reject >=1 plan per kernel?") is exactly the gate that will silently pass for halo kernels — the architect will produce schematically-valid YAML and the implementer will still produce a pe.csl that deadlocks on the corner PE. Author's own kill-criterion fires.

Q2 (does it address halo_recv_unblock / dsr_queue_fabric_init / collectives_2d specifically?): No. halo failures (6/7) are protocol failures inside fn/task bodies: which branch reaches unblock_cmd_stream, whether the fabin_dsd is async with the right ut_id, whether the recv is posted before the send, whether per-PE recv-count varies by edge. The proposed schema has fields {imports, exports, task_bindings, pe_branches: [{guard, behavior}], fabric_ops: [{role, color, queue, async, ut_id}]}. "behavior" and "fabric_ops" are where the bugs live — and either those become free-form prose (in which case validation can't touch them) or they become exhaustively schematized (in which case the schema is now a half-built CSL AST and the architect is writing CSL in a different syntax). dsr_queue failures are similar: which queue ID is reserved, what order @initialize_queue is called, top-level vs in-fn comptime — none of which the schema validates without effectively becoming a typechecker. collectives_2d failures (2/4) are struct-param mismatches that translation_facts DID extract correctly and the implementer ignored anyway.

Q3 (prior art?): Yes, partial — and the partial is not encouraging. Plan-then-execute (ReWOO, Plan-and-Solve, AlphaCode-style two-stage) shows lift on tasks where the plan is decomposable into independent subtasks (math word problems, multi-hop QA). For code translation specifically: WaferLLM's OSDI'25 paper (which this repo cites in ARCHITECT_CONTEXT) uses a similar prose-architect → CSL-impl split — that's where this framework's current architect role comes from. Their reported lift is on perf, not pass-rate on novel kernels. MLIR-style lowering with typed intermediates works because the IR has a formal semantics and a deterministic lowering — that's not what an LLM-authored typed plan is. The closest LLM analog with rigorous evidence is constrained decoding / grammar-constrained generation (Picard, JSON-Schema-constrained), which forces SYNTACTIC validity, not semantic correctness; pass-rate lift on hard tasks is small (~5pp) and concentrated in tasks where syntactic errors dominate. The failures here aren't syntactic — they compile-fail or deadlock-fail on protocol violations. No cited evidence that LLM-authored typed plans with validation against an external file produce real lift on protocol-translation tasks. Yellow flag.

Q4 (10x smaller version <1 day?): Yes, and the author should be required to run it before approval. Take 3 hours: pick the 6 halo-failing kernels' captured architect outputs from the last hybrid sweep, hand-extract what the structured plan WOULD have been (architect-as-oracle), then check whether ANY of those plans would have prevented the actual implementer failure. If even 1 of 6 fails reveal the implementer would have produced a different pe.csl given the structured plan, that's signal. If the manual plan looks indistinguishable from the prose DESIGN already produced, kill it. This costs zero LLM tokens and answers Q1 directly.

Q5 (expected lift on 6/15 baseline?): +0 to +1 kernel, with non-trivial probability of -1 (regression from architect respin instability or implementer over-anchoring on an over-constrained schematic plan). The honest p50 is unchanged from baseline. The mechanism by which it could win is if the implementer is currently mis-reading the architect's prose and the structural spec disambiguates — that's a real but small effect, and the failing cluster doesn't sit on ambiguity in the prose architect output (manual inspection of halo failures shows the architect correctly describes the halo protocol; the implementer just doesn't emit the unblock_cmd_stream call on the boundary branch). The structural spec doesn't have a field for "did the implementer remember to call unblock_cmd_stream on every guarded branch" without becoming a per-line checklist, at which point it's a different intervention (a post-implementer linter, which would be more direct).

Two additional concerns:

(a) Re-prompt loops on architect failure are a known source of cost blow-up. "Reject and re-prompt with typed diff" sounds clean but in practice the LLM produces a near-identical plan with the same semantic error and the loop terminates either on attempt-cap or on a degenerate "wrap the violating field in a free-text escape" which the author already flagged as the schema-degradation path. Realistic worst case: 2-3x architect cost per kernel for marginal gain.

(b) The author's claim "eliminates ~30% of failed implementer attempts (estimated from manual classification)" needs the classification shown. The pattern from translation_facts (0W/2L/17T over 19) is that estimates of "obviously this would help" from manual inspection have repeatedly NOT survived A/B contact. The same author-confidence pattern is here. The author's risk note is unusually self-aware — that's good — but the kill-criterion they propose is too generous (one rejection per kernel is trivially achievable with a strict schema and still no semantic lift).
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Drop the architect rewrite entirely. Instead, write a 50-line post-implementer linter that runs cslc-grounded checks for the 3 known cluster failure modes ON the emitted pe.csl: (i) every guarded PE branch (if get_x_coord/get_y_coord) reaches unblock_cmd_stream in some path, (ii) no @fmovs on a fabric DSD without .async = true, (iii) no @initialize_queue / @bind_data_task outside top-level comptime, (iv) collectives_2d struct uses NUM_PES not dim_size. If any check fires, emit a contract-fix repair prompt (existing bucket C path) with the specific violation cited. This is the same idea — fail-fast on a structural property — but applied where the failures actually live (in pe.csl, not in the plan) and grounded in cslc rather than in YAML schema validation. Engineering cost: 1-2 days. Expected lift: same or higher than the proposal (still small, +1 kernel realistic), but the verdict mechanism is cheap enough to run as an in-loop check rather than gating on architect respin. Critically: the ground_gotcha.py grounding helper already exists and can validate the linter rules against real cslc, so the linter inherits cslc-grounded ground truth instead of regex-derived. Use ab_translation_facts.py replay harness to A/B it on the 19 captured implementer outputs in ~30 minutes before any prod deploy.

all_critiques.name: Compile-and-edit inner loop (cslc-in-the-loop drafter)
all_critiques.critique:
This is largely a re-skin of the existing bucket-B repair path, not a structurally new mechanism, and it targets the wrong half of the failure mode.

WHAT THE FRAMEWORK ALREADY DOES (the proposal seems unaware): benchmark_csl.py:39 already invokes cslc + cs_python on the real bundle, captures stderr per step into a structured transcript (parse_instrumented_stdout), and feeds it into csl_bundle_fix_with_review (prompt_cuda2csl.py:1179) via {command_transcript} + {failure_reason} + {layout_text} + {current_code}. That prompt is sent BACK TO THE SAME implementer session on every bucket-B verdict, and the outer loop runs up to reviewer_max_attempts=10 of these (cuda2csl.py:608). Today's "outer" loop is, for a compile failure, already: draft -> cslc-via-benchmark -> stderr -> re-prompt-implementer with stderr -> redraft. The proposal's "new" inner loop is the same arrows with two things removed: the reviewer call (~1 LLM, ~30s) and the cs_python run (which is skipped anyway when compile fails — there's no simulator cost to amortize). The author's own claim that "by then bucket-routed repair (A/B/C) has been triggered which re-builds prose" is incorrect for the syntax case: bucket B does NOT re-call the architect; it goes straight to the implementer with stderr + layout in hand. Bucket A only fires when the reviewer judges the design itself wrong, which is exactly the case where you should NOT short-circuit it.

Q1 (vs semantic_bridge/translation_facts): structurally different on injection-source (execution-derived vs pre-baked), but structurally IDENTICAL on injection-shape (text into implementer prompt before code emission) and structurally identical on REPAIR shape to what bucket-B already does. The novelty reduces to "skip the reviewer and stay in the same chat session." That's a parameter tweak, not a new mechanism.

Q2 (cluster fit): the proposal's strongest claim is halo_recv_unblock = "wrong @bind_local_task / @activate / fabric DSD field names." But the r4 halo workflow finding (memory: "canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses") and the fact that 3 hand-curated halo gotchas just shipped today both point the other way: halo failures are NOT primarily compile-time. The model writes code that compiles and runs to completion with the wrong protocol — wrong activation ordering, wrong unblock timing, wrong fabric DSD field SEMANTICS even when field NAMES are right. cslc returns rc=0 and the inner loop exits "successfully" into the existing reviewer, which is where we are today. Same for dsr_queue_fabric_init: most of those die at runtime on queue underflow / fabric init order, not at compile. Only collectives_2d (c2d_params.x vs .y) is a clean compile-error case, and that's 2 kernels. Of the 9 failing kernels, the upper bound on "compile-error-only failures cslc can catch that bucket-B isn't already catching by attempt 2" is generously 2; realistic is 0-1.

Q3 (prior art): the closest external analogue is self-edit / self-debug loops (SELF-DEBUG, Reflexion, AlphaCode-style execute-and-edit). They DO show lifts, but the published lifts are on (a) tasks where the test signal is binary and pure (LeetCode pass/fail) and (b) baselines that do NOT already have a reviewer-routed repair loop with execution feedback. The delta here is small precisely because the baseline already does the execute-and-feed-back step. No cite I can produce shows compile-only inner loops adding lift over a baseline that already feeds compile stderr into a fresh implementer prompt — because nobody builds that baseline as the comparison.

Q4 (10x smaller version): yes, and it would falsify the proposal in <4h. Just patch _benchmark_current_code to early-return on cslc rc!=0 with stderr stuffed into failure_reason, AND set reviewer_max_attempts=4 but skip the reviewer call when failure_reason starts with cslc-style "file:line: error:". That gives you "tight syntax-only repair loop" with maybe 30 lines changed and zero new infra. If THAT moves halo from 1/7 -> 3/7, the full proposal is worth building. My prediction is it moves 1/7 -> 1/7 because the cslc rc==0 failures are the hard ones.

Q5 (honest lift): from 6/15 -> 6/15 or 7/15. I estimate +3% (0.5 kernels) expected, with the realistic ceiling at +13% (2 kernels: maybe one collectives_2d, maybe one dsr that happens to be syntactic). Cost-benefit is poor because the SAME engineering hours could go to (a) instrumenting the architect with executable mesh-pattern stubs from csl_mesh_patterns.py, (b) building the CUDA-side IR that Phase 1 explicitly deferred (typed AST of kernel launches + memory access shapes), or (c) a runtime-trace-derived oracle that catches the rc==0 semantic errors halo actually hits — any of which addresses a class the current pipeline genuinely doesn't see.

Specific risk not in the author's note: oscillation IS the failure mode, not the edge case. The grounded-halo r2/r3 results (0/5 each, drafters fabricated builtins/syntax/error messages even WITH cslc grounding) are direct evidence that this model under this prompt shape patches symptoms and invents fixes when handed cascading errors. The author's "detect non-converging edit distance" mitigation is exactly what r4 tried (escalate after cap); r4 was 0/5.

One thing the proposal gets right: the wall-time / $ estimate is reasonable, and the integration is genuinely small (1-2 days is real). The cost isn't the problem; the wrong-bottleneck targeting is.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: 10x smaller version (4 hours, falsifies in one sweep): in _benchmark_current_code, when cslc exits non-zero, short-circuit the reviewer entirely and re-prompt the same implementer session with a stripped-down "cslc errors: <first 3 file:line: error: lines>; patch only those lines; re-emit the full file" message, up to 3 times before the normal benchmark/review path resumes. No new wrapper, no harness, no planId for halo or dsr. Run on the 9 failing kernels. If lift is +0 or +1, the full proposal is dead-on-arrival. If it's +3 or more, the bottleneck assumption was right and the full version is worth building. This experiment costs ~$5 and one sweep; the full proposal costs 2 eng-days + $15 + opportunity cost on the IR work that Phase 1 deferred.

all_critiques.name: Compile-and-edit inner loop (cslc-in-the-loop drafter)
all_critiques.critique:
This proposal is largely a re-packaging of bucket-B that the proposal itself admits exists, just with the reviewer/architect amputated and a tighter token budget. Concretely:

1. Structurally NOT different from existing repair. Read cuda2csl.py:1469 + benchmark_csl.py:243-258 + workflow_common.py:368-391 + prompt_cuda2csl.py:1179 (csl_bundle_fix_with_review). The outer loop already does: write code -> run commands_wse3.sh (which IS cslc on the real bundle directory) -> capture per-step stderr with idx markers -> dedupe cslc warnings (_dedupe_cslc_warnings, the exact fix-1-error-per-line-block normalization the proposal wants) -> head+tail clip via _clip_head_tail(head=400, tail=1600) -> stuff into the bucket-B fix prompt together with reviewer_rationale, debugger sub-agent report, layout, and builtin whitelist -> feed back to the SAME Opus session and ask it to re-emit. That is exactly "draft -> compile -> feed error lines back -> redraft." The proposal's "top-3 error lines" is a strict information subset of what bucket-B already passes; this is "translation_facts but smaller and execution-derived" which is a distinction without a difference w.r.t. structural shape: the model still receives a textual error blob before re-emitting. Translation_facts was 0W/2L/17T over 19 attempts; the prior was a richer signal than 3 cslc error lines and didn't move the needle. The author's "execution-derived not pre-baked YAML" framing is true but irrelevant — bucket-B's transcript is already execution-derived.

2. Does NOT address any of the three failing clusters specifically. The proposal calls these "syntax-shaped" failures cslc names "precisely on a specific file:line." That's the assumption I would push hardest on. halo_recv_unblock failures aren't typically "undeclared identifier" — they're semantic: the agent uses the wrong @bind_local_task/@activate combination, picks a fabric DSD field that exists but has the wrong meaning, or fails to call sys_mod.unblock_cmd_stream() at the right moment. cslc compiles many of these (the program type-checks; it just deadlocks or computes wrong values), so the stderr the inner loop would feed back is empty or warning-only. The r4 halo workflow already established this empirically: "cslc-grounded + canonical hints to rewriter -> 0/5 — canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses." Same root cause hits here: when cslc DOES name a file:line, bucket-B already handles it (most W1 attempts that compile go on to fail at runtime — that's where the bucket budget is spent). The cases where cslc errors are NOT precise are exactly the cases the proposal hopes to fix.

3. No external prior art is cited in the proposal, and the closest analogue (Self-Debug / Self-Repair on HumanEval-style tasks) shows roughly 5-15% lift on Python where the execution trace is cheap, the model is fluent in the language, and errors map 1:1 to fixes. CSL is a DSL with ~zero pretraining mass, and Cerebras compiler errors are famously cryptic ("DSR dispatch context error" type stuff). The author's own risk note flags this: "if cslc errors are too cryptic (cascading errors from a single missing import), the model patches symptoms, not cause, and oscillates." That's the modal case here, not the edge case. The r4 grounded-halo experiment is the strongest prior-art-in-this-repo data point and it landed at 0/5.

4. A 10x smaller version exists already and was effectively run: bucket-B IS the compile-and-edit loop with 8 outer iterations. The marginal experiment to test "is there lift if we strip the reviewer and give the model 3 error lines instead of a full transcript?" is one prompt-template tweak: replace csl_bundle_fix_with_review's transcript block with the first 3 cslc error lines, set --skip-reviewer, re-run the halo+dsr subset. That's an afternoon, not 1-2 days. If it doesn't lift on the 9 failing kernels in <1 day of evals, the full proposal won't.

5. Realistic lift: 0-1 of 9 failing kernels move, i.e. 6/15 -> ~6.3/15. Best case I can construct is one collectives_2d kernel where the cslc error message names c2d_params.x vs .y and the inner loop catches it 1 attempt earlier than bucket-B does today — saving budget that the existing outer loop also recovers via wasted_attempts accounting. The 6/9 halo kernels are dominated by runtime/semantic failures and the 2/3 dsr_queue kernels involve composed initialization patterns whose errors cascade. +3% lift estimate, dominated by variance.

Two harder downside risks the proposal underweights:

(a) Multi-turn perturbation. The implementer thread is already 8-deep with reviewer turns; adding 4 inner micro-iterations per outer attempt potentially pushes the conversation into 30+ turns. Context overflow guards (_llm_call_with_trim_on_overflow at cuda2csl.py:1078) fire and silently trim the architect's design memo, which is the worst thing to drop. The proposal doesn't say whether the inner loop runs in a fresh session or appends to self.messages — the latter compounds drift, the former throws away the reviewer/architect context that bucket-B relies on.

(b) cslc wall time. The proposal says "30-90s per invocation" for these bundles. Actual measured cslc time on collectives/halo bundles is 60-180s because they spawn multi-PE expansions. 4 inner iterations x 90-180s = 6-12 minutes per attempt, x 8 attempts x 15 kernels = roughly 12-24 hours added to a sweep that today runs in ~10 hours. Author's "1.5x today's wall time" is optimistic by ~2x. At Argo Opus rates the proposal's $15 estimate is also low — the inner-loop prompts still carry layout.csl (often 200-400 lines) so "~5x shorter" is wrong; closer to 1.5-2x shorter.

What I'd actually do instead, ranked by expected lift:

(i) An ablation that's cheaper to run than the full proposal: --skip-reviewer + 2 extra outer attempts. Tests "is reviewer-routing the bottleneck, or is it that the model can't fix these at all?" If lift is 0 (likely), then the inner-loop is also 0 by reduction.

(ii) Real IR work that the framework hasn't tried: a CUDA-side typed-AST IR that names the parallel pattern (stencil-with-halo, scan, broadcast-then-reduce, etc.) and a small library of CSL realizations for each pattern, then retrieves the realization at architect time. This is structurally different from semantic_bridge (which was prose) and translation_facts (which was CSL-side YAML facts). The CSL-side half was deferred per the user's note — the missing half is "what pattern is this CUDA implementing" not "what's the syntax of @bind_local_task." Pattern recognition is the actual bottleneck on halo_recv_unblock.

(iii) Reference-CSL leak in a controlled way: instead of hiding pe.csl, hide it but expose a structurally-similar pe.csl from a different kernel in the same cluster (e.g. for halo kernels, show 7pt-Stencil's working pe.csl). The compute-leak canary already exists to enforce per-kernel hiding; relaxing to per-cluster is one assertion change. Higher information-content than 3 cslc error lines.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Strip the proposal to its minimal testable claim: in cuda2csl.py:1704, change csl_bundle_fix_with_review's prompt to prepend "FOCUS ON THESE 3 CSLC ERRORS FIRST: <first 3 file:line: error: lines from transcript>" extracted from the existing per-step stderr that benchmark_csl already captures. No new cslc invocation, no new wrapper, no per-kernel bundle pointer — just re-ranking what bucket-B already has. ~30 lines of code, ~2 hours, re-run on the 9 failing kernels in one hybrid sweep. If THAT doesn't lift, the full inner-loop won't either. Predicted result: 0-1 kernel lift, dominated by variance. If you want a real swing, spend the 1-2 day budget on (ii) above instead — CUDA-side pattern-typed IR with retrieval at architect time.

all_critiques.name: Specialist syntax-fixer model (small/fast) gated by cslc
all_critiques.critique:
The proposal misdiagnoses the bottleneck. I pulled the last-attempt cslc stderr from the most recent sweep (run_20260611_19*) for the 9 currently-failing kernels. The actual error distribution:

- 7pt-Stencil: `variable of type 'comptime_struct' must be comptime-known` at `extern const memcpy_params: comptime_struct;` — wrong storage class. NOT in the proposal's regex set (`undeclared identifier|expected token|wrong number of arguments|no member named`). Even if it were, the fix requires knowing that comptime_struct must be a `param`, not `extern const` — that's a CSL idiom rule, not a line-level typo. And the 16 'unused entry in module instantiation' warnings stacked above it show the architect set up the wrong contract — a 2-line edit by Haiku won't reconcile a layout.csl that instantiates kernel.csl with 5 params the kernel doesn't accept.
- Single-Tile-Matvec, FFT-1D-2D, Residual: `name 'f_tic' was not declared during layout evaluation`. This matches the proposal's regex (looks like 'undeclared identifier'), but the symbol is missing from the BINDING (layout.csl @export_symbol + host commands.sh symbol map), not from the file the implementer wrote. A line-local fixer staring at pe.csl will helpfully add a stub `fn f_tic()`, which is exactly wrong — `f_tic` is a host-callable that must come from the timestamp library, properly exported through layout. This is the failure mode that destroyed semantic_bridge and translation_facts: localized 'help' that makes a different mistake.
- Game-of-Life: `cannot export symbol of type '[6]u32'` — architecture decision (SoA vs AoS, marshal type). One-line edit can't fix.
- Cholesky, Mandelbrot: `only 'var' and 'extern const' variables may be uninitialized` — requires cross-file reasoning (is this param coming from host or in-module?).
- GEMV-Collectives-2D: `FATAL: hcf (halt and catch fire)` — RUNTIME trap, not even a compile error. Regex won't even fire.

So on the 9 failures, 0 are clean syntax-typo-class errors that a line-local fixer can correctly resolve without seeing layout.csl + commands.sh + the export contract. The premise that 'B currently re-runs full Opus on the full prompt for what is often a 2-line typo' is not supported by the data — what B re-runs full Opus on are mostly contract/architecture errors that already routed to bucket C or A, plus a few semantic-class errors that need exactly the multi-file context Opus already has.

Now, the structural questions:

1. STRUCTURALLY different from semantic_bridge / translation_facts? Partially. The author is right that gating on execution signal (cslc fired) and routing to a different model is a real difference — it adds a branch, not context. That's why I rated 'unlikely' instead of 'dead-on-arrival'. BUT: the FAILURE MODE shape is identical. semantic_bridge failed because algorithm-level prose didn't address syntax-level failures; translation_facts failed because RAG'd gotchas already covered the surface and IR added perturbation. This proposal will fail because line-local edits can't address the cross-file contract failures that dominate the failing set. Same family of failure: 'localized intervention applied to a problem whose locality is wrong.'

2. Does it address halo_recv_unblock (6/7), dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3), or collectives_2d (2/4)? No. Halo failures are about @block/@unblock dataflow correctness across recv tasks (the very thing the curated halo gotchas couldn't get LLMs to do); a syntax-fixer doesn't help. DSR queue / fabric init failures throw 'initialization for this queue has already been set' / 'maximum input queue is 7' (saw both in the data) — these are state-tracking errors across an entire pe.csl, not a typo at one line. Collectives_2d failures are about the multi-axis broadcast/reduce dance the architect chose wrong. None of these clusters has the line-localized syntax-typo shape the fixer targets.

3. Prior art for cheap-syntax-fixer-after-expensive-model-draft in code translation? Self-Debug (Chen et al. 2023) and CodeT (Chen et al. 2022) used execution feedback as a loop signal but routed BACK to the same model — they didn't find a cheap specialist helped beyond what bigger-model self-repair gave. SWE-agent / Aider use cheap models for whole-task edits, not as a syntax-fix layer beneath a stronger one. The closest analog is LSP-style auto-fix integrations (linter → suggested fix), and those work on languages with mature linter rule sets — CSL has neither. I'm not aware of published work showing a Haiku-class model wins over Opus self-repair on a domain Opus has weak training coverage for (which CSL is). Yellow flag confirmed.

4. 10x smaller version that proves the principle in <1 day: Yes, and it's worth doing because it kills this idea cheaply. Take the 9 failure traces I just extracted. Manually prompt Haiku 4.5 with each failing pe.csl + the 3 stderr lines + the builtin whitelist, ask for a one-line fix. Re-run cslc. If 0/9 compile (my prediction), the role-based pipeline change is unwarranted. Half-day of work, zero plumbing. The author should do this BEFORE writing the role.

5. Expected lift on 6/15 baseline: 0 to +1, most likely 0. If by luck the fixer happens to convert one of the 'undeclared layout symbol' kernels by hallucinating a plausible stub that compiles AND passes the numeric check (very low probability — passing numeric_check requires correct host-bound timestamp readout), then +1. Realistic expectation: zero. I'd bet small money against any lift.

The author's risk note acknowledges the right risk ('classifier regex misroutes a semantic bug to the fixer, fixer makes the wrong edit') but underestimates how dominant that mode is — it isn't a mitigatable edge case, it IS the modal case in the current failure set. The mitigation 'limit fixer to 2 invocations' caps the cost of being wrong but doesn't deliver any wins.

One more thing the proposal doesn't acknowledge: cost claim is wrong-signed. The current B-bucket repair already passes context-trimmed history (per the implementer's _llm_call_with_trim_on_overflow path); claiming it 'burns Opus tokens on a 2-line typo' overstates current cost. Adding the fixer adds Haiku calls on top of, not in place of, the eventual Opus call when the fixer misroutes (which it will, per item 2). So net cost goes UP, not flat as claimed.

The fact that this LOOKS like a hybrid-cost-optimization (which we know worked at the outer level) is precisely the rhetorical trap that gets the framework to spend cycles on it. The outer hybrid works because Sonnet+Opus see DIFFERENT prompts/contexts and explore different basins (genuine search diversity). The inner hybrid here would have Haiku see a STRICTLY SMALLER context than Opus and try to fix what Opus couldn't — that's not the same shape, it's the opposite shape.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Skip the new role entirely. Instead: do the half-day empirical kill-test described in (4). Extract the 9 last-attempt failure traces from run_20260611_19* (I already have them), hand them to Haiku with the proposal's exact prompt template, re-run cslc. Report compile pass rate and (for compilers) numeric pass rate. If 2+ kernels go from fail to pass, escalate to the full proposal. If 0-1, kill the idea and write up the experiment so it stops getting re-proposed. Total cost: ~2 hours of Haiku calls + 1 hour of analysis. If a smaller-but-real version of the idea survives the kill-test, the salvageable variant is probably NOT a new role but a single 'syntax_retry' parameter on the existing bucket-B implementer: when cslc fails with a regex-matched syntax error AND the previous attempt's stderr matched the same regex, swap the implementer model to Haiku for that single retry (proves whether model-swap-on-stuck helps without the architectural complexity of a fourth role).

all_critiques.name: Specialist syntax-fixer model (small/fast) gated by cslc
all_critiques.critique:
This is a re-skin of the existing debugger sub-agent (debugger_agent.py, 357 LOC, already wired through cuda2csl.py around lines 1627-1703) with three superficial tweaks: (a) classifier-regex gating instead of bucket-B + concrete-verb gating, (b) Haiku instead of Sonnet/Opus, (c) edit-only framing instead of structured-JSON-patch framing. The execution-signal gating already exists — should_fire() at debugger_agent.py:128 keys on stderr-bearing concrete-verb actions ("cslc", "compile", "grep", etc.). Substituting a regex for "undeclared identifier" doesn't add a new mechanism; it narrows an existing one.

Hard answers to the questions:

(1) Structurally different from semantic_bridge / translation_facts? Partially yes (it does add a decision branch keyed on cslc exit) but the new role IS still "another LLM with a curated prompt", and the curation it adds (stripped CSL + 3 error lines + builtin_whitelist_block) is a strict subset of what the implementer fix-prompt already includes (cuda2csl.py:1620 already threads builtin_whitelist into the bucket-B repair). Wrapping a subset of context in a different model call is decoration, not a new mechanism. The "edit-only, no algorithm change" framing is also just a prompt instruction — both the reviewer's recommended_patch and the debugger's recommended_patch already say this; the implementer routinely ignores it. A different model with the same instruction won't change that.

(2) Does it address one of the 9 failing clusters specifically? No. Look at what halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail), dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fail), and collectives_2d (2/4 fail) actually are. csl_knowledge_base.py:226 describes them as "API surface confusion": missing `.dim_params = c2d_params.x` in module import, missing dest_dsr_ids/src0_dsr_ids/src1_dsr_ids arrays, missing halo recv/unblock protocol orchestration, missing color/queue/DSR fabric wiring. These are not "undeclared identifier" or "wrong arg count" — they are MISSING WHOLE STRUCTURES that the implementer never wrote. cslc on a kernel that forgot half the dsr_queue protocol does not emit "undeclared identifier on line 47"; it emits errors about uninitialized queues, missing exports, or runs to a deadlock. A syntax-fixer cannot synthesize the missing collectives_2d import block from a 3-line cslc error. The proposal targets a failure mode (typo-class) that isn't actually in the current 9-kernel residual.

(3) Prior art? The two cited precedents are wrong-genre. (a) "Cheap-then-expensive at OUTER level works" (run_hybrid_sweep.sh Sonnet→Opus) succeeds because the WHOLE second attempt re-runs the whole pipeline with a stronger model — it's not a syntax-narrowed sub-call. (b) Standard refactor LLMs (Aider, Cursor edit mode) use small models for edits, but those operate when the EDIT TARGET IS KNOWN and the human supplies the goal. There is no published evidence that a syntax-only sub-model lifts pass-rate on code-translation tasks where the unsolved residual is API-shape errors. Yellow flag confirmed.

(4) 10x smaller proof? Yes, and it's nearly free: grep the existing reviewer transcripts for the failing 9 kernels, count how many failures land in pure "undeclared identifier / wrong arg count / no member named" vs structural/protocol misses. If <20% are syntax-shaped, the upper bound on this proposal is ~1 kernel of lift. Strong prediction: <10% are syntax-shaped, because the implementer is Opus, not a junior dev — its remaining failures are conceptual, not typo-class. Do this grep BEFORE building anything; it's a 30-min experiment that probably kills the proposal.

(5) Realistic lift on 15-kernel from 6/15? 0. The Opus+Sonnet union ceiling argument in the proposal is actually evidence AGAINST: if both models leave the same residual mistakes, those residuals are at the conceptual layer (which Opus is better at than Haiku), not the typo layer (which both already fix). Adding a weaker model with less context cannot improve on a stronger model with more context for the same problem. The "smaller model with one job does better" intuition holds when the job is genuinely simpler than the larger model's job — but cslc-shaped errors on real CSL code require knowing the collectives_2d / halo / DSR vocabulary the Opus run already had access to.

The proposal's own risk note flags "shape risk: looks like more prompting." That's the right concern and the rebuttal ("gated by execution signal, different model, narrower task") describes the existing debugger agent, not a new mechanism. The debugger agent fires today on bucket-B + concrete-verb (debugger_agent.py:151-155), reads stderr (cuda2csl.py:1655-1678), and emits a structured patch. If the proposal is "use Haiku for that role instead of the orchestrator's primary model" — that's a 1-line config change, do it as an experiment first before building a new role.
all_critiques.smaller_variant:
Three smaller experiments that strictly dominate the full proposal:

(A) [30 min, zero code] Grep the last sweep's transcripts for the 9 failing kernels. Bucket failures into (i) pure syntax (undeclared identifier, wrong arg count, no member named), (ii) protocol/structure (missing import block, missing export, missing halo protocol), (iii) semantic (wrong algorithm). If (i) is <2/9 attempts, kill the proposal. This is the proof-of-principle.

(B) [2 hours] Re-point the existing DebuggerAgent's _llm_call to Haiku via XKERNEL_DEBUGGER_MODEL env var (debugger_agent.py:301 — single constructor arg). Run the 15-kernel sweep with XKERNEL_DEBUGGER=1 + Haiku. This tests the "smaller model, same role" hypothesis without building a new role or new regex classifier. If Haiku-in-debugger-slot doesn't move the needle, the syntax-fixer-as-new-role won't either.

(C) [1 day, if A and B are positive] Tighten the existing bucket-C contract-fix path (cuda2csl.py:1602-1620) to ALSO fire on syntax-shaped stderr, not just contract violations. Reuses all existing plumbing, no new role, no new model call.

If the proposal must be built as written, ship it behind a flag, run it on the 15-kernel benchmark only, and kill if lift is 0/15 — don't iterate on it the way semantic_bridge and translation_facts got 19+ attempts before being cut.

all_critiques.name: Layout-anchored constrained decoding via skeleton injection
all_critiques.critique:
Three load-bearing problems, ordered by severity.

(1) The failure-mode diagnosis is wrong, and that breaks the proposal's central claim. I read /home/USER/xkernel/kernels/Laplacian2D-Halo/CSL/layout.csl and pe.csl. layout.csl exports exactly six symbols: `tile`, `new_tile`, `time_buf_u16`, `step`, `f_tic`, `f_toc`, `f_memcpy_timestamps`, `f_enable_timer`. NONE of the names the proposal cites as 'invented by the model' (`f_recv_n`, `recv_north_task`, `RX_DONE_TID`) appear in layout.csl. The RX task naming is entirely internal to pe.csl — it's a local_task_id bound to a free-form task name. A skeleton extracted from layout.csl literally cannot constrain `RX_DONE_TID` vs `f_recv_n` because layout.csl does not mention either. Same story for the `memcpyParams.x_config` vs `x_in_config` example: layout.csl only ever calls `memcpy.get_params(px)` and forwards the opaque struct; the field-name confusion lives in how pe.csl unpacks it, downstream of the contract. The skeleton would fill in correctly the things that were never broken (`step`, `f_tic`, `f_toc` — already covered by the explicit f_tic/f_toc requirement at prompt_cuda2csl.py:281) and provide zero constraint on the parts that actually fail.

(2) Structurally identical to translation_facts, dressed differently. I read translation_facts.py. The extractors `_extract_export_names` (line 156), `_extract_set_tile_code_fields` (line 136), `_extract_declared_task_ids` (line 102), `_extract_imports` (line 119), `_extract_host_launch_sequence` (line 201) ALREADY lift exactly the surface the proposal wants. translation_facts rendered them as YAML; this proposal renders them as a code template. Same input set, same information content, different presentation layer. The 19-attempt A/B (0W/2L/17T) didn't fail because the model couldn't parse YAML — it failed because that surface area is already well-covered by RAG'd gotchas + layout being in-context, AND because the bugs aren't there. Re-rendering it as Python-string code scaffolding does not change what bytes the model has to work with.

(3) Skeleton-as-template is actively dangerous for an idiomatically-diverse target. I diffed pe.csl across kernels: Game-of-Life uses `recv_north_color`/`recv_north_iq`/`recv_north_task_id`/wse2-wse3-branched `@get_data_task_id` and a `data_task` named `recv_north(val: u32)`. Halo uses `RX_N`/`rx_n_iq`/`RX_DONE_TID` and a plain `task f_rx_done() void` activated by a counter. These are not surface variants — they're entirely different concurrency idioms (data-task-per-wavelet vs local-task-on-completion-counter). A skeleton baked from layout.csl + 'canonical halo pattern' would pick one; for the other half of the corpus it forces the wrong design. The author's mitigation ('detect parse failures and fall back') doesn't catch this: parsing succeeds, the skeleton is well-formed CSL, but it pre-commits to the wrong concurrency shape — and the implementer prompt says 'do not change signatures'. This is the failure mode that killed halo-gotcha r4 (canonical patterns too composed to fit the local kernel). Skeleton injection is r4 with a parser.

Secondary issues: cost is understated — the parser-and-canonicalizer for f_send/f_rx_done/f_compute task wiring is the hard part, not lifting @export_name calls; that's the part that needs to encode idiom choice. 3-5 days is a CSL-parser-from-scratch estimate and CSL has comptime conditional routing that's painful to handle generically. Also, prompt_cuda2csl.py already does substantial scaffolding (the f_tic/f_toc hard requirement at L281; the @export_symbol must-be-inside-comptime requirement at L292) — these are exactly the no-failure-mode anchors the skeleton would provide, and they're already in.

Outside evidence: constrained decoding (grammar-constrained generation, e.g. llama.cpp gbnf, OpenAI structured outputs) and template-completion (FILM, CodeT5+) are validated for syntactic regularity, NOT for matching a target program's idiom to a source program's algorithm. The closest published precedent is type-driven program synthesis (Hoogle, Synquid) — those work when the type IS the spec; here the layout.csl signatures are necessary but vastly underspecify the program. MLIR lowering passes use templates but they encode TRANSFORMATIONS between fixed-semantic IRs, not free generation. I'm not aware of a published win for 'lift skeleton from one of two source files, inject as fill-in template, let LLM complete' on real code translation at this complexity.

Real lift estimate: maybe +1 kernel (one of the dsr_queue_fabric_init failures where the field-name confusion is at the layout boundary, not the params unpack), as likely -1 from forcing the wrong idiom on a halo kernel. Net 0-1, with high variance and 3-5 days of eng.
all_critiques.smaller_variant:
Yes — and it would refute the proposal in <1 day. Instead of building the parser-and-template pipeline, do a 2-hour prompt experiment: for the 9 failing W1 kernels, manually hand-write the 'skeleton you must match' (signatures of `step`/`f_tic`/`f_toc` + the @export_symbol pe.csl-side mirror block + import lines) and inject as a new prompt slot. Use the existing q_translate_cuda_to_csl_bundle. Run 3 attempts per kernel (27 total LLM calls, ~$20). If this manually-curated, idiom-free, perfect-fidelity skeleton doesn't move halo_recv_unblock pass-rate above 1/7, the parser+template version cannot do better — it can only be a noisier version of the same intervention. This A/B is cheap and falsifies the central claim before any parser work. If the result IS a win, the next step still isn't the parser — it's figuring out WHICH part of the hand-skeleton mattered (just signatures? full export block? imports?) before automating.

A different small variant worth running independently: differential repair. Take a failing pe.csl from attempt N, diff its @export_symbol / @bind_local_task block against the inverted layout.csl @export_name list, and inject the diff as a structured error to the repair attempt: 'layout exports X with type fn(u16)void, your pe.csl exports it with type fn()void.' This is mechanical contract-checking, not skeleton injection — and it addresses the actual class of failures (contract mismatch) without committing to a program shape. contract_check.py exists already; check whether it's wired into the C-bucket repair path. That's the real proposal hiding inside this one.

all_critiques.name: Layout-anchored constrained decoding via skeleton injection
all_critiques.critique:
Three hard problems.

(1) STRUCTURALLY IT IS translation_facts WITH DIFFERENT DECORATION. The proposal extracts exports, @get_local_task_id literals, set_tile_code field names, and imports — those are exactly the four primitives translation_facts.py (_extract_export_names, _extract_declared_task_ids, _extract_set_tile_code_fields, _extract_imports) already regex'd from layout.csl. translation_facts was wired into 3 prompt slots, A/B'd over 19 attempts → 0W/2L/17T, torn out (tasks F2-F5 then R1-R5). The proposal's "structural scaffolding vs declarative facts" framing is a delivery-format distinction; the information content is the same regex over the same file. Worse, the model ALREADY sees the raw {layout_text} dumped verbatim into the implementer prompt (prompt_cuda2csl.py:243) PLUS a prose paragraph (lines 325-338) listing "which task IDs layout.csl exports, what fields its struct params contain, which compile-time params get passed through" and explicitly threatening "undeclared identifier — a contract violation". Skeleton injection would be the fourth restatement of the same constraint to a model that's already ignoring restatements 1-3.

(2) IT DOES NOT ADDRESS THE HALO BOTTLENECK (6/7 of the failures). The author motivates the proposal with "model invents recv_north_task when layout exports f_recv_n." Looked at Laplacian2D-Halo/layout.csl: failures are not about export-name mismatch on the contract surface — they are about wsync/advance/microthread queue plumbing in the BODY. PROGRESS confirms this: r2/r3/r4 halo workflows all hit 0/5 because "canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses". The protocol logic lives inside function bodies, which is precisely what the skeleton leaves blank. Skeleton fixes a contract problem the model doesn't have on halo kernels and leaves the body problem it does have.

(3) THE dsr_queue_fabric_init CLAIM IS WRONG. The author cites `memcpyParams.x_config` vs `.x_in_config` as fixable by a layout-side skeleton. Field names of memcpy_params come from `<memcpy/get_params>` library headers, NOT from layout.csl — layout passes the whole struct as a single field (`.memcpy_params = memcpy.get_params(Px)`). A regex over layout.csl cannot recover internal field names of imported library structs. translation_facts hard-coded these in _IMPORT_FIELD_SCHEMAS and still got discarded.

(4) "CONSTRAINED DECODING" IS A MISNOMER. Real constrained decoding masks logits at sample time (grammars, FIM models trained on it). This is prompt-template injection asking the model to fill blanks — nothing prevents it from emitting a wrong name. The author's own risk note concedes this ("model is forced into the wrong contract" — but it isn't actually forced, the LLM can emit whatever it wants). No published evidence that prompt-side skeleton injection beats "include the contract + tell the model to obey it" for code synthesis of this complexity; FIM literature only validates the technique for FIM-trained base models.

(5) THE ONLY CLUSTER WITH A PLAUSIBLE CASE IS collectives_2d (c2d_params field names ARE recoverable from layout.csl). 2/4 fail today; optimistic conversion is 1 extra pass. translation_facts had a dedicated _IMPORT_FIELD_SCHEMAS["<collectives_2d/pe>"] block saying literally "use NUM_PES, not .dim_size" — discarded as inert.

Expected lift: 0 to 1 kernel (0 to +6.7pp). Realistic point estimate ~3pp. Cost: 3-5 eng days for a parser whose null hypothesis (no lift) has strong precedent.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: YES, and it should run before any parser work. For ONE collectives_2d failing kernel and ONE halo failing kernel, hand-author the skeleton (10 minutes each), drop it into the implementer prompt for those two kernels only, run 5 attempts with/without. If 0/5 vs 0/5 on both (which the translation_facts precedent predicts), kill the project for ~$20 of compute and 1 hour of eng. If the collectives_2d kernel goes 0/5 → 3/5 (which would be the strongest evidence for the proposal that the corpus can produce), THEN build the parser for the 2-4 collectives kernels only — not the full 30. The current proposal skips this falsification step and budgets the parser first; that's the same mistake that burned translation_facts.

all_critiques.name: Self-critique against cslc-grounded checklist
all_critiques.critique: Hard verdict: this is translation_facts re-packaged as a confirmation prompt, and translation_facts was killed 0W/2L/17T (tasks #46–55). The "checklist generator" is materially the same machinery that already exists in /home/USER/xkernel/code_translation/translation_facts.py: _extract_export_names, _extract_imports, _extract_declared_task_ids, _extract_set_tile_code_fields, validate_facts_against_builtins. The proposal even bullet-lists the exact four static-analysis sources translation_facts already extracts (imports, exports, task-binding fn names, DSD struct fields). The author's claim that "the criteria are auto-derived not authored, so they can't drift from reality" is true of translation_facts too — and translation_facts STILL didn't lift. Putting the same facts in a downstream YES/NO prompt instead of an upstream FACTS block does not add information; it adds a turn. (1) Structural-difference question: the only real difference vs translation_facts is positional — facts injected AFTER draft, not before. That changes "context" to "self-critique." But self-critique without an outside grader is a known weak loop; the same Sonnet/Opus that hallucinated @import_module "<math>" five lines ago will rubber-stamp it five lines later because it sees its own prior output as authoritative in-context. Author flags this risk and proposes monitoring YES rate — fine, but the mitigation is "kill it fast," which is a sign the experiment is structured to fail-cheap rather than to win. (2) Cluster mapping: NONE of the three failing clusters are import-name / export-name / bind-fn / DSD-field bugs. halo_recv_unblock failures (6/7) are about ORDERING and ARMING of @block/@unblock around recv tasks and color routing — the gotcha in csl_builtins.yaml line 292+ already names sys_mod.unblock_cmd_stream, and the kernels still fail because the protocol shape is wrong, not because the symbol is misspelled. dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3) is about WSE-2 vs WSE-3 queue-vs-color polymorphism and fabric DSR setup ordering — translation_facts already surfaces reserved queue IDs and arch; passing 5 YES/NO items won't fix shape. collectives_2d (2/4) is composition of x_color/y_color row+col reductions — also a protocol/shape failure, not a "did you import a thing that exists" failure. The bug class the checklist catches (imported a nonexistent module, called a nonexistent export, bound a nonexistent fn, used a missing DSD field) is empirically rare in the current failure mix because RAG'd gotchas + builtin_whitelist_block (already wired at cuda2csl.py:1404, 1573, 1598, 1620, 1715) catch most of it BEFORE implementer emits. The proposal's own cost note quietly admits this: "skip the LLM call if all 5 items pass automatically" — meaning the static checker alone would resolve most cases without the LLM, which by definition produces zero lift over running the static checker alone, which is just re-running translation_facts pre-flight, which got 0W. (3) Prior art: self-critique / self-refine loops on code (Reflexion, Self-Refine, Self-Debug Chen 2023) consistently show that critique without an outside oracle gives small gains on tasks where the model's prior is already strong, and ZERO or negative gains on tasks where the prior is weak — which is exactly the regime here (Opus 4.7 plateaued at 6/15). LeanDojo / Coq tactic search / MLIR lowering work specifically moved away from LLM self-critique toward typed/verified oracles (the type-checker IS the critic) because LLM self-critique on formal code rubber-stamped its own errors. The proposal's "oracle" is csl_builtins.yaml lookup — which doesn't need an LLM in the loop; just gate the draft on the static check and re-prompt with the failed item, no YES/NO turn. (4) The wasted-cycle-savings argument (~90s saved on 30% of attempts) is double-counting: when the static checker catches an issue, you can just nudge directly to fix it (one extra implementer call, no critique turn) — the YES/NO model call is pure overhead. (5) "+1 Opus call" undersells the variance hit: Opus self-critique on a 200-line CSL file with 5 items + minimal-diff affordance is closer to 3-5K output tokens not "minimal patch"; in practice the model will rewrite the file. That's a second implementer call dressed as a critic — the framework already has best-of-N for that and it caps at the Sonnet+Opus union ceiling (6/15). Real expected lift on the 15-kernel bench: 0-1 kernel = 0-7pp. Most likely 0pp because the static checker layer is already doing the catchable work via builtin_whitelist_block + RAG'd gotchas. Distinguishing this from translation_facts on novelty grounds requires showing failures where the implementer DID violate a machine-checkable layout-export/builtin-arity constraint AND a downstream prompt the model would treat as authoritative-correction (not as its-own-prose-restated). I'd want to see, from the existing W1 failure verdicts, a count of "unknown symbol / wrong arity / missing import" cslc errors as a share of the 9 failures. If that share is <20% (my prior, based on the cluster mix), this proposal is dead-on-arrival; my "unlikely" rating assumes it's 20-40%.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Yes, and the smaller version exposes the proposal as redundant. Skip the LLM YES/NO turn entirely: run the static checker (which already exists as validate_facts_against_builtins + the four _extract_* functions in translation_facts.py) on the post-implementer draft, and if it fails, send ONE deterministic nudge ("@import_module 'X' is not in csl_builtins.yaml; layout.csl exports {Y, Z}; rewrite to use only those") and re-call the implementer once. No critique model in the loop. Eng cost: 4 hours (the extractors already exist; wire them into a post-draft validator + nudge template). If this 10x-smaller version gives 0pp lift on the 15-kernel bench (which is my prior — translation_facts already did the upstream version of this and got 0W), kill the whole line of inquiry. If it gives 1-2pp, you've proven the principle without paying for the YES/NO turn, and the YES/NO version is still strictly worse on cost. Either way, you don't need the full proposal. This is exactly the test that should be run BEFORE the 2-3-day eng investment, not after. A useful redirect: spend the 2-3 days on the actual bottleneck — halo_recv_unblock is 6/7 fail and the discarded r2/r3/r4 halo-gotcha workflows show the framework can't currently mine the @block/@unblock protocol shape from canonical examples. That's a real IR-shaped gap (multi-task control-flow / arm-disarm protocol IR), not a "did you spell the import right" gap.

all_critiques.name: Self-critique against cslc-grounded checklist
all_critiques.critique:
The proposal collapses on contact with the actual failure distribution. I scanned the most recent 15-kernel hybrid sweep (results/hybrid_sweep_20260614_210137/) and looked at the terminal-attempt stderr on each failing kernel. The four checklist categories — (a) imports against csl_builtins.yaml, (b) @export_symbol names against layout, (c) @bind_*_task targets, (d) DSD struct field names — would have flagged ~0 of the ~10 actual failures examined. Concretely:
- Laplacian2D-Halo last attempt: `tensor_access = |i|{Mt} -> src[i * @as(i16, Nt)]` — fails because `src` is a fn-argument pointer, not because of any import/export/binding/struct-field. The checklist YES-answers all 4.
- Residual / GEMV-Collectives-2D: `layout_mod.get_x_coord()` called at module scope. `layout_mod` IS imported; failure is a scope/comptime constraint. Checklist YES-answers all 4.
- Game-of-Life: `@export_symbol(&generate, "generate")` — the symbol's name matches what layout expects; the failure is type-shape (fn vs variable). A name-equality check would say YES.
- FFT-1D-2D: `f_east: [2*Nz]f16` size-expression comptime issue. Not an import/export/binding/field.
- Cholesky / Mandelbrot / GEMM-Collectives-2D / Laplacian2D-Reduce: runtime kernel-stall (`received 0 bytes`). No compile-time signal exists for the self-critique to consume.
