- GEMV (sonnet): error fires inside `collectives_2d/pe.csl:1157` — DSR ID assignment collision in library code. The implementer's import name is correct; the constraint violated is a numeric-allocation invariant the checklist doesn't model.
So on the 9 W1 failures the proposal claims to address, the structural answer to Q1 is: this IS the same shape as translation_facts — "machine-extractable surface facts injected into the model loop." The only differences are (i) extraction runs after the draft not before, and (ii) the model answers YES/NO instead of consuming prose. Neither difference changes what facts are available. translation_facts already extracted the same imports/exports/bindings/field schemas (translation_facts.py lines 119-198 are exactly the proposed extractors), got A/B'd at 0W/2L/17T, and was pulled. The proposal re-runs that experiment with a YES/NO wrapper.

Q2 — addresses which cluster: none specifically. halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail) is dominated by (a) recv-task scope/ordering, (b) edge-PE deadlock from hardcoded neighbor counts, (c) async-vs-sync fabric DSD discipline. dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fail) is dominated by DSR-ID arithmetic collisions inside library code. collectives_2d (2/4 fail) is dominated by comptime-scope errors and DSR-id reuse, not import-name errors. None of the three clusters' modal failure is checklist-shaped.

Q3 — prior art outside this repo: I'm not aware of published code-translation work where pre-cslc self-critique against a 4-item structural checklist moved the needle on a hard benchmark. Self-consistency / self-critique results in coding (e.g. Self-Refine, Reflexion) generally show benefit when the critic has access to an EXECUTION signal the generator didn't have. Here the proposal explicitly runs BEFORE cslc, so the critic has strictly less signal than the existing reviewer (which fires after benchmark with the actual stderr in hand). That's the wrong direction — the existing reviewer is the one with leverage; an additional critic upstream of execution is the weaker variant.

Q4 — 10x cheaper proof: yes, and it should be run first. Take the existing translation_facts.py extractor (it already builds the 4 lists), grep across results/hybrid_sweep_20260614_210137/**/final_result.json for last-attempt failures, and for each failure ask: does extract_layout_facts(kernel_dir) on the draft pe.csl report any of the 4 categories as mismatched? If the answer on the 9 W1 failures is "0–1 mismatches detected," the lift ceiling is 0–1/15 and the experiment is dead before any LLM call. From the spot-check above the answer looks like 0/9, so the ceiling is ~0% lift.

Q5 — actual expected lift on 15-kernel benchmark from 6/15 baseline: 0%, possibly -1 kernel (regression risk from the model rubber-stamping YES and the wrapper consuming a budget slot, or producing a 'minimal patch' that corrupts a previously-compiling draft). Author's own risk note flags the rubber-stamping failure mode, which is the dominant one.

Additional concerns the proposal underrates:
- The 30% "wasted cslc cycle saved" claim is unsourced. By grep over the same sweep, only 3 attempts across all 15 kernels show an undeclared-identifier-class error that the checklist would catch pre-cslc — that's ~3/100 attempts, not 30%, and saving 90s of cslc on 3 attempts is unmeasurable.
- "Minimal-diff parsing of the response" is a regression vector. The reviewer→implementer loop's main risk today is the implementer rewriting code in ways that lose previously-working pieces. Adding a second model that emits minimal patches without compile-grounding adds exactly that risk before cslc has run.
- The reviewer already runs post-cslc with the real stderr and routes to bucket A/B/C. Adding a pre-cslc critique with strictly less information is duplicative work.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: There IS a useful smaller variant, but it isn't an LLM call: ship the static checker WITHOUT the model wrapper. Take the 4 extractors (already in translation_facts.py), run them as a PURE PYTHON gate on the implementer's draft before cslc, and on a hard fail (e.g. @import_module path not in csl_builtins.yaml; @export_symbol name not in layout's expected exports), short-circuit to a deterministic repair-prompt that names the specific mismatch — no model self-critique, no YES/NO theater. Cost: 4 hours. If it fires on ~3% of attempts as the grep suggests, lift is 0-1 kernels, but at least the cost is also ~0 and you learn the true mismatch rate empirically. If the mismatch rate turns out to be <5%, that's a definitive kill signal for the full LLM-wrapped version. If it's >20% (which I doubt based on the sweep evidence), THEN the LLM wrapper becomes defensible. Run the cheap version first; do not approve the 2-3 day eng spend until the mismatch-rate measurement is in hand.

all_critiques.name: Reference-bundle retrieval for nearest neighbor pe.csl exemplar
all_critiques.critique:
Five hard problems, ordered by severity.

(1) The feature extractor is wrong for exactly the failing kernels. The proposal extracts features "from layout.csl" but the W1 failures cluster on kernels that don't have a single pe.csl/layout.csl pair. 25-Point Stencil has 7 .csl files (routes/switches/task/oned_exch/nop/consts/util) with no layout.csl at the conventional path. BiCGSTAB/CG/PCG each have layout.csl + layout_bicgstab.csl plus blas.csl + kernel.csl + kernel_<solver>.csl. SpMV-Hypersparse has subdirectories (allreduce2R1E/, hypersparse_spmv/). The feature extractor will silently read the wrong file or no file, and the "top-1 nearest neighbor" will be selected from a corrupt feature space for ~half the failing corpus. This is a "ran on the easy case, broke on the hard case" trap.

(2) The cluster sizes don't support the retrieval premise. halo_recv_unblock has 7 kernels, 6 fail, 1 works (7pt-Stencil or Laplacian2D-Halo). That single working neighbor is structurally simpler than the 6 failures — it's the easy case of the cluster. Injecting it as an exemplar for 25-point-Stencil invites the implementer to collapse to a single-file shape and skip the routes/switches/task decomposition the kernel actually needs. Same problem in dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fail) — the one working neighbor is the lower-complexity case. Nearest-neighbor only helps when neighbors are comparable in complexity; the W1 failure pattern is precisely that the failing kernels are MORE complex than the passing ones in their cluster.

(3) The "structurally different from semantic_bridge/translation_facts" argument is weaker than the proposal admits. Yes, granularity differs (whole file vs. atomic fact). But the deeper reason those failed is that W1 failures are not knowledge failures — they're composition failures. The model already saw the relevant csl-examples chunks via TF-IDF; the working 7pt-Stencil pe.csl IS in that corpus. Switching from chunked to whole-file retrieval moves the same content from "retrieved as needed" to "always present in prompt at 2k tokens." That's a context-budget tradeoff, not a fundamentally new signal. The "worked example" literature lift (in-context code generation studies) was measured on Python/Java where the model is already fluent; CUDA→CSL has the language-fluency gap that turns exemplars into miscopies.

(4) The compute-leak guard claim is true at the canary level but misses the firewall's intent. The author is correct that the canary keyed to the target's fn name won't false-positive on a neighbor's pe.csl. But the original "layout visible, compute hidden" invariant exists so the translator can't see the answer. Once you systematically inject other kernels' pe.csl as neighbors, you are training the model on a peer-leaked corpus — kernel A learns CSL syntax from kernel B's solved compute, then kernel B (in a later sweep, after curriculum drift) learns from kernel A's solved compute. Across enough sweeps this is exactly the regurgitation drift the canary was added to prevent. The proposal needs an explicit "exemplar pool excludes the cluster of the target kernel," not just "exemplar != target."

(5) Cost is understated. "2-3 days" budgets the implementation only. The real cost: a unit test for the compute-leak interaction (claimed), a regression test for selection stability (claimed), AND a per-attempt instrumented sweep to verify the exemplar isn't actively mis-leading (not claimed). The discarded experiments (translation_facts, semantic_bridge) burned weeks in A/B replay specifically because "looked plausible, didn't survive contact" was only discoverable through full sweeps. Plan +1 week for proper A/B, not 3 days.

What's actually likely to happen: on the 15-kernel W1 sweep, halo cluster (6 failures) sees 0-1 new passes — probably Laplacian2D-Reduce if anything, since it's the closest neighbor to 7pt-Stencil. dsr_queue_fabric_init (2 failures, BiCGSTAB/CG/PCG vintage) sees 0 new passes because the failing kernels are multi-file and no single-file exemplar bridges that. collectives_2d (2 failures) might see 1 if there's a comparable-shape working neighbor — but the cluster-gated KNOWN_GOTCHAS_W1 already covers most of the same surface. Realistic outcome: 6/15 → 6 or 7 out of 15, with non-trivial risk of one regression as a misleading exemplar pushes a borderline-passing kernel off the cliff. Net expected: +0 to +1 pass, NOT a step-change.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Yes, and it's the right first move. Pick the worst cluster (halo, 6/7 fail). Hand-pick a SINGLE exemplar pair: 7-Point-Stencil pe.csl as the exemplar, inject it verbatim into the implementer prompt for THREE targets — 25-Point-Stencil, Residual, and one other halo failure. Run 5 attempts each. Total: 15 LLM runs (~$5, half a day of wall-clock). If even ONE new pass appears AND no regression vs control, the principle is proven and the full feature-extractor/retrieval engineering is justified. If zero new passes, kill the full proposal. This skips the entire feature-extraction / similarity-scoring / index-build cost (2 of the claimed 3 days) and answers the actual question (does whole-file exemplar injection help) directly. Critically: the smaller variant uses the EASIEST mapping (hand-picked best exemplar for each target) — if it can't win there, the retrieval-based version with selection error definitely won't.

all_critiques.name: Reference-bundle retrieval for nearest neighbor pe.csl exemplar
all_critiques.critique:
Three load-bearing problems, each grounded in this repo's evidence.

(1) PRIOR ART IN THIS REPO ALREADY RAN THIS EXPERIMENT AND IT FAILED. The tutorials A/B (results/cross_model_tutorials_ab.md, 2026-05-31) is materially the same shape: whole-file CSL tutorial programs injected with agent-specific dispatch (architect→READMEs, implementer→CSL fns), 217-chunk broad and 29-chunk narrow variants. Across Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7, and gpt-oss-120b on 4 hard kernels, net pass-count delta vs baseline was 0/0/0. The report's verbatim conclusion: "knowledge layers below the implementer raise the quality of generated CSL without changing whether it passes the benchmark." The proposal's claim that "whole-file exemplars are what the model actually generalizes from" is asserted against direct evidence to the contrary on this exact pipeline. The author flags this as "shape risk" then dismisses it with "translation_facts was a glossary, this is a worked example" — but the I config of the tutorials A/B was already worked examples (entire pe_program.csl files from topic-11-collectives etc.), not a glossary.

(2) THE COMPUTE-LEAK GUARD IS NOT THE INVARIANT BEING PROTECTED. cuda2csl.py:938-1029 extracts a canary line from the TARGET kernel's reference compute file only. Injecting Laplacian2D-Halo's full 269-line pe.csl into the 25-Point Stencil translation will pass the canary check trivially — that's the author's "mitigation." But the canary's PURPOSE is to prevent the agent from regurgitating the reference solution. The benchmark invariant is "the agent translates from CUDA, not from a working CSL"; cross-kernel exemplar injection violates that invariant for siblings in the same cluster, which is exactly where the proposal would inject. For halo_recv_unblock (6/7 failing), the only large working exemplar is Laplacian2D-Halo (pe.csl 269 lines) and stencil_3d_7pts in benchmark-libs — the failing kernels share DSD setup, halo color routing, and recv-unblock idioms with these by construction. A "passing" 25pt-Stencil after seeing 7pt-Stencil's full pe.csl would be epistemically void; the framework would have built a measurement contamination, not a translation lift. This is worse than no lift.

(3) THE STRUCTURAL FIT IS BACKWARDS FOR THE FAILING CLUSTER. The failing kernels are precisely the multi-file ones. 25-Point Stencil is 7 files / 1583 lines (layout 248, oned_exch 166, task 804, util 52, routes 126, switches 80, consts 107). The "30 working kernels" pool advertised in the proposal — when grep'd for pe.csl — has 14 single-file entries (GEMM, GEMV, Cholesky, Wide-Mult, Laplacian2D-Halo, Laplacian2D-Reduce, LorenzoPredictor-Tile, Game of Life pe_program.csl, etc.). The nearest-neighbor over layout.csl features will tend to retrieve single-file siblings for multi-file targets, because layout.csl is similar but the compute decomposition is the actual difficulty. The implementer is already single-shot; handing it a 269-line pe.csl when it needs to emit 1500 lines across 7 files actively misleads on shape, not just algorithm.

Answers to the hard questions: (1) Not structurally different from semantic_bridge/tutorials at the shape that matters — all three are "inject more text before implementer." Granularity isn't the axis that drove those failures; the implementer doesn't have the headroom to use either. (2) Generic "more context" — no cluster-specific lift mechanism. For halo, the existing 269-line Laplacian2D-Halo + 11 distilled gotchas + cluster-keyed RAG already saturate the surface; for dsr_queue_fabric_init the working pool is tiny (likely 1-2 exemplars, all siblings); for collectives_2d the available exemplars are sibling-contaminated. (3) The external prior art the author would cite is in-context learning for boilerplate-heavy code generation (codex/CoT papers showing few-shot exemplar lift on HumanEval-style tasks); none of that work involves a domain where the "exemplar" pool is six items, sibling-overlapped, and competes with already-saturated RAG. (4) See smaller_variant. (5) Expected lift is at or below 0 wins out of 9 failures, with a non-zero chance of contamination-driven false-positive passes that look like wins but invalidate the benchmark.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Yes, and it would kill the idea in <1 day. Run a single A/B on the halo_recv_unblock cluster only: pick the 1-2 currently-passing halo kernels as exemplar source (Laplacian2D-Halo, 7pt-Stencil), inject the full passing pe.csl into the implementer prompt for the 6 failing halo kernels, with an EXPLICIT contamination audit step that diffs the produced pe.csl against the injected exemplar (line-equivalence ratio, function-name overlap). If contamination ratio is high and pass rate is up, you've measured nothing real. If contamination is low and pass rate is up, then expand. If pass rate is flat (the predicted outcome based on the tutorials A/B precedent), discard. ~1 day eng for the diff harness, ~$0.40 sweep cost. Critically: do NOT skip the contamination audit. Without it, this experiment is uninterpretable for the same reason the compute-leak canary exists in the first place. A still-smaller variant: skip implementation and instead run a single manual injection (25pt-Stencil receiving Laplacian2D-Halo's pe.csl) to inspect what the agent does with it — 2 hours total. If the agent copies large blocks verbatim, you have your answer without building any infra.

all_critiques.name: Programmatic compile-error to gotcha-KB feedback (active learning, no LLM)
all_critiques.critique:
Three concrete reasons this is dead-on-arrival or near it:

(1) **Same shape as translation_facts, with a more brittle source signal.** The proposal disclaims the comparison ("structurally NOTHING like translation_facts: there is no extra prompt context here"), but that's wrong. translation_facts injected structured CSL-side facts at the implementer; this proposal injects structured CSL-side gotcha entries at the implementer (via the existing KB injection path the proposal itself names: `for_implementer()`, csl_knowledge_base.py:1323). The delivery channel is identical. The only difference is the *authoring* pipeline (auto-mined vs hand-curated). The author flags this exact risk ("if the model isn't acting on KB entries, growth doesn't help") and then proposes "measure pass-rate lift" as mitigation — but that's a *detection* mechanism, not a fix. translation_facts was killed for exactly this reason after 19 attempts. The KB-injection channel has a known low conversion rate from "fact present in prompt" to "fact acted on in generation"; adding more entries at the bottom of the pile doesn't change conversion rate.

(2) **The error signal is dominated by cascade noise and meta-errors, not the patterns that matter.** I sampled `final_result.json` from the existing results tree. The most common stderr in Single-Tile-Matvec failures is `error: Unable to open ./src/layout_matvec.csl: no such file or directory` — a *bundle staging path* error, not a CSL language error. This will normalize into a top-N pattern that has zero translation signal. The real W1 failure clusters are halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail), dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fail), collectives_2d (2/4 fail) — these are *semantic/mesh-topology* failures where the cslc error is far downstream of the root cause (or the code compiles and runs wrong, producing no cslc error at all). Mining error text won't surface a gotcha that says "you need to call `@unblock` after `@recv_data` on stencil edges" — that pattern doesn't show up as a normalized cslc error, it shows up as a hang or wrong-result. Author's own mitigation ("require reproducer to compile-fail with the same error class") strands the long tail of *runtime* failures and *no-error wrong-output* failures, which is most of the W1 bottleneck.

(3) **N≥3 across distinct kernels is the wrong threshold for the corpus that exists.** With 15 kernels × 8 attempts × N sweeps, the patterns that will cross N≥3-distinct-kernels are the *already-known* ones (halo edge handling, DSR queue init) that hand-curation already covered (#35, #57, #65). The long-tail patterns that are still killing the 9 failing kernels are by definition *infrequent* — one kernel doing one weird thing — and N≥3 across distinct kernels filters them out. Lower the threshold to N=1 and you regress to the LLM-drafter failures of r2/r3 (fabricated patterns from one-off noise).

Other holes: prior art for "auto-mined compiler-error gotcha library for code translation" is thin. LLVM/MLIR error catalogs exist as *documentation* (LLVM diagnostics, the Rust compiler error index) but the data they're built from is the *compiler's source*, not user attempts. Closest comparable is competitive-programming auto-hint mining (CodeContests, AlphaCode) where the lift over the hand-curated baseline was small (~1-2pp) and they had 10^5+ attempts, not 10^3. The proposal's claim of "120 failures/sweep × n sweeps = real data corpus" is true but the *signal-to-noise* in those failures is dominated by harness issues (bundle paths, missing files) not translation issues.

Author's risk note ("lowest shape risk of all 6 proposals") is also wrong — this has *medium* shape risk because it's the third iteration on the same shape (semantic_bridge → translation_facts → mined-gotchas) and the first two failed for reasons that this iteration doesn't structurally address.

Bottom line: if hand-curated grounded halo gotchas just shipped and we don't yet have the resweep number, building an *automated* pipeline to produce more entries of the same shape before knowing whether the hand-curated ones moved the needle is premature. Measure first.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: 10x smaller, useful version: spend 4 hours, not 4 days. Write a one-shot script (50 LOC) that walks the existing results tree, extracts every unique normalized stderr, dedupes, and writes a flat ranked list with kernel attribution. No promotion logic, no ground_gotcha integration, no diff gate. Read the list with human eyes for 30 minutes. If you find 3+ patterns that (a) are real CSL language errors not harness noise, and (b) aren't already in `KNOWN_GOTCHAS_W1_FAILURE_PATTERNS`, *then* the full proposal's premise is validated and worth the 4-day build. If you find 0-2, you've killed the proposal at 5% of the cost and learned that the signal isn't there. This also has the side benefit of producing a hand-curatable shortlist for the *next* round of grounded gotchas — which is what task #65 already proved works. Concretely: `find results/cuda2csl -name final_result.json -exec jq -r '.attempts[] | select(.status=="fail") | .transcript[] | .stderr' {} + | grep -oE 'error:.{1,200}' | sed 's/[0-9]\+/<N>/g; s/[a-z_]\+\.csl/<F>/g' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -40` — that's literally the experiment, runnable today.

all_critiques.name: Programmatic compile-error to gotcha-KB feedback (active learning, no LLM)
all_critiques.critique:
Empirically tested the premise against the actual sweep data (17 kernels, 134 attempts, 130 failures, 123 compile-fails in /home/USER/xkernel/code_translation/results/cuda2csl/run_2026061*). Four hard problems the proposal underweights:

(1) The cslc error stream is mostly cascade noise. The top normalized pattern is 'semantic error in module imported here' (102x) and 'failed to parse program requested here' (26x) — both are the compiler saying 'the real error is one import-level down.' These dominate the histogram and would generate worthless gotchas under the proposed templating ('error: semantic error in module imported here seen 102x'). The 'extract 5 lines around file:line' heuristic captures the wrong site for cascade errors; you have to walk the import chain to the root, which the proposal doesn't scope.

(2) The non-cascade errors that DO pass N>=3 are largely already in the KB. 'only var and extern const may be uninitialized' fires 40x in the last sweep and that gotcha was hand-curated in r5 (Library .csl files gotcha) AND in the collectives_2d gotcha #3 AND in the topic-11 corner-PE gotcha. The model is being shown those entries via cluster-gated injection and still emits the error 40x. The bottleneck is model retention / prompt-slot saturation, NOT KB coverage. Mining more variants of the same error doesn't address the failure mechanism.

(3) The halo_recv_unblock cluster (6 of the 9 failing kernels, the dominant W1 bottleneck per PROGRESS) typically fails as a RUNTIME D2H 0-bytes hang, not a compile error. The miner has zero signal there. In the specific sweep I sampled, 7pt-Stencil/Residual/Game-of-Life all compile-fail before reaching runtime, but the conceptual bug (which PE skipped unblock_cmd_stream) is one cslc literally cannot diagnose — so even when compile-failed those attempts contribute noise to the histogram, not signal toward the halo bottleneck.

(4) The 'structurally different from translation_facts' claim overstates it. The OUTPUT lands in the same KNOWN_GOTCHAS_W1_FAILURE_PATTERNS string at the same for_implementer() slot. translation_facts lost 0W/2L/17T at that slot. The source-of-truth being mined-from-real-errors vs. extracted-from-IR doesn't change the prompt-slot saturation failure mode that killed translation_facts. The author flags this risk in the 'real risk' note but then doesn't downweight expected lift for it.

What actually worked (task #65 halo gotchas) involved a human reading cascade-failed compiles, understanding WHY each error occurred, mentally constructing the canonical fix, then grounding it. The miner produces mechanical templates ('Compile error X seen N times. Trigger: regex.') — that's a restatement of cslc's own output, not a fix. The model already sees cslc's output in the debugger sub-agent loop. Adding the same string to the KB pre-implementer doesn't add information; it adds repetition.

Prior art yellow flag: no public work I can point to on auto-mining compile errors into a corpus-level LLM-prompt KB for code translation. Closest analogs (Self-Debug, MAGIS, SymPrompt) keep error feedback in the inner loop of a single generation, not as a KB grower. The mechanism the proposal proposes is novel, which here is bad — multiple smarter teams haven't built it because the cost/benefit doesn't pencil.

Cost-benefit: 3-4 eng-days for a build that addresses 0-1 kernels of the 9 failing. Worse, it builds infrastructure (miner + grounding gate + diff promotion) whose maintenance burden persists even after it stops paying lift. If it ships and underperforms, ripping it out costs another day.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Yes — a 1-day version is so directly probative it should run BEFORE the 3-4 day version. Hand-pick the top 5 non-cascade normalized error patterns from the existing 17-kernel sweep results (grep error: lines from results/cuda2csl/run_2026061*/*/final_result.json — I already ran this; the candidates are 'declaration shadows another symbol' 8x, 'failed to evaluate expression for array dimension' 4x, 'variable of type X must be comptime-known' 3x, plus 1-2 more). Write 5 prose gotchas by hand reading the failing CSL files. Drop them into KNOWN_GOTCHAS_W1_FAILURE_PATTERNS. Re-run the hybrid sweep on the 9 failing kernels. If that doesn't move 6/15 to 7/15 or 8/15, the full miner won't either — the bottleneck is not KB coverage. If it DOES move, then automate (and you've already validated which error classes to target, sparing the cascade-handling problem). The 1-day version captures ~all of the expected lift at ~10% the cost AND tells you whether the bigger build is worth doing. Running 3-4 days of automation before this 1-day test is the wrong sequence.

all_critiques.name: Sub-kernel cslc probe gate before bundle assembly
all_critiques.critique:
Q1 (structural difference): Yes, partly. semantic_bridge and translation_facts injected text BEFORE the implementer wrote code (priors); this injects executable verdicts AFTER, in the repair loop. That's a real shape change — error attribution vs. context priming. BUT the repair loop already receives a full cslc stderr_tail clipped to 400+1600 chars (see cuda2csl.py:1675), plus the debugger sub-agent (which already runs targeted compile probes per DEBUGGER_AGENT_DESIGN). So the marginal new signal is "which fragment lit up cslc," not "what cslc says." That marginal-localization-only view is much narrower than the proposal pitches it as. Closer in shape to the debugger agent than to translation_facts; the question is whether sub-fragment locality buys what the debugger doesn't already buy.

Q2 (does it address a specific failing cluster?): Weakly. The author admits the right intuition — fragment-locality fits READER-side fixes (typo, wrong import field, arity). But the actual failure modes:
  - halo_recv_unblock (6/7): the post-mortem said canonical patterns are 'too composed to fit minimal harnesses'. That was about WRITING gotcha snippets — the proposal's claim that READING is different is plausible but unverified. A halo-recv bug like 'unblock called from wrong task context' or 'wrong color routes' is INHERENTLY cross-fragment (task↔color↔queue↔DSR↔fabric setup all interact). Fragment-isolated compiles will pass these because routes live in layout.csl, not pe.csl. Probe says 'ok' on each piece while bundle still fails.
  - dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3): the named bug class (dsr id collisions, queue 0/1 ownership) IS cross-fragment by definition — two functions colliding on DSR 6 is the bug, but each function alone compiles. The proposal explicitly flags this as the risk and offers no mitigation beyond 'demote it for those classes,' which means it doesn't help the cluster it claims to target.
  - collectives_2d (2/4): these need the full mesh harness (c2d_params, set_rectangle ≥ 2x2) to even instantiate; single_pe and send_recv_2x1 harnesses will reject the snippet on import_module failures unrelated to the real bug.
So the proposal targets a generic 'better error attribution' improvement that does NOT cleanly fit any of the 3 failing clusters. The clusters that DO benefit from fragment-local checks (typos, wrong builtin arity) are precisely the ones cslc already nails in the bundle pass with a clear pointer line.

Q3 (prior art): Closest analogue is incremental/separate compilation in MLIR/LLVM lowering pipelines and the 'shrink ray' pattern from delta debugging (creduce, C-Reduce, llvm-reduce). Those help HUMANS triage; published evidence of them moving the needle on LLM-driven code-translation pass-rate (vs. just being a developer convenience) is essentially absent. The closest LLM-loop precedent is ToolWriter / Self-Debug / LDB (LLM Debugger) using runtime feedback — those report 5-15% lifts on competitive programming, but the baseline there is 'no execution feedback at all.' We already have execution feedback (full cslc stderr + debugger probes). Net: no specific prior art for sub-program slicing as a CSL/MLIR-style translator booster. Yellow flag.

Q4 (10x smaller version): Yes, and it's the right first move. ~2 hours, not 1 day: pick the 9 failing kernels' final-attempt pe.csl files from results/, wrap each one's @import_module block, each fn body, each color/DSR decl block in the existing 3 harnesses, run cslc, and tabulate (a) what fraction of bundle-level errors get reproduced by some fragment, (b) what fraction of fragments compile clean while the bundle fails, (c) is the surfaced error materially better-localized than the bundle's. If (a) is < 50% — most bundle errors don't reproduce fragment-isolated — kill the proposal. If (b) is high — most fragments pass while bundle fails — the signal is too sparse to act on. This dry-run uses existing artifacts and existing harnesses; it requires zero new code beyond a fragment splitter (~80 lines).

Q5 (honest lift estimate from 6/15): 0-2 kernels (0-13pt). Most likely +1 (collectives_2d typo case, maybe one halo case where the bug is a wrong @import_module field name). Negative tail risk: if probe adds an authoritative-sounding 'fragment X passes' to the repair prompt that misdirects the implementer away from the real cross-fragment bug (halo/dsr both have this shape), it could regress. I'd budget +6% expected (vs the proposal's implied 10-20%), with non-trivial probability of 0% or -7%.

Other specific concerns:
- Fragment extraction from a 200-line draft via AST-walk is harder than it sounds: CSL fns frequently reference comptime params, imports, and module-level consts defined elsewhere in the file. Splitting them in isolation will produce 'undefined symbol' noise that swamps the real bug. The proposal hand-waves this as 'wrap in HARNESS_SINGLE_PE' but the harness only provides memcpy_params and M, N — every real fn touches more.
- The +30-90s per attempt cost is per-FRAGMENT serial in singularity_gate (cslc is gated). For a kernel with 8 fns + 4 import blocks + 3 DSR decls, that's 15 cslc runs ≈ 150-300s, not 30-90s. Across 8 attempts × 15 kernels that's an extra 5-10 hours per sweep, not 15-25 min.
- The proposal does NOT address the W2 iterative-solver problem (memory note: cycles_send is host-RPC-bounded for those kernels — no amount of better translation-time signal fixes a measurement-bottleneck). Author correctly scopes to W1 but the framework PM should note this proposal can't touch the biggest known cycle-reduction gap.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Don't build the wiring. First, run the 2-hour DRY analysis on the 9 failing pe.csl files: extract fragments, compile them in existing harnesses, count (a) bundle-error reproduction rate, (b) fragment-passes-while-bundle-fails rate, (c) error-message localization improvement. Decide go/no-go from numbers, not intuition. If go, scope to ONE error class with measured locality (import field names is the most plausible) — not 'all of them with category demotion.' That's a 1-day build, not 2-day, and avoids the trap of building general infra for a benefit that exists only on a narrow slice. Skip the bucket-B wiring entirely for v1; instead inject the fragment verdict into the existing debugger sub-agent's stderr_tail prompt as one extra structured block — that hits the same surface area with ~30 lines of glue and no new control flow.

all_critiques.name: Sub-kernel cslc probe gate before bundle assembly
all_critiques.critique:
Q1 (structural difference): Yes, structurally different from semantic_bridge / translation_facts — those injected text BEFORE the implementer; this injects a structured cslc-grounded signal AFTER it, in the repair loop. That's a real architectural distinction. BUT the repair loop already gets the real cslc stderr with file/line/column (cuda2csl.py:1670-1678 trims to head=400/tail=1600 of the failing transcript). The marginal info a fragment probe adds is "this snippet also fails when isolated" vs the existing "the full file fails here at line N". For most fragment-local errors (typos, builtin arities, import field names) the bundle-level cslc message already pinpoints them. The proposal is structurally novel; the SIGNAL it adds is largely redundant with what repair already sees.

Q2 (does it address the specific failing clusters): No — and the evidence cuts the other way. I sampled the actual cslc errors on the failing W1 kernels. The halo and collectives_2d failures are dominated by errors like: `builtin is only valid during layout evaluation @export_name(...)` (wrong file — fragment passes single_pe harness, fails in real layout binding), `name 'x_tile' was not declared during layout evaluation @export_symbol(ptr_x, ...)` (cross-file symbol coupling), `param dim_memcpy ... may be uninitialized → failed to evaluate expression for array dimension` (param-to-sizing chain across the whole comptime graph), `semantic error in module imported here @set_tile_code(...)` (failure surfaces in layout.csl referring to a pe.csl import). These are exactly the cross-fragment / cross-file composition failures the proposal's own risk note flags as out-of-scope. The dsr_queue_fabric_init cluster IS in scope (DSR id collisions across functions) but only when the collision is intra-file AND the harness preserves the colliding DSR allocator state — fragment isolation defeats that by construction.

Q3 (prior art for code translation): MLIR/LLVM lowering passes do use per-op verifiers, but those are static type/IR checks on a canonical IR, not isolated re-compilation of source fragments inside a separate harness. The closest analogue I know — CompilerGym / TVM autotuners — gate on the full compile, not synthetic sub-modules. Spectacularly, the CUDA→SASS / Triton→PTX world does NOT do fragment-isolated probes for repair guidance; they iterate on the full module because the bottlenecks are exactly cross-fragment (register pressure, shared-mem aliasing, layout legality). No citation. Yellow flag.

Q4 (10x smaller version): Yes, and it should be the gate before you build the full probe. Write a 50-line script that takes the LAST 10 failed pe.csl drafts from results/cuda2csl/run_20260611_*, runs ground_gotcha.ground_csl_snippet() on the function bodies extracted by a crude regex, and for each draft prints: (a) did any isolated fragment fail? (b) was that fragment's error already in the bundle-level stderr_tail the repair loop saw? If (a)∧¬(b) is rare (<25% of drafts), the probe adds nothing the repair loop doesn't already have. Cost: 4 hours. This is mandatory diligence — the framework has burned three rounds on signals that overlapped with existing ones (semantic_bridge, translation_facts, r2/r3 halo drafters).

Q5 (expected lift on 15-kernel from 6/15): ~2-5% (i.e., maybe 1 additional pass, more likely 0). The 9 failures are not bottlenecked on "the implementer doesn't see which fragment broke" — they're bottlenecked on "the implementer doesn't know how to compose layout.csl ↔ pe.csl ↔ run.py for the halo recv pattern," which is upstream of the fragment view. The halo gotcha post-mortem from this June already concluded "canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses" — the PROPOSAL'S REPLY that the *reader* side fits where the *writer* side didn't is plausible but unverified, and given the actual halo errors I sampled hit cross-file coupling, the asymmetry the author hopes for is probably not real here.

Meta-risks: (i) The +30-90s/attempt with 8 attempts × 15 kernels × multiple sweeps adds real wall-clock that competes with sweeps that DO move the number. (ii) Fragment extraction by AST-walk on draft CSL is non-trivial — the framework doesn't have a CSL parser, only the cslc binary; you'll be writing brittle regex extraction that breaks on the next prompt revision. (iii) Most concerning: the repair loop currently feeds 2KB of REAL stderr to the LLM and STILL fails 9/15 — the LLM doesn't lack error visibility, it lacks the cross-file composition mental model. Adding a second structured error signal on top of an existing one that's already being ignored is a class of intervention the framework has tried and discarded twice.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: The 10x smaller version (Q4 above) is itself the right next step, but it's a DIAGNOSTIC, not a feature: run ground_csl_snippet over the last 10-20 failed drafts and measure the overlap between fragment-probe verdicts and the stderr the repair loop already gets. If overlap >75%, kill the proposal. If <25%, the proposal becomes interesting and should be re-evaluated. If 25-75%, scope the probe to ONLY error classes where overlap is low (likely: nothing; possibly: intra-file DSR collisions if the harness preserves allocator state). Higher-leverage alternative the proposal doesn't consider: instead of compiling fragments, compile the ACTUAL failing pe.csl WITH a swap-in synthetic minimal layout.csl, which would address the cross-file coupling errors that dominate the real failures. That's a one-day spike and would test the actually-bottlenecking hypothesis (\"the implementer can't see what layout.csl needs from it\") rather than the not-bottlenecking one (\"the implementer can't see which line is broken\").

all_critiques.name: Static halo-recv counting linter (compile-time invariant check)
all_critiques.critique:
Hard critique, answering the five questions in order.

(1) STRUCTURAL difference from semantic_bridge / translation_facts: weaker than the author claims. The author says "it returns a binary verdict that gates routing, not extra prompt text." That is a real structural change — but only on the success path. On the FAILURE path (which is the whole point of the linter, since the kernels we care about are the failing ones), it must inject a textual explanation back into the bucket-C repair prompt — otherwise the model has no idea what to fix. So in steady state on the halo cluster, this IS extra structured prompt text injected before/around the implementer call, decorated with "the linter said so." translation_facts already lost 0W/2L/17T precisely because RAG'd gotchas covered the same surface and IR added perturbation without lift. The risk of the same outcome is high.

(2) Specificity to a bottleneck cluster: yes, this one targets halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail) directly, which is the right cluster to target. But the framing "the bug class is mechanical (count of recvs doesn't match count of unblocks)" is wishful. Looking at the actual passing idioms in this repo, halo control flow is NOT a single arithmetic pattern. Game-of-Life uses per-direction running counters (num_west_recv, num_east_recv, num_ns_recv) mutated inside recv tasks, with @block/@unblock sequencing via task_ids and a 4-state machine (send / sync_fwd / fwd_east_west / sync_send). Laplacian2D-Halo uses a single RX_DONE_TID fired per-async-receive when extent completes — no running counter at all. Laplacian2D-Reduce adds an extra norm-color reduction layered on top. A linter that "computes expected_recv per PE from send_dsd extents" only handles the Laplacian shape; for the Game-of-Life shape there is no scalar "expected recv count" — the counter is conditional on which neighbors sent. The author's mitigation ("start in advisory mode, measure FP rate") is honest but the FP rate prediction is the proposal's load-bearing assumption and it is most likely high.

(3) Prior art: there is no public prior art for "static halo-counter linter for CSL-like dataflow language" because CSL is niche. The closest analogs are MLIR verifier passes for affine/linalg dialects (these work because the IR is constructed by the compiler, not parsed from human/LLM output) and Verilog/Chisel linters for handshake protocols (Verilator's UNUSED, Spyglass clock-domain checks — these work on a fixed structural surface that has standardized over decades). For LLM-emitted code: CodeT, Self-Debug, Reflexion all use compiler/test feedback, not custom static analyzers; no published result shows that hand-written static checkers on top of LLM output systematically beat "give the LLM the failing test or compiler error." This is a yellow flag bordering on red. The conceptual cousin that does work — fuzzing/property-based-testing as oracle for LLM code generation (e.g., CodeRosetta) — uses an executable oracle, not a static one. Which suggests the right answer is NOT a static linter at all but a runtime probe (see smaller variant below).

(4) 10x smaller version that proves the principle in <1 day: yes, and it should be done first. Skip the AST walker, skip the topology arithmetic. Instead: take the 6 currently-failing halo kernels' last-attempt drafts (we have them on disk in results/), hand-compute the recv-count-vs-unblock-threshold mismatch for each, and write the corrective sentence by hand. Re-run JUST the implementer with that sentence prepended. If hand-curated, oracle-grade corrections don't unstick 3+/6, the linter cannot possibly help — because the linter is strictly worse than hand-curated text. This experiment is 4 hours, not 4 days, and it falsifies the proposal cheaply. Cost-benefit demands it before any AST work.

(5) Expected lift on 15-kernel benchmark: I'd estimate +0 to +1 kernels (6/15 → 6-7/15), most likely +0. Reasons: (a) halo failures are rarely "off-by-one in the unblock counter" — when you read the actual transcripts (per PROGRESS.md, A1/A2/B1 halo workflow iterations all hit 0/5), the dominant failure modes are wrong DSR/queue lifecycle, missing fabric-init, mis-typed RX_DONE_TID firing semantics, and composed multi-task sequencing — not arithmetic counter mismatches. (b) The 3 halo gotchas shipped today (item 65) already target this surface with hand-curated text; their lift is the upper bound on what a noisier auto-extractor of the same information can deliver. (c) Bucket-C re-routing already exists; the marginal value is the verdict, and a noisy verdict (false-positive on Game-of-Life-style counters) would degrade routing.

Bottom line: structurally similar to a discarded experiment, targets the right cluster but with the wrong mental model of the failure (arithmetic vs. dataflow-protocol sequencing), no external precedent, and the 4-hour falsification test should run before any 4-day build. If the 4-hour test surprises me (3+/6 unstick with hand-graded recv-count corrections), reconsider.
all_critiques.smaller_variant:
Yes, two smaller variants, in this order:

(a) 4-hour oracle test: for each of the 6 failing halo kernels, manually inspect the latest draft pe.csl, hand-compute the recv-count-vs-unblock mismatch (if any), and prepend a one-sentence correction to a fresh implementer call. If <3/6 unstick with oracle-grade corrections, the full proposal is dead. If 3+/6 unstick, build the smallest possible linter that handles ONLY the Laplacian-shape pattern (single RX_DONE_TID per extent), skip the Game-of-Life-shape (per-direction running counter) entirely.

(b) Replace the linter entirely with a runtime probe: instrument the draft pe.csl with a watchdog timer + per-direction recv counters that dump to stdout on hang, run on cs_python_sdk simulator for 1s with tiny mesh, and feed the actual observed counter values back into the bucket-C repair prompt. Has the oracle property the static linter lacks (it sees what really happened), works uniformly across both halo idiom shapes, and reuses the existing cslc-grounding infrastructure (ground_gotcha.py). Eng cost is comparable; expected lift is materially higher because the signal is true rather than estimated.

all_critiques.name: Static halo-recv counting linter (compile-time invariant check)
all_critiques.critique:
Three serious problems.

(1) STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCE FROM translation_facts IS THINNER THAN CLAIMED. The proposal frames itself as "binary verdict gates routing, not prompt text" — but the verdict message ("PE(0,1) expects 3 recvs but unblocks at 4") is itself text injected into the C-bucket prompt. Net effect: structured-fact-extraction-over-CSL feeds new prose into a repair LLM call. That is the same shape as translation_facts (which also produced YAML facts consumed as prompt text), with two superficial deltas: (a) it runs post-draft instead of pre-draft, (b) it triggers a routing decision. translation_facts also gated behavior in a sense (it set the implementer's prior on field names) and still lost 0W/2L/17T. The "gating" framing is a rhetorical move, not a mechanism change.

(2) THE HALO IDIOM IS NOT SINGULAR — THE LINTER'S MENTAL MODEL DOESN'T MATCH THE CANONICAL CODE. I read the two canonical references the repo treats as ground truth. Game of Life (kernels/Game of Life/CSL/pe_program.csl:149-165) uses a SENTINEL-CHAIN idiom: the last async fmovs in a direction-set carries .activate=sync_fwd_task_id, and edge PEs call @activate directly. There is NO "expected = N" counter and NO recv_done threshold to lint against. Laplacian2D-Halo (kernels/Laplacian2D-Halo/CSL/pe.csl:1-30) uses a COUNTER idiom (RX_DONE increments a counter, fires COMPUTE at num_halos_expected). benchmark-libs/stencil_3d_7pts uses a third, param-driven library-import idiom. So the "every halo kernel has expected=N somewhere we can lint" premise is empirically false in the very directory the proposal cites. A linter that only knows counter-threshold patterns will false-negative on sentinel-chain drafts (most failing models will gravitate to the simpler sentinel form, since it's what Game of Life shows); a linter that knows both will need topology-sensitive idiom classification before it can even decide which arithmetic to check. That's not a 3-4 day project, that's a partial CSL type-checker.

(3) WRONG BUG CLASS. PROGRESS notes say r3/r4 halo-gotcha workflows failed because "drafters fabricated builtins/syntax/error messages" and "canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses." The failure mode in halo_recv_unblock cluster is IDIOM SELECTION, not off-by-one counter arithmetic. If the model picks the wrong async/sync model, the wrong color routing, or the wrong queue layout, the linter (which checks counter thresholds against send extents) will compute on garbage and either (a) silently pass because there's no recv_done to find, or (b) emit a count mismatch that misdirects the C-bucket repair away from the real bug. Best case: the linter never fires on the actual failure mode. Worst case: it emits confident-sounding misdirection that wastes a repair attempt.

(4) FALSE-POSITIVE RISK ON THE 84 PASSING BUNDLES. The author already flagged this, but it's underweight. Edge-PE arithmetic + axis-major mesh decompositions + c2d_params transforms means the topology computation needs to handle: row/col-major PE indexing, partial-mesh (sub-rectangle) topologies, per-PE comptime params evaluated from layout-side string-template arithmetic, and (for Power Method / iterative kernels) iteration-driven dynamic send counts. Getting <5% FP across 84 heterogeneous bundles requires actually implementing send/recv liveness over a comptime-evaluating walker. The "if FP stays high it joins translation_facts in discard" exit is honest but means the realistic outcome is another 3-4 days for the same null result.

(5) PRIOR ART IS THIN AND CAUTIONARY. LLVM MachineVerifier and Verilator-style lints work because their IR has explicit liveness/typing. Neural-translated DSL drafts don't. I don't know of published code-translation work where a post-hoc topology linter measurably lifted neural-translation pass rates; the closest analogues (LLM4Decompile, TransCoder repair loops) repair on compile-error/test-fail signal, not on author-written topology invariants. Author should be skeptical when the proposal has no external prior art AND has local prior art (translation_facts) that died for adjacent reasons.

Expected lift: 0-1 additional pass on the 15-kernel set, contingent on the C-bucket repair LLM picking up the mismatch as a count error rather than an idiom error. Most likely outcome: 0 net new passes, possibly -1 from misdirection on a sentinel-chain draft that the linter false-positives.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: YES — and the smaller variant is what should actually be tried first, because it's also the falsifier for the full proposal. ONE DAY SPIKE: run the proposed extractor (without orchestrator integration, without C-bucket routing) in pure read-only mode against the 84 passing bundles in knowledge/explored/successes/ + the 9 currently-failing W1 halo drafts saved in results/. For each, emit: (a) "I could compute expected_recv per PE = Y/N", (b) "I detected an unblock threshold to compare against = Y/N", (c) "verdict = pass/mismatch/inapplicable". If the verdict is "inapplicable" on >40% of passing bundles (likely, given the sentinel-chain idiom), OR if the verdict mismatches passing bundles (FP >5%), OR if it doesn't reliably catch the known-failing drafts (i.e., the bug isn't where the linter looks), kill the proposal — no orchestrator wiring, no 3-4 day eng. This spike is also valuable independent of the proposal: it produces a frequency table of which halo idioms appear in the corpus, which informs whether the next halo gotcha should target counter-style or sentinel-style failure. If I were forced to pick the single most useful thing to do here, it would be this spike SCOPED TO produce that idiom-frequency table, and explicitly NOT to build the linter as a gate.

all_critiques.name: CUDA-vs-CSL property-based equivalence sweep using existing CUDA refs
all_critiques.critique:
Aims at the wrong bottleneck. The 9 W1 failures are dominated by halo_recv_unblock (6/7), dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3), and collectives_2d (2/4) — these translations don't compile or crash at fabric init / DSR-allocation / halo-recv timing. A K=8 random-input equivalence gate runs only on translations that already passed the bundled test, so it sees ZERO of the 9 broken ones. Upper bound on lift is therefore "reclassify currently-passing translations as flaky" — which on a 6/15 baseline is NEGATIVE-leaning, not positive, unless the bucket-B re-route lands a fix, and the framework already shows that the budget/repair bucket isn't the bottleneck (reviewer-max-attempts 4→8 gave 0/14 marginal lift).

The author's claim of "lowest risk of being shaped like translation_facts" is half-right: as a verdict gate it IS structurally different from the two discarded prose/YAML injections. But the proposed bucket-B routing payload ("M=37,N=29,K=11 diverged max_rel_err=0.14") IS prompt-time context on the repair turn, so on the only path where it could lift pass-rate, it reverts to the exact shape that already failed twice. Worse, the random-size space is not free: CSL bundles bake fabric_dims, PE grid (P=4), and tile sizes (Mt=14,Kt=14,Nt=14) into commands.sh. Most "random" (M,N,K) will crash the CSL harness for reasons unrelated to translation correctness, producing false-flaky verdicts that demote good translations. Inspect of GEMM/CSL/commands_wse3.sh and the CUDA mains (which accept N/M/K via argv) confirms a deep impedance mismatch: the CUDA ref is host-orchestrated and shape-agnostic, the CSL is a tiled SUMMA hard-wired to a specific 4x4 PE grid. Per-kernel "shape range" extensions to spec.yaml are NOT 5 days; they require redesigning each CSL bundle's parameterization, which is the bulk of W1 itself.

W2 relevance is zero by the user's own auto-memory: iterative-solver cycles_send is host-RPC-bounded by run.py's Python loop, so output-correctness fuzzing cannot inform the cycle metric.

No prior art exists for this shape on kernel-translation tasks. Csmith/Alive2 do property-based compiler testing but target the COMPILER not the translation; their domain (small synthesizable C, peephole equivalence) is fundamentally different. Random-input fuzzing of finished binaries catches off-by-one boundary bugs — fine for "tile-boundary off-by-one" the author cites, but that is not the documented failure cluster on the 9 W1 fails.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Yes — kill the build, do the experiment in under a day: take the 6 currently-passing translations, run each at 2-3 spec-legal perturbed sizes (e.g. multiples of the baked P*Mt grid), see how many degrade. If 0/6 degrade, premise is falsified — abandon. If ≥3/6 degrade, you've learned something real but STILL need to verify the bucket-B repair payload actually steers fixes before building the K=8 gate. This 1-day probe replaces the 5-day build and is the only honest path forward. Cost: ~30 min of cslc+sim per kernel × 6 = ~3 hours wall-clock, zero new code beyond a 50-line param-sweep wrapper around the existing benchmark_csl.run_staged_bundle.

all_critiques.name: CUDA-vs-CSL property-based equivalence sweep using existing CUDA refs
all_critiques.critique:
The proposal solves a problem the failure data says doesn't exist on the bottleneck, and it can't physically run on most of the failing kernels.

1. STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCE FROM SEMANTIC_BRIDGE / TRANSLATION_FACTS — yes, real. This is an execution-time verdict gate, not an in-prompt context insertion. The author's risk note correctly identifies this. So it dodges the specific failure mode of those experiments (prompt perturbation without signal). But shape isn't the issue; targeting is.

2. DOES IT ADDRESS HALO_RECV_UNBLOCK / DSR_QUEUE_FABRIC_INIT / COLLECTIVES_2D? No. I read csl_knowledge_base.py: the halo cluster's distilled gotchas are all structural/init-time — `sys_mod.unblock_cmd_stream()` not called, `@initialize_queue` discipline, `@bind_local_task` top-level-comptime-only, hardcoded 4-neighbor recv-counts deadlocking boundary PEs, microthread ID pool exhaustion. dsr_queue_fabric_init is the same family. These kernels don't compile, or they hang at memcpy_h2d, or they deadlock before producing outputs. They don't "pass on the bundled input and fail on an adversarial input" — they produce no output at all. K=8 randomized inputs cannot fail-route something that never made it to a first verdict. The 9 W1 failures are structural, not numerical-edge-case.

3. THE PROPOSAL CAN'T EVEN RUN ON MOST OF THESE KERNELS. Laplacian2D-Halo's spec pins Mt=Nt=4, mesh=2x2, M=N=8 — the fabric layout, color routing, queue allocations, and halo buffers are baked into the CSL bundle at cslc time via out.json params. You cannot pass `--params=M=37,N=29` to an already-compiled multi-PE bundle; you would have to re-translate per random shape. For single-PE GEMM/GEMV this works; for the halo cluster and collectives_2d cluster (which IS the bottleneck — 8/9 of the failing kernels), it's incoherent. The proposal silently assumes shape-as-runtime-arg semantics that CSL doesn't have for the fabric kernels.

4. PRIOR ART — property-based equivalence on CUDA↔CSL or CUDA↔assembly translation: I can't cite anyone doing this for accelerator DSLs. Differential fuzzing exists for compilers (Csmith, EMI) but those exercise *compiler bugs* given a single correct source, not *translation correctness* across two distinct DSLs. The closest plausible analogues (DeepSeek's CUDA-to-Triton work, KernelBench evals, MLIR conversion testing) all gate on a single canonical input set. Yellow flag: there's a reason — for fabric-baked kernels, the input shape is part of the program, not an argument. Author cites no prior art; I find none.

5. CUDA REFERENCES MAY THEMSELVES BE WRONG — the author flags this. Looking at Laplacian2D-Halo/CUDA/kernel.cu the boundary handling differs from the CSL bundle's `Mt=Nt=4 2x2 mesh` assumption; the CUDA ref's comment says it "accepts arbitrary M, N" but the CSL bundle does not. Reconciling these per-kernel is the real engineering cost, undercounted in the 5-day estimate. Realistic: 2-3 days per fabric kernel for the comparator, ~3 weeks for the 9 W1 + 6 W2 set.

6. AUTHOR'S OWN ADMISSION KILLS IT FOR W1: "raises the floor (catches bad translations) more than the ceiling (doesn't generate new translations)". On a 6/15 baseline where the gap to 15/15 is 9 zero-output kernels, raising the floor under the 6 produces zero new passes. The proposal's stated mechanism — converting binary passes into a stratified pile — yields W1 lift of exactly 0 unless one of the current "passes" is actually wrong (possible, but then you'd LOSE a pass, not gain one; that's negative lift on this metric).

7. THE INTERESTING ANGLE THE PROPOSAL UNDERSELLS — for W2 (cycle reduction), the optimizer currently has only cycle-count signal. A robustness gradient could in principle help select between candidate optimizations. But the W2 bottleneck per MEMORY.md is that iterative solvers' cycles_send is host-RPC-bounded — Power_Method/BiCGSTAB/CG/PCG all measure host↔device cmd-stream sync, not on-device compute. Random-input robustness has zero bearing on that. The one W2 win cited (7pt-Stencil 2129→1076 via comptime_value_tuning) wasn't blocked by lack of robustness signal; the implementer just rarely produces the working transformation. K=8 doesn't help the implementer.

8. WHAT IT WOULD ACTUALLY CATCH — for single-PE algorithmic kernels (GEMM, GEMV, Mandelbrot, Histogram) the mechanism is sound but those kernels mostly pass already and aren't in the failure cluster. So the cost lands on the working set and the benefit lands nowhere.

Verdict: orthogonal to the actual bottleneck, mechanically blocked on the dominant failure cluster, and gives the W1 metric a 0 by construction.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: A genuinely cheap variant exists and would settle this in <1 day: pick the 3 single-PE algorithmic kernels currently passing (GEMM, GEMV, Mandelbrot) and run K=3 randomized inputs through CSL run.py + CUDA kernel.cu by hand. Do any of the current "passes" actually fail on random inputs? If yes — the binary verdict is hiding real bugs and the full proposal becomes more interesting (though still not for the W1 metric). If no — the entire premise (that single-input passes are masking translation bugs) is false and the proposal is dead. This is one afternoon of work and answers the load-bearing question. Do NOT build the spec.yaml extensions, kernel-class tolerance system, or bucket-B routing until the cheap version shows current passes are actually flaky. Separately, if the team wants a "better IR" approach: skip this and look at the *CUDA-side* IR the original Phase 1 plan deferred — a typed AST of the CUDA kernel that explicitly tags thread/block/shared-memory roles, fed to the analyzer as structured input rather than free-form prose. That at least addresses the analyzer's current "free-form CUDA prose" weakness, which is upstream of all 9 failures.

all_critiques.name: Symbolic SMT check of recv/unblock parity from layout
all_critiques.critique:
Five hard problems, in descending order of fatality.

(1) The encoding misrepresents the actual CSL halo pattern. I inspected a passing halo file (sandbox/cuda2csl/game-of-life_5no6shgo/.../stencil_3d_7pts/pe.csl). The pattern is `@block(ut_rx_n)` etc. — `@block` takes a *microthread handle* and waits for that one async @fmovs to finish, guarded by `is_n_edge`. There is no "recv_count == threshold" counter anywhere. `sys_mod.unblock_cmd_stream()` is a separate concept (yields the host command stream, unrelated to halo recv parity). The proposal conflates `@block(microthread_handle)` (per-edge per-microthread join) with a hypothetical counting unblock that fires "when recv_count == threshold." That counting pattern does exist in some collective idioms, but it is not the recurring halo-failure shape. Encoding a model that doesn't match the real semantics produces confident wrong answers — exactly the "encoding is wrong" failure mode the author flags as highest-risk.

(2) Structural equivalence to discarded translation_facts. The proposal differs in DECORATION (Z3 instead of YAML) but not in SHAPE: it's a separate analysis pass that produces structured advice fed back to the implementer/repair LLM, with no closed loop against cslc. translation_facts was 0W/2L/17T over 19 attempts; semantic_bridge had the same shape and was also discarded. The lesson the framework already paid for is: "structured advice before the implementer" does not move pass-rate when the implementer's failure is syntactic/idiomatic, not contractual. The SMT verdict ("PE (0,1) hangs at recv=3 threshold=4") is just a fancier prose hint than a YAML fact — the repair LLM still has to produce correct CSL syntax to act on it. There is no reason to believe the LLM is better at translating SMT verdicts to correct fabric code than at translating YAML facts.

(3) The bottleneck identification is wrong. PROGRESS.md and the discarded r2/r3/r4 halo-gotcha rounds say the halo failure mode is "drafters fabricated builtins/syntax/error messages" and "canonical patterns too composed to fit minimal harnesses." Nothing in the evidence trail says "works on 4x4 hangs on 5x3." If parametric-mesh hangs were the actual cluster recurrence, we'd see it in benchmark logs — but the benchmark runs each kernel at a single fixed mesh, so we'd never observe the "production-size" bug class this proposal targets. The proposal invents a failure mode to justify a tool.

(4) Z3 encoding of CSL fabric semantics is a research project, not a 7-10 day prototype. Microthread arbitration, color routing, fabric backpressure, multi-task activation chains, and the interaction between `@activate`, `local_task_id`, and `unblock_cmd_stream` are not a "small fragment" — they're the entire halo idiom. Any subset small enough to encode in a week will exclude the semantics that actually cause the hangs. The 60s timeout fallback to "inconclusive" makes this a no-op on hard cases, which are the only ones we care about.

(5) The "validate against known-passing bundles" mitigation does not address the false-negative cliff. Validating "encoding says OK for kernels we know pass" only tests the encoding's specificity. The interesting question is: does the encoding correctly *catch* the bug in a failing kernel? There's no plan for that — and you cannot construct ground-truth "this is the SMT-detectable bug" labels without manually debugging each failing translation, at which point you've done the human work the tool was supposed to amortize.

Prior art is also weak. SMT for concurrency bugs (e.g. CBMC, ESBMC, SMT-encoded actor systems) works on languages with stable, documented semantics. CSL has neither a public formal semantics nor a model-checking community. No CUDA→{anything} translator I know of uses SMT to gate output, and MLIR lowering uses pattern-rewrite verification, not SMT counterexample-guided repair. The "yellow flag" the questioner asks about should be red.

Realistic outcome: 7-10 days of engineering, an encoding that passes the 3 known-good bundles by construction (you tuned it until it did), gates 1-2 attempts on the 6 failing halo kernels with verdicts the repair LLM either ignores or "fixes" by changing the wrong thing, net 0 or -1 on pass-rate, and an SMT dependency to maintain.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Yes, and the smaller variant exposes the proposal's weakness rather than salvaging it. 1-day version: write a pure-Python concrete simulator (no Z3) that, given a layout (W,H) and a draft pe.csl, enumerates every (x,y), counts the number of `@block(ut_rx_*)` calls under the edge guards, and counts the number of `@fmovs` recv-microthread launches under those same guards. Flag any PE where `block_count != fmovs_count`. This catches the actual common bug ("forgot to guard the @block with the matching is_edge check") in O(100 lines) without Z3, without symbolic execution, and without inventing a recv-counter model that doesn't exist in CSL. If even this simpler concrete check doesn't move pass-rate over 3-5 attempts on the 6 failing halo kernels, the SMT version certainly won't — and you've learned that in a day instead of two weeks. If it DOES move pass-rate, ship the lint and never build the SMT version. Either way, the SMT proposal as written has no path to being the right answer.

all_critiques.name: Symbolic SMT check of recv/unblock parity from layout
all_critiques.critique:
Q1 (structurally different from semantic_bridge / translation_facts?): YES structurally — this is verification-on-the-draft post-implementer, not context-injection pre-implementer. That's the right kind of structural difference. Credit given. But the dependency chain it introduces — draft must be syntactically valid CSL AND structured around the recv-counter idiom for the encoder to bind any variables — collapses the structural difference in practice. The 6/7 halo failures aren't all "right shape, wrong threshold"; per the canonical Game-of-Life pe.csl (353 lines, 30+ block/activate/unblock sites including sync_fwd/sync_send/fwd_east_west/recv_{N,S,E,W}/start_next_gen state machines using @activate as the cross-task signal, not @unblock), the canonical pattern is a multi-channel handoff (recv counter → @activate fwd task → fwd counter → @activate next_gen), not a single "recv == threshold → @unblock" predicate. The proposal's symbolic model encodes the trivial fragment, not the actual idiom that's failing to be generated.

Q2 (addresses a specific cluster?): Nominally yes — halo_recv_unblock. But the cluster's real failure mode is "the draft never composes the multi-phase state machine," not "the draft composes it correctly except for an off-by-one in the threshold expression." Off-by-ones are the case SMT shines on; structural omissions (missing fwd_east_west task entirely, using @unblock where @activate is needed, missing the @block-self-on-entry that arms the next round) are not catchable by a counter-parity solver. The r4 halo-gotcha experiment (0/5) and the bottleneck doc's "canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses" finding both point at composition-failure, not threshold-arithmetic.

Q3 (prior art for SMT-checked code translation?): SMT verification of fixed concurrency protocols (TLA+/Promela/SPIN) is mature, but that's verification of human-authored specs of known protocols, not catching LLM translation bugs. The closest analog — SMT-checking LLM-generated code (Dafny/Verus/Coq with LLM drafters) — typically reports that verification rejects most LLM drafts on encoding-mismatch grounds, not real bugs, and the human time to triage false positives swamps the lift. No public result I'm aware of shows SMT-as-verifier closing the loop on a halo-fabric translation task. Yellow flag is appropriate; not red, but the author's own "most-promising failure mode: the encoding is wrong" admission is the correct prior.

Q4 (10x smaller pilot possible?): YES, and the author proposes it: advisory mode against the 3 known-passing halo bundles (Game of Life, 7-Point Stencil, Laplacian2D-Halo). This is the right gate and it's cheap (1-2 days, not 7-10). My strong recommendation: do ONLY the pilot. If the encoder cannot parse the Game-of-Life canonical pattern without throwing or false-positiving — and it almost certainly cannot, given the multi-channel @activate handoff above — kill the proposal at the pilot, no further investment. Do not pre-commit the 7-10 day build.

Q5 (honest lift estimate): Best case if the encoding works AND the failing drafts have the right shape AND the repair LLM can act on (pe=(0,1), recv=3, threshold=4) feedback: 1-2 kernels of the 6 halo failures move (lift 6/15→8/15, +13pp). Realistic case given the canonical-pattern gap and the "encoding is wrong" risk: 0-1 kernels (lift 0-7pp). Expected value ~+3pp. Lower than the ~+5-7pp a halo-specific few-shot prompt with the Game-of-Life canonical state machine inlined would likely deliver at 10% of the eng cost. Phase-1 translation_facts burned 19 attempts at 0W/2L/17T on a structurally similar bet (structured info, right cluster, wrong layer); this proposal's expected ROI is worse, not better, because of the higher eng cost.

Specific structural objections: (a) The encoder assumes draft is parsable enough to extract a send/recv/unblock graph — the failing drafts at the 6/7 halo bucket include ones that fabricate builtins or get the task-id wiring wrong, which fail extraction, not SMT. (b) is_edge guards are not the only conditional shape — the canonical kernels use `if (num_ns_recv == num_ns_nbrs) @activate(...)` with per-direction counters AND a separate total counter, which the proposal's "recv_count_{N,S,E,W}" model doesn't quite match (it conflates per-direction with aggregate). (c) "unblock_fires_at_step_k" is a discrete-time abstraction over CSL's async-fabric semantics — the author's own risk note (async fabric reordering, microthread arbitration) is the cliff and they have no concrete plan for it beyond "advisory mode." (d) Even when SMT returns a clean counterexample {pe=(0,1), recv=3, threshold=4}, prior bucket-C repair evidence in this repo shows the LLM tends to over-correct: changing the threshold to 3 globally and breaking interior PEs. The counterexample must come with "and here are the constraints for the other PEs you must NOT break," which the proposal doesn't specify.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: The author's own advisory-mode pilot IS the right 10x-smaller variant, and it should be the entire commitment for now (1-2 days, not the full 7-10). Concrete bound: 2 days to (a) write the layout/pe parser, (b) encode the recv-counter-threshold fragment in Z3, (c) run against Game of Life, 7-Point Stencil, Laplacian2D-Halo. Kill criteria, declared up front: if ANY of the 3 canonical kernels false-positives, or if the parser cannot extract the multi-channel state machine (it almost certainly cannot for Game-of-Life's sync_fwd/sync_send/fwd_east_west three-phase handoff), shelve the SMT direction permanently. A cheaper non-SMT variant worth piloting in parallel (half a day): a halo-specific few-shot template that inlines the Game-of-Life canonical state-machine skeleton (sync_fwd + sync_send + fwd_east_west + recv_{N,S,E,W} + start_next_gen with all the @activate/@block wiring) as a fillable template for the implementer, gated on cluster=halo_recv_unblock. This addresses the actual failure mode (composition, not threshold arithmetic) at 1/20th the cost. If the few-shot template wins on even 1 of the 6 halo failures, that beats SMT's expected value.

all_critiques.name: csdb wavelet replay as automatic failure diagnosis
all_critiques.critique:
STRUCTURAL CHECK vs prior failures (Q1): Genuinely different from semantic_bridge/translation_facts in shape. Both discards were prompt-time content injected before the implementer, generic across kernels, and substitutable by RAG. This is failure-time evidence sourced from the specific failing artifact — cannot be pre-cached, keyed to the candidate's actual fabric. Pass on Q1. HOWEVER the author oversells "structurally far." The implementer that ultimately writes the patch is unchanged; only the debugger sub-agent's pre-thinking has new input. Debugger v1 already shipped with stderr_tail + reviewer_rationale and DEBUGGER_AGENT_DESIGN.md notes v1's lift was "marginal." The delta here is "feed debugger ground-truth instead of stderr fragments" — that's a meaningful upgrade but not a category change.

BOTTLENECK MATCH (Q2): Sharply targets halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail) — sdk_debug_shell has a literal `--backpressure` flag and `instr-trace tasks` showing "waiting on recv" state, which IS the halo cluster failure mode. Partially targets dsr_queue_fabric_init (the runtime-assert subset). Does NOT target collectives_2d (those fail at compile/correctness, not hang). Honest scope is ~6-7 of 9 failing kernels, not all 9.

PRIOR ART (Q3): YELLOW FLAG. General pattern (runtime evidence → LLM repair) is well-validated by Self-Debug, SWE-agent, AutoCodeRover — but those use Python tracebacks / pytest failures, not multi-PE dataflow trace state. No published system does csdb-style hardware/sim trace → LLM-driven HDL/dataflow repair at this complexity. The closest analogues all involve much more structured runtime signals (a Python exception with line numbers is qualitatively different from "PE(2,1) blocked on color 9 with 2/3 wavelets").

CORE UNDERWEIGHTED RISK: The trace tells the LLM "WHICH PE is stuck" and "on WHAT color/wavelet count." That is a symptom, not a cause. Halo failures in this repo are structural — wrong @unblock placement, missing @advance_wavelets count, wrong fabric_in_dsd binding. Knowing PE(2,1) is the stuck one does not tell the implementer which line in pe.csl to change. The debugger sub-agent still must reason symptom→fix using the same halo gotchas that have already failed to land working patches (per the r2/r3/r4 halo-workflow discards). Adds info but doesn't change the reasoning chain that's been bottlenecking.

TOOLING FEASIBILITY: Confirmed real. `/home/USER/cs_sdk-1.4.0/csdb` and `sdk_debug_shell` both have click-based CLIs with explicit --x/--y/--color/--fmt/--artifact_dir/--backpressure flags. Subcommands map directly to the proposal (wavelet-trace trace, instr-trace tasks/trace/uthreads). Author's parsing-brittleness risk is real but bounded — pinning SDK 1.4.0 plus a regression test on one known-hang bundle controls it. Author's "verify SDK allows re-running with trace enabled programmatically" risk is genuinely unresolved and is the #1 thing to spike before committing to design.

EXPECTED LIFT: Optimistic +20% (8/15→9/15, +2 kernels in halo cluster). Realistic given debugger v1 marginal precedent: +7-13% (7-8/15). Bear: 0% — the trace is too symptomatic vs structural. Weighted estimate: ~+10pp pass rate (7/15). The 4-6 day cost is recoverable, but only marginally — comparable in cost to several prior efforts that returned 0.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: YES, and this should be GATING. Phase 0 (1 day, no code commits): pick 3 known halo-hang artifacts already on disk from prior sweeps. Run csdb/sdk_debug_shell manually on each. Hand-format raw output (truncated to 2KB) and paste it into the debugger sub-agent's prompt as a new section. Run the existing debugger agent on each. Check: does Sonnet-4.6 produce a different recommended_patch than the run without the trace? Does any of the new patches actually fix the kernel? Decision rule: 0/3 = kill the project (LLM can't use the evidence even when given it perfectly — the 4-6 day parser build is sunk cost). 1/3 = build the smaller integration only for the backpressure case; defer parser. 2-3/3 = proceed with the full design. This avoids the failure mode that killed translation_facts (build first, A/B after, discover the LLM was indifferent to the new slot). The hand-curated phase-0 is the cheap, falsifiable version of the whole thesis.

all_critiques.name: csdb wavelet replay as automatic failure diagnosis
all_critiques.critique:
Grounded against the actual repo and SDK, this is half a good idea built on a couple of unverified assumptions, and it bumps into prior art that the author has noted but underweighted.

What checks out: (a) debugger_agent.py is real, its trigger verbs already include 'csdb'/'wavelet'/'trace'/'cs_readelf', and DebuggerInput.stderr_tail is genuinely thin for halo hangs — so the slot to fill exists; (b) simfab_traces/ directories DO get emitted by default in benchmark sim runs (verified in /home/USER/csl-examples/benchmarks/*/out/), so 'no extra recompile required' is approximately true.

What doesn't check out: (1) The proposal repeatedly says 'invoke csdb to dump per-PE wavelet trace + task state and parse it.' csdb is an INTERACTIVE shell (subcommands: target/image/memory/register/wavelet — no --help, no obvious batch driver). The batch-friendly tool is actually sdk_debug_shell wavelet-trace / instr-trace tasks. So the headline tool is wrong — the design needs to be rewritten around sdk_debug_shell, and the author hasn't actually tried it. (2) sdk_debug_shell wavelet-trace REQUIRES --x --y --color as inputs. You cannot ask it 'which PE is stuck?' — you must already know the (x,y,color) triple to query a trace. The diagnosis the proposal wants to extract is upstream of the tool it plans to call. You'd need a separate per-PE scan (loop over every PE and color, parse for backpressure/empty queues) — that's a non-trivial parser, not the 'small Python state machine' claimed. The 4-6 day estimate is light by a factor of ~2. (3) 'SDK_TRACE=1' is invented; the author flags 'verify per SDK docs' but the proposal is structured as if it's known to work.

Prior-art collision the author acknowledges but downplays: the v1 debugger A/B 'showed marginal lift per past A/B'. The proposal's distinction ('v1 fed stderr; this feeds simulator ground truth') is real but narrow — the bottleneck on the failing halo cluster, per PROGRESS and the grounded-gotcha work that just landed (#65 hand-curated halo gotchas from r3+r4 evidence), is NOT 'the LLM doesn't know which PE is stuck' but 'the LLM doesn't know the canonical halo-recv-unblock idiom and fabricates wsetb_ctrl-style builtins.' Knowing PE(2,1) is stuck on color 9 with 2/3 wavelets received does not, by itself, tell the implementer to use teardown wavelets or the right activate_task pattern. The diagnostic identifies the symptom; the cure is still 'inject the right canonical pattern,' which is what the grounded gotchas already do.

Structural shape vs translation_facts: the author is right that it's failure-time not prompt-time, but the LOAD-BEARING question is whether the implementer can act on per-PE-stuck-on-color-N information any better than it acts on the existing reviewer rationale 'PE blocked waiting for halo recv.' translation_facts failed not because of WHEN it injected but because the implementer ignored the structured grounding when it conflicted with its own prior. There is moderate reason to fear the same here: 'PE(2,1) stuck on color 9' is more specific but still leaves the fix space open, and the implementer's failure mode on this cluster is fabrication of plausible-sounding builtins, which more diagnostic specificity does not directly counter.

Addressable population math: 6/7 halo failures + 2/3 dsr + 2/4 collectives = ~10 attempts/sweep. Of those, the proposal only helps cases that (a) cslc-compile, (b) sim hangs (not asserts with useful stderr, not compile-fails). On the halo cluster specifically, my read of the recent progress notes is that a substantial fraction fail at compile time on hallucinated builtins — those get zero benefit. Best-case the proposal touches 4-6 attempts per 15-kernel sweep. Realistic conversion to actual passes: 0-2 of those. Expected lift over 6/15 baseline: ~+0 to +2 kernels (+0 to +13 pp), most likely +0 to +1 (~+3 pp).
