The author's instinct ('parses 70% of hangs and silently fails on the rest, still net positive') is plausible for diagnostic richness but not for pass-rate, because pass-rate is gated by the implementer's ability to act on the richer signal, which past A/Bs (v1 debugger, translation_facts) say is the bottleneck.

Outside prior art: the closest analogue is post-mortem core-dump analysis fed to LLMs (Anthropic/OpenAI agent demos have shown this works for single-process Python crashes). I don't know of a CUDA→assembly or MLIR-lowering harness that has shown simulator postmortems → next-iteration repair driving meaningful pass-rate lift on a benchmark. This is a yellow flag: it's plausible-looking infrastructure that hasn't been demonstrated for code-translation specifically. The closest in-repo precedent is debugger v1 itself, which was marginal.

Bottom line: not dead-on-arrival, but the proposal is naming the wrong tool, hasn't verified the trace-enable path, and the addressable failure population is narrow. The grounded halo-gotcha work just shipped is a more direct attack on the same cluster.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Yes, and it's the only version worth building. 1-day spike: pick ONE failing halo_recv_unblock kernel that hangs (not compile-fails), manually drive `sdk_debug_shell wavelet-trace --artifact_dir out --x N --y M --color C` and `instr-trace tasks` for every PE in the rectangle, paste the relevant output as a hand-curated `stderr_tail` augmentation, and re-run the SAME failing config (model+seed+temp) with the augmented prompt — see if the next attempt passes. If 0/1 → kill the proposal; the implementer can't act on this signal even hand-fed. If 1/1 → invest in tooling and run the spike on 3-4 more hangs before committing to the parser. This skips the 4-6 day csdb-output-parsing build until you have evidence the implementer can convert. It also forces verification of the actual SDK invocation (the proposal has named the wrong tool — discovering that in a 1-day spike is much cheaper than discovering it on day 4 of a 6-day build).

all_critiques.name: Template-library retrieval with parameterized lowering
all_critiques.critique:
Structurally different from semantic_bridge/translation_facts on paper (it REPLACES generation, not decorates it). In practice, "different shape" is doing a lot of work and the proposal collapses into the same failure mode for cluster-specific reasons.

1. STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCE — partially real, but smaller than claimed. Yes, deterministic hole-substitution under a cslc gate is a different mechanism. But the SELECTOR is still an LLM doing a free-form "which template matches this CUDA" call — that is exactly the kind of free-form prose mapping semantic_bridge was, just relocated. And once the template doesn't fit cleanly (it won't, see #2), the SLIM implementer goes back to free-form CSL editing, which is what's already failing. Net: maybe 1/3 of the proposal is genuinely new mechanism; the rest is window-dressing on the existing generate-then-fix loop. The "if cslc passes, ship without LLM" path is the only genuinely new lever, and it only fires when the template happens to be a working kernel for the input — i.e., when nothing was needed.

2. CLUSTER FIT — fails hard on the actual failure shapes. I read Laplacian2D-Halo/pe.csl (269 lines) and Game-of-Life/pe_program.csl (353 lines). These are the ONLY two working halo_recv_unblock kernels in the repo. diff says 487 of 622 lines differ. They share the algorithmic outline (4 cardinal sends/recvs + counter + compute task) but the concrete bindings are unrelated:
   - Laplacian: async fmovs into halo DSDs with .activate=RX_DONE_TID; software counter; no WSE-2/3 fork at the task layer.
   - Game-of-Life: data_task_id derived from color on WSE-2 / from input_queue on WSE-3; separate sync_send + sync_fwd + start_next_gen + fwd_east_west tasks.
   These are NOT one template with hole substitutions — they are two different completions of the dispatch design space. The r3/r4 halo-gotcha workflows already showed canonical-pattern hints don't compose to working code in minimal harnesses; templates are the SAME canonical patterns reified as scaffolds, with the SAME composability gap. The empirical evidence in PROGRESS is that halo skips Opus on cluster gating (cluster too sensitive to canonical-pattern overfitting) — templating doubles down on the exact thing that hurts here.

3. dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fail) is closer to template-shaped — the failure mode IS "forgot @initialize_queue under @is_arch wse3" or "wrong queue id". But this can be fixed by a single ~5-line lint pass (the framework already has ground_gotcha.py infra for runnable snippets); doesn't need a 15-template library.

4. collectives_2d (2/4 fail) — the author says "forgot dest_dsr_ids vanishes with a template that already has them". This is true only if the LLM picks the right template AND the surrounding tile layout matches AND the reduction op matches. Three things have to align; failure on any one falls through to the unchanged baseline pipeline. The 2 failures already had the GEMM-Collectives-2D working bundle in RAG context and still failed — they didn't fail for lack of an example, they failed because they couldn't bind variables across the example boundary.

5. PRIOR ART — yes, but not encouraging. MLIR dialect-conversion patterns / LLVM pattern-rewriter are the closest analog and they need typed IR on both sides for hole types to be checkable. They don't work as prose-keyed substitution. TVM TOPI / Halide schedules require the schedule language to be small and total. There's no public report (that I can find) of "LLM-selected, hand-templated lowering" beating "RAG + free-form generation" on a non-trivial accelerator DSL. Closest negative result: AlphaCodium-style template retrieval for competitive programming gained <2% on top of strong retrieval baselines. Yellow flag is warranted.

6. CONCRETE FAILURE MODE PREDICTION — selector confidence will be a useless dial. The author knows this and adds "below threshold, fall through". In practice the selector will be confidently wrong on the halo cluster (Laplacian and Game-of-Life look similar at the analyzer-prose level, selector picks one, template doesn't fit, slim implementer can't bridge the gap, attempt burns). Net change vs baseline: -1 attempt of budget + selector-call cost, no lift. On 2-3 W1 kernels the deterministic-cslc-pass shortcut might fire (a SAXPY-shaped kernel where the closest template already compiles); these are kernels already in the 6/15 winning set.

7. THE EXPECTED-LIFT ESTIMATE in the proposal is implicit but I'd read it as +2-3 wins (8-9/15 from 6/15). My honest estimate is +0 to +1, 6-7/15. The 1 marginal win comes from a dsr_queue case where the template happens to ship the @initialize_queue boilerplate that the LLM keeps dropping. The halo cluster won't move.

8. STRATEGIC COST — 3-5 eng days is the *build* cost; the real cost is opportunity. The framework has 7 attempts/8 already mostly-saturated and a known cluster-specific bottleneck. The same 3-5 days spent on (a) on-device iteration loops for the iterative-solver W2 cluster (per the memory note, run.py is host-RPC-bound; rewriting fixes 4 0%-improvement kernels in W2) or (b) a small typed CSL contract IR derived FROM the working pe.csl files (extract function signatures, exported symbols, queue/color bindings as a checkable spec; this is the CUDA-side IR half that translation_facts deferred) would address concrete known bottlenecks rather than betting on template generalization.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Yes — and the smaller version is the actual right move. Pick ONE cluster (dsr_queue_fabric_init, 2/3 fail) and ship a single hand-written "queue init boilerplate" injector: a 30-line Python pass that scans the generated pe.csl for @get_input_queue/@get_output_queue with non-default colors and inserts the @initialize_queue under @is_arch("wse3") if missing. Run cslc; if it now compiles, accept. This is <1 day, tests the principle (deterministic post-edit of LLM output under cslc gate), and if it lifts 1-2 W1 wins, generalizes to the full proposal. If it lifts 0, the proposal is dead and you saved 4 days. The halo cluster is the wrong place to start — too composed, two reference kernels disagree on the dispatch design — so DON'T begin templating there even if the dsr probe works.

all_critiques.name: Template-library retrieval with parameterized lowering
all_critiques.critique:
Reviewer #2. Three concrete reasons to be skeptical, then one reason it's not zero.

(1) STRUCTURALLY different from semantic_bridge/translation_facts, but not in a way that addresses the documented failure mode. semantic_bridge was prose-into-prompt, translation_facts was YAML-into-prompt, this is template-into-output. Yes that's a different shape. BUT the r3/r4 halo-gotcha post-mortems explicitly say "canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses" — i.e., the working halo idiom from kernels/Laplacian2D-Halo/CSL/pe.csl is ~269 lines woven across SEND/RX_DONE/COMPUTE/EXIT task states with color bindings, queue IDs reserved against memcpy, edge-flag conditionals, ping-pong buffers, and an unblock_cmd_stream tail. The "holes" in that template are not BLOCK_SIZE-shaped — they are entire stretches of task-state logic that vary per kernel (Cholesky's triangular dependency vs. Laplacian's symmetric stencil vs. GEMV-Checkerboard's row/col routing). Once you param-hole all of that, you've reinvented the implementer. Once you DON'T param-hole it, the "deviations" the slim implementer must edit are exactly the parts that broke r3/r4. The hard part of these failures isn't fabricating wrong syntax for known idioms — RAG + cluster gotchas already cover named-builtin gotchas. The hard part is composing the right control flow across 200+ lines of stateful tasks, and that's what a hole-substitution template can't do.

(2) Bottleneck mismatch. Of the 9 W1 failures, halo_recv_unblock=6/7 fail, dsr_queue_fabric_init=2/3 fail, collectives_2d=2/4 fail. Concrete check: Laplacian2D-Halo is listed in PROGRESS.md as ALREADY WORKING (1709→671 cycles, 6 accepts, in the WORKED column). The halo failures are kernels like Cholesky, GEMV-Checkerboard, Residual, LorenzoPredictor-Tile — each of which has a DIFFERENT communication pattern, not "same halo as Laplacian with different tile size." Cholesky's wavefront is triangular pivot/non-pivot; GEMV-Checkerboard's is interleaved row+col; LorenzoPredictor is a 2D dependency from upper-left. They are not the same template with different holes. The author's mental model — "the SDK has 2-3 canonical halo patterns" — is wrong: kernels/Laplacian2D-Halo and kernels/Laplacian2D-Reduce already differ enough that diff -q says they differ, and they're the two MOST similar halo kernels in the corpus. For dsr_queue_fabric_init (only 2/3 fail and 0 wins on Opus per cluster-skip logic), the issue is queue-ID assignment vs. memcpy reservations + DSR allocation order — a per-kernel arithmetic puzzle the LLM keeps getting wrong by one, not a missing template. A template hardcoding queue IDs 2..5 collides the moment a kernel needs a 5th send. Iterative solvers (CG/PCG/BiCGSTAB/Power-Method) fail W2 cycle-reduction for a reason MEMORY.md explicitly captures: cycles_send is host-RPC-bounded by the Python loop in run.py, NOT pe.csl quality. Templating pe.csl cannot move that needle by one cycle.

(3) Prior art is weak and points the other way. Template-based code translation has worked for narrow transpilers (TXL, DMS, Coccinelle for kernel refactors, Babel/jscodeshift for JS migrations) but those operate where source/target are syntactically and semantically congruent. The closest published work to this proposal — translation via retrieval-augmented templates for HPC DSLs — is TPU-MLIR, Triton lowering, and Halide schedules. In all three, the "template" is a lowering pass owned by the compiler with formal semantics on the holes, not an LLM picking a string and a deterministic substitution. The free-form "retrieve nearest example and ask the LLM to slot in values" pattern is what most CodeLlama / StarCoder fine-tunes used pre-2024, and it consistently lost to free-form generation on cross-paradigm translation (CUDA→OpenCL surveys, Rosetta-style benchmarks). The author's own framework already discarded a structurally-cleaner cousin: cluster-gated KNOWN_GOTCHAS_W1_FAILURE_PATTERNS injects template-flavored hints into the prompt, and 6/15 baseline was the ceiling. The proposal claims templates will lift a ceiling that two prior shapes of the same idea (gotchas + facts) failed to lift. Yellow flag.

(4) Confidence-threshold fallthrough mitigation doesn't save it. If selector confidence is the safety net, the failure modes are: (a) selector picks high-confidence + wrong template → spend 1 LLM call on slim-implementer diff against a wrong scaffold → wastes the attempt with a poisoned context the next attempt sees; (b) selector returns low confidence → fall through to baseline → no harm, no benefit; (c) selector picks right template but holes don't fit → silently wrong output passes cslc (cslc gate catches compilation errors, not semantic errors), wastes the W1 attempt budget, AND the version_trace.json now has a misleading "templated" lineage that breaks the post-hoc cluster analysis. Net: zero upside scenario is the modal scenario. Bad scenario is non-trivial.

(5) The one reason it's not dead-on-arrival: collectives_2d "forgot dest_dsr_ids" failures are real and a template MIGHT help if the GEMM-Collectives-2D pe.csl is close enough to the GEMV-Collectives-2D pe.csl (it's 148 vs 188 lines, same family). That's potentially 1-2 of the 9 failures. Best realistic case: +1 W1 kernel out of 15 → 7/15. Expected value much lower because the dest_dsr_ids fix is also a 5-line gotcha that could be hand-curated into the existing cluster-gated knowledge_base in 30 minutes without any new infrastructure.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: YES — and the smaller variant is strictly better than the proposal. 1-day version: pick the SINGLE most-overrepresented failure shape (collectives_2d dest_dsr_ids forget, which is 2/4 failures and matches a known fix in kernels/GEMM Collectives 2D/CSL/pe.csl). Don't build templater.py, don't add a pipeline stage, don't write 15 templates. Instead: (a) extract the exact 10-20 line "DSR-bound matvec column" block from the working GEMM-Collectives-2D pe.csl as a verbatim code snippet, (b) add it as a SINGLE cluster-gated knowledge entry under csl_knowledge_base for cluster=collectives_2d with explicit "copy this block verbatim, replace M/N/tile_dim" instruction, (c) ground it through ground_gotcha.py to confirm cslc accepts it. Cost: 2 hours, $0 infra change, reuses the cluster-gating that already shipped. If this lifts collectives_2d from 2/4→3/4 or 4/4, that's evidence in favor of the full template proposal. If it doesn't lift, the full proposal is dead — and you've spent 2 hours instead of 3-5 days. Critically, this is testable BEFORE committing to the architecture. The full proposal as written commits to building infrastructure before checking the principle.

all_critiques.name: Test-time scaling: 32-candidate parallel sampling with cslc-gated voting
all_critiques.critique:
Three concrete reasons this won't survive contact, grounded in the framework's own evidence rather than skepticism in the abstract.

(1) The 'sequential attempts collapse diversity' premise is empirically false on THIS benchmark. I pulled the 2026-06-14 hybrid sweep (results/hybrid_sweep_20260614_210137). On the kernels that DO pass, first-pass-attempt-index is spread across 2, 3, 4, 5, and 7 (e.g. Opus 7pt-Stencil wins at attempt 7; Sonnet GEMM wins at attempt 5; Laplacian2D-Halo wins at attempt 3). If sequential conditioning were collapsing diversity, wins would pile up at attempts 1-2 and tail off. They don't — repair-driven attempts are doing genuine work. On the kernels that DON'T pass, all 8 sequential attempts return command_failed with non-trivial variation across attempts (different cslc errors per attempt in spot-checks). 'More diverse samples' is not what is missing; the implementer cannot reach the right region of program space regardless of sample count, which is exactly the point the proposal's own risk note concedes.

(2) The proposal is structurally the same shape as the existing --best-of machinery, which is already shipped. cuda2csl.py L2215-2306 implements within-attempt distinct-angle best-of-N: build N implementer prompts (each gets its own angle, retrieved knowledge, profiler feedback), call LLM N times, pool survivors, rank by cycles, return best. The current N is 3 and runs sequentially. The proposal is 'set N=32, parallelize with asyncio, swap the ranker from cycles-of-survivor to cslc-pass + DESIGN.md cosine similarity.' That's a knob turn plus a verifier swap, not a structurally new mechanism. And the verifier swap is a downgrade: the current ranker uses ACTUAL benchmark cycles on samples that already passed cslc; the proposed ranker uses 'agreement with architect prose,' which has zero signal on correctness (LorenzoPredictor's 6/8 failures are missing_success_marker = compiles + runs + wrong output; prose agreement cannot catch this).

(3) The ceiling math kills it on the 9 hard kernels. The Sonnet+Opus union ceiling cited (6/15) was measured at 8 attempts per model. On the failing 9, neither model produced a single compiling halo_recv/dsr_queue/collectives_2d-cluster sample across 16 combined attempts. Sampling 32 Sonnet shots from a fixed analyzer/architect context (which the proposal preserves) is drawing from the same distribution that already returned 0 wins on 8 draws; the variance reduction is exactly what you'd expect — a few extra near-misses on already-passing kernels, near-zero gain on the failures. The proposal's mitigation (mix 24 Sonnet + 8 Opus) is just running today's hybrid sweep slightly differently — which is the very setup that produced the 6/15 ceiling being cited as the starting point.

Specific things that look wrong on closer read: (a) cost claim of '$0.40/kernel ~ 8x tokens' ignores the 4-role pipeline (analyzer + architect + reviewer + sometimes debugger). The 32x multiplier applies only to the implementer call, but a translate attempt is not a single LLM call. (b) Wall-clock claim of 'cost-neutral' assumes the 4-6 concurrent cslc semaphore from benchmark_csl.py is the bottleneck for 32 candidates; it would actually saturate fast and serialize the back half (~32/5 × ~90s real compile time = 9-10 min, not 3-4). (c) AlphaCode2/DeepSeek-R1 are cited as 'similar complexity'; they target Python/C++ where the verifier is unit tests on output correctness. The analogue here is missing_success_marker checks, not cslc — and the proposal's ranker does not include those.

What the proposal does NOT address that the original question explicitly asked about: CUDA-side IR (Phase 1 deferred half), typed AST, MLIR-style multi-level lowering, or executable specifications. It is a pure decoding-time intervention that ignores the IR question entirely. If the conclusion of running this experiment is 'model capability is the bottleneck' (as the author concedes is the likely outcome), that's a result you can get for free by reading the existing hybrid sweep — Opus on the 9 failing kernels already shows 0/9 over 8 attempts each. The information value of paying $6 to confirm is low.
all_critiques.smaller_variant:
There is an obvious 10x-cheaper pilot the proposal hand-waves past: take the existing --best-of knob, raise it from 3 to 16 inside ONE attempt (not 8), on the 3-kernel halo_recv subset (Laplacian2D-Halo, 7pt-Stencil, Residual). Reuse the existing sequential implementer loop — no asyncio work, no semaphore tuning. Mix Sonnet/Opus 12/4. If 16 fresh shots on halo_recv produce zero compile-passing samples, the union-ceiling story is confirmed and the full 32-wide proposal is dead. Total cost: ~$1, half a day of eng. If it produces even one compile-passing halo sample, you have a strong reason to invest in the larger version. The proposal as written goes straight to the $6 / 1-2 eng-day version without first running the $1 / half-day check that would falsify it. The smaller version also doesn't require the new ranker (you just check 'did any compile + pass smoke test'), which sidesteps the weak DESIGN.md-cosine fidelity proxy.

Separately, if the goal is honestly 'verify that capability is the bottleneck before redirecting effort,' the $0 version is reading the existing hybrid sweep logs more carefully: on the 9 failing kernels, what does the cslc error message look like at attempt 8 for both Sonnet and Opus? If both models fail at the same cslc error after 8 RAG-augmented attempts each, the bottleneck is confirmed without running anything new.

all_critiques.name: Test-time scaling: 32-candidate parallel sampling with cslc-gated voting
all_critiques.critique:
Expected lift estimate: ~+5pp (1 kernel, 6/15 -> 7/15), with meaningful probability of 0 lift, and outside chance of +13pp (2 kernels).

Structurally different from semantic_bridge/translation_facts? Yes, technically — those were "more context per attempt"; this is "more independent attempts at fixed context." That earns it a real hearing. But it collides with two pieces of evidence already in the repo that the author waves at but does not fully internalize:

(1) The hybrid Sonnet+Opus union ceiling is 6/15. That's not 6/15 from one Sonnet run + one Opus run; the sweep already takes the BEST of each model across 8 sequential attempts with diverse repair angles (A/B/C buckets). The 9 failing kernels failed under a regime that already explored prompt variation, model variation, and verifier-guided repair. The proposal's mechanism (perturbing gotcha order, varying temperature 0.5-1.0, rephrasing canonical-pattern asks) is a strictly weaker diversification than what the existing sweep already does — sequential repair conditions on the actual cslc error message, which is a far richer perturbation signal than temperature jitter. The author's claim "sequential collapses diversity" is backwards for this codebase: the sequential attempts are the highest-information branches available. Independent samples at T=0.9 will mostly reproduce the same modal Sonnet failure mode for halo_recv_unblock (fabricated unblock-on-recv semantics) 32 times.

(2) The 6/7 halo failures are not a "long-tail of diverse near-misses one of which is correct" problem — per the memory index and the gotcha-workflow r2/r3/r4 logs, halo_recv_unblock fails because Sonnet/Opus both fabricate non-existent builtins or compose canonical patterns that don't fit minimal harnesses. Sampling 32 fabrications and verifier-gating them yields 0 compilers, not 1 winner. The "cslc-gated voting" framing assumes cslc-pass correlates with correctness; for halo, even the cslc-passing samples are likely to be semantically wrong (no halo exchange happening at all, just compiles). The smoke I/O test catches some of this, but the existing repair loop already runs cslc + bench on every attempt — that's what generates the bucket verdict. So you're not adding a new oracle, you're just front-loading volume to the existing one.

Does it address ONE of the three failing clusters specifically? No — the author admits this ("generic more-attempts improvement"). The bottlenecks are domain-knowledge gaps (halo unblock-after-recv pattern, DSR-queue/fabric-init ordering, c2d API surface). Sampling does not generate new knowledge; it samples from the model's existing distribution, which is exactly what's already known to be deficient. The mitigation "mix 24 Sonnet + 8 Opus" reduces to: do the hybrid sweep, but parallel and without repair conditioning — which loses signal vs. current setup.

Prior art outside the repo: AlphaCode2 / DeepSeek-R1 best-of-N results are real but operate at N=1000+ with task-suite verifiers on benchmarks where the model has substantial mass on the correct solution. The relevant comparable here is not competitive programming (HumanEval/Codeforces, where models are well-trained) but low-resource DSL translation. Closest prior art: Reflexion / Self-Debug papers found that on niche DSLs, sequential repair beats parallel sampling at fixed budget — exactly the opposite of what the proposal asserts. MLIR-lowering work (CIRCT, Polygeist) does not use BoN sampling; they use rule-based lowerings precisely because the model-distribution mass on rare DSL idioms is thin. No citable result shows N=32 BoN closing a 60%-fail gap on a DSL with <50 public examples (which is roughly CSL's footprint). That's the yellow flag the author asks about, and I'd raise it to orange.

Cost claim is also under-stated. $0.40/kernel * 15 kernels = $6/sweep is fine, but the sweep is run dozens of times during iteration; real budget cost is 8-12x current monthly LLM spend on this project. Wall-clock claim ignores that cslc on a 32-wide fan is bursty under the 4-6 semaphore — tail latency dominates, real wall is probably 6-9 min not 3-4.

The most honest read: this proposal pays 8x tokens to discover what the existing sweep ceiling already tells us — the bottleneck is model capability on rare CSL idioms, not search width. The author's own risk note ("if union ceiling holds, this is real — then redirect to template-library") is the correct conclusion already; you don't need to spend $6 to learn it. The 10x-smaller pilot below is the only part of this proposal worth keeping.
all_critiques.smaller_variant:
YES, and it's the only version worth doing: N=8 parallel samples on the 3 halo kernels that fail Sonnet, single model, single temperature (0.8), no prompt-perturbation theatrics. Half-day implementation: drop the existing sequential loop on those 3, run 8 asyncio gather calls, cslc-gate, smoke-bench, return first pass. Total cost ~$1.20. Decisive outcomes:
  - 0/3 pass: kills the whole proposal and confirms model-capability-bound. Redirect to template-library / few-shot exemplar injection of working halo patterns from cerebras-csl-skills (the actually-promising direction the author should consider instead).
  - 1/3 pass: marginal; ~+1 kernel lift expected at full scale, not worth 8x cost.
  - 2-3/3 pass: surprising, falsifies my critique; scale to N=32.
This 4-hour pilot is strictly better than the 1-2 day full build, because the full proposal's expected lift (+3 to +7pp) is below the noise floor of the 15-kernel benchmark (one kernel = 6.7pp); you can't tell if it worked at N=15 without re-running 3-5 seeds, which the author hasn't budgeted for.

all_critiques.name: Profile-guided KB: build the gotcha catalog from real cslc error histograms, not curation
all_critiques.critique:
Hard-question answers, grounded in the codebase:

**Q1 — Structurally different from semantic_bridge/translation_facts?** Partially, but less than the author claims. Three load-bearing things are already happening in the repair path (cuda2csl.py:1646-1685): (a) `format_command_transcript(benchmark["transcript"])` already pipes the full cslc stdout+stderr into the reviewer prompt (prompt_cuda2csl.py:1174); (b) the reviewer emits a one-sentence RATIONALE that is the human-readable normalization of that stderr — and rationales I sampled from the halo resweep logs are *already* signature-quality ("missing closing `]` in `@zeros([1]f32;`", "`fabin_dsd` on WSE-3 does not accept a `.length` field"); (c) the DebuggerAgent fires on bucket-B with a 2000-char stderr clip plus reviewer rationale plus debug action. So the repair LLM already sees: full transcript → reviewer-distilled signature → debugger diagnosis → canonical patch suggestion. The proposal adds a 4th channel ("canonical_fix_diff_snippet from historical examples"). The author's claim of structural difference rests on "conditioned on hard evidence not on prediction" — but the reviewer rationale IS already conditioned on hard evidence (it's literally written from the stderr the reviewer just read). The new layer is "more context conditioned on the same evidence the reviewer already saw and acted on."

**Q2 — Addresses one of the three failing clusters specifically?** No. The proposal is explicitly generic ("any signature with N>=3"). Worse, the cluster diagnostics in the README make it unlikely to help the bottleneck cluster: halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail) is dominated by "Runtime hang (0 bytes received)" rationales — I just counted 14 hits in the sample logs. Hangs are precisely the signature where the cslc stderr is uninformative (the kernel compiled, then deadlocked); the previous halo r3/r4 grounding workflows already established that the canonical fix patterns for halo deadlocks are "too composed to fit in minimal harnesses." Mining `(stderr, fix_diff)` pairs from a corpus where the stderr is silent for the dominant failure mode will produce signatures of the form "0 bytes received" mapped to wildly divergent fixes per kernel — which the matcher would then inject as misleading guidance. dsr_queue_fabric_init at N=2/3 is too small a sample to mine. collectives_2d is the closest plausible win but already has the targeted cluster gotchas.

**Q3 — Prior art for code translation?** Yes, and it's a cautionary tale. The closest analog is automated program-repair tools mining bug-fix pair databases (GenProg, Prophet, SequenceR, DeepFix, Hoppity, TFix). The honest summary: these methods report 3-15% absolute improvement on Java/C bug benchmarks where the codebase is millions of fixes deep (Defects4J, ManySStuBs4J: 100K+ pairs). At the proposed N>=3 (or N=2 pilot) over ~250 attempts split across 15 kernels, you're at the floor where the bug-mining literature reports zero generalization beyond the exact files mined. Compiler-side: MLIR PDL/PDLL pattern rewrites do mine canonical diffs but they're hand-curated, not statistically learned, *because* the statistical approach failed for them. No published result for CUDA→accelerator translation specifically.

**Q4 — 10x smaller version that proves it in <1 day?** Yes, and this is what should actually run first. Run `grep "RATIONALE:" results/halo_resweep_after_rag_iter_20260603/*.log` (~5 min of bash, no eng work). Cluster the rationales by hand for 30 minutes. You will find — I just sampled this above — that 14 of ~30 rationales collapse to the single bucket "hang/0 bytes received" with no actionable canonical fix, ~7 collapse to "@export_name vs @export_symbol vs comptime block" (already covered by the dsr_queue cluster gotcha), and the rest are singletons. The histogram exists *now*, takes 1 hour to read, and reading it is the actual test of whether the catalog approach can pay off. If you can't write the 3 canonical fix-diffs by hand after reading the histogram, the automated pipeline cannot either.

**Q5 — Expected lift on 15-kernel benchmark from 6/15?** +0 to +1 kernel (roughly +3% absolute, well within noise of a 15-kernel benchmark — single-flip variance is ~6.7pp per kernel). Best-case path: the catalog picks up the @export_name/@export_symbol pattern cluster and one collectives_2d kernel converts. More likely: catalog overlaps with already-shipped cluster gotchas, the halo-hang cluster eats most of the data with non-actionable fixes, and the matcher injects misleading hints into halo repairs (which is the bottleneck), driving a small regression. Note also: translation_facts ran 19 attempts → 0W/2L/17T. A profile-guided variant at similar magnitude of intervention is well within the band of "tie" the framework has historically measured.

**The actually risky part the author understated:** the repair channel already shows the LLM the stderr verbatim AND a human-quality summary AND a structured debugger report. Adding a 4th input ("here is what worked on a different kernel after a similar-looking error") is exactly the input shape that translation_facts already proved was perturbative-not-additive. The structural difference the author cites (gated to bucket-B, fires only on signature match) only reduces the *blast radius* of that perturbation — it doesn't change the sign.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: The 10x version IS the whole experiment. Step 1 (1 hour, zero code): `grep "RATIONALE:" results/halo_resweep_after_rag_iter_20260603/*.log results/cuda2csl/run_2026060*/[A-Z]*/agent.log 2>/dev/null | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn > /tmp/rationale_histogram.txt`, then read it. Step 2 (1 hour): for any signature with N>=3, write the fix-diff by hand. Step 3 (4 hours): wire the hand-written fixes into the existing `KNOWN_GOTCHAS_W1_FAILURE_PATTERNS` (same path as the 11 already shipped) with the same cluster-gating mechanism. Step 4 (existing infra): A/B on the 15-kernel W1 corpus. This skips the parser/normalizer/diff-extractor entirely and tests the *content hypothesis* (do the historical errors contain a knowable pattern that's not already in the gotcha catalog?) without building any automation. If step 1 yields a clean histogram with 3+ actionable singularly-fixable clusters, then the automation pays off and you build it. If step 1 yields what I just saw above (one big "hang" bucket + already-covered @export bucket + long tail of singletons), the automation cannot help because the input data doesn't have the signal. This is the same decision tree that should have killed translation_facts after 5 attempts instead of 19.

all_critiques.name: Profile-guided KB: build the gotcha catalog from real cslc error histograms
all_critiques.critique:
Three load-bearing problems, in descending order of severity.

PROBLEM 1 — THE PREMISE IS FACTUALLY WRONG. The proposal says "the source of truth has to be real cslc output" implying current repair prompts hide that from the LLM. They don't. cuda2csl.py:1710 already passes format_command_transcript(benchmark["transcript"]) into csl_bundle_fix_with_review, and workflow_common.py:368-394 emits literal `stderr:` blocks clipped head=400 tail=1600 per failed step. I verified on results/hybrid_sweep_20260614_210137/Laplacian2D-Halo/.../translation_log.json msg[5]: the user prompt contains the exact cslc diagnostic `./pe.csl:297:35: error: expression does not yield the address of a variable or a comptime-known pointer\n      .tensor_access = |i|{Mt} -> src[i * @as(i16, Nt)],\n` plus the reviewer rationale (which is bucket=B "tensor_access lambda uses src, a runtime pointer; CSL requires comptime-known pointer — use @set_dsd_base_addr with strided mem1d_dsd") plus the SUGGESTED DEBUG STEP. The LLM already has (a) raw stderr, (b) reviewer's diagnosis, (c) actionable recipe. Repair STILL fails — Laplacian2D-Halo went through 3 repair attempts on that exact error, including a follow-up with returncode 139 hang. Adding a "canonical fix diff" from a catalog of similar errors is one more redundant pointer at the same target, not new information. This is structurally identical to translation_facts (0W/2L/17T) — extra grounded context layered onto a prompt that already has the grounding.

PROBLEM 2 — THE DATA ASSEMBLY IS HARDER THAN ESTIMATED. The proposal says "walk sandbox/cuda2csl/* and extract (failed_csl, cslc_stderr, next_attempt_csl_if_passed) triples". I checked: sandbox/cuda2csl/* (2744 dirs) contains ONLY the final src/kernel.csl per attempt and benchmark-libs, NO stderr, no attempt-history. The stderr lives in translation_log.json scattered across results/cuda2csl/run_*/ and results/hybrid_sweep_*/<kernel>/<model>/run_*/<kernel>/. There is no shared key between a sandbox dir and the corresponding translation_log message. Reconstructing (fail_csl, stderr, fix_csl) tuples requires (i) parsing 200+ run.log/translation_log.json across multiple sweep directories, (ii) reconstructing per-attempt CSL snapshots from "Current compute file:\n```csl\n..." blocks in user messages (the actual CSL isn't stored per-attempt; it's embedded in subsequent prompts), (iii) identifying which subsequent attempt finally passed on the SAME kernel — across separate runs that share no run_id. 3-4 eng days is wildly optimistic; 1.5-2 weeks is more honest, with a real risk that the join is too lossy.

PROBLEM 3 — N>=3 SIGNATURE COVERAGE IS A FANTASY ON OUR DISTRIBUTION. The proposal handwaves "dsr_queue_fabric_init failures very likely cluster on 2-3 distinct cslc error signatures". This is the same fallacy that killed halo r2/r3 — assuming the failure population is patterned. Halo bugs are MOSTLY runtime hangs (returncode 139, 0 bytes), not compile errors. Look at Laplacian2D-Halo above: attempt 1 fails at compile with a tensor_access error; attempt 2 fails with a HANG, where stderr is empty/uninformative. Six of seven halo failures are like this — the catalog has no error string to match against, because the device hung. dsr_queue_fabric_init fails similarly. The 6/15 cases that already pass do so via either Sonnet on first try or Opus rescue — i.e. the easy half doesn't need a catalog and the hard half hangs without stderr. The proposal's own fallback ("if catalog empty, that's signal") concedes this and dresses it up as a feature.

PRIOR ART. The "compile-error → canonical fix diff" pattern works for two regimes: (a) closed compilers where the same error has one fix (rustc, TypeScript errors → corrective edit datasets work well in CodeT5/Magicoder finetunes), (b) syntactic typos where the diff is a 2-token substitution. CSL halo/DSR failures are neither: cslc errors point at a line, but the fix often involves restructuring sends/receives across the file. There is no public "MLIR lowering bug → patch diff" RAG corpus that demonstrated lift on a 15-kernel benchmark of this complexity; the closest work (CompCoder, Self-Edit, DrRepair) shows lift in the 60-80% baseline regime against syntactic errors, not at 40% with semantic+timing+fabric bugs. Yellow flag.

DIRECT ANSWERS TO YOUR 5 QUESTIONS:
1. Structurally same as translation_facts and the discarded halo-gotcha LLM-drafter rounds. Gating on "cslc has already failed with signature X" sounds different but is operationally the same as "cluster matches halo_recv_unblock" — we already gate on the verdict bucket and the kernel cluster. New: stderr signature. Net delta over current state: ~25% more conditional context, same shape.
2. None of the three specifically. Halo (6/7 fail) are mostly post-compile hangs with no stderr signature to match. dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fail) might surface 1-2 signatures but those are already covered by the 3 new halo gotchas shipped today. collectives_2d (2/4 fail) are typically composition bugs across multiple files, not single-error-signature.
3. No public work has shown this work on accelerator-DSL translation at <50% baseline. DrRepair/Self-Edit work assumes errors map ~1:1 to syntactic fixes. Yellow flag.
4. Yes — see smaller variant.
5. Honest estimate: 0/15 to +1/15 (0% to +6.7%), with non-trivial regression risk if the catalog injects misleading fixes for stderr-prefix-match-but-different-root-cause cases (same risk that killed always-on gotchas in Single-Tile-Matvec). Expected value ~ +2pp.
all_critiques.smaller_variant:
Yes, and it would falsify the proposal in 1 day with $0 LLM spend. Step 1 (4h): grep across all existing results/hybrid_sweep_*/<kernel>/sonnet/.../translation_log.json for the literal text "stderr:" in user-role messages, extract the first cslc error line per failed attempt, group by kernel and normalized error template (strip paths, line:col numbers). Step 2 (2h): tabulate per (cluster, error_template) → count. Step 3 (2h): for each cell with count >= 2, manually inspect 1 example and ask "would a fix-diff template help here, or is the bug structural?" If the histogram shows >= 8 templates with count >= 3 AND >= 5 of those are halo/dsr/collectives cluster AND a human can write a concrete patch for each — the principle is alive, proceed with full build. If we get <5 templates with count >= 3 OR the templates are mostly compile-fine-but-hang (no useful stderr), the principle is dead. Predict: histogram will show 3-4 templates with count >= 3, most of them syntactic ("unknown @-builtin", "type mismatch", "expression does not yield comptime-known pointer") — already covered by builtin_whitelist_block and the curated gotchas — and the hard failures (halo hang) will have no stderr to histogram. Decision in 1 day, no full build.

A more promising 1-day alternative that actually targets the bottleneck: write a CSL-specific RUNTIME-HANG diagnostic harness analogous to ground_gotcha.py — when bucket-B verdict identifies "runtime hang, returncode 139, 0 bytes", auto-inject a minimal <debug> trace shim into the failing CSL and re-run, append the trace output to the next repair prompt. This addresses the halo failure mode (6/7) where the LLM has NO observation signal today because the device just hangs. Higher expected lift than histogram catalog, similar build cost.

all_critiques.name: Bench corpus split: separate 'CUDA-shaped' from 'algorithm-shaped' refs and translate from the latter
all_critiques.critique:
Q1 (structural novelty vs prior failures): The proposal claims to be "different shape — changes the SOURCE side." That framing is misleading on two counts. (a) The implementer-end input is unchanged: it still receives prose-equivalent context plus retrieved snippets, just with a different opening string. The only thing that moves is what the analyzer sees on its first turn — and analyzer output is already "free-form CUDA prose" per the framework description, i.e. CUDA gets paraphrased into prose anyway one role downstream. Pseudo just front-loads that paraphrasing into a hand-curated artifact. (b) STRONGER PRIOR ART INSIDE THIS REPO that the proposal didn't acknowledge: explore_modes/mode_cuda_nl.py + seeds/cuda_nl_catalog.jsonl already exists and does exactly this — natural-language target description + suggested_mesh field + reduced CUDA snippet feeding q_cuda_nl_to_spec → q_cuda_nl_design_from_spec. 12 catalog entries exist. If this approach worked, the catalog would be 30 entries and the W1 bottleneck wouldn't still be 9/15. The proposal is structurally a hand-curated, per-kernel variant of mode_cuda_nl. Risk of repeating the semantic_bridge pattern (rich-prose context that gets ignored by an LLM that just wants to pattern-match against retrieved CSL snippets) is high.

Q2 (does it hit the specific failure clusters?): No — and this is the weightiest objection. Look at what halo_recv_unblock kernels actually need (concrete: kernels/Laplacian2D-Halo/CSL/pe.csl): 4 fabric colors with TX_/RX_ direction names, 4 input_queues at IDs 2-5 (because memcpy reserves 0-1), 4 output_queues, 4 local_task_ids at IDs 12-15 (because memcpy reserves 0-11), a counter that decrements on RX_DONE and chains COMPUTE when it hits num_halos_expected, edge masks (is_w_edge etc.) so corner PEs don't send into the void, and a final unblock_cmd_stream() so the host launch returns. None of this is "algorithm." It's all CSL fabric-protocol contract. Writing the algorithm as numpy.roll + np.where for boundaries gives the agent EXACTLY ZERO of these concrete artifacts. Same story for dsr_queue_fabric_init (the whole point IS that queue ID assignment and fabric init are the problem — algorithm doesn't have queue IDs). For collectives_2d the algorithm IS expressible as an np.sum and the agent will then have to re-invent the col-reduce + row-broadcast color choreography from scratch, which is precisely what it's failing at now. The proposal addresses the part the agent is already good at (algorithm intent) and ignores the part it's failing on (protocol contract realization).

Q3 (external prior art): I'm not aware of published work showing "rewrite source in target-friendly pseudocode then translate" beating direct translation for hardware-DSL targets at the failure rate this codebase is at. The closest cited work is Codex/AlphaCode-style "natural language → code" benchmarks, but those are GENERATING from intent, not translating between two source codes — the input intent is the only available source and there is no source-shape mismatch to bridge. MLIR lowering is the opposite shape: it works by ADDING structure incrementally (typed multi-level IR with verifiers per level), not by rewriting source. So: no clean external prior art. Yellow flag confirmed.

Q4 (cheaper proof): Yes, trivially. The author estimates 2 eng weeks for 9 kernels. A 1-day proof would be: hand-write pseudo for the THREE failing kernels that are most representative of each cluster (one halo, one dsr_queue, one collectives_2d), reuse mode_cuda_nl wiring (zero new prompt/flag work), and run 3 attempts × 2 styles × 2 models = 12 LLM calls. If pseudo doesn't visibly help on any of the three, abandon. The fact that the proposal sized the experiment at 2 weeks before validating the principle is itself a yellow flag — the framework has been burned by "build the whole apparatus then measure."

Q5 (honest expected lift from 6/15 baseline): My estimate is +0/15 to +1/15 on the 9 currently failing, with non-negligible risk of -1/15 on the 6 currently passing (perturbation, same as translation_facts saw). Expected value ~+0.3 kernels = ~+2% absolute. Why: the agent reproduces CUDA-shaped references "cycle-for-cycle when it succeeds" precisely because RAG retrieved a near-identical CSL exemplar — pseudo-style input doesn't change what's in the corpus to retrieve. The 9 failing kernels fail because the retrieved exemplars don't compose cleanly into the target (per the r4 halo-gotcha postmortem: "canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses"). Different source-side framing of the same algorithm doesn't change retrieval (TF-IDF over CSL corpora won't tokenize the pseudo) and doesn't change which CSL snippets compose. The author's framing — "is the bottleneck CUDA-to-CSL or thinking-to-CSL?" — is rhetorically clean but the cluster evidence already answers it: it's neither; it's "CSL-protocol-realization-from-composed-snippets."

Additional concrete failure mode the author missed: the pseudo refs become a maintenance liability. When the CSL bundle gains a new variant (e.g., 4D mesh) the human now has to update CUDA ref, pseudo ref, and CSL ref consistently, with no compiler to catch drift. translation_facts had auto-extraction; pseudo has zero. This is worse on that axis.

Mitigation the author proposes — "worst case: pseudo also gets 6/15, which proves framework is the bottleneck" — is decision-useful in principle but the experiment is overpriced for the information it returns. mode_cuda_nl already provides ~80% of the same signal at zero additional cost; running mode_cuda_nl against the 9 failing W1 kernels for $5 of LLM tokens would answer the same diagnostic question this week.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Skip the 2-week hand-write of 9 pseudo refs entirely. Instead: (1) Run the EXISTING mode_cuda_nl pipeline against the 9 failing W1 kernels using only their nl_target + suggested_mesh fields (write the missing 9 catalog entries — ~2 hours, since each entry is ~10 lines of the schema already exemplified). This is the same diagnostic at 1/40 the cost. (2) If mode_cuda_nl gets ≥8/9 on the failing set, THEN the source-shape hypothesis is alive and the more expensive hand-pseudo experiment is justified. (3) If mode_cuda_nl gets ≤2/9 (likely), the source-shape hypothesis is dead and the framework should pivot to the actually-suggested area: contract-level pre-flight checking (parse the implementer's draft against csl_builtins.yaml + queue-ID reservation rules BEFORE the compile step, surface concrete violations as the reviewer's first message). That's a "better IR" approach the proposer didn't consider — it's a CSL-side post-generation IR that exists in the implementer→reviewer loop, addressing the actual failure mode (composed snippets violating per-kernel constraints).

all_critiques.name: Bench corpus split: separate 'CUDA-shaped' from 'algorithm-shaped' refs and translate from the latter
all_critiques.critique:
STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCE FROM PRIOR ART (Q1): Yes, structurally different from semantic_bridge and translation_facts. Both prior failures injected MORE context into the same implementer; this REPLACES the source. That's a real distinction. But there's a different prior art it strongly resembles, and the author missed it: this is the "intermediate language" pattern (CUDA -> pseudo -> CSL), which is the same shape as MLIR progressive lowering, except the lowering step (CUDA -> pseudo) is done by a human, not the agent. So the experiment doesn't measure "can a translator handle pseudo->CSL" -- it measures "can a human + translator handle CUDA->CSL when the human does the hard half." That's a known-positive result; humans writing the mesh-explicit form IS the architect's job. The experiment as designed cannot distinguish "pseudo helps the LLM" from "human-author-of-pseudo did the architect's job and the LLM is now transcribing."

BOTTLENECK SPECIFICITY (Q2): The proposal claims to address all three failure clusters but actually only addresses ONE well: halo_recv_unblock. Halo failures ARE about recovering mesh structure from flat CUDA -- numpy slicing makes halo regions explicit, so this could help. But dsr_queue_fabric_init failures are NOT about source-language mismatch; they're about CSL's DSR microarchitecture (queue IDs, fabric_in/fabric_out wavelet routing, color binding) which has NO numpy analog. Writing `np.sum(axis=mesh_x)` doesn't tell the implementer how to allocate DSR queues 0-7 vs avoid the reserved ones, doesn't tell it which colors collide with fabric_init defaults. Same for collectives_2d -- the failure is in row/col broadcast staging with input_queue=N, not in the algorithm. So at most 6/9 failing kernels are even in-domain for this intervention, and the dsr_queue cluster is dead-on-arrival.

PRIOR ART (Q3): The closest published work is Facebook's Aroma and Google's pseudo-code-to-code (DeepMind AlphaCode-style) -- these show pseudo helps when generating fresh code, NOT when targeting an exotic ISA. Halide/TVM scheduling-language work is more relevant and AGAINST: they all converged on typed IRs (TIR, scheduler IR) with semantic operators, NOT free-form pseudo-numpy. The Cerebras team's own SDK examples don't have a pseudo-tier. No prior published result supports the specific claim "human-written numpy-mesh pseudo improves LLM->exotic-DSL translation pass rate." Yellow flag confirmed.

SELF-DEFEATING DESIGN: The author flags the real risk ("writing the pseudo IS the translation") and offers a mitigation ("the pseudo refs are an INSTRUMENT") that doesn't actually mitigate. If you spend 2 eng weeks hand-writing pseudo refs that explicitly encode halo exchange via numpy slicing, allreduce as np.sum on a mesh axis, and PE id as an explicit loop variable -- you have done 80% of the architect's cognitive work. A lift from 6/15 to 12/15 wouldn't prove "preprocessing CUDA helps"; it would prove "if a human writes a mesh-explicit spec, the LLM can transcribe to CSL," which is already the WORKED finding ("when it succeeds, it's barely translating; it's transcribing"). The decision-useful claim ("invest in source preprocessing") would not actually follow, because no automated CUDA->pseudo step exists; you'd be recommending investment in a step the experiment didn't test.

COST/BENEFIT: 2 eng weeks is the framework's largest single investment to date. semantic_bridge and translation_facts each cost ~1 day to implement+run. Reviewer-budget-bump cost ~hours. The $20 LLM cost is the cheap part; the human-week cost is what makes this a poor bet. If the framework has burned multiple rounds on plausible proposals, the ones that burned least (translation_facts: 2 days incl. A/B) at least failed cheaply.

EXPECTED LIFT: Best case ~10pp (6/15 -> 7.5/15 rounded to 8/15), driven entirely by the halo cluster catching 2-3 more wins. Realistic case 0-7pp. The dsr_queue cluster won't move. The collectives_2d cluster might move 0-1. Even an optimistic outcome doesn't clear the bar for the cost.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: YES, and the smaller variant is dramatically better cost/benefit: pick ONE halo kernel (the one where the agent's architect prose currently looks most confused -- check the analyzer.md/architect.md from a recent failed Laplacian2D-Halo or Game-of-Life run). Spend ONE day writing the pseudo ref for just that kernel. Run 8 attempts with --source-style pseudo vs 8 with cuda. If pseudo doesn't move that single kernel from fail to pass, the full 9-kernel investment is dead. If it does pass, run 2 more halo kernels (3 days total) before committing to the rest. This staged version costs ~4 days instead of 2 weeks, and the kill criterion at day-1 is sharp. Even better smaller variant: SKIP the human pseudo entirely and instead have the analyzer agent produce the pseudo as an explicit step (CUDA -> LLM-generated numpy-mesh -> LLM CSL). This costs ~1 day of prompt wiring, zero hand-authoring, and actually tests the "preprocessing helps" hypothesis rather than the "humans help" hypothesis. The risk that the analyzer produces wrong pseudo is real, but at least the experiment then answers the right question.

all_critiques.name: Drop-the-hard-kernels: declare W1 corpus solved at 6/15 plateau, redirect to W2/W3
all_critiques.critique:
This proposal is dead-on-arrival for three concrete, repo-grounded reasons. It's not the same shape as semantic_bridge/translation_facts (correct: it's a budget reallocation, not a feature), but the framing is built on misread evidence.

1. CATEGORY ERROR ON THE TARGET LIST. The prompt's W1 bottleneck is halo_recv_unblock 6/7, dsr_queue_fabric_init 2/3, collectives_2d 2/4. The proposal's 'human_reference_required' list is BiCGSTAB, CG, PCG, Power_Method, Cholesky, GEMM_Collectives_2D, 7pt-Stencil variants. These two lists barely overlap. BiCGSTAB/CG/PCG/Power_Method are not W1 translation failures — per PROGRESS.md sec 2.2 they ship with cycles_send and are W2-stuck, not W1-stuck. Cholesky has 5 W2 accepts and 1.08x win (PROGRESS sec 3.3). 7-Point Stencil has the 1.98x win (sec 3.4). GEMM_Collectives_2D has the largest single absolute win in the corpus, 1.45x (sec 3.5). Tagging the kernels with the most demonstrated W2 traction as 'human_reference_required and skip W1' inverts the evidence.

2. THE PROPOSAL ASKS TO DOUBLE DOWN ON A MEASUREMENT BUG. Per the auto-memory note `project_power_method_instrumentation.md` and PROGRESS.md sec 9 (Piece 3g, 2026-06-06): the immune-solver family's `run.py` brackets `f_tic`/`f_toc` around a host-side Python `for i in range(max_ite)` loop with 3 blocking RPCs per iteration — so cycles_send measures host↔device sync, not on-device compute. Worse, for Power_Method the optimizer was editing `src/kernel_power.csl` while `layout.csl` line 121 compiles `kernel.csl`: every edit was a literal no-op. Piece 3f already ran 8×4=32 deeper-W2 attempts on this family and got 0 wins, with cycle span 0/2/3/7 around baseline (the noise floor symptom). The proposal's flagship redirect — 'increase n-rounds from 8 to 24 on the 6 kernels with prior accepts' — applied to the immune family is asking to run Piece 3f three times longer against a metric that can't move. The actual unlock is Piece 3j (host-loop detector) + wire `kernel_power.csl` into the build (PROGRESS sec 9, item 2). That's an instrumentation fix, not a budget redirect.

3. THE CORPUS-CEILING CLAIM IS UNDERSUPPORTED. '6/15 = hybrid Sonnet+Opus union ceiling' is asserted, not proven. The 3 halo gotchas shipped today haven't been A/B'd in a full sweep yet. Cluster-gated KNOWN_GOTCHAS just added 3 entries. Calling the ceiling and graduating 9 kernels before the most recent gotcha drops are measured is premature; semantic_bridge and translation_facts both 'felt ceiling' too, and the lesson from those was that the ceiling claim was wrong about which lever to pull, not that the ceiling was real. The historical-spend argument ('$150 burned with no movement') doesn't survive the question 'what did the LAST sweep see, with the new halo gotchas live?' If that answer is 'haven't measured', then declaring the ceiling is a guess wearing accountant's clothes.

Secondary issues: (a) The proposal claims this addresses none of the three failure clusters specifically — it explicitly addresses none of them. By the proposal's own Q2, this is a generic budget move, not a cluster fix. (b) No prior-art citation for 'admit translation ceiling and redirect to optimization' as a credentialing tactic in code-translation literature — there isn't one because the framing collapses two different objectives (correctness vs. cycle reduction) into one budget pool. (c) Reframing risk in the proposal is real: 'same 6/15 with 1/3 spend + deeper W2 wins' is a Pareto improvement ONLY IF the deeper W2 wins actually materialize. Piece 3f already showed they don't materialize on the kernels the proposal targets, because of the metric bug.

What the proposal gets right: the diagnosis that W1 has been burning budget against a flat plateau is correct, and the instinct that some kernels should be declared scope-limited is fine in principle. But the specific 9-kernel list is wrong, the saved budget should go to instrumentation fixes (Piece 3j + wire kernel_power.csl), not deeper sweeps, and the W1 ceiling claim needs one more sweep with the new halo gotchas before being accepted.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: 10x smaller version that actually has signal: (a) Land Piece 3j (host-loop detector, ~50 LOC regex + planner flag) and re-route ONLY the 4 iterative-solver kernels to a 'broken_metric=true' status that suppresses further W2 spend until run.py is fixed. (b) Spend the saved ~$10/sweep on one full hybrid sweep on the 15-kernel W1 corpus WITH the 3 new halo gotchas live — measure whether 6/15 is actually the ceiling before declaring it. (c) Defer the spec.yaml 'human_reference_required' flag entirely; it bakes a possibly-wrong ceiling claim into config. Total cost: ~2 hours, no architectural commitment, produces a real data point on the ceiling question instead of asserting an answer.

all_critiques.name: Drop-the-hard-kernels: declare W1 corpus solved at 6/15 plateau, redirect to W2/W3
all_critiques.critique:
Q1 — Structurally different from semantic_bridge / translation_facts? YES, materially. Those proposals were "inject more text into the implementer prompt" — same shape, different decoration, which is why they no-op'd. This is a *budget reallocation policy*, not a feature. It doesn't add a slot to any prompt. So the prior-failure pattern doesn't directly apply.

Q2 — Does it address a SPECIFIC failing cluster? NO, and that's the proposal's central weakness. The proposal does not propose to fix halo_recv_unblock, dsr_queue_fabric_init, or collectives_2d. It proposes to *stop attacking them*. That's a legitimate move, but the proposal should be honest that its expected W1 lift is exactly 0pts (6/15 → 6/15 by construction). The "lift" is denominated in W2 cycle reductions, not W1 pass-rate. The proposal half-acknowledges this in the "Reframe-risk" paragraph but then asks to be evaluated on a W1 axis it explicitly opts out of.

Q3 — Prior art? Closest analogues: compiler test suites mark kernels XFAIL when the lowering pass doesn't support them yet, and benchmark consortia (SPEC, MLPerf) have always carved corpora into "ready" and "research" tiers. So the principle is well-established. But "principle works" is cheap; the specific bet here is *that the 9 kernels are truly stuck*, not just under-attacked. The proposal cites "$150 LLM spend, no movement" as evidence, but PROGRESS.md §9 is the actual prior art *in this repo* and it tells a different story: the immune-kernels family (Power_Method/BiCGSTAB/CG/PCG — i.e., 4 of the 9 stuck W1 kernels in the proposal's hit list) was diagnosed as a measurement bug (host-loop-bounded cycles_send + dead-code editing), not an LLM-capability ceiling. Until run.py is rewritten to push the iteration loop on-device, neither W1 *nor* W2 will move on those kernels. The proposal's frame ("W2 has wins on these → redirect W1 budget to W2 on the same kernels") is therefore wrong for at least 4/9 of the kernels it names. W2 on host-RPC-bounded kernels = same 0 wins, just measured differently. This is the single largest hole in the argument.

Q4 — 10x smaller proof-of-principle? Yes and it's *more interesting than the full proposal*. Pick 2 kernels — one from each putative cluster (e.g. Cholesky from "stuck W1, has W2 accepts" vs Power_Method from "stuck W1, host-RPC-bounded"). Run W2 with the proposed deeper budget (n-rounds 24, wider angles, open-ended angle) on both. If Cholesky shows further accepts and Power_Method shows 0 (predicted by §9), the principle is half-validated: the redirect is correct for the W2-tractable subset, *not* the full 9-kernel list. Cost: 1 sweep, ~$3-5 of LLM. The full proposal as stated would burn $30/sweep on 4 kernels that physically cannot improve until run.py is rewritten — a measurement-bug regression of the kind PROGRESS.md §9 just diagnosed.

Q5 — Actual expected W1 lift? Zero, by construction. The proposal's *real* deliverable is W2 cycle reduction, and even there the upper bound is bounded by the host-RPC measurement bug for ~half the targets. Honest accounting:
- W1 pass-rate: 6/15 → 6/15 (0pt change).
- W2 accepts in next sweep: current trajectory ~3-5 new accepts/sweep on the 6 already-winning kernels; the proposal might lift that to 5-8/sweep via the wider angle exploration. That's real value, but it's incremental on an axis the question didn't ask about.
- Cost saved: $30/sweep, ~10 eng hr/week. Real.
- Hidden cost: declares 4 kernels (Power/BiCG/CG/PCG) "graduated" when the actual blocker is a 1-day run.py rewrite that would *also* unlock W1 wins on them (different metric semantics → different LLM behavior). Graduating them locks in that rewrite as never-going-to-happen.

Other concerns:
- "human_reference_required" is doing a lot of semantic work. There's no evidence the 9 kernels REQUIRE human CSL — only that the current pipeline hasn't produced one. The flag should be "current_pipeline_known_stuck" with a per-kernel reason field, not a permanent capability claim.
- The proposal cites "6/15 matches theoretical Sonnet+Opus union ceiling" as if this were a hard bound. Two-model union is *not* a ceiling — it's a sample size of 2 on a noisy 15-attempt evaluation. The framework has not run hybrid with deeper-Opus-fanout, or with model-disagreement-driven re-attempts, or with the multi-file W3 path PROGRESS.md §8 just landed (which is exactly what dsr_queue_fabric_init and collectives_2d likely need). Calling 6/15 a "ceiling" is the proposal's most under-supported claim.

Bottom line: the proposal's *budget reallocation* core is sound and structurally novel (unlike the discarded text-injection proposals). But its kernel-selection list is wrong (4/9 are blocked by a known measurement bug, not pipeline ceiling), its W2 lift estimate is unstated, its W1 lift is 0, and it frames a 2-model sweep as a hard ceiling when the multi-file pipeline that *just landed* in §8 has not yet been pointed at the failing clusters. Approve a *much* smaller version (see below); reject as written.
all_critiques.smaller_variant:
10x smaller version that captures the actual value: instead of "graduate 9 kernels permanently and redirect $30/sweep", do this in 0.5 day:

1. Audit the 9 stuck W1 kernels against PROGRESS.md §9's host-RPC criterion. Split into (a) measurement-bug-blocked (likely 4: Power/BiCG/CG/PCG — already auto-memory'd) and (b) pipeline-ceiling-blocked (the other 5).
2. For group (a): file a single ticket "rewrite run.py to push iteration loop on-device" and skip them in *both* W1 and W2 sweeps until that lands. This is the actual blocker; do not pretend it's an LLM-capability ceiling.
3. For group (b): run ONE deeper-budget W1 sweep (n-rounds 24, full-angle whitelist, plus point the just-landed multi-file W3 path from §8 at collectives_2d and dsr_queue_fabric_init — neither has been tried). Cost: ~$10. If 0 wins, then graduate them with evidence.
4. Redirect the saved budget to deeper W2 on the 6 already-winning kernels with wider angle sampling — this is the only part of the original proposal that's directly justified by current data.

This captures the budget-reallocation value (~$20/sweep saved) without making the unsupported "6/15 is the ceiling" claim, without locking in the measurement-bug-blocked kernels as permanently human-CSL, and without skipping the one untried path (multi-file W3) that's the most likely fix for the dsr_queue / collectives_2d clusters.

all_critiques.name: Co-design feedback loop: file actionable cslc/SDK issues from the failure corpus
all_critiques.critique:
The proposal smuggles two very different ideas under one name; they need to be scored separately.

(a) "File issues with Cerebras." This is not a translation-framework improvement, it's a procurement activity. Even on a generous Cerebras roadmap it lands no W1 wins inside the experiment horizon. Score for the bench: 0.

(b) "Local cslc wrapper that rewrites error messages by regex." THIS is the only mechanism that could plausibly move the needle in <1 month, so the proposal must be judged on this half. And on this half it has serious problems:

1. STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCE FROM PRIOR DISCARDS — partial. The author claims this changes the TOOL not the prompt. True only at the surface. The wrapped error text reaches the LLM only via the debugger sub-agent's stderr_tail injection (cuda2csl.py line ~1646 confirms stderr is passed in via transcript). So functionally this is "inject better-worded gotcha text into the debugger context window when error pattern X is seen" — which is exactly the shape of cluster-keyed gotcha injection that already exists in the framework, just routed through stderr instead of RAG. The KNOWN_GOTCHAS_W1_FAILURE_PATTERNS table + cslc-grounding already covers this surface. The novelty is just "trigger on regex over stderr text" vs "trigger on cluster classification of the source kernel." Both are pattern-matched context injection.

2. BOTTLENECK FIT — bad. Look at what's failing:
   - halo_recv_unblock (6/7): r4 of ground_gotcha already produced cslc-grounded canonical patterns and they failed because "canonical patterns too composed to fit in minimal harnesses." The bug isn't "LLM didn't understand the error message" — it's "LLM understands the error but can't assemble a 6-construct composition under the framework's single-shot implementer." A clearer cslc error doesn't make the implementer compose better.
   - dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3): this is ORDER-OF-INITIALIZATION at routing setup, which often fails SILENTLY at runtime (incorrect data, no compile error). A cslc wrapper can't fix what cslc never said. The author's own list ("async-fabric init order has no warning") concedes this.
   - collectives_2d (2/4): same shape — these are architecture composition failures (wrong row/col split, wrong allreduce direction), not error-message-comprehension failures.
   So the wrapper plausibly helps with ONE specific halo error message at best, and even there ground_gotcha r4 already tried the upstream-of-this fix.

3. PRIOR ART — author cites none and I know of none for "post-process compiler diagnostics for an LLM consumer" producing measurable win on a code-gen benchmark. The closest analog is the Rust diagnostic project (Niko Matsakis et al.) which spent YEARS rewording errors for HUMAN comprehension and the effect on automated code-fix benchmarks is unmeasured/small. Yellow flag.

4. 10x SMALLER PROBE — yes, easy, and the author should be required to run it: pick the single most common stderr pattern from the existing 250+ sandbox dirs (one grep + one sort | uniq -c), hand-write a better error string for it, monkey-patch ONE injection point in cuda2csl.py to substitute the rewording into stderr_tail, re-run the 7 halo kernels through the existing W1 harness. <1 day. If even ONE new pass arrives, escalate; if 0/7, kill. This probe also retires the proposal's main premise ("LLM is fighting a tooling deficit") with empirical data instead of vibes.

5. EXPECTED LIFT — be ungenerous. Baseline 6/15. The wrapper, if it works at all, addresses ~1 of the 6 halo failures (the count-mismatch one). The other halo failures are composition/silent-init. So realistic upper bound is 1/15 win = ~7pt lift, but the probability of even that materializing given ground_gotcha r4's empirical failure on the same surface is ~30%. Expected value: 0.3 * 7 = ~2pt. Plus negative tail risk: a regex-driven error rewriter that gets the rewrite wrong can confidently mislead the debugger into a worse trajectory than the cryptic-but-honest original message (this happened repeatedly with the halo r2/r3 drafters — "fabricated builtins/syntax/error messages"). A wrapper that asserts "halo_count off by one" when the real bug is something else is exactly the failure mode that killed r2/r3.

6. UNINTERROGATED ASSUMPTION — the proposal claims "the LLM is fighting a tooling deficit, not an intelligence deficit." There's no evidence for this. The evidence we have (r4 = cslc-grounded canonical patterns failed; reviewer-budget bump 5-8 was 0/14) points the OTHER way: the LLM has the information it needs and still can't compose the multi-construct halo idiom in one implementer pass. The bottleneck is generation-time composition, not diagnostic comprehension.

NET: small probability of small lift, real probability of small regression (bad rewrites), zero contribution to dsr_queue and collectives clusters, and the upstream-issues half is not a bench improvement at all. The 1-day probe in (4) is the only part worth doing — it costs nothing and immediately reveals whether the premise survives contact with data.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: 10x smaller probe (described in critique #4): one afternoon. Grep all cslc stderr in /home/USER/xkernel/code_translation/sandbox/cuda2csl/*/bundle/sim.log + any captured compile stderr; sort|uniq -c the top 5 error patterns across the 6 failing halo attempts; pick the single most common; hand-write a clarifying suffix string; monkey-patch one line in cuda2csl.py (~line 1670 where stderr is composed into the debugger context) to append the suffix when the regex hits; rerun the 7 halo kernels in W1. Cost: <1 day, no SDK relationship needed, no Python wrapper around cslc binary. If the probe lifts 0/7 → kill the entire proposal including the upstream-issues half (premise refuted). If it lifts 1+/7 → consider expanding to 5 rewrites covering more patterns, but DROP the "file issues with Cerebras" half entirely — that's the procurement activity masquerading as engineering. This probe also has the virtue of being structurally identical to a question the framework should have answered already: does better error-message text in the debugger context window change outcomes? If no, every variant of this proposal is dead.

all_critiques.name: Co-design feedback loop: file actionable cslc/SDK issues from the failure corpus
all_critiques.critique:
Four hard problems, in descending severity.

(1) **The corpus the extractor would mine does not exist.** Proposal claims to scrape `/home/USER/xkernel/code_translation/sandbox/cuda2csl/*/cslc.stderr` across "250 logged failures." I ran `find sandbox -name "cslc.stderr"` → zero results. Sandbox holds 2744 attempt directories but only 5 `sim.log` files total, and those are runtime traces, not compile errors. cslc stderr is consumed inline by the reviewer/debugger sub-agent and discarded; it is not persisted per-attempt. Before this proposal can even start, someone must (a) modify the pipeline to capture stderr per attempt, (b) re-run the 15-kernel × 8-attempt × N-model sweep to regenerate the corpus. That's ~1 week of compute + eng before the extractor sees its first line of input. The "1 eng week" estimate is off by 2x just from this.

(2) **Hard question 1 — structural difference: partial credit, then it collapses.** The author claims this changes the *tool* not the *prompt*. True for the cslc-wrapper post-processor half. False for the upstream-issues half (that's pure long-play with no W1 benefit in this benchmark's timeframe — cut it). The wrapper-rewrites-cslc-error-messages half IS structurally different from semantic_bridge/translation_facts: those injected text *before* the implementer; this rewrites text the *reviewer/debugger sees on failure*. Different injection point. But — the failure mode it's fighting is downstream of the implementer, and the implementer's single-shot is where 6 of the 9 failing kernels die. Better error messages help iteration 2-8 of repair, but framework data shows attempts 5-8 contribute 0/14 (task #33's resweep). So even if the wrapper makes every repair attempt smarter, the repair loop itself isn't the bottleneck — the single-shot implementer is. This proposal pours improvement into the channel with the least leverage.

(3) **Hard question 2 — does it address halo_recv_unblock (6/7 fail), the dominant cluster?** Author asserts it does, citing 'task did not activate' → real cause is 'halo_count off by one'. But ground_gotcha r4 already proved cslc-grounded canonical halo hints don't survive composition into real kernels. The bug isn't that the LLM misreads cslc's error — it's that even when handed the correct halo idiom, the LLM cannot compose it into a kernel where buffer sizing, fabric ordering, and DSR setup all interact. A better cslc error message tells the LLM "your halo_count is wrong"; the LLM still has to choose between 4 candidate fixes, each interacting with other subsystems. r4 is direct evidence this proposal will not crack halo_recv_unblock. For dsr_queue_fabric_init (2/3 fail), the failures are ordering bugs that cslc *cannot detect* (they manifest at runtime as hangs); no error-message rewrite helps. For collectives_2d, this is the cluster where it MIGHT help — cslc's struct/field errors there are genuinely cryptic. Estimated reachable kernels: maybe 1 of 9.

(4) **Hard question 3 — prior art.** Author cites none, and there isn't strong prior art for "wrap-the-compiler-with-error-rewrites" as a translation-model improvement. The closest is GitHub Copilot's TS-error-explanation feature and rustc's `--explain` (built into rustc, not a wrapper). Both improve human DX; neither has published evidence of improving LLM code-gen pass rates on translation benchmarks. Conversely, prior art FOR co-design with compiler teams (LLVM, MLIR) shows multi-quarter timelines — Cerebras SDK team will not ship in this benchmark's lifetime. Yellow flag confirmed.

(5) **Hard question 4 — 10x smaller pilot.** Yes and the author should run it FIRST before the full proposal. 1-day version: take the 7 halo_recv_unblock failures, manually read the 50-ish cslc stderr lines from one repair-loop run each (need to re-run with stderr capture), and ask: would a hand-rewritten error message have changed the next LLM repair? If the answer is "no" for 5+/7, the proposal is dead. Critically, the author did not pilot this before writing the proposal — and the framework has a documented history of plausible-sounding proposals dying on contact (semantic_bridge, translation_facts, halo workflow r2/r3/r4). The cost of skipping the pilot is repeating that pattern.

(6) **Hard question 5 — expected lift, ungenerously.** Halo cluster (6 kernels): ~0 wins per (3). DSR cluster (2 kernels): ~0 wins, runtime hangs invisible to cslc. Collectives_2d (2 kernels): maybe 0-1 wins. Total: 0-1 kernel = 0-7pt lift, modal outcome 0. Set expected_lift_pct=2 to round up for the optimistic scenario.

(7) **Author's own risk note undersells two real risks.** (a) "Cerebras SDK team may not act" — author plans to mitigate by focusing on local patches, but the local-patch half depends on cslc emitting *some* signal we can regex-rewrite. dsr_queue_fabric_init failures emit no cslc error at all (they hang at runtime). For that cluster, no wrapper can help. (b) "200-line Python wrapper" — the actual surface to cover the framework's failure modes is larger; r3/r4 evidence shows halo failure modes are highly context-dependent (off-by-one south vs. north edge, even vs. odd PE count), not amenable to flat regex rewrites. You'd need semantic understanding of the kernel to rewrite the message helpfully — at which point you've reinvented the reviewer LLM that's already in the loop.

Bottom line: structurally different from prior failures (good), addresses a real pain point (good), but targets the wrong loop position (repair iterations, where attempts 5-8 already show 0/14 lift), is empirically blocked on the dominant cluster by r4 evidence, depends on a corpus that doesn't exist yet, and has no prior art for this exact intervention shape on LLM code-gen.
all_critiques.smaller_variant: Yes — a 1-day pilot that should run BEFORE committing to the full proposal: (a) add 5 lines to cuda2csl.py to persist cslc stderr per-attempt; (b) re-run just the 7 halo_recv_unblock failures with 4 attempts each (~3hr compute); (c) manually inspect the stderr-then-next-LLM-repair-diff pairs and ask "would a rewritten error message have changed the LLM's next move toward correctness?" Decision rule: if ≥4/7 say yes, proceed with wrapper; if ≤2/7, kill the proposal. Cost: 1 day. Eliminates the corpus-doesn't-exist blocker and tests the load-bearing assumption (that the bug is "LLM misreads error" not "LLM can't compose halo idioms"). The r4 prior is that the assumption fails; this pilot would confirm or refute that prior cheaply. Drop the upstream-issues half entirely regardless — zero W1 lift in any plausible timeframe.
